text_kjv: He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.

commentary.narrative: The second refrain returns to the formula of verse 2 but now with richer imagery. The opening ak ('he alone') is repeated, maintaining the narrowing focus. But here, the psalmist moves beyond the abstract declaration of trust to use concrete metaphors drawn from the natural world and military experience. The 'rock' (tsur) was already an ancient image for stability, refuge, and divine protection in Israelite thought. When the psalmist says God is his rock, he is claiming that God is as immovable, as solid, as reliable as the geological foundation of the land itself. Salvation (yeshuat) is paired with this image, suggesting that deliverance is not a momentary rescue but an enduring state rooted in God's nature.
commentary.narrative_continued: The third image—'high fortress' or 'defense' (misgab)—shifts from natural geology to military architecture. A misgab is a fortified high place, a stronghold from which defenders can see enemies approach and resist siege. The psalmist claims God is this high fortress. The final line introduces an important admission that The Covenant Rendering clarifies: the psalmist will not be 'greatly moved' (rabbah, 'greatly'). The qualifier rabbah is often removed in later manuscript traditions and in some translations, but it is significant. It acknowledges that the psalmist may indeed experience some shaking, some emotional or spiritual disturbance. But he will not be overthrown. This honest admission—that faith does not mean invulnerability but rather that one's ultimate foundation is unshakeable—is a mark of the psalm's spiritual realism. By verse 7 (the final refrain), the psalmist will drop the qualifier 'greatly,' suggesting that the act of meditating on God's sufficiency has deepened his confidence further.

word_study.meaning: From an ancient root meaning 'to bind, to constrain, to form.' Tzur literally means 'rock' or 'stone' and becomes a metaphor for protection, refuge, and stability. The psalmists use tzur more than any other biblical image for God—it appears over 30 times in the Psalter.
word_study.significance: The rock is not merely a hiding place but an immovable foundation. In covenant theology, God's character is as unchanging and dependable as stone. In Latter-day Saint thought, Christ is the 'rock' upon which the Church is built (Matthew 16:18), and the image is crucial to understanding both stability and the principle that true security is found in Christ.

word_study.meaning: A noun from sagab, meaning 'to be high, to be inaccessible.' Misgab denotes a fortified high place, a refuge that is elevated above the reach of attackers. It combines the ideas of height, strength, and refuge.
word_study.significance: While tzur (rock) emphasizes unchanging foundation, misgab emphasizes elevation and protection from immediate assault. Together, these images suggest God is both the unshakeable ground beneath and the inaccessible refuge above. The metaphor is particularly apt for someone under siege or threat.

word_study.meaning: From the verb mut, meaning 'to totter, to be shaken, to be displaced.' The verb suggests not merely emotion but actual displacement from one's position. It is used in Joshua 10:11 for the shaking of the earth itself.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's refusal to be 'moved' is not emotional calm but metaphysical stability. He will not be dislodged from his position of trust. The phrase 'not greatly moved' (lo emot rabbah) is a Hebraism that means the shaking will be minor compared to the immobility of the psalmist's foundation.

word_study.meaning: An adverb meaning 'much, greatly, abundantly.' It modifies the degree or extent of what follows.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of rabbah in verse 3 is theologically important because it acknowledges the reality of disturbance while affirming that such disturbance will not be ultimate. The psalmist is not claiming invincibility but perseverance. This is a mature faith that does not deny struggle.

cross_references.connection: A song of Moses declaring that God is a rock—'The Rock, his work is perfect... a God of faithfulness and without iniquity'—establishing the theological foundation for the psalmist's metaphor.
David's own song declaring God as his rock, fortress, and deliverer—paralleling Psalm 62:3 almost identically and showing David's consistent use of these metaphors.
Jesus teaches that the wise build on the rock (petra), and the house does not fall when the flood comes—transferring the psalmist's rock metaphor to the foundation of discipleship.

Nephi and Lehi tell their Lamanite captors that if they build on the rock of Christ, the gates of hell will not prevail—showing how The Book of Mormon applies the ancient psalm's image of God as rock to faith in Christ.
The Lord promises that those who rely on His word 'shall not be moved' (echoing the psalmist's declaration) and shall overcome all temptations.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, both Egypt and Mesopotamia used rock and fortress imagery for divine protection and royal stability. However, the Israelite use is distinctive: God is not merely strong but is presented as the ground of existence itself. Rocks in the Levantine landscape are not merely obstacles but the visible bones of creation. A fortress in the context of ancient Israel would be familiar to anyone who had experienced siege warfare—a place of last refuge where the elevated position allowed defense against numerically superior forces. The mention of a 'shaking' or 'moving' (mut) suggests the psalmist understands himself as vulnerable to actual displacement—whether through political exile, military defeat, or loss of position. The qualifier rabbah ('greatly') may reflect a historical moment in David's life when he experienced real instability, such as during his years fleeing from Saul, when even his conviction in God could be tested by circumstantial pressure.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 4:34-35 shows Nephi building his foundation on Christ: 'O Lord, I will trust in thee forever. I will not put my trust in the arm of flesh.... Thou art my rock and my salvation.' Helaman 5:12 declares that 'whosoever shall put their trust in God shall be supported in their trials, and their troubles, and their afflictions.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes God as the rock and foundation of salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 10:69 teaches that the Church is built on the rock of revelation, with Christ as the cornerstone. D&C 38:2 emphasizes that God is 'in the midst' of His covenant people, providing strength and refuge. D&C 84:36-37 promises that those who keep the covenants shall 'become the sons of Moses and of Aaron and the seed of Abraham, and the elect of God.' The rock language in the Doctrine and Covenants consistently applies to Christ and to the covenant foundation of the Church.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, initiates are taught that Christ is the rock upon which the Church is built. The architectural symbolism of temples (strong foundations, high spires visible from afar) mirrors the psalmist's metaphors of rock and fortress. The temple itself becomes a misgab—a high place set apart from the world where the covenant is sealed and refuge is found.

commentary.christological_typology: The rock that the psalmist trusts is ultimately Christ. In 1 Corinthians 10:4, Paul teaches that the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness was Christ. In Matthew 16:18, Jesus says 'upon this rock I will build my church,' identifying Himself as the unshakeable foundation. The psalmist's declaration that he will not be 'greatly moved' prefigures the stability offered by faith in Christ, which is described in Hebrews 12:27 as a kingdom that 'cannot be shaken.' The rock and fortress are typological of Christ as the source of all spiritual and eternal stability.
commentary.application: For modern covenant makers, this verse teaches that faith in God provides actual, metaphysical stability—not the removal of difficulty but an immovable foundation beneath the difficulty. When a member of the Church experiences trial—illness, persecution for belief, family conflict, or loss—the psalmist's declaration becomes operative: God is the rock upon which to stand, God is the fortress from which to resist spiritual assault. The psalmist's candor about being 'somewhat moved' (though not greatly) gives permission for honest acknowledgment of struggle while maintaining ultimate trust. In the context of covenant, we stand on Christ, the rock, and find ourselves fortified against the disturbances of mortality. The fact that the psalmist uses military metaphors (fortress, defense) suggests this is not sentimental comfort but active, militant faith—we are not passive victims but defenders of our covenant position, standing in the fortress that God provides. The qualifier rabbah also teaches that even when we do feel shaken—and the honest life includes such moments—this shaking is not the final word. The rock does not move.

text_kjv: How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence.

commentary.narrative: The psalm now shifts focus from the psalmist's trust in God to address the enemies directly, answering the opening question with prophetic judgment. The opening 'How long?' (ad anah) is a rhetorical question that expresses both exasperation and confidence that the threat is temporary. The enemies are not abstract but coordinated: they 'imagine mischief against a man.' The verb that underlies this—tehotetu—means to assault, to rush upon, to set oneself against. This is not casual malice but organized conspiracy. The psalmist does not name himself but refers to himself as 'a man,' perhaps to indicate that he is but one person facing a multitude. The dramatic rhetorical reversal then announces the fate of the conspirators: they will be crushed ('ye shall be slain all of you'), and their apparent strength will prove illusory.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final pair of images is crucial: the enemies think of themselves as strong ('a bowing wall' and 'a tottering fence'), but the psalmist reverses their self-assessment. They are not fortresses but collapsing structures. A wall that bows inward (natuy) is on the verge of collapse. A fence that totters (dechuyah, 'pushed, thrust, driven back') has already lost its structural integrity. These are images of imminent collapse—the enemies appear to be strength, but they are actually fragility. The psychological and spiritual inversion is profound: the enemies see themselves as assembled strength; the psalmist sees them as structures about to fail. This is not mere metaphor but theological declaration: God's enemies, no matter how organized or numerous, are fundamentally unstable because they are not rooted in God. The verse thus answers the implicit question that the opening psalms raised: what happens to those who do not trust God but instead conspire against those who do?

word_study.meaning: A question formula meaning 'until when, how long.' It is used in the Psalms to express both lament and challenge—a demand that a situation change or be resolved.
word_study.significance: The question is not asked passively but with authority. The psalmist is not begging for relief but announcing that the threat is temporary. This is the language of prophecy, not of weakness.

word_study.meaning: From the verb thahat, meaning 'to devise, to plot, to imagine.' In context, it means to set upon, to rush against, to assault with coordinated intent.
word_study.significance: The term suggests premeditation. The enemies are not acting in blind rage but have thought out their assault. This makes their failure more significant—planned evil still fails before God.

word_study.meaning: Qir means 'wall.' Natuy is from the verb natah, meaning 'to bow, to bend, to incline.' A wall that bows inward or outward has lost its structural integrity and is about to collapse.
word_study.significance: The image is of a structure that appears to be a wall but is actually compromised. It is a metaphor for enemies who appear strong but are fundamentally unsound. The visual image of a bowing wall would be immediately recognizable to anyone in an ancient siege situation—it was a sign of imminent breakthrough.

word_study.meaning: Gader means 'fence.' Dechuyah is from the verb dachah, meaning 'to push, to thrust, to drive.' A tottering fence is one that has been pushed so many times it has lost its structure.
word_study.significance: Where the wall is an image of grand military structure, the fence is the more modest enclosure. Together, the images suggest that enemies at every level—from the highest to the lowest—will collapse. No enemy, whether great or small, will withstand.

cross_references.connection: David similarly faces enemies who assault him, yet declares confidence that even if an army encamps against him, his heart will not fear—expressing the same defiance grounded in trust in God.
David refuses to slay Saul, declaring that God will judge between them—trusting God's judgment rather than his own violence, and demonstrating faith that God will ultimately vindicate the righteous.
The way of the Lord is a stronghold to the upright but ruin to evildoers—expressing the principle that the same God who protects the righteous judges the wicked.

No weapon formed against the servant of the Lord shall prosper, and every tongue that rises against him shall be condemned—a later prophetic echo of the psalmist's declaration of protection and judgment.

The Lord declares that He will defend the Saints and 'confound all those who have spread lying reports about my people'—showing how the psalmist's confidence in God's judgment is affirmed in Restoration revelation.

commentary.historical_context: The language of conspiracy and organized assault suggests a situation of political threat, possibly drawing on David's experience fleeing from Saul or during his reign when rival claimants to the throne conspired against him. The image of a bowing wall carries concrete resonance in the context of siege warfare, which was a dominant feature of ancient Near Eastern warfare. A wall that bowed inward was in imminent danger of collapse, and soldiers would concentrate their assault on weak points. The image of a fence, by contrast, is more modest—suggesting enemies at various levels of power all face the same judgment. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian royal texts, enemies of the king are regularly depicted as weak and unstable, even when they present military challenge. This rhetorical inversion—making the enemy appear weak—may have served both psychological and theological purposes in ancient Israel: it bolstered confidence and affirmed that the king's position was rooted in cosmic order, not mere military might.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:6 records Ammon's declaration that the Lord has given him strength to defend his kinsmen against their enemies—a similar confidence that God judges those who conspire against His people. Helaman 10:7 shows the Lord giving Nephi sealing power, indicating that the Lord will validate the righteous servant's judgments. 3 Nephi 16:10-15 records Christ's declaration that those who do not believe His words will be smitten and destroyed—the same judgment principle the psalmist invokes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:7-8 teaches the Saints to forgive their enemies and leave judgment to God, who will repay according to righteousness. D&C 103:25-26 promises that the Lord will 'fight the battles' of Zion while the Saints remain faithful. The Doctrine and Covenants consistently emphasizes that vindication and judgment belong to God, not to the Saints' hands—a principle the psalmist operates within.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the principle that God will protect the covenant people and judge those who oppose them. The endowment teaches that those who break covenants will face judgment. The psalmist's declaration of judgment on enemies who conspire against him parallels the temple teaching that the Lord, as judge, holds all power and will ultimately vindicate the faithful.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's experience of being conspired against and his trust that God will judge his enemies prefigures Christ's passion. Jesus was the subject of organized conspiracy (the Sanhedrin's plot, Judas's betrayal) yet trusted God's judgment and vindication. In Luke 22:69, Jesus tells the Sanhedrin that He will be seated at the right hand of God—a declaration of vindication through resurrection. The Gospels present Jesus's enemies as ultimately facing their own collapse (the fall of Jerusalem, the destruction of the Temple), validating His trust that God, not His enemies, would have the final word. The image of collapsing walls and fences is also typological of Jericho, whose walls fell before Joshua's army—a picture of God's power to overthrow those who oppose His people.
commentary.application: For modern covenant makers, this verse teaches an important principle: to maintain trust in God even while facing real, organized opposition does not mean denying the reality of the threat but reinterpreting it. The enemies are real; the conspiracy is actual. But their ultimate failure is certain because they are not rooted in God. For those who experience persecution—whether social, professional, or familial—because of their faith, the psalmist's question 'How long?' becomes operative. The threat is temporary. Those who conspire against the righteous appear strong but are fundamentally unstable. This does not mean the righteous will never suffer loss; rather, it means the ultimate outcome is already determined. The psalmist invites us to see through the appearance of enemy strength to the reality of enemy fragility. Covenant makers who trust in God stand on the rock; those who oppose God stand on structures about to collapse. The invitation is to refuse fear and to trust in the Lord's judgment and vindication.

text_kjv: They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah.

commentary.narrative: This verse deepens the portrait of the enemies by revealing not just what they do (conspiracy) but their methods and their character. The opening phrase 'They only consult' (ak mi-see'eto yaa'atsu) is noteworthy because of the repeated use of ak ('only, alone')—the same word that began the psalmist's own affirmations in verses 2 and 3. Where the psalmist says he trusts in God 'only,' the enemies consult 'only' about how to bring him down. This verbal parallel shows that the psalmist and his enemies are oriented in opposite directions—one toward God alone, the other toward conspiracy alone. The word 'excellency' or 'elevation' (see'eto, 'his height, his dignity, his position') indicates the psalmist holds a position of honor or authority that the conspirators wish to dismantle.
commentary.narrative_continued: The characterization of the enemies as those who 'delight in lies' (yirtzu kazav) shows they are not merely pursuing practical goals but taking pleasure in deception itself. They love the act of lying. Then comes perhaps the most devastating image: 'With their mouths they bless, but inside they curse' (be-fiv yevarekhu u-be-qirbam yeqalelu). The contrast between outward speech and inner reality reveals the nature of political conspiracy in any age: the enemies smile while cursing, offer public affection while harboring private hatred. This is the lie that underlies all their other lies—the lie of their own hearts. The word 'Selah' (sela, likely 'pause' or 'interlude') marks a moment of pause, giving time for the listener to absorb the disturbing portrait of conspiracy and hypocrisy. The pause also shifts the perspective—from observing the enemies to observing the psalmist's endurance of their duplicity.

word_study.meaning: From the verb ya'ats, meaning 'to counsel, to advise, to plot together.' It denotes deliberative planning, the gathering of minds to determine a course of action.
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes premeditation and coordination. The enemies are not acting impulsively but have assembled to plan their assault. This makes their conspiracy a matter of collective will, not individual weakness.

word_study.meaning: From the verb nasa, meaning 'to lift up, to raise, to exalt.' See'et denotes lifting, elevation, or eminence. It refers to a position of honor, dignity, or authority.
word_study.significance: The word suggests the psalmist (David) holds a position from which he can be 'cast down.' This language is royal—David's position as king is what the conspirators wish to dismantle. The enemies are not envious of his wealth alone but of his authority and dignity.

word_study.meaning: Ratzah means 'to be pleased, to delight, to take pleasure in.' Kazav means 'lie, deception, vanity.' The phrase means they take pleasure in lies themselves.
word_study.significance: The emphasis is not on the practical benefit of lying (that they lie to achieve a goal) but on their joy in the lie itself. This suggests a spiritual condition—they love falsehood for its own sake, which is a mark of opposition to truth and to God.

word_study.term_original: בְּפִ֥יו יְ֝בָרֵ֗כוּ / וּבְקִרְבָּ֥ם יְקַלְלוּ (be-fiv yevarekhu / u-be-qirbam yeqalelu)
word_study.meaning: Barak means 'to bless, to praise, to kneel before.' Qalal means 'to curse, to lighten, to make light of.' The contrast is between outward verbal blessing and inward curse.
word_study.significance: The split between mouth and heart reveals the core duplicity of the enemies. In Hebraic thought, the mouth and heart are the seat of identity—what comes from the heart is what the person truly is (Matthew 12:34). The enemies' hearts curse even as their mouths bless, making them fundamentally divided and false.

word_study.meaning: The etymology is uncertain, but the term likely means 'pause,' 'interlude,' or 'lift up.' It appears 71 times in the Psalms and seems to mark a musical or liturgical break in the text.
word_study.significance: Selah creates space for reflection. After the portrait of enemies who curse inwardly while blessing outwardly, the pause allows listeners to absorb the reality of human deception and to recommit themselves to trust in God's knowledge of hearts.

cross_references.connection: Warns that fervent lips with an evil heart are like glaze on an earthen vessel—smooth and deceptive on the surface but hollow within, paralleling the enemies' false blessing and inner curse.
Jesus condemns the Pharisees as whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside but full of hypocrisy inside—using the same principle of exposure that the psalmist applies to his enemies.
David spares Saul's life but declares that God will judge between them—trusting God to see the truth that humans hide behind false appearances.
Describes the worthless person who speaks with perverted mouth, winks, shuffles feet, and points fingers—a portrait of the conspiracy that Scripture condemns, paralleling the psalmist's enemies.
Alma warns his son that small deceits lead to larger ones—a principle that applies to those who take pleasure in lies as the psalmist's enemies do.

commentary.historical_context: The portrait of enemies who offer public blessing while harboring private curse is a consistent feature of ancient Near Eastern royal literature. Egyptian execration texts list enemies who should be destroyed, and Mesopotamian literature frequently warns of conspirators who smile while planning betrayal. In the context of David's reign, such conspiratorial activity was well-documented historically—Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15) involved precisely this kind of duplicity, with Absalom winning people's hearts through false blessing while plotting to seize the throne. The image of being cast down from a position of elevation (see'et) is particularly resonant in the context of ancient Near Eastern warfare and politics, where the goal of conspiracy was often not merely to eliminate a rival but to humiliate him—to bring him from elevation to degradation. The fact that the enemies take pleasure in lies (yirtzu kazav) may also reflect the spiritual understanding in Israel that such delight in falsehood marks one as opposed to the God of truth.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 10:17 describes lawyers and judges who pervert judgment through lies, gaining power while their hearts are set against truth—a portrait similar to the psalmist's enemies. Helaman 2:3-4 tells of the Gadianton robbers who worked by secret combination and murder, hiding behind false oaths and appearances of righteousness. The Book of Mormon frequently illustrates the principle that those who take pleasure in deceit are fundamentally opposed to God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:36-37 teaches that truth comes from God and that the devil cannot speak truth because he is 'the father of lies.' Those who take pleasure in lies, as the psalmist's enemies do, align themselves with opposition to God. D&C 76:103-106 describes those who 'love and make a lie' as those who will be consigned to outer darkness, suggesting that delight in falsehood is a mark of spiritual separation from God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires making and keeping truthful covenants before God, who 'knows all hearts.' The contrast between outer word and inner curse that the psalmist describes is precisely the kind of hypocrisy the temple ordinances expose and call people to repent of. The temple teaches that before God, all hearts are known, and no secret curse can be hidden.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's experience of enemies who smile while cursing prefigures Christ's passion. Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss (Matthew 26:48-49)—the ultimate expression of blessing given while cursing the recipient. The chief priests, elders, and scribes offer false testimony against Jesus while maintaining an appearance of religious righteousness (Matthew 26:59-61). Christ's trust in God to see beneath outward appearance to inner reality parallels the psalmist's conviction that God alone knows the truth. In John 2:24-25, the evangelist notes that Jesus 'needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man'—a divine knowledge that exposes the enemies' deception. The Gospels present Christ's enemies as precisely the kind of conspirators the psalmist describes: outwardly righteous, inwardly full of hatred and deception.
commentary.application: For modern covenant makers, this verse teaches the sobering reality that betrayal often comes with a smile. In professional, familial, or ecclesiastical contexts, those who conspire against you may do so while maintaining an appearance of friendship. The verse does not call us to paranoia but to discernment. The psalmist's response is not to retaliate with his own curse but to trust God's perfect knowledge of all hearts. Modern believers are invited to do the same: when we encounter duplicity and false blessing, we can trust that God sees what is hidden. This does not mean passivity—we should protect ourselves and others from those acting in bad faith. But it means we do not fight such enemies with their own weapons (lies and curses) but by maintaining integrity and trusting God's judgment. The psalm also implicitly warns against becoming like the enemies—allowing ourselves to bless with our mouths while our hearts curse, maintaining false appearances while harboring bitter thoughts. Instead, we are called to integrity: the blessing and curse of the covenant maker should match the reality of the heart, making us persons of truth before God and others.

text_kjv: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.

commentary.narrative: The psalm returns to the refrain, but with a crucial shift. Where verse 2 began with an assertion—'Truly my soul waiteth upon God'—verse 6 is a command: 'My soul, wait thou only upon God.' The psalmist is now preaching to himself. This is not passive acceptance but active redirection. Having described the threat of enemies (verses 4-5) and their deception, the psalmist must now reset his inner orientation. The soul has been pulled toward fear, toward calculation of threats, toward consideration of counter-strategies. The command brings it back to stillness and silence. The word 'only' (ak) returns for the third time in the refrain, creating a rhythmic insistence on singular focus. Nothing else receives attention—not the numbers of enemies, not their cunning, not their apparent strength. Only God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final phrase shifts language slightly from verse 2. Where verse 2 spoke of yeshuah ('deliverance, salvation'), verse 6 speaks of tiqvah ('hope, expectation, waiting'). The Covenant Rendering notes that this shift broadens the scope from immediate rescue to comprehensive expectation. The psalmist is not merely asking God for emergency intervention in the present crisis but is reorienting his entire future toward God. He is saying that his fundamental stance toward what comes is one of expectation directed toward God. This verse also marks the midpoint of the psalm's refrain cycle. Verse 2 opened with the refrain; verse 7 will close it. But by verse 6, having meditated on God's sufficiency (verses 2-3) and confronted the reality of enemies (verses 4-5), the psalmist has deepened his conviction. By the final refrain (verse 7), the qualifier 'greatly' from verse 3 will be dropped—the psalmist's confidence will have matured from 'I will not be greatly moved' to 'I will not be moved.' This arc shows how contemplation of God's nature and explicit rejection of enemy temptations deepen faith.

word_study.meaning: From the verb damam, 'to be silent, to be still.' The verb is in the imperative form—a command, not a declaration. The form domi literally means 'be silent, be still.'
word_study.significance: The shift from declaration (verse 2) to command (verse 6) shows self-address. The psalmist is coaching his own inner self toward discipline. The imperative mood suggests this is not automatic but requires conscious effort and will.

word_study.meaning: From the root qavah, 'to wait, to hope, to expect.' Tiqvah denotes hope, expectation, or waiting. It is broader than yeshuah (deliverance), encompassing a future orientation and trust.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, tiqvah broadens from the immediate deliverance of verse 2 to a comprehensive expectation about the future. The psalmist is not just asking 'Will God rescue me from these enemies?' but 'In whom am I placing my hope for all that comes?' The answer: only in God.

cross_references.connection: Repeats the same self-command: 'Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God'—showing the pattern of the psalmist counseling his own inner person to reorient toward God.
Though father and mother may forsake, 'the Lord will take me up'—a declaration of expectation (tiqvah) placed in God when earthly supports fail.

Paul teaches that the Scriptures were written to teach us patience and comfort through hope (elpis in Greek, the equivalent of tiqvah)—suggesting that verses like Psalm 62:6 function to retrain the inner person toward God.
Describes God as the God of 'a lively hope' (literally, living expectation)—applying the psalmist's tiqvah to the Christian understanding of resurrection and eternal life in Christ.
The prophet declares 'the Lord is my portion,' and waits quietly (domi) for the Lord's salvation—directly echoing the language and sentiment of Psalm 62:6.

commentary.historical_context: The shift from declaration to command in the refrain reflects an ancient practice of self-exhortation in the face of threat. In Egyptian wisdom literature, the sage addresses his own heart or soul to maintain composure and virtue. In Mesopotamian literature, kings speak to their own inner selves to steel their will for battle. This practice is not unique to Israel but becomes particularly prominent in the Psalms as a form of spiritual discipline. The refrain structure (appearing in verses 2, 6, and implied again in verse 7) suggests this psalm was designed for liturgical repetition. The worshipper would not merely hear the psalmist's declaration once but would hear the refrain multiple times, allowing it to reshape inner orientation through repetition. The shift from yeshuah (deliverance) to tiqvah (expectation) may also reflect a development in the psalmist's understanding. After hearing the refrain once (verse 2), he contemplates the rock and fortress (verse 3), confronts the enemies (verses 4-5), and then by verse 6, he recognizes that his need is not merely for temporary rescue but for a reorientation of his entire future expectation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:41 teaches that the prayers of the righteous should be full of faith and patience—the combination of tiqvah (expectation) and dumiyyah (silence, patient waiting). Moroni 10:3 invites readers to 'ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, if these things are not true,' trusting in God's response—an expectation placed entirely in God's hands. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows covenant makers redirecting their own hearts toward God when temptation or fear arises.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:18 promises that those who continue in faith will 'have hope and be made perfect in all things.' D&C 121:7-8 teaches that the foundation of hope is faith in God and trust in His covenant. The Doctrine and Covenants emphasizes that hope (tiqvah in Hebrew terms) is not optimism about circumstances but trust in God's ultimate vindication of the righteous.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment ceremony includes moments where the initiate must redirect inner orientation toward covenants and promises despite visual and auditory elements designed to test that orientation. The principle of the psalmist's command to himself—'My soul, wait only upon God'—mirrors the covenant maker's commitment to maintain faith and expectation in God despite seeming obstacles or voices calling in other directions.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's experience in Gethsemane and on the cross included precisely the discipline the psalmist commands: a redirection of His own will toward God. In Luke 22:42, Jesus prays 'not my will, but thine, be done'—commanding His own soul, as it were, to submit to God's will despite the reality of suffering. In Matthew 27:46, even as Christ cries out 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' He remains addressing God—maintaining expectation (tiqvah) in God even in apparent dereliction. The Gospels present Christ's entire ministry as an extended example of the discipline of maintaining singular focus on God's purposes despite distraction, threat, and temptation. Christ is the perfect embodiment of the psalmist's command to the soul to wait only upon God.
commentary.application: For modern covenant makers, this verse teaches that faith is not a feeling that happens to us but a practice we perform on ourselves. When anxiety rises, when enemies gather (whether literal or metaphorical), when the threats seem overwhelming, the psalmist's command becomes operative: 'My soul, wait thou only upon God.' This is not a suggestion but an imperative. We must actively redirect our own attention. The shift in the verse from immediate deliverance (yeshuah) to comprehensive expectation (tiqvah) broadens the application: we are not just asking 'Will God get me out of this crisis?' but 'Am I placing my fundamental trust and expectation in God, not just for today but for all time?' In family crises, in professional uncertainties, in health struggles, in social or political upheaval, the covenant maker is invited to silence the soul—to stop the frantic internal conversation about what might go wrong, what others might do, what we cannot control—and to redirect the entire fabric of expectation toward God. This is done repeatedly, in the small moments of daily life. Each time we choose trust over anxiety, we are repeating the psalmist's command to the soul. Over time, this practice trains the inner person, so that by the time of the final refrain (verse 7), we can say with deeper conviction that we will not be moved. The expectation has become habitual.

text_kjv: He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a decisive shift in the psalmist's confidence. After the instruction to wait silently before God in verses 1-6, the speaker now articulates absolute trust without qualification. The phrase "He only is my rock and my salvation" echoes the opening of the psalm, but with a crucial difference noted by The Covenant Rendering: verse 3 included the qualifier "greatly" when addressing the threat against the soul ("I will not be greatly shaken"), acknowledging the magnitude of danger. Here, all hedging language has been removed. The period of silent waiting—of not defending oneself, of not speaking one's own defense—has produced a transformation: the speaker moves from qualified confidence to unqualified certainty.

The triadic repetition of God's protective attributes (rock, salvation, defense/high fortress) demonstrates that the psalmist's security is not partial or circumstantial. These three terms are not three separate supports but three expressions of a single reality: God's character is utterly reliable. The word "moved" (Hebrew mot, from the root meaning "to shake" or "to slip") suggests the loss of solid ground beneath one's feet—a displacement. The negative construction "I will not be moved" declares that no circumstance, no adversary, no social upheaval will dislodge the speaker from this foundation.

word_study.meaning: A rock or crag; used metaphorically for a place of refuge, strength, and immovable stability. In ancient Near Eastern thought, a rock could be a naturally fortified position or a symbol of divine permanence.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'rock' rather than 'fortress' or 'shelter' emphasizes geological permanence—something built into the very fabric of creation, not constructed by human hands. For the psalmist under social attack, this is profound: safety is not found in human alliance but in a reality as permanent as stone.

word_study.meaning: Deliverance, rescue, safety; often used in military or personal crisis contexts. The root suggests 'spaciousness' or 'broad places'—a sense of being brought to safety where one can breathe.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract salvation but concrete rescue from the immediate threat of slander and social destruction. God's salvation is the opening out of a confined, threatened space into freedom.

word_study.meaning: A high fortress, tower, or elevated refuge; a place elevated above the surrounding terrain. The prefix mi- means 'from' or 'out of,' suggesting movement away from danger into height.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'high fortress,' capturing the sense of elevation and superior position. The psalmist is lifted above the reach of adversaries, not standing on equal ground with them.

word_study.meaning: To shake, slip, slide, or move from a stable position; used of tents shaking in wind or feet sliding on treacherous ground.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is visceral—it suggests the feeling of losing one's footing. The psalmist asserts that no force will cause such displacement. This connects to the anxiety of verses 2-3, where the soul's 'shaking' was the underlying terror. Now that shaking has ceased.

cross_references.connection: Uses identical language of God as 'rock' and 'fortress' in the context of deliverance from enemies, showing the consistent metaphorical language for God's protective nature throughout the Psalter.
Describes God as 'The Rock, his work is perfect' and establishes God's constancy and perfection as the foundation for trust, directly paralleling the theological claim of this verse.
Hannah's prayer declares 'There is none holy as the LORD,' emphasizing exclusive reliance on God alone, mirroring the absoluteness of 'He only' in this verse.
Also uses 'rock' imagery and describes God bringing the psalmist up from a slimy pit and setting his feet on a rock, illustrating the transition from peril to stability that this verse affirms.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern understanding of 'rock' as refuge was not merely poetic. In the Levantine landscape, caves and rocky outcroppings served as actual places of refuge during conflict. David himself famously hid in the cave of En Gedi (1 Samuel 23-24). However, for the psalmist under social attack—facing slander rather than military siege—the 'rock' is metaphorical: it represents an inner, spiritual stability that no amount of social pressure can erode. The language of 'defense' (misgab) also suggests military fortification, yet the enemy here is not armed but vocal. This reframing of vulnerability is key: the psalmist's true adversary is not a military threat but the threat to one's reputation and standing in the community.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:12 expresses a similar confidence: 'Now when our hearts are sorrowful, yea, even unto that degree that we cannot cast them out,' suggesting that waiting silently before God leads to transformed certainty. The Nephite experience of maintaining faith through persecution parallels the psalmist's journey.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:3-4 establishes the temple as 'my rock and my salvation' in latter-day context, showing how the image of God's house as a stable refuge persists in Restoration revelation. D&C 19:23 also speaks of Christ as 'a rock and his foundation sure,' demonstrating that Christ fulfills the 'rock' typology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language of being 'moved' or 'unmoved' connects to the covenant principle of standing firm in faith. The temple is presented in Latter-day Saint teaching as the place where God makes His character visible—where the abstract assurance of verses 1-6 becomes concrete experience through ordinance and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is identified as 'the rock' throughout the New Testament (1 Corinthians 10:4, Matthew 16:18). The promise 'I will not be moved' prefigures Christ's unshakeable nature and His invitation to believers to stand upon Him as the sure foundation. In Doctrine and Covenants 50:44, the Lord promises that those who build upon His rock 'shall not be moved.' The psalmist's personal declaration here becomes, in Christian interpretation, an affirmation that Christ's character is that immovable rock.
commentary.application: For modern believers facing social pressure, reputation attacks, or the anxiety of instability, this verse offers a radical reorientation: one's security does not depend on social standing, approval, or circumstance, but on a relationship with God that is immovable by nature. The application is not passive resignation but active choice—choosing to rest one's entire weight on God rather than on self-protection, human approval, or circumstantial advantage. The progression from verses 1-6 (silent waiting) to verse 7 (confident declaration) suggests that genuine confidence emerges only after periods of restraint and trust, not before them. In contemporary covenant life, this means that the quiet work of faith—the times of not defending oneself, not explaining oneself, not fighting for one's reputation—prepares the soul for a deeper kind of assurance that no external circumstance can shake.

text_kjv: In God is my salvation and my glory: the rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 deepens the preceding affirmation by adding a stunning element: not only does God provide salvation and defense, but God is also the source of the psalmist's 'glory' (kavod). This is a psychologically and spiritually significant claim. Under social attack, especially in an honor-shame culture like ancient Israel, one's glory—one's reputation, significance, and social weight—is precisely what is under threat. The enemies of the psalmist (implied from the context of verses 2-4) have attacked this glory through slander and lies. Yet the psalmist makes an extraordinary claim: that even this glory, this sense of personal significance and worth, does not originate within himself or depend on others' opinion, but derives entirely from God.

The Covenant Rendering captures a nuance the KJV misses: the glory 'rests on' God, not merely 'is in' God. This suggests dependency—the way weight rests upon a foundation. The psalmist is saying that his fundamental worth, his kavod (a word that literally means 'weight' or 'heaviness,' suggesting importance and solidity), has its foundation in God's esteem, not in the esteem of those who slander him. The phrase 'rock of my strength' and 'refuge' repeats imagery but in a new register: after establishing that God alone is trustworthy (verse 7), the psalmist now applies this truth to the deepest wound of social attack—the threat to one's sense of self-worth. The final phrase, 'is in God,' is repeated for emphasis, closing the verse with the certainty that everything the psalmist possesses—salvation, glory, strength, refuge—converges in one source.

word_study.meaning: Glory, honor, weight, significance. The root meaning is 'heaviness' or 'weightiness'—suggesting that which carries importance or substance. In honor-shame cultures, one's kavod is one's reputation and standing in the community. God's kavod is His visible manifestation of power and character.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the psalmist's kavod 'rests on' God—a remarkable admission that even his sense of worth and significance is not self-generated but depends on divine sustaining. This addresses a deep spiritual wound: in an honor culture, slander and lies aim precisely at one's kavod. The psalmist responds by locating his true kavod outside the reach of slanderers, in God's estimation.

word_study.meaning: As in verse 7, a rock or crag representing stability and refuge; here in the construct phrase 'rock of my strength' (tzur uzzi), emphasizing the source of power and resilience.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'rock' from verse 7 signals that the foundation is unchanging, even as new dimensions of trust are added. The rock is not just defensive but the source of strength itself—the psalmist does not merely hide behind God but draws power from this relationship.

word_study.meaning: Might, strength, power, defense. Often used to describe the power of God or of a fortress. In personal contexts, it refers to the resilience and capability a person possesses.
word_study.significance: The 'rock of my strength' suggests that God is both the source and substance of the psalmist's resilience. This is not boasting in personal vigor but recognition that all capacity to endure comes from one's relationship with God.

word_study.meaning: Shelter, hiding place, refuge. From the root meaning 'to hide' or 'to take shelter'; suggests both the act of hiding and the place of safety itself.
word_study.significance: The stacking of three protective terms (rock, strength, refuge) suggests comprehensive security—no aspect of the psalmist's need is left unmet. This addresses anxiety holistically: the person finds stabilization (rock), empowerment (strength), and shelter (refuge) all in God.

cross_references.connection: David declares that God is 'a shield for me: my glory' (kavodi), directly paralleling this verse's claim that glory belongs to God, not to human opinion.

Speaks of faith that is 'much more precious than of gold' and 'may be found unto praise and honour and glory,' showing how genuine faith leads to true honor that comes from God rather than human sources.
God declares 'I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory I will not give to another,' establishing that God is the ultimate source of all glory and honor.
Paul renounces confidence in the flesh and grounds his boasting entirely in Christ, mirroring the psalmist's redirection of trust from self-generated worth to God-given significance.
Also uses the language of God as refuge and strength ('I will cry unto God most high; unto God that performeth all things for me'), showing the consistent pattern of comprehensive trust.

commentary.historical_context: In the honor-shame culture of ancient Israel, a person's kavod—their standing, reputation, and weight in the community—was not merely a matter of pride but of survival. Access to resources, protection, and opportunity all depended on one's honor rating. Slander, as implied in Psalm 62:4, was therefore a devastating weapon: it aimed at the very foundation of social existence. The psalmist's claim that his true kavod 'rests on' God rather than on community opinion was countercultural and radical. It represents a spiritual liberation from the tyranny of public perception. This does not mean the ancient Israelite was indifferent to community standing, but rather that they grounded their fundamental worth in a relationship with God that transcended social volatility.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:38 teaches that true glory comes from God: 'And now, as ye have desired that I should give unto you a name that ye shall not be forgotten, behold I have caused that my name shall be written upon all the holy temples of my people,' showing that permanent significance derives from God's act, not human memory.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 128:22 emphasizes that the work of God gives lasting significance: 'And now, my dearly beloved brethren and sisters, let me assure you that these principles in relation to the dead and the living, correspond with those presented in the New Testament.' The principle is that true worth and memory are secured through God's work, not through human reputation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant emphasizes that individual worth is established and sealed by God Himself, not by social status or worldly accomplishment. The temple endowment teaches that one's true identity and significance are revealed through the ordinances, transcending earthly social hierarchies. The sealing ordinances specifically teach that relationships and identities can be made permanent and meaningful beyond mortality—a kavod that endures eternally.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies this principle radically. Though stripped of earthly glory, beaten, and subjected to public shame, Jesus maintained perfect knowledge of His identity and worth as the Son of God. John 17:5 records Christ's claim that He had glory with the Father 'before the world was,' and this glory could not be taken from Him by crucifixion. The promise of John 17:24 that believers will see and share in Christ's glory is grounded in this same principle: true kavod comes from relationship with God through Christ, not from worldly circumstance. The psalmist's faith prefigures the paradoxical glory of Christ—a glory most visible in apparent humiliation.
commentary.application: In contemporary covenant life, this verse addresses a pervasive modern anxiety: the fear of social disapproval and the pressure to build and maintain one's reputation. Social media, professional advancement, and cultural status all create pressures to secure one's 'glory.' This verse invites a reorientation: one's fundamental worth is not negotiable through circumstance or opinion because it is grounded in God's estimation. For members facing criticism, slander, or social pressure (whether within or outside the Church), this offers liberation—not from responsibility to act righteously, but from the psychological tyranny of constant reputation-management. The application is to regularly ask: 'Whose glory am I seeking? Am I resting my sense of self-worth on God's steadfast regard, or on the shifting opinions of others?' This cultivates what might be called 'God-rooted confidence'—a stability that permits genuine service, because one is not perpetually defending one's significance.

text_kjv: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 9, the psalm shifts decisively from personal meditation to public exhortation. Through verses 1-8, the psalmist has been working out his own faith in the hearing of others—a form of testimony. Now the speaker becomes a teacher, calling the community to the same trust he has discovered. The Covenant Rendering repositions the syntax to place 'pour out your hearts before him' at the beginning, followed by 'Trust in him at all times,' suggesting that the act of complete vulnerability (pouring out) precedes and enables the state of trust. This is significant: trust is not achieved by willpower or discipline alone, but by the radical act of emptying oneself before God—holding nothing back, defending nothing, keeping no secret reserve.

The verb shifkhu, 'pour out,' is visceral and physical. In biblical usage, it describes pouring out water (Psalm 79:3), pouring out blood in sacrifice (Leviticus 17:4), and even pouring out one's soul in desperate prayer (1 Samuel 1:15). This is not polite petition but total self-disclosure. The communal address (am, 'people, nation') transforms what might have been a private psalm into an invitation for all who listen to participate in this posture. The parenthetical 'Selah' signals a pause—time for the hearer to let the instruction settle, to consider whether they are willing to be so vulnerable. The closing affirmation, 'God is a refuge for us' (plural), extends the promise of verse 7 (singular, 'I will not be moved') into a corporate reality: the refuge is not just for the psalmist but for all who make this commitment to transparent trust.

word_study.meaning: To trust, rely on, have confidence in. The root suggests throwing oneself upon something or someone, entrusting one's weight to them. It carries a connotation of abandon—the word is used of resting, lying down in security.
word_study.significance: Batach is not mere intellectual belief but a physical and emotional stance of reliance. To 'trust in God' is to throw oneself upon Him, to cease holding oneself up through one's own effort. This is why it must be connected to the act of 'pouring out'—one cannot throw oneself on God while holding reserves back.

word_study.meaning: To pour, pour out, shed. Used of pouring liquids, shedding blood, and especially in poetic contexts, emptying oneself of emotion, complaint, or prayer before God. The Covenant Rendering notes the visceral power of this verb.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'pour out' rather than 'confess' or 'pray' emphasizes completeness and irreversibility. Once poured out, liquid cannot be recovered or controlled. This captures the psalmist's call to total vulnerability before God—a holding back of nothing.

word_study.meaning: Heart; the seat of emotion, will, intention, and understanding in Hebrew thought. Not merely feeling but the center of one's being—one's true self, including hidden thoughts and desires.
word_study.significance: To 'pour out the heart' before God is to make the interior self transparent. There is nowhere to hide, no facade maintained. This is why it requires courage—it is the opposite of self-protection.

word_study.meaning: As in verse 8, shelter or hiding place; from the root 'to hide.' Here, God becomes the place where one can hide, but only after having been completely revealed.
word_study.significance: The seeming paradox is profound: only by pouring out completely and ceasing to hide can one truly find refuge. The place of safety is not found by maintaining boundaries but by crossing them entirely.

word_study.meaning: A term of uncertain meaning; possibly 'pause,' 'interlude,' 'lift up,' or 'forever.' Appears 71 times in the Psalms. Most scholars view it as a direction for pause or transition, allowing time for reflection or for a musical interlude.
word_study.significance: The placement of 'Selah' here suggests that the listener needs time to absorb what is being asked. The instruction to 'pour out your heart' is challenging—Selah gives space for hesitation, for the struggle that occurs when one is asked to be completely vulnerable.

cross_references.connection: Hannah tells Eli, 'I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD,' showing that pouring out one's heart before God is the posture of prayer that God honors.
Paul instructs, 'In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God,' paralleling the call to transparent petition before God without holding back.

The psalmist recalls, 'I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise,' indicating that communal worship is the context for learning to pour out one's heart.
Exhorts believers to 'draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith,' using similar language of authenticity and complete vulnerability before God.
Teaches that confidence before God comes from knowing He is 'greater than our heart' and from dwelling in a place of transparent conscience, aligning with the principle of pouring out before Him.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern worship, petitions to deities often followed formal, prescribed patterns. The Mesopotamian prayer formula and Egyptian temple inscriptions show that worshipers typically approached the divine with carefully structured language and maintained social hierarchy even in the act of prayer. The psalmist's call to 'pour out your heart'—to move beyond formal petition to transparent, unguarded speech—represents a distinctive aspect of Israelite faith. The God of Israel was understood to desire not perfect performance but authentic relationship. Archaeological evidence from personal prayer inscriptions (such as those found at Kuntillet Ajrud) shows that ordinary Israelites did indeed engage in direct, unmediated address to God, suggesting that this personal, vulnerable mode of prayer was genuinely practiced, not merely idealized.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:26 teaches 'Pour out your hearts in your closets unto your Father; yea, when ye are alone and in your secret places, cry unto God,' directly echoing this verse's call to complete vulnerability in prayer and extending it to the injunction that such pouring out should be constant, not occasional.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1 records the Lord's invitation: 'Hearken and hear, O ye my people, saith your God, even Jesus Christ, your Redeemer,' followed by calls to those who will listen. D&C 59:8 emphasizes that the Lord 'hath said: Thou shalt love thy God with all thy heart,' requiring the same wholehearted commitment that 'pouring out' represents.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple recommend interview and the personal covenants made in the endowment require a form of this 'pouring out'—acknowledgment before witnesses of one's commitment, with nothing held back. The principle that God sees all hearts and that integrity requires alignment between exterior profession and interior reality is taught in temple ceremonies. The call to 'trust in him at all times' resonates with the eternal nature of temple covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the perfect embodiment of 'pouring out' before God. In Gethsemane, Luke 22:44 records that He prayed 'more earnestly' with sweat 'as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground'—a physical manifestation of the spiritual act of pouring out one's entire self. Hebrews 5:7 describes His prayer 'with strong crying and tears' and willingness to be heard through reverent submission. The invitation in this verse to pour out one's heart finds its ultimate meaning in Christ, who poured out His soul unto death (Isaiah 53:12) in perfect trust in the Father.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse addresses a primary obstacle to spiritual growth: the reluctance to be fully vulnerable before God. Cultural conditioning, psychological self-protection, shame, and fear of judgment all conspire to keep believers maintaining some facade even in prayer. This verse calls for radical authenticity—bringing not just approved thoughts and gratitude, but anger, doubt, confusion, despair, and all the contents of one's actual inner life before God. The application includes: (1) Regular practice of unguarded prayer, pouring out what is actually present rather than what should be present; (2) Recognition that God is not shocked or disappointed by human struggle; (3) The understanding that trust grows through such vulnerability, not despite it; (4) Willingness to teach others, as the communal address suggests, that this kind of prayer is not a failure of faith but its deepest expression. The modern believer might ask: 'What am I holding back in my prayers? What part of my interior life am I still defending rather than offering to God? What would change if I ceased performing faith and simply poured out my actual condition?'

text_kjv: Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 is a devastating social commentary delivered after the call to trust and transparency in verse 9. Having invited the community to pour out their hearts before God (verse 9), the psalmist now explains why this is necessary: all human sources of trust and confidence—whether lowborn or highborn—are ultimately insubstantial. The Covenant Rendering's distinction is crucial: 'Common people are only a breath; important people are a lie.' The parallel structure creates a chiasm: common people are hevel (emptiness, vapor), while important people are kazab (a deception, a false claim). Both social classes fail as reliable sources of support, but in different ways. Ordinary people lack substance—they have nothing solid to offer. Important people possess apparent substance, but it is false—their claims to reliability, wisdom, and protective capacity rest on illusion.

The metaphor of the scales (moznayim) draws from imagery associated with divine judgment and justice (compare Daniel 5:27, where Belshazzar is 'weighed in the balances, and art found wanting'). When both classes are placed on the scales of cosmic reality, they rise upward together—not because they are light in weight, but because they weigh less than hevel itself. Hevel, the 'breath' or 'vapor' that defines the theme of Ecclesiastes, is the psalmist's measurement of absolute worthlessness. To weigh less than hevel is to be so insubstantial as to be unmeasurable. This is not a counsel of misanthropy but of reorientation: if human sources are this unreliable, then all hope must be relocated to God. The verse therefore functions as the logical foundation for verse 9's command to trust in God 'at all times'—not as an option among alternatives, but as the only rational response to the complete unreliability of human support structures.

word_study.meaning: Vapor, breath, wind, nothingness; anything without substance, permanence, or purpose. The root suggests something fleeting or evanescent. This is the key word of Ecclesiastes, where it appears over 30 times to describe the futility of earthly pursuits.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'breath' captures the sense better than 'vanity.' Breath is something you produce with your mouth, expel, and it vanishes. It is the image of profound impermanence. When the psalmist says humans are 'hevel,' he is claiming they are as insubstantial as one's own exhaled breath—present for a moment, then gone.

word_study.meaning: A lie, falsehood, deception; something that claims to be one thing while being another. The root suggests breaking faith or creating a false impression.
word_study.significance: Unlike hevel (which is simply empty), kazab is actively deceptive. The 'men of high degree' are not merely insubstantial but actively misleading—they present themselves as reliable, weighty, and worthy of trust, but this presentation is false.

word_study.meaning: Sons of Adam; mankind generally, but in this parallel construction, specifically the common people as opposed to the powerful. The term emphasizes common humanity.
word_study.significance: The construction 'sons of Adam' reminds the hearer that all humans, regardless of social class, share the fundamental nature of mortality and limitation. They are all Adam's descendants—shaped from dust (Genesis 2:7), all subject to the human condition.

word_study.meaning: Sons of a man; in social context, this refers to men of standing, importance, or nobility. The single word 'ish' (man) in the construct suggests those who have achieved or inherited prominence.
word_study.significance: The parallel structure suggests that whether one appeals to common folk or to the powerful, both fail. The term bney ish may also carry ironic weight—they are merely 'sons of man' too, despite their pretensions to greater substance.

word_study.term_english: to be laid in the balance
word_study.meaning: Placed on scales, to go up (or rise). The scales (moznayim) are the instrument of weighing and thus of measuring value or truth. To 'rise' on the scales means to weigh less.
word_study.significance: The image is of objects being measured by weight. In ancient commerce and law, the scales determined true value. When the psalmist says people 'rise' on the scales, he uses language of cosmic judgment—when weighed against ultimate reality, they float upward because they have no weight at all.

cross_references.connection: The opening proclamation, 'Vanity of vanities... all is vanity,' uses hevel repeatedly to describe all human effort and accomplishment, establishing the worldview that underlies this verse's dismissal of human sources of trust.
Uses scale imagery in judgment: 'Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting,' similarly employing the scales as a measure of ultimate worth and truthfulness before God.
Describes all nations as 'less than nothing, and vanity' before God, using similar language of human insignificance when measured against the divine reality.
Uses the wisdom formula 'One... two... three... four' to introduce absolute statements, paralleling Psalm 62's use of structural repetition to emphasize unchanging truths about human reliability.
Jesus teaches that life is more than food and raiment, and that worrying about sustenance reflects misplaced trust in material and human sources rather than in God's provision.

commentary.historical_context: In the honor-shame culture of ancient Israel, social status determined access to resources, protection, legal standing, and personal security. People oriented their entire lives around securing and maintaining their standing in the community. The psalmist's claim that both high and low people are equally unreliable would have been shocking. He is not denying that powerful people have resources or influence—he is claiming that such things are fundamentally unstable and untrustworthy. This reflects a genuine historical insight: ancient Near Eastern political history shows repeated cycles of uplifted leaders falling into shame, exile, or death. Powerful dynasties collapsed. Wealthy merchants lost their fortunes. The psalmist may be speaking from experience of such reversals. Archaeologically, the cycles of prosperity and destruction visible in settlement patterns across the Levant would have reinforced this understanding that human power and security are temporary and unreliable.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 28:31 warns that certain will 'heap up treasures upon the earth, which moth and rust doth corrupt, and thieves break through and steal,' echoing the psalmist's teaching that human possessions and status are insubstantial. Helaman 13:36 teaches a similar lesson about trusting in riches: 'For behold, ye do love money, and your substance, and your fine apparel.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:32 warns that in the last days, 'there shall be men standing in that generation, that will not pass until they shall see an overflowing scourge,' suggesting that human social structures and authorities cannot protect from divine judgment. D&C 121:1-2 teaches that reliance on human leadership or worldly power is ultimately futile when that power is exercised unrighteously.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that true authority and power are not located in worldly hierarchies but in covenants with God. The order of the temple, with its emphasis on truth and its stripping away of worldly status markers, embodies the principle that human social standing has no ultimate significance. All covenants are made equally before God, regardless of social status in the world.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ's life repeatedly demonstrates the principle of this verse. He rejected worldly power (Matthew 4:8-10), warned against trusting in human leadership (Matthew 23:8-10), and showed that even when surrounded by powerful opponents and betrayed by followers, His true reality and weight were not diminished. His crucifixion—the ultimate stripping away of worldly honor—paradoxically revealed His true weight and glory. The resurrection shows that what the world deemed worthless (the executed prophet) is in fact of infinite worth in God's scales. The invitation to 'take up thy cross and follow me' (Mark 8:34) implicitly accepts the psalmist's assessment: worldly security is vanity; only trust in God is substantial.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse cuts against powerful cultural currents. Societies measure worth through status, accumulation, social media presence, professional rank, and network influence. The psalmist's assessment—that all such measures are 'lighter than vanity' in cosmic weight—is radically countercultural. The application is not to despise people of authority or to reject all human relationships, but to recalibrate one's fundamental trust. A modern believer might ask: 'On whose approval or support am I ultimately depending? A boss, colleague, family member, community group? Am I basing my sense of security on their favor or position? What would change in my life if I accepted that all human sources of security are, in ultimate terms, insubstantial?' This leads to liberation: freed from the need to please everyone or to maintain status, a believer can act with integrity and courage. Paradoxically, this detachment from human judgment often leads to more genuine and healthy relationships—because they are no longer burdened with the demand that they provide ultimate security. The verse invites the modern member to make the same shift the psalmist made: from seeking refuge in human alliance to seeking refuge in God, and to teach others this same reorientation.

text_kjv: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 applies the truth of verse 10 to specific forms of false security. After establishing that all human sources of trust are insubstantial (verse 10), the psalmist now warns against three specific temptations: (1) trusting in oppression, (2) finding significance in robbery, and (3) becoming attached to increasing wealth. The Covenant Rendering's phrasing is precise: 'Do not trust in extortion; do not put empty hope in robbery.' This unpacking clarifies what the KJV might obscure: the issue is not merely the acquisition of wealth through unjust means, but the psychological trap of thinking such acquisition provides security or significance.

The first prohibition addresses osheq (oppression, extortion)—acquiring wealth or power through violence or exploitation. The danger is subtle: the person who becomes wealthy through oppression might think themselves secure, believing that their ill-gotten strength will protect them. But verse 10 has already established that all such power is vanity. The second warning targets gazel (robbery, theft)—and the verb used is 'put empty hope,' connecting back to hevel (breath, emptiness) from verse 10. To find significance in robbery is to become hevel oneself—as insubstantial as the act of taking. The third prohibition addresses the most common temptation: the gradual attachment to increasing riches even if acquired justly. Chayil (wealth, strength, army) can increase legitimately, but the heart's attachment to it is the spiritual danger. The phrase 'set not your heart upon them' (al tasitu leb) echoes the vocabulary of trust and dependence—it is not just about external behavior but about where one's fundamental reliance is placed.

word_study.meaning: As in verse 9, to throw oneself upon, to trust or rely upon; here used in the negative imperative.
word_study.significance: The repetition of this key term from verse 9 creates a frame: 'Trust in God at all times' (verse 9) now has its inverse explicitly stated: 'Do not trust in oppression.' The choice is binary—one trusts either in God or in substitutes, but not both with equal weight.

word_study.meaning: Oppression, extortion, crushing; wrongful taking of another's rights or possessions. The verb suggests pressure applied to extract something unjustly.
word_study.significance: To 'trust in oppression' is to believe that one is safe because one has power over others. But such power is fragile—it depends on continued ability to oppress, and it provokes resistance. The psalmist recognizes that security built on injustice is inherently unstable.

word_study.meaning: To become empty, insubstantial, vain. The verb form is derived from the noun used in verse 10.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this by 'put empty hope': to trust in robbery literally makes one empty (hevel). One absorbs the character of what one puts faith in. This is a form of spiritual physics—false trust is self-emptying.

word_study.meaning: Robbery, theft, the act of taking wrongfully from another. The verb carries a connotation of violent or forceful taking.
word_study.significance: Gazel is more acute than osheq—it is sudden, forceful taking rather than systematic oppression. The psalmist's warning encompasses both slow exploitation and sudden violent acquisition.

word_study.meaning: Wealth, substance, strength, army, might. The root suggests capability, resources, and power. Can refer to military strength, accumulated resources, or personal capability.
word_study.significance: Chayil is not inherently sinful—it is simply capacity and resources. The problem arises when 'heart' (leb, one's fundamental orientation) is set upon it. The warning is about what one loves and depends upon, not about wealth itself.

word_study.meaning: To set, place, or fix one's heart; idiomatically, to direct one's attention, affection, or dependence toward something.
word_study.significance: This phrase occurs frequently in wisdom literature when warning against misplaced desire or attachment. To 'set one's heart' on riches is to make them one's ultimate concern, essentially committing one's soul to them. This is the spiritual danger.

cross_references.connection: Paul teaches that 'the love of money is the root of all evil,' identifying the attachment to wealth (rather than wealth itself) as spiritually destructive—paralleling this verse's warning about setting one's heart on riches.

Jesus warns, 'Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth,' directly echoing this verse's principle that life and security are not found in increasing wealth.
States that 'he that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house: but he that hateth gifts shall live,' teaching that profit obtained through wrongful means brings instability to one's whole life.
The prophet condemns those 'that store up violence and robbery in their palaces,' showing how unjust acquisition becomes a form of spiritual disorder affecting everything one possesses.
Similarly warns against trusting in wealth and riches, and asks 'None of them can by any means redeem his brother,' establishing that economic security cannot provide ultimate protection.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, wealth accumulation typically occurred through one of three means: legitimate trade and agriculture, royal grant (the king's favor), or conquest and extraction (including slavery and taxation). The psalmist's warning against trusting in 'oppression' (osheq) would have been particularly pointed for those who acquired wealth as royal officials, tax collectors, or military commanders—roles that involved systematic extraction from others. Archaeological evidence shows that such acquired wealth could be rapid, but political instability meant it was equally fragile. A change in regime, a palace coup, or a failed military campaign could erase wealth and status instantly. The psalmist's warning reflects both moral principle (such wealth is wrongly obtained) and historical realism (such wealth is unstable). The warning against becoming 'vain' (hevel) in robbery suggests that wrongfully obtained goods carry a spiritual weight—they implicate one in injustice and make one spiritually hollow.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 1:27-28 teaches that the Church is blessed 'with more riches, and abundance of flocks and herds, and with greater herds upon all the face of the land,' but only when the people are righteous and not attaching their hearts to wealth. When they turn to pride and acquisitiveness, spiritual decline follows. Helaman 6:17-21 shows how the pursuit of wealth through dishonest means leads to spiritual destruction and ultimately to violence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:26-27 teaches that riches and fine things lead to complacency and worldliness unless the heart is set on building God's kingdom. D&C 6:7 emphasizes that God's gifts are given for the benefit of the community, not for selfish accumulation: 'Seek not for riches but for wisdom.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that all possessions are ultimately God's, held in stewardship rather than absolute ownership. The law of consecration, entered into through covenant, embodies the principle that one's heart must be set on God's purposes rather than on personal accumulation. The temple garment itself is a daily reminder of covenants that supersede economic allegiances.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ exemplified the principle of this verse in His rejection of Satan's offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them' (Matthew 4:8-9) in exchange for worship. His teaching in the Sermon on the Mount warns against 'mammon' (Matthew 6:24) and teaches that 'no man can serve two masters.' His instruction to the rich young ruler—to sell all and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21)—was not a universal command but a diagnosis: this man's heart was set on riches, making it impossible for him to follow Christ.
