The verse thus establishes a theological sequence: human sin is real and overwhelming; but God is the one who addresses it; and he does so through a covering, an atonement that removes sin's power.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the words/matters of iniquities have become strong / have overpowered.' Gavru is the past tense of gabar, meaning to be strong, mighty, or to overcome. Avonot is the plural of avon, meaning iniquity, guilt, or depravity.
word_study.significance: The verb gavru is active—it does not say 'I struggle with sin' but 'sin has overpowered me.' This anthropomorphizes sin as a force with agency. It reflects an ancient theology that recognizes sin as something more than individual moral failure; it is a power that works in human beings. The Covenant Rendering's 'when the weight of wrongdoing overpowers me' captures the sense of sin as a burden that exceeds human capacity to bear.

word_study.meaning: Transgressions, rebellions, revolts. Pesha refers specifically to rebellion against God's authority, a deliberate turning away. It is a more volitional sin than avon (iniquity), which can include both willful and unwillful transgression.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'iniquities' (avonot) to 'transgressions' (pesha'im) moves from general guilt to specific rebellion. The parallelism in the verse acknowledges both types of sin: the general depravity that overwhelms and the specific rebellions that require forgiveness.

word_study.meaning: You will atone for them, you will cover them over, you will make propitiation. From the root k-p-r (kaphar), which is the verbal root of kippur (atonement). The root carries meanings of 'to cover,' 'to wipe away,' 'to make expiation.'
word_study.significance: This is perhaps the most theologically loaded word in the verse. The k-p-r root is the very foundation of Israel's sacrificial system and atonement theology. It appears in Leviticus 16 in the context of the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), when the high priest would cover (k-p-r) the sins of the people through the sprinkling of blood and the scapegoat ritual. To use tekhaprem here is to claim that God, like the high priest, has the power to cover and remove sin. The Covenant Rendering's 'you cover over our rebellions' is precise—the image is of covering something so it no longer appears, making it invisible to God's eye. This is not mere forgetting; it is a deliberate, divine act of removing the guilt that separates creature from Creator.

cross_references.connection: Declares that all have sinned and 'come short of the glory of God' (echoing the overpowering nature of sin) and that God offers redemption through Christ, who is the 'propitiation' (the covering, the atonement).

Describes the scapegoat ritual of Yom Kippur, where the high priest confesses sins over the goat, which then 'carries away' all iniquities—the concrete enactment of the 'covering' mentioned in this verse.
The Suffering Servant passage: 'the Lord hath laid on him the iniquities of us all'—describing the messianic fulfillment of the atonement theme in this verse.
Lehi teaches that the atonement of Christ overcomes the power of sin and makes repentance possible—directly paralleling the theology of verse 4.
Modern revelation: 'I, the Lord, forgive sins unto those who confess their sins before me and ask forgiveness'—establishing God's willingness and power to atone for transgressions.

commentary.historical_context: The psalm assumes the sacrificial system as backdrop. In ancient Israelite practice, when someone was aware of sin—whether deliberate transgression or inadvertent guilt—they would bring a sacrifice to the temple. The priest would then perform the kaphar (atonement) ritual, which involved sprinkling blood and sometimes burning parts of the offering. The term tekhaprem would have evoked this entire system for Israelite worshipers. The shift from singular 'me' to plural 'our' suggests corporate confession, likely in a communal worship context. The mention of both avonot (iniquity—more general depravity) and pesha'im (rebellion—more specific transgression) reflects the comprehensive awareness of sin's scope: it includes both what we do deliberately and what we are guilty of by nature. The recognition that sin 'overpowers' (gavru) the individual reflects an anthropology in which human beings are not fully autonomous moral agents but are affected by powers larger than themselves—an insight particularly relevant in contexts of post-exilic Judaism, where the community felt the weight of historical judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 2:8-10 teaches that 'the Messiah cometh in the fulness of time' and that 'he offereth himself a sacrifice for sin' to make 'repentance and redemption' possible. Alma 42:9-15 explains that 'justice' cannot be set aside, but God provides 'mercy' through the atonement—the paradox of verse 4, where God both acknowledges sin's overwhelming power and covers it over. Mosiah 3:11-12 speaks of Christ taking upon himself the sins of the world.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:37 teaches that 'the Lord can do all things' and among his powers is the forgiveness of sins. D&C 19:16-18 reveals that Christ 'suffered...the pain of all men' in order that the Father could offer forgiveness. The principle of verse 4—that only God can cover what overpowers humanity—is foundational to the atonement as revealed in D&C. Section 45:3-5 explicitly connects Christ's atonement to the covering (kaphar) of sin: 'Wherefore I command you to repent...that ye may be forgiven.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The mention of tekhaprem (covering/atonement) has direct bearing on the temple, where the atonement of Christ is understood as the reality to which all previous sacrifices pointed. The Latter-day Saint temple teaches that Christ's atonement is both individual ('that one might atone for the sins of all mankind') and communal (we are brought into that atonement through covenant). The passage from confessing sin (verse 4's admission) to having it covered (by God's act of atonement) mirrors the temple's movement from awareness of human need to receipt of divine grace.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is thoroughly Christological. The high priest's covering (kaphar) of sin on Yom Kippur was an anticipatory type of Christ's atonement. Christ is the 'propitiation for our sins' (1 John 2:2)—he is the one who performs what the psalmist here asks: covering over, making atonement for, removing the weight of transgression. The shift in the verse from singular 'me' to plural 'our' anticipates Christ's inclusive atonement—he covers not one person's sin but the transgressions of all humanity. Hebrews 9:11-14 explicitly interprets the Day of Atonement and the high priest's work as types of Christ's sacrifice once for all.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to the pattern of repentance. First comes honest acknowledgment: 'When the weight of wrongdoing overpowers me.' This is not minimizing sin or pretending it's not a serious problem. It is admitting that sin has power. Second comes confessing before God: the shift from 'me' to 'our' invites the individual to identify not as a solitary sinner but as part of a community that struggles together. Third comes faith in God's atonement: 'thou shalt purge them'—trusting that the covering, the removal of guilt, is God's prerogative and promise. In practice, this means regular repentance—not from a posture of self-loathing but from a posture of trust that God genuinely has the power to cover and remove sin. It means bringing specific sins, specific rebellions, before God in prayer, not as mere introspection but as genuine petition for the atonement that is available through Christ.

text_kjv: Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple.

commentary.narrative: After acknowledging sin's power and God's atonement, the psalmist shifts to describing the joy of those who are brought into God's presence. The verse opens with an ascription of blessedness (asher, often translated 'blessed') over one who is chosen and brought near to God. The Hebrew verbs tivchar ('you choose') and utqarev ('you bring near') both place the initiative entirely with God. Access to the divine presence is not achieved but granted. The psalmist is not describing someone who, through moral effort, has earned a place in God's house. Rather, God himself selects and invites. To 'dwell in your courts' (yaskon chatzerekha) is to inhabit the spaces of the temple—to live in continuity with the divine presence. The image is not momentary visitation but sustained dwelling, though in the temple's literal sense it would have meant pilgrimage and festival seasons. Then the perspective shifts from singular to plural: 'we shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house' (nisb'ah bituv betekha). This sudden shift from 'the man whom thou choosest' to 'we' invites the entire community of worshipers to identify with the blessedness described. 'Goodness' (tuv) here means not merely moral virtue but fullness, abundance, what sustains life. To be satisfied with the goodness of God's house is to experience sufficiency, the sense that all legitimate longing is met. The final phrase, 'the holiness of your temple,' grounds this experience in the actual sacred space—not abstract spirituality but the concrete reality of the temple building, with its curtains, altars, and presence of God.

word_study.meaning: Blessed, happy, fortunate. Often appears at the opening of psalms to describe the spiritual happiness that comes from alignment with God. Not mere pleasure but deep, covenantal joy.
word_study.significance: The word asher (blessed) appears throughout the Psalter to describe those whose lives are ordered by covenant with God. It denotes not feeling but objective status—to be blessed is to be in right relationship with God, which naturally produces joy. This verse declares that the person chosen and brought near by God possesses deep, essential happiness.

word_study.meaning: You choose, you select, you prefer. From the root bachar, meaning to choose, select, or pick out. Implies discernment and deliberation.
word_study.significance: The choice is God's, not the worshiper's. God looks upon humanity and selects those whom he will bring into covenant relationship. This reflects the election theology of Israel: not earned but given. In the context of verse 4's confession of sin and atonement, this is remarkable—despite sin, God still chooses to bring people near.

word_study.meaning: You cause to approach, you bring near. From the root qarav, meaning to come near, draw close, approach. Can have both spatial and relational significance.
word_study.significance: Again, the initiative is God's. The verb is in the causative form—God is the active agent bringing near. In the context of the temple, this could be literal (granting access to the sacred spaces) but also relational (establishing intimacy, closeness). The pairing of 'choose' and 'bring near' suggests that God's choice naturally results in relational closeness.

word_study.meaning: Will dwell in your courts. Yaskon is from shakan, meaning to dwell, settle, inhabit. Chatzerekha is the plural of chatzer, meaning courtyard or enclosed space. The temple had a series of courts (outer court, inner court, etc.), each with deeper access to the holy place.
word_study.significance: To dwell (not merely visit) in God's courts is the hope expressed. This suggests a sustaining, ongoing relationship rather than momentary encounter. The imagery of courts evokes the actual geography of the temple—concentric circles of sacred space, each bringing the worshiper deeper toward the presence of God.

word_study.meaning: We will be satisfied / fulfilled with goodness. Nisba is from saba, meaning to be full, to have one's fill, to be satisfied. Tuv means goodness, beauty, abundance, well-being.
word_study.significance: To be satisfied is to have one's deepest hunger met. The image is not of moral achievement but of feast, of abundance. The Covenant Rendering notes that this satisfaction language appears elsewhere (e.g., Psalm 63:6) where presence with God is experienced as feast. This is the ultimate desire—not to work for God but to dwell with God and experience the abundance of his presence.

word_study.meaning: Holy temple / Holy palace. Qedosh means set apart, holy, sacred. Heikalkha is the temple building, the palace of God. The heikhal is the inner sanctuary, the most sacred space.
word_study.significance: The temple is not merely a building but the dwelling place of the Holy God. Its holiness derives from God's presence. By extension, those who dwell in the courts of this holy temple are brought into contact with holiness, are transformed by proximity to the sacred.

cross_references.connection: Also celebrates those who dwell in God's house: 'How amiable are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord.' Uses nearly identical language and theology.
Promise that seeking God leads to finding him—underlying the theology of verse 5 that God brings near those he chooses.
Teaches that through Christ's atonement, believers have 'boldness to enter into the holiest' and have been 'brought near by the blood of Jesus.'
Articulates the same theology: 'God...hath chosen us' and 'made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus'—a spiritual enactment of dwelling in God's courts.

Modern revelation on the gathering of the elect: 'That ye might be gathered unto my bosom...when the day of his coming shall arrive, when he shall sit down upon his throne to reign with power and great glory.'

commentary.historical_context: The temple's physical layout involved concentric courtyards—an outer court accessible to Israelites, an inner court for priests, and the Holy of Holies accessible only to the high priest on Yom Kippur. The term 'courts' (chatzerot) would have evoked this geography. To 'dwell in the courts' would have meant participating in the life of the temple—attending feasts, bringing offerings, standing within the sacred space. The promise of satisfaction (nisba'ah) with the 'goodness of the house' reflects the practice of eating portions of sacrificial meals within the temple precinct (Deuteronomy 12:7)—the temple was not merely a place of solemnity but also of celebration and nourishment. The shift from singular ('the man whom thou choosest') to plural ('we shall be satisfied') reflects the actual practice of communal worship—individuals came to the temple but experienced it as a community of worshipers gathered in God's presence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 8:11-12 describes Lehi's vision of the tree of life, where those who partake experience satisfaction and joy—a parallel to being satisfied with the goodness of God's house. Alma 32:42 teaches about the joy of bearing fruit through faith, a spiritual equivalent of dwelling in God's abundance. Mosiah 2:41 promises that those who keep the commandments will be blessed and have contentment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1 addresses the 'people of my church' and speaks of being gathered and brought near. D&C 88:62-63 teaches that all things are sustained by light and truth, which emanates from God—a spiritual principle underlying the 'goodness of thy house.' D&C 105:10 speaks of the blessing promised to those who are faithful: 'Wherefore I command you to repent...and be faithful.' Section 131:1-4 describes the conditions of celestial glory and the families who dwell there, extending the temple theology into eternal perspective.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: This verse is profoundly connected to temple theology. The courts of the physical temple become in Latter-day Saint understanding a symbol of progression through covenants toward the presence of God. Temple workers, who 'dwell' in the temple regularly, experience the ongoing refreshment described in verse 5. The temple recommend system reflects the theology of 'choosing' and 'bringing near'—only those God has called forth through their faith and covenants are granted access. The satisfaction experienced by those who regularly attend the temple—feeling the Spirit, making covenants, being reminded of God's goodness—directly enacts verse 5.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate one chosen and brought near by God. Hebrews 4:14-16 describes Jesus as having 'passed into the heavens' and as a 'merciful and faithful high priest' who grants access to the throne of grace. The satisfaction promised in verse 5 is ultimately fulfilled in Christ—he is the reality toward which the temple pointed. Those who come to Christ (the antitype of the temple's holy place) experience the dwelling with God that verse 5 describes. John 1:14 ('the Word became flesh and dwelt among us') is the ultimate fulfillment of 'dwelling in thy courts.'
commentary.application: This verse teaches about the blessing of belonging to God's covenant community. It reasserts, after the confession of verse 4, that despite human sin, God chooses to bring people near. The shift from singular to plural invites individual readers to see themselves as part of a community selected and brought near by God. In modern practice, this finds expression in temple attendance—regular worshipers in the temple literally dwell in God's house and experience the satisfaction described. But it also applies beyond the temple: being part of a ward community, participating in sacrament meeting, studying scripture together—these are ways modern Latter-day Saints 'dwell' in God's house and experience satisfaction. The verse challenges isolationism; it affirms that the deepest joy comes through dwelling in community with God and with others who have been brought near by his choice. It also provides comfort to those who feel unworthy: you are not chosen because you deserve it; you are chosen because God, in his mercy, decides to bring you near. That choice is the source of blessing.

text_kjv: By terrible things in righteousness wilt thou answer us, O God of our salvation; who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea:

commentary.narrative: The psalm now expands its vision outward from the intimate worship of the temple to cosmic scope. God answers the prayers of those in Zion, the psalmist indicates, 'by terrible things in righteousness.' The word 'terrible' here translates nora'ot, which means 'awesome things, fearsome acts'—God's interventions in human history and nature are overwhelming in their power. But these awesome deeds are never arbitrary; they are always be-tsedeq, 'in righteousness,' meaning they set things right, restore justice, establish order. God does not display raw power for its own sake. Rather, the terrible and awesome acts by which God answers prayer are righteous acts—they are expressions of God's commitment to justice and right relationship. The verse then identifies God by title: 'O God of our salvation'—not merely a powerful God but one who delivers, who rescues, who saves. The scope expands further: this God is 'the confidence of all the ends of the earth'—the farthest reaches of the known world look to this God for security. And 'them that are afar off upon the sea'—even those separated by vast distances, who travel on the dangerous seas, find their trust in this God. The movement from the particular (the worshipers in Zion's courts) to the universal (all ends of the earth, distant seas) suggests that God's character as revealed in the temple is not limited to Israel but extends to all creation. All who learn of this God become partakers of the confidence he provides.

word_study.meaning: Awesome things, terrible/fearful things, mighty deeds. From the root yara, meaning to fear or be afraid. Nora'ot describes acts that inspire awe and fear—overwhelming displays of power.
word_study.significance: The word denotes not cruelty but overwhelming power that inspires reverent fear. In the context of God answering prayer, nora'ot suggests that when God acts in response to human petition, the results are powerful, visible, undeniable. God does not answer prayer timidly or incompletely. The Covenant Rendering's 'awesome deeds' captures the sense of power that evokes reverence.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, right action, justice, that which is correct and proper in God's order. Tsedeq encompasses both God's character (he is righteous) and his acts (he acts righteously).
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'awesome deeds' (nora'ot) with 'righteousness' (tsedeq) is crucial. God's power is never divorced from justice. When God acts, he acts to restore tsedeq—to set things right. This prevents the portrayal of God as a capricious despot with unlimited power. Every terrible thing God does serves the purpose of establishing righteousness. The translator notes that 'God's awesome deeds are not arbitrary displays of power but expressions of tsedeq—they set things right.' This is the foundational principle of God's character in Israelite theology.

word_study.meaning: You will answer, you will respond, you will reply. From the root anah, meaning to answer, respond, or fulfill. In the context of prayer, it means God responds to the petitions brought before him.
word_study.significance: The verb ta'aneinu connects back to verse 3's 'you who hear prayer.' Hearing naturally leads to answering. God does not merely hear prayer passively; he answers with action. The awesome deeds of verse 6 are God's answers—his responses to prayer.

word_study.meaning: God of our salvation, God of our deliverance. Yesh'a means salvation, rescue, deliverance from danger. The title emphasizes God's character as liberator and savior.
word_study.significance: This title appears frequently in the Psalter and defines God not in abstract theological terms but in terms of his saving action. He is the God who has delivered Israel from Egypt, who rescues the righteous from enemies. For a community praying in the temple, 'God of our salvation' invokes the entire history of God's rescues and implies that he will continue to save those who call upon him.

word_study.meaning: Confidence, security, that in which one trusts. From the root batach, meaning to trust, rely on, find security in.
word_study.significance: To speak of God as the 'confidence' (mivtach) of distant peoples is to suggest that even those who have not directly encountered the temple or Israel's God find their security in relationship with him. It is an assertion of God's universal appeal and availability—peoples everywhere can trust him.

word_study.term_english: ends of the earth / afar off upon the sea
word_study.meaning: Far ends of the earth and distant/far seas. Qatzve means extremities or ends, eretz means earth/land, rechokam means distant or far. This indicates the remotest reaches of the known world.
word_study.significance: The geographical imagery expands the scope of the psalm dramatically. It is not merely Israel but all humanity, even those most distant and separated by danger (the sea), who come within the scope of God's saving purpose. This universalism anticipates later prophetic vision (Isaiah 45:22: 'Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth').

cross_references.connection: Also celebrates God's salvation extended to 'all the ends of the earth': 'His right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory...that all the ends of the earth may see the salvation of our God.'
Describes God's power as unsearchable yet his compassion extended to those who wait upon him, echoing verse 6's pairing of terrible deeds with salvation.
Paul quotes Psalm 19:4 on the Gospel being declared 'to the ends of the world,' applying the universalism of verse 6 to the proclamation of Christ.
Nephi speaks of the Lord's work being 'manifest in the flesh' for 'all the ends of the earth,' directly applying verse 6's universal scope to Christ's atonement.
Modern revelation on the universal character of God's light and truth: 'The light which is in all things, which giveth life to all things...shineth eternity; therefore, must abide the law.'

commentary.historical_context: The imagery of 'ends of the earth' and 'distant seas' reflects the geographical perspective of ancient Israel. From the vantage point of Jerusalem, the edges of the known world were indeed remote and mysterious—desert wastes in some directions, vast sea distances in others. The mention of 'those afar off upon the sea' evokes the dangers of ancient maritime travel. That even distant, vulnerable peoples could find confidence in the God of Israel is a remarkable theological claim in the ancient world, where gods were typically conceived as limited to particular territories or peoples. The phrase 'by terrible things in righteousness' may allude to historical events—the plagues of Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea, victories over enemies—through which God had demonstrated both awesome power and righteous purpose. Later post-exilic thinking, reflected here, extends this pattern: God's interventions in world history, while appearing terrible to enemies, serve the purpose of establishing justice and saving the righteous.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:33-35 speaks of the power of God extended 'unto all the ends of the earth,' and Alma 37:4-5 teaches that the plates will 'go forth unto all nations.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes that God's saving power extends beyond Israel to all peoples. 3 Nephi 15:11-24 records Christ teaching of 'other sheep' who will hear his voice, extending the scope of verse 6's universalism.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:1 opens the Doctrine and Covenants by addressing the book 'To the inhabitants of Zion, and to the inhabitants of the earth'—immediately establishing that God's word extends to all. D&C 77-88 teach about God's universal governance and the extension of his light and truth to all creation. D&C 42:55-56 speaks of the gospel being 'preached to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people'—the ultimate extension of verse 6's principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is understood in Latter-day Saint theology as the place where God's saving purposes are most clearly revealed and where covenants connecting individual to cosmic patterns are made. The endowment ceremony includes imagery of all humanity being invited to come unto God—a ritual enactment of verse 6's universal scope. The phrase about 'all the ends of the earth' becoming confident in God finds modern expression in the principle of temple work for all deceased persons, regardless of nationality or era.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is both the 'awesome deed of righteousness' by which God answers prayer and the 'God of our salvation' whom all the ends of the earth may trust. His atonement is the terrible and righteous act par excellence—the crucifixion is the ultimate revelation of both divine power and divine justice. Colossians 1:15-20 describes Christ as 'the image of the invisible God' through whom 'all things...were reconciled' and through whom God's peace extends throughout creation. Revelation 5:11-14 envisions worshipers 'from every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation' singing the song of the Lamb, a liturgical fulfillment of verse 6's universalism.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that God's intervention in human affairs—whether historical, personal, or cosmic—follows a pattern: awesome deeds, always in righteousness. For modern believers, this reframes how we interpret difficulties and God's answers to prayer. When God acts, it may be in ways that seem dramatic or difficult—what the psalmist calls 'terrible things'—but the underlying principle is always tsedeq, the setting right of what has been wrong. This invites trust even when God's ways seem incomprehensible. Additionally, the universal scope of verse 6 invites modern Latter-day Saints to see their faith as participating in God's global work of salvation. The confidence God offers is not reserved for the righteous few but is available 'to all the ends of the earth'—a principle that underlies missionary work and temple work for all humanity. Finally, the pairing of awesome power with righteousness offers a corrective to thinking of God as either a distant, non-interventionist deity or an arbitrary power. The God of Psalm 65:6 is involved, powerful, and trustworthy because his power always serves justice and salvation.

text_kjv: Which by his strength setteth fast the mountains; being girded with power.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the transition from the psalmist's personal experience of forgiveness (verses 1-5) to the cosmic scope of God's power. The mountains—immovable, eternal symbols of stability—are not self-sustaining but actively established and maintained by divine strength. The imagery shifts from the intimate (God hears prayer, forgives sin) to the monumental (God holds the physical world together). This is not poetic decoration; ancient Israel understood mountains as the literal pillars of the world, the most permanent fixtures of creation. By asserting that God 'sets fast' the mountains through his strength, the psalmist is declaring that nothing in creation is independent of God's constant, deliberate action.

The picture of God 'girded with strength' (ne'zar bi-gevurah) uses the image of a warrior's belt or waistband, the very piece of armor that holds a warrior together and ready for battle. God's power is not latent or potential—it is his active readiness, his binding, his constant state. The verb mekhin (from kun, 'to establish, to set, to prepare') emphasizes deliberate construction and ongoing stability. Mountains do not merely exist; they are positioned and held in place by an act of sustained divine will.

word_study.meaning: To establish, set in place, prepare, make firm. The root kun describes deliberate construction or arrangement, not accidental formation. In the qal participle form here, it emphasizes ongoing, present action—God continuously establishes.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in creation accounts and covenant language. God kun ('established') the heavens and earth; covenants are kun ('established, set fast'). The mountains are not merely static; they are actively sustained by divine decree.

word_study.meaning: Power, strength, might, energy. Refers to physical force and the capacity to act. In Hebrew, koach is the raw, tangible power to accomplish—not abstract authority but concrete force.
word_study.significance: God's koach is the power that moves creation. This is the same word used for human strength and labor (cf. Ecclesiastes 9:10, 'with all thy might [koach]'). It grounds divine power in something comprehensible—the strength to do work.

word_study.meaning: Girded with strength/might. The verb azar means to gird, to bind up like a warrior tightening his belt. Gevurah is strength, might, the forceful capacity for action. The image is of God wrapping himself in strength as armor or readiness.
word_study.significance: This is warrior language. God is not distant or passive but visibly armed, deliberately prepared, actively ready. The metaphor suggests constant vigilance and readiness—gevurah emphasizes forceful, kinetic strength.

cross_references.connection: God surveyed all he had made and saw that it was very good—this foundation of creation is what Psalm 65:7 declares is continuously upheld by divine strength.
Help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth; like Psalm 65:7, it affirms God's active sustenance of the created order.
All things were created by and for Christ, and in him all things hold together—a direct NT echo of God's ongoing establishment of creation.
Korihor is asked how the earth hangs suspended; Alma affirms that the support of the earth is through God's word—paralleling the psalmist's declaration of divine sustenance.
Christ upholds all things by the word of his power—the same active, present-tense sustenance affirmed in Psalm 65:7.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern cosmology shared by Israel, mountains were understood as cosmic pillars—they represented permanence, the unchanging order of creation. Ugaritic texts, Egyptian tomb paintings, and Mesopotamian creation myths all portrayed mountains as the structural foundation of the world. To claim that God 'establishes' mountains was to claim absolute dominion over the very architecture of existence. The image of God 'girded with strength' evokes the iconography of warrior kings and gods depicted in Levantine art—the belt or waistband was the symbol of readiness and power. By applying this imagery to the invisible God, the psalmist makes God's sustaining power visible and comprehensible to an agrarian people who understood strength through labor, armor, and the grip of a warrior's readiness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See Alma 30:44, where Alma teaches that God's word holds the earth suspended in space—a Book of Mormon parallel that echoes Psalm 65:7's assertion of divine sustenance through active power (gevurah).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:41-47 describes the power by which God sustains all things: 'The light of the sun, the light of the stars, is the light of Christ. And the stars are they, by which you may navigate.' God's sustaining power is equated with light and order—just as Psalm 65:7 declares God's strength as the organizing principle of creation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where heaven and earth meet, where God's sustaining power becomes tangible and accessible. The temple's architecture—with its pillars, its foundations, its careful ordering—reflects the cosmic order established by the strength described in Psalm 65:7.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the embodiment of the divine strength (gevurah) that sustains all things. Hebrews 1:3 explicitly identifies Christ as the one who 'upholds all things by the word of his power.' In the Restoration, Christ is understood not as a static savior but as the active, present agent of creation's ongoing coherence. The mountains established by God's strength in Psalm 65 are ultimately established through Christ's power.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 65:7 teaches that stability and permanence in life do not come from our own efforts but from alignment with God's sustaining power. Just as mountains are 'set fast' only through divine establishment, our spiritual foundations are secure only as we remain girded with the strength that comes from discipleship. In times of uncertainty, this verse invites us to recognize that the world's apparent chaos—political upheaval, natural disaster, personal fragmentation—is not ultimate; it is held within God's deliberate, active, sustaining power. To trust in this power is to trust that we, like the mountains, are being held in place by a strength greater than our own.

text_kjv: Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 deepens the cosmic scope of verse 7 by introducing chaos as the counterpoint to divine order. The 'roaring of the seas' (shaon yammim) is not metaphorical—it is the literal, physical threat that ancient maritime peoples experienced. The sea in ancient Near Eastern theology represented primordial chaos, the force that existed before creation and constantly threatened to return and undo the world. This is not a peaceful nature poem; it is a declaration of God's authority over forces that genuinely terrify. The parallelism between 'the roaring of the seas,' 'the roaring of their waves,' and 'the uproar of the nations' (hamoun le'ummim) is theologically profound: cosmic chaos and political turmoil are equated. The same divine power that stills the seas stills human rebellion and unrest.

The verb mashbiach ('he stills, he silences, he quiets') emphasizes decisiveness—God does not negotiate with chaos or gradually manage it; he silences it. This is not compromise but dominion. For the psalmist's original audience—likely exilic or post-exilic Judeans living under foreign imperial power—this verse carried concrete political meaning. God's ability to still the tumult of nations meant that Israel's current political powerlessness did not reflect cosmic reality. The same God who holds back the chaos of the sea can hold back the chaos of empires.

word_study.meaning: To still, to silence, to quiet, to calm. The root shabach means to make quiet, to hush, to subdue noise. In the hiphil stem (mashbiach), it emphasizes active causation—to cause silence, to force quietness.
word_study.significance: This is not gentle calming but forceful silencing. The verb suggests dominion over resistance. God doesn't soothe the sea; he quiets it authoritatively. This is covenant language—God shabbachs (quiets) enemies and chaos for the sake of his people.

word_study.meaning: Roaring, tumultuous noise, uproar, din. Often refers to the sound of water or the sound of crowds. In Isaiah 17:12, shaon describes the roaring of many peoples; in Psalm 42:7, it describes the roar of waterfalls.
word_study.significance: Shaon is not neutral sound—it carries threat and power. It is the voice of forces that are wild, uncontrolled, dangerous. God's ability to still shaon is the ability to subdue the untamed.

word_study.meaning: Tumult, uproar, commotion of nations/peoples. Hamoun refers to noise and commotion caused by crowds or multitudes; le'ummim is the plural of le'om, 'nation, people.' The phrase literally means 'the commotion of nations.'
word_study.significance: The psalmist explicitly equates physical chaos (seas, waves) with political chaos (nations). Both are expressions of the same primordial disorder that God subdues. This frames political unrest not as merely human conflict but as cosmic rebellion against God's order.

cross_references.connection: God separates the waters and calls them 'seas'; creation begins with establishing boundaries against chaos. Psalm 65:8 shows God continuously enforcing those boundaries.
The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of glory thunders over the mighty waters—parallel imagery of God's sovereign voice subduing the sea's power.
Jesus stills the storm and the sea; he performs the exact action attributed to God in Psalm 65:8, demonstrating his divine identity.
In the final restoration, 'there was no more sea'—the ultimate fulfillment of Psalm 65:8, where the force of chaos is permanently subdued.
The Nephites witness God's power manifested in the subduing of the land and the Lamanites; this reflects the ancient psalm's equation of cosmic and political order.

commentary.historical_context: In Ugaritic mythology (the religious context closest to ancient Israel's own), the god Baal's greatest victory is over Yam, the personified sea and chaos. This mythological framework shaped how Israel understood the world. The sea was not merely a body of water; it was the embodiment of the forces opposed to creation and order. When the psalmist declares that God stills the seas, he is claiming for Israel's God the victory that other Near Eastern peoples attributed to their gods. Furthermore, the explicit parallel between the roaring of the seas and the tumult of nations reflects the genuine political turbulence of the Second Temple period. For exilic and post-exilic Jews living under Persian, Greek, and later Hellenistic rule, this verse was a comfort: the God who holds back the Mediterranean could hold back foreign empires.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See 1 Nephi 18:8-20, where Nephi experiences tumultuous seas and invokes God's power to still them. The pattern is repeated: physical and spiritual chaos are both subdued by covenant obedience and faith in God's power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:32-34 describes the sea heaving itself beyond its bounds—a sign of the last days. Psalm 65:8 frames the alternative: the God who commands the seas to stay within their boundaries is sovereign over historical upheaval.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple symbolism, the Sea (the brass sea in Solomon's temple) represented both the chaos subdued by creation and the waters of eternal life. Psalm 65:8 affirms that the temple is built on ground consecrated by God's authority over all chaos.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus stilling the storm (Mark 4:39, 'Peace, be still') directly fulfills the promise of Psalm 65:8. His authority over the sea demonstrates his identity as the God of Israel. In the Restoration, this becomes a type of Christ's ongoing power to still the tumults of human experience and bring order to the chaos of sin and rebellion.
commentary.application: Psalm 65:8 offers perspective to modern Saints facing personal, social, or political turmoil. The verse teaches that chaos—whether literal (natural disaster) or figurative (social upheaval, institutional collapse)—is not the ultimate reality. The ultimate reality is God's sovereign authority to quiet these forces. For covenant members, this means that our interior peace does not depend on external order. Even when the nations rage and institutions crumble, the God who commands the seas can command the storms in our lives. The application is not passive resignation but active trust in God's ultimate authority over all forces, seen and unseen.

text_kjv: They also that dwell in the uttermost parts are afraid at thy tokens: thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 9 shifts from the cosmic drama of creation's sustenance to the universal recognition of God's power. The 'uttermost parts' (qetsavot, the extreme margins of the inhabited world) are moved to awe and fear by God's 'tokens'—the visible signs and wonders by which God demonstrates power. This verse asserts that no corner of creation exists beyond God's reach or awareness. Even those living at the world's edges—those farthest from Israel's center—witness and respond to God's acts. The verse then pivots to a stunning personification: God 'makes the gateways of morning and evening shout for joy' (tarnin can mean both 'shout' and 'resound'). The very cycles of day and night—the most constant, predictable phenomena—are portrayed as conscious, joyful responses to God's power.

This is not merely meteorological observation; it is theological assertion. The daily cycle of dawn and dusk, which marks time and seasons and harvests, is presented as an act of worship. The earth itself, through its rhythms, celebrates God. For an agrarian people dependent on predictable seasons and regular rainfall, this verse is profound: the movements of sun and stars that sustain your life are not mechanical but are expressions of joy in God's power. The structure of reality is not indifferent mechanism but continuous celebration of the divine. Those who recognize this—who witness these 'tokens' (ototekha)—stand in awe rather than presumption.

word_study.meaning: Extremities, edges, uttermost parts, boundaries. From the root qets, meaning 'end' or 'edge.' Plural form emphasizing the plural margins of the inhabited world.
word_study.significance: These are not merely distant places but the conceptual boundaries of the known world. In ancient geographical understanding, the qetsavot were the limits beyond which civilization was thought not to extend. To affect those at the qetsavot is to demonstrate authority over all creation.

word_study.transliteration: otot (plural); otot Elohim in other contexts
word_study.meaning: Signs, tokens, wonders, miraculous acts. From ot, a sign or marker that points to something beyond itself. In Hebrew, otot are not arbitrary miracles but divinely ordained demonstrations of power that communicate meaning.
word_study.significance: Otot are signs that must be interpreted—they are revelatory. This word is central to the plagues in Egypt (otot va-mopetim, 'signs and wonders'). God's tokens are not random displays but communications of divine will and power.

word_study.meaning: Outgoings, exits, points of departure. Literally 'things that go out.' In context here, it refers to the rising points of the sun (dawn) and moon (dusk)—the places where light 'goes out' or appears.
word_study.significance: The word emphasizes that dawn and evening are not passive phenomena but active 'goings out.' They are movements, releases of light and energy. The poetic identification of these moments as 'gateways' frames them as thresholds between divine action and human awareness.

word_study.transliteration: tarnin (from ran, to shout or sing)
word_study.meaning: To shout, to cry out, to sing, to resound. In the hiphil form here, it is causative: to cause to shout or resound. Can refer to joyful shouting or the ringing sound of musical instruments.
word_study.significance: The root ran appears in ranah (to sing, shout) and is deeply connected to celebration, victory, and joy. This is not silent acquiescence but vocal, exuberant response.

cross_references.connection: God's invisible attributes are clearly seen in what he has made, arousing both awe and accountability; parallel to Psalm 65:9's assertion that creation's tokens are witnesses to all peoples.
The heavens declare God's glory and the firmament shows his handiwork; like Psalm 65:9, creation itself is portrayed as an active witness to divine power.
Alma asks Korihor how the earth remains suspended and answers that it is through God's word; the daily stability witnessed by all peoples testifies to God's power.
God's light and truth pervade all creation, sustaining it; the regularity witnessed in verse 9 reflects this universal divine presence.
God who created the heavens and stretched them out, and gives breath to those upon it, is the light to the nations; parallel to the universal witness of Psalm 65:9.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient cosmography divided the world into center and periphery. Israel understood itself as living at a relatively central location (the land between two seas, at the crossroads of major trade routes), with other peoples living progressively farther away. The 'uttermost parts' would have included the distant reaches of the known world—perhaps the lands beyond the Mediterranean, the extremes of the desert, or the far horizons visible from high mountains. The concept of qetsavot also carried theological weight: the farther from God's temple (the center), the farther from God's presence—or so it might have seemed. This verse subverts that assumption. The God whose power is visible at the extremes is not localized to the temple but universally effective. The reference to dawn and dusk is grounded in ancient agricultural rhythms: the precision of sunrise and sunset, the predictability of the seasons, were signs of divine order that farmers depended upon for survival.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See 2 Nephi 27:23, where God's word reaches all people in all nations; Psalm 65:9's assertion that God's tokens are witnessed even at the uttermost parts finds a Restoration parallel in the global reach of the gospel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 declares God's word to be truth and his voice to speak from heaven to all people; the tokens witnessed in Psalm 65:9 become, in the Restoration, the specific testimony of the restored gospel reaching to all peoples.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple's positioning in the center of the covenant people's lands reflects the assumption challenged by Psalm 65:9: God's presence is not confined to the temple building but reaches to the uttermost parts. In Restoration theology, temples are built on the margins (e.g., South Africa, South America) to emphasize that God's power is indeed accessible everywhere.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the light of the world (John 8:12); the daily light of dawn and dusk that 'shouted for joy' in Psalm 65:9 points to Christ as the ultimate token of God's power and presence. His resurrection at dawn and his ascension are the supreme 'tokens' that demonstrate God's dominion over creation.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 65:9 teaches that God's power and presence are not confined to church buildings, sacred spaces, or any particular location. The tokens of God's power—the regularity of creation, the faithful patterns of nature, the evidence of divine order—are universally accessible. This is liberating: you do not have to travel to a sacred center to witness God's tokens; they surround you daily. The dawn and dusk that appear in your life are invitations to recognize and rejoice in divine power. Furthermore, the application extends to testimony: your awareness of God's tokens in your own life—the patterns of divine care, the answered prayers, the moments of clarity—are themselves a form of witness that can reach others, even those at the uttermost parts of your circle of influence.

text_kjv: Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 descends from cosmic theology to the concrete physical reality of Palestinian agriculture. The 'visit' (paqadta) is a key Hebrew theological term: when God 'visits' (Hebrew paqad), consequences follow. In other contexts, paqad means to visit with judgment (Exodus 32:34, 'I will visit upon you your sin') or with blessing (1 Samuel 2:21, 'the Lord visited Hannah'). Here, the visit results in saturation of the earth (va-teshoqqeha, 'you water it, you overflow it'). The abundance is extraordinary: the 'stream of God' (peleg Elohim) is 'full of water' (male mayim). This is not the trickle of a seasonal wadi but a full, flowing watercourse—a metaphor for the heavenly source of rain that the farmer cannot control but completely depends on.

The verse is structured to show God's complete involvement in the agricultural cycle: God visits, waters, enriches, prepares grain, and prepares the earth that will receive the grain. The farmer's work (plowing, planting) is not mentioned; the focus is entirely on God's invisible labor. The Hebrew parallelism in the last phrase—'you prepare their grain, for this is how you have prepared the earth'—creates a loop: God prepares the earth so that it will be ready to receive and nurture the grain that God has already prepared. The causality is entirely divine; human agency is assumed but theologically secondary. For an ancient agricultural society, this is radical: the difference between feast and famine, survival and death, is not ultimately determined by human skill or labor but by the 'stream of God' being full or empty.

word_study.meaning: To visit, to attend to, to number, to appoint, to inspect. The root paqad is multivalent: it means to turn attention toward someone or something, with the result that change occurs. Can mean to punish (paqadti et-chata'tchem, 'I will visit upon you your sins') or to bless (paqad et-Sarah, 'the Lord visited Sarah').
word_study.significance: Paqad is a covenant term. God 'visits' his people in the sense of activating his covenant commitment. Here, the visit to the earth triggers the entire cycle of blessing. It is not absentee divinity but active, present engagement.

word_study.meaning: To water abundantly, to saturate, to soak, to overflow. The root shaqaq means to desire intensely or to overflow. In the hiphil form, it means to cause to be saturated or drenched. The Covenant Rendering notes 'you water it, you overflow it'—emphasizing the abundance beyond mere sufficiency.
word_study.significance: This is not spare rainfall but lavish, saturating water. The imagery suggests abundance, excess, blessing beyond the minimum needed for survival. Compare to the language of Deuteronomy 28:12, where God opens the heavens to 'pour rain upon your land.'

word_study.meaning: Peleg: a stream, channel, watercourse, irrigation channel. Literally 'divided water' (from palag, to divide, to split). The phrase 'stream of God' is unusual in scripture—it is not an earthly river but a metaphor for the heavenly source of moisture. Elohim: God, the divine power.
word_study.significance: The image is of an irrigation system dividing and distributing water—here, the source is not earthly but divine. This suggests a heavenly reservoir sustaining the earth. The agricultural imagery is concrete but points to a heavenly prototype. In Restoration thought, this parallels the waters of life that flow from God's throne (Revelation 22:1).

word_study.transliteration: taashrennah (from ashar, to be rich, to become wealthy)
word_study.meaning: To enrich, to make rich, to cause prosperity. From ashar (to be rich, wealthy). In the hiphil form, it emphasizes God's causative action in making the earth prosperous. Often translated 'greatly enriches' due to the intensive force of the root.
word_study.significance: The earth is not left in bare sufficiency but is actively made rich, prosperous, abundant. This language of richness and wealth is applied to the physical landscape—divine blessing is not merely spiritual but material.

word_study.transliteration: tekin (from kun, to establish, to prepare)
word_study.meaning: To prepare, to establish, to make firm, to arrange. Appears twice in verse 10. The root kun is central to creation theology (the earth is kun, 'established'; covenants are kun, 'made firm'). Here it emphasizes deliberate preparation.
word_study.significance: The same verb used for establishing mountains (verse 7) is used for preparing grain and earth. All levels of creation—cosmic and agricultural—share the same divine establishment.

cross_references.connection: The land drinks rain from heaven, and the Lord cares for it continually; directly parallel to Psalm 65:10's assertion that God visits and waters the land.
In creation, there was no rain but a mist that watered the earth; Psalm 65:10 shows the mature creation system where rain (peleg Elohim) sustains fertility.
As rain comes down from heaven and waters the earth, making it produce seed, so God's word accomplishes its purpose; Psalm 65:10 parallels this divine nurturing action.
Leave your debts and go into the fields; God will provide—reflects the covenant confidence of Psalm 65:10 that the divine stream sustains provision.
The allegory of the olive tree shows the Lord tending the vineyard with water and nourishment; Psalm 65:10's image of divine care for growth parallels this Restoration vision.

commentary.historical_context: Rainfall in ancient Palestine was (and is) notoriously unpredictable. The Mediterranean climate brings winter rains (October to April) followed by a dry summer. Famine could strike within a single generation if rains failed. The 'river of God' (peleg Elohim) is not a reference to any actual river in Palestine but a metaphorical way of describing the heavens as a reservoir. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, the gods are portrayed as opening the 'windows of heaven' to release water; the psalmist uses similar imagery. The phrase peleg Elohim is unique in the Hebrew Bible and may be the psalmist's creative way of describing both the dependence on rain and the hidden, divine source of all moisture. For a Palestinian farmer, to speak of God visiting the earth and filling it with water was to speak of the most essential blessing—literally the difference between survival and death.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See Alma 37:41-42, where the Nephites are promised that if they keep God's commandments, 'the Lord God will make all things manifest unto you.' The pattern of verse 10—God reveals blessing through attentive care—parallels the Nephite experience of divine provision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:16-20 commands Saints to be grateful for the fruits of the earth and promises that the earth will 'yield its increase' to those who obey. Psalm 65:10's vision of divine visitation and enrichment is the theological foundation for this promise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where heaven and earth intersect. The 'river of God' that flows from the divine presence (Revelation 22:1) is connected to Psalm 65:10's vision. The Restoration teaches that covenant obedience opens the heavens and brings divine blessings into the physical world.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the living water (John 4:13-14); he fulfills the promise of Psalm 65:10 by providing spiritual sustenance. The 'stream of God' that flows full of water is ultimately Christ himself, the source of all true nourishment. In the Resurrection, Christ becomes the rain that causes the earth to bring forth its increase.
commentary.application: Psalm 65:10 invites covenant members to recognize that material blessing and spiritual blessing are not separate domains. The provision of daily bread is not beneath God's concern but is a central manifestation of his covenant care. In modern terms, this might speak to: (1) Gratitude for the actual physical blessings of food, shelter, and provision—not to be taken for granted but recognized as expressions of God's visitation. (2) Trust that God continues to 'visit' his people—not just in personal spiritual experiences but in practical, material care. (3) Recognition that our participation in provision (farming, working, serving) is secondary to God's primary action. As Paul writes, 'Neither he that planteth is any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase' (1 Corinthians 3:7). The application is to live with the security that comes from recognizing your dependence on divine care, and to respond with gratitude and faithful work.

text_kjv: Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 zooms in on the precise mechanics of agricultural blessing, moving from the macro level (the stream of God) to the micro level (individual furrows and ridges in the field). The psalmist is describing the exact moment when seeds germinate and crops begin to grow—the moment of maximum vulnerability and maximum dependence on God's care. The sequence is theologically significant: water, settlement, softening, blessing. The farmer has already plowed, creating ridges (raised portions where seed is planted) and furrows (the valleys between). These are now 'drenched' (tlameyha raveh, 'its furrows are drenched abundantly') with water that the farmer cannot provide. The ridges are 'settled' (nacheth gedudeyha, literally 'descended upon'), broken down by the weight and penetration of water and gentle rain. The soil becomes 'soft' (temoggenah, 'dissolved, broken down'), transformed from hard, compacted earth into workable, life-giving medium. Only then does God 'bless the springing' (tsimchah tebarekh)—the germination and growth that can now occur.

This is not poetic decoration; it is precise agricultural observation rendered as theology. The farmer cannot force germination; the farmer can only prepare the ground. God must transform the hard earth into living medium and then awaken the seed to life. The four verbs (waters, settles, softens, blesses) describe four stages of divine action that together constitute a single blessing. For a farmer working in a Mediterranean climate with limited water, each of these actions would be desperately prayed for. The verse celebrates God's intimate involvement in the most humble agricultural process—not just rain from heaven but the precise, measured action that prepares soil and awakens life.

word_study.transliteration: tlameyha raveh (from tam, furrow, and ravah, to be or make saturated)
word_study.meaning: Tlameyha: furrows, the plowed grooves in a field. Raveh: saturated, drenched, abundantly watered. The construction conveys intensive saturation—not just watering but abundantly drenching.
word_study.significance: Furrows are the channels where water flows and where seeds nestle after planting. To soak the furrows is to ensure that moisture reaches deep into the soil and will sustain growth. The focus on furrows (not the ridges where seed actually sits) shows attention to the hidden infrastructure of growth.

word_study.transliteration: nacheth gedudeyha (from nachath, to descend, settle; gedud, ridge, clod)
word_study.meaning: Nacheth: to descend upon, to settle, to press down. Gedudeyha: its ridges, its clods (compacted lumps of earth). The phrase describes the action of water and rain descending upon and settling the ridges, breaking them apart.
word_study.significance: This is the action that follows the initial drenching: the persistent, gentle pressure of moisture and weight that breaks down compacted earth. It is divine patience working through natural process—not violent but inevitable and transformative.

word_study.transliteration: birbibim temoggenah (from rabib, shower of rain; mogag, to dissolve, to soften)
word_study.meaning: Birbibim: showers, gentle rains. Temoggenah: you cause it to dissolve, to soften, to become pliable. The root mogag suggests melting, dissolving—a transformation from hardness to fluidity.
word_study.significance: The verb temoggenah is tender and precise: it is not harsh or violent transformation but gentle dissolving. The showers (rabibim) do their work gradually and persistently, turning resistant, hard earth into receptive, living soil.

word_study.term_english: blessest the springing / bless the sprouting
word_study.transliteration: tsimchah tebarekh (from tsimach, to sprout, grow; barak, to bless)
word_study.meaning: Tsimchah: its springing, its growth, its sprouting vegetation. Tebarekh: you bless, you consecrate, you empower. The verb barak means to bless, to invoke blessing upon, to cause flourishing.
word_study.significance: The final action is explicitly a blessing—the moment when life emerges from the prepared ground. The blessing is not a separate gift but the culmination of the entire process of preparation. Growth cannot occur without the prior four actions of divine care.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom delights in the habitable earth and rejoices in it; Psalm 65:11 similarly portrays creation as the object of divine delight and careful cultivation.

Jesus teaches that the kingdom grows by itself—the farmer sleeps and rises and the seed grows, but God provides the increase. Psalm 65:11 illustrates this principle: the farmer prepares, but God brings forth the sprouting.
Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the increase; Psalm 65:11's sequence of divine actions shows the principle that human and divine labor are coordinated but God's blessing is determinative.

Alma teaches that faith is like a seed; the word is nourished and grows. The agricultural metaphor of Psalm 65:11 (growth depends on water, settlement, softening, blessing) parallels the spiritual growth requiring faith and divine nurture.
If you keep God's statutes, your land will yield its increase; Psalm 65:11 shows the divine mechanism of blessing—water, softening, growth—that is conditional on covenant obedience.

commentary.historical_context: The detailed agricultural vocabulary of Psalm 65:11 reflects intimate knowledge of Palestinian farming. Furrows (tlamim) are the grooves created by the plow, where water naturally flows and where seeds are placed. Ridges (gedudim) are the raised portions between furrows. The Palestinian farmer, working in the region's dry season (May-September), depends entirely on winter rains (October-April) to soak the fields for planting and early growth. Once the field is plowed in autumn and seed is placed in the furrows, the farmer is essentially helpless—everything depends on sufficient, well-timed rainfall. Too much rain causes erosion and washout; too little causes drought. This verse reflects the anxiety and hope of farmers who have done all they can and now wait for God. The precise observation of how water works on soil—dissolving clods, settling ridges, awakening dormant seed—would resonate with farmers who studied these processes carefully. The theology is embedded in precise observation of nature.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See Jacob 5, the allegory of the olive tree, where the Lord tends the vineyard, watering, nourishing, and grafting. The sequence of careful, detailed actions in Psalm 65:11 parallels the Lord's meticulous cultivation of his people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:43-62 promises Saints that if they dedicate themselves to building God's kingdom, he will prepare the way and bless their labors. The pattern of verse 11—divine care for the details of growth—underlies the promise that God will not abandon his covenant people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where heaven's waters flow into the earthly world. The 'stream of God' (verse 10) and the gentle showers of verse 11 are ultimately the blessing of the temple—the place where divine power enters the created world to sanctify and transform.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the seed that falls into the ground and dies but brings forth much fruit (John 12:24). Psalm 65:11's description of how God prepares the soil and blesses the springing describes the process by which Christ's redemptive power bears fruit in believers' lives. The softening of hard earth mirrors the softening of the human heart through the Atonement.
commentary.application: Psalm 65:11 teaches covenant members that spiritual growth, like agricultural growth, requires patience and divine care. The verse illustrates that growth has multiple stages: (1) Foundational nourishment (being watered by God's word). (2) Settlement and breakdown of resistance (the hard places in our hearts being gently dissolved). (3) Gentleness and adequacy (the showers are sufficient, not overwhelming). (4) Blessing (the emergence of new spiritual life). The application is to recognize that spiritual growth is not instantaneous, that divine care works through process, and that impatience is a form of faithlessness. Just as the farmer cannot force sprouting but must wait for the proper season, the covenant member cannot force spiritual transformation but must trust the timeline of divine blessing. Additionally, the verse invites us to recognize that the setbacks and dry seasons of the soul—when we feel like hard, compacted earth—may be necessary preparation for the blessing of growth.

text_kjv: Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 12 brings the entire agricultural cycle to triumphant culmination. The year is 'crowned' (ittarta) with God's goodness (tovatkha)—the agricultural year, which begins with plowing and planting and ends with harvest, is portrayed as an achievement, a crowned victory. The image of a crown emphasizes that the completed year is the crowning accomplishment of the entire process. But then the verse shifts to an even more dramatic image: God's paths 'drop fatness' (ma'galekha yir'apun dashen). The metaphor is of God traveling through the land—perhaps in a chariot, like an ancient king making a triumphant tour—and as the divine chariot wheels roll over the earth, they leave behind 'fatness' (deshen), the richness of oil and grain and abundance.

This is not a distant God blessing from afar but an intimately present God moving through the landscape, transforming it through his passage. The 'paths' or 'tracks' (ma'galim) are the routes of travel—where God has gone, abundance follows. The image is almost tactile: you could trace God's presence by following the trail of abundance left behind. For the Psalmist's audience, this would evoke the image of a victorious king or a god moving across the land, and fertile abundance springing up wherever that divine presence passes. The verse takes the invisible God and makes his presence visible through its results. You cannot see God, but you can see the 'fatness'—the overflowing richness—that marks where God has been and what God has done. The entire psalm culminates in this vision: God's power holds the mountains firm, stills the chaos of seas and nations, marks the daily cycle with joy, visits and waters and prepares the earth, and finally travels through the land leaving abundance in his wake.

word_study.transliteration: ittarta (from atar, to crown, to encircle)
word_study.meaning: To crown, to place a crown upon, to encircle with a crown. The image is of placing a wreath or diadem on someone's head as a sign of honor, completion, or victory. Atar can also mean to turn or encircle.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that the year is honored, completed, marked as special. The crowning suggests that the agricultural cycle is not merely a natural process but a divine accomplishment worthy of recognition and celebration. The year itself is treated as a being that can be crowned—a personification emphasizing the year's importance.

word_study.meaning: Goodness, blessing, prosperity, benefit. Tov is one of the most fundamental Hebrew words: God saw creation and beheld that it was tov ('good'). Tovah (the feminine noun form) emphasizes the concrete manifestation of goodness—actual benefit and blessing.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract divine benevolence but concrete blessing—crops harvested, food stored, families fed. God's tovah is measured in material reality. The goodness of the year is visible and tangible.

word_study.transliteration: ma'galim (from agal, to roll, to turn)
word_study.meaning: Paths, tracks, ruts, trails. From the root agal (to roll), the word can refer to wheel ruts left by chariots or the winding paths of travelers. The Covenant Rendering notes 'wagon tracks,' emphasizing the image of a chariot or vehicle passing through.
word_study.significance: The word emphasizes that these are not invisible paths but visible marks—tracks that can be seen and followed. God's presence is marked by the trail of blessing left behind. This grounds the abstract divine presence in observable, physical reality.

word_study.transliteration: yir'apun (from rapah, to drip, to drop, to overflow)
word_study.meaning: To drip, to drop, to overflow, to stream down. The root rapah suggests liquid overflowing or trickling down. In the hiphil form here, it is causative: to cause to drip or overflow.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes abundance so excessive that it overflows and drips down—it is not contained or measured but overflowing. The image is of richness so full that it cannot be contained but spills out.

word_study.meaning: Fatness, richness, abundance, the richest portion of a sacrifice or food. In sacrificial language, dashen refers to the fat portions most pleasing to God. In food language, it refers to rich, nourishing, luxurious food. The word carries connotations of abundance and luxury.
word_study.significance: Dashen is not mere sustenance but richness and luxury. To say that God's paths drip with dashen is to say that abundance, even excess, marks where God's presence has passed. This is language of celebration and overflowing blessing, not bare sufficiency.

cross_references.connection: Joseph's sheaf rises and stands upright while the other sheaves bow down; Psalm 65:12's image of the year crowned with goodness parallels the vision of abundance that God grants to Joseph.
The blessings of obedience include crops so abundant that they cannot be contained; Psalm 65:12's vision of paths dripping with fatness echoes the covenant promise of overflowing provision.
The barns will overflow with grain and the vats will overflow with new wine; Psalm 65:12's language of abundant overflow parallels the eschatological vision of divine provision.
God promises to open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing until there is not room enough to receive it; Psalm 65:12's overflowing abundance reflects this covenant promise.

All things are created by the word of the Lord and sustained by the word of his power; Psalm 65:12's vision of God's paths bringing abundance reflects the Restoration teaching of sustained divine action.

commentary.historical_context: The image of God traveling through the land as a chariot or king was deeply rooted in ancient Near Eastern royal ideology. Pharaohs were depicted making processional tours through their lands, leaving order and blessing in their wake. The metaphor of abundant fields following a divine visitation reflects the idea that a god's presence transforms the landscape. In Ugaritic texts, Baal's passage through the sky brings rain and fertility. The Hebrew psalmist adapts this imagery: God's 'wagon tracks' through the land become channels of blessing. The emphasis on 'fatness' (dashen) as the marker of abundance reflects the reality of ancient Palestinian agriculture: a good year meant not just survival but surplus—grain stored, oil pressed, prosperity visible and tangible. The image of paths dripping with fatness would have been almost unimaginable wealth to a subsistence farmer: it represents the dream of overflowing abundance, the fantasy of a year so blessed that richness literally drips from the earth.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: See 1 Nephi 2:19-20, where Lehi's family prospers in the wilderness because of obedience, and the Lord 'did prosper us in the land.' The pattern of Psalm 65:12—covenant obedience resulting in overflowing abundance—appears throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:16-21 teaches that 'in the season thereof' each herb and fruit brings forth food, and those who are grateful receive more abundantly. The pattern of Psalm 65:12 is Restoration doctrine: divine blessing overflows to those who covenant with God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where heaven's abundance flows into the earth. The river that flows from the throne of God (Revelation 22:1) becomes, in the Psalm 65:12 vision, the 'stream of God' that marks the land with blessing. The temple represents the point where God's paths intersect with earthly reality, bringing abundance.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of the promise of Psalm 65:12. His path through the earth—his ministry, his death, his resurrection—leaves behind blessing that overflows to all nations. The 'fatness' that drips from his tracks is the spiritual abundance of the gospel—grace, mercy, redemption—that flows from his passage through human history. His resurrection is the supreme 'crowning of the year'—the completion and triumph of God's redemptive purpose.
commentary.application: Psalm 65:12 invites covenant members to (1) Recognize that God's presence in their lives should result in visible, tangible blessing—not merely interior spiritual experience but concrete improvement in circumstances, relationships, and capacity. To test whether we are living in God's paths is to ask: are the 'wagon tracks' of my obedience leaving behind abundance, or narrowness? Are my relationships, my work, my influence marked by overflowing blessing? (2) Understand that blessing is not selfish accumulation but is meant to be visible, to be followed by others, to mark the path for those who come after. The 'paths' that drip with fatness are visible routes that others can see and follow. Our blessed lives should create visible trails of goodness. (3) Trust that the God who 'crowns the year with goodness' honors faithful work and will bring cycles and seasons to completion. In times when we have planted and watered but have not yet seen the harvest, Psalm 65:12 teaches that God oversees the harvest and will bring it to completion. The crown awaits the year that is faithful to the pattern God has established.

text_kjv: They drop upon the pastures of the wilderness: and the little hills rejoice on every side.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 65:13 is the climactic conclusion of a psalm celebrating God's provision and blessing over creation. The psalmist has moved from confession of sin (verses 1–3), to confidence in God's answered prayer (verses 4–5), to witness of God's power over nature (verses 6–12), and now concludes with creation itself responding in joy and abundance. This final verse captures the sensory reality of divine blessing: moisture—essential for life in ancient Near Eastern agrarian societies—falls upon places that are ordinarily dry and unproductive. The wilderness pastures, which might seem marginal or even hostile to human settlement, are transformed into places of fruitfulness and celebration. The image is not merely descriptive but deeply theological: God's blessing reaches even to the edges, the forgotten places, the seemingly cursed lands. Nothing falls outside His providential care.

word_study.meaning: Root רעף (rʿp) means to drip or trickle, often referring to the falling of rain or dew. The Niphal imperfect form conveys ongoing, cascading moisture. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'drip with moisture' captures the continuous, beneficent nature of the provision. This is not violent downpour but gentle, sustaining precipitation—the kind that ancient farmers depended on for survival.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'drip' rather than 'pour' or 'rain' emphasizes abundance that is also gentle and measured. In Hebrew poetic thought, this kind of subtle, persistent blessing often symbolizes God's intimate, personal care.

word_study.meaning: Neʾot (plural of naʾah) refers to pastures or meadows—places where flocks can graze. Midbar is wilderness or steppe—land that is typically arid, sparse, and on the margins of settlement. Together, they denote the pastoral regions on the edge of civilization, places that depend entirely on seasonal rain.
word_study.significance: The psalmist deliberately highlights the blessing of marginal lands, not merely the fertile river valleys or cultivated fields. This theological move suggests that God's blessing is comprehensive and reaches even to forgotten places. For ancient Israel, whose livelihood depended on both grain and herds, these wilderness pastures were vital to survival.

word_study.meaning: Tachgornah is from the root חגר (chgr), meaning to gird, encircle, or wrap around—literally to put on a belt or garment. Gil is joy, gladness, exultation. The metaphor personifies the hills as if they are dressing themselves for a festival, wrapping joy around themselves like a festive garment. The Covenant Rendering captures this vividly: 'wrap themselves in joy.'
word_study.significance: This anthropomorphism is central to the psalm's theology. The hills are not inert matter responding mechanically to precipitation; they are celebrants responding to blessing. The image suggests that creation itself recognizes and participates in God's benevolence, responding with conscious joy and gratitude. This resonates with the broader biblical theme that all creation praises God (cf. Psalm 148).

word_study.meaning: This term (from the root סבב, meaning to circle or encompass) indicates completeness and totality—not just one hill or region, but all the hills, everywhere. The KJV's phrase captures the circularity and totality of the image.
word_study.significance: The 'every side' imagery completes the picture of comprehensive blessing. The blessing is not partial or regional but universal and complete across the land.
