restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's people are described as 'willing to enter into a covenant with their God' and make visible commitments to righteousness (Mosiah 5:5-8), though not precisely wearing sackcloth. More directly, Alma the Younger's conversion results in visible transformation — his 'rebirth' is marked by changed appearance and demeanor, making him visibly identified with righteousness after having been identified with rebellion (Alma 36).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:10 describes the wicked as those who 'love darkness rather than light.' The psalmist's visible commitment through sackcloth is the opposite — a visible marking of light and devotion. D&C 45:57 teaches about the last days when the righteous will be 'made bare' or 'revealed,' suggesting that visible faith will eventually be vindicated.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Sackcloth is a form of spiritual preparation and humiliation before God, themes central to temple worship. The psalmist's constant wearing of sackcloth is a sustained temple-like state of preparation and humility before the Lord, even in the marketplace and family life.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus' entire Passion narrative is a fulfillment of this verse and Psalm 69 generally. Jesus is stripped, humiliated, and made a spectacle before mockers (Matthew 27:27-31, John 19:1-5). He is made 'a reproach' and becomes a 'byword' — crucified between thieves, mocked by passersby, ridiculed with 'King of the Jews' inscribed above Him. His visibly marked suffering (the cross itself being His equivalent of sackcloth) makes Him an object lesson for the world. Yet this ultimate fulfillment transforms the meaning: through His mockery and humiliation, He purchases redemption. The psalmist's willing endurance of reproach thus becomes a type of Christ's voluntary submission to shame for the sake of God's people.
commentary.application: Verse 12 concludes the psalm's opening section with a hard truth: faithful devotion to God, especially when it is visible and radical, makes one conspicuous, marked, and subject to mockery. In a secular age where religious commitment is increasingly treated as eccentric or embarrassing, this verse validates that such treatment is not new. Yet it also challenges modern disciples to consider what visible marks of our faith we bear. Are we willing to be 'bywords' for our commitment to God? Or do we hide our faith to avoid becoming a proverb? The application is not to seek out mockery or be provocative, but to maintain authentic faithful practices even when they make us conspicuous — fasting when others feast, wearing modest clothing when others dress provocatively, attending temple when others spend sabbath differently, speaking about faith when others avoid the topic. The psalmist teaches us that such visibility is costly but meaningful; God sees and honors what the world mocks.

text_kjv: Draw nigh unto my soul, and redeem it: deliver me because of mine enemies.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist moves from lament into urgent petition, deploying two distinct Hebrew redemption verbs to amplify his plea. Geʾalah (redeem) evokes the kinsman-redeemer—the near relative bound by blood covenant to rescue a family member in distress. Pedeni (ransom) invokes a commercial transaction, as though the psalmist's soul has been seized and must be purchased back. By layering these verbs, the author appeals to God on multiple grounds: as both intimate family protector and as the only power with sufficient wealth to buy him free. The phrase 'because of mine enemies' is theologically astute—it shifts the motivation from the psalmist's merit to God's own honor. If the enemies triumph by destroying the righteous, God's name is diminished. This transforms a personal cry into a plea for divine vindication.

word_study.meaning: To redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer, to recover something lost through family obligation. The gōʾēl was the near relative legally bound to restore a family member's inheritance or freedom (Leviticus 25:25-26, Ruth 3:11). The verb carries covenantal weight—it assumes family solidarity and binding obligation.
word_study.significance: In the Psalms, when God is asked to act as geʾēl, the psalmist is claiming the relationship of covenant kinship. God is not a distant judge but a near redeemer whose honor is bound up with Israel's deliverance.

word_study.meaning: To ransom, to redeem by payment, to liberate from captivity or death by a price. Unlike geʾalah (which emphasizes family obligation), padah emphasizes transaction and exchange—a commercial redemption. Often used for the ransoming of the firstborn (Exodus 13:13, Numbers 3:46-51).
word_study.significance: The pairing of geʾalah with padah suggests God must act both as covenant kinsman and as powerful redeemer who can literally buy the psalmist's freedom. The Covenant Rendering makes clear that both verbs operate together: intimate obligation plus sovereign power.

word_study.meaning: The life force, the self, the person as a living being. In Hebrew psychology, the nephesh ('soul') is not a disembodied spirit but the vital principle that animates the body—the throat, the breath, the desire, the whole person in his vulnerability.
word_study.significance: When the psalmist says God should 'draw near to my nephesh,' he is asking God to approach the very center of his existence in its moment of greatest peril. This is not abstract spiritual language but concrete plea for the preservation of life itself.

cross_references.connection: Boaz is called a 'mighty man of valour' and identified as a near kinsman-redeemer (gōʾēl), exemplifying the role the psalmist asks God to fill—one bound by covenant obligation to rescue a vulnerable kinsman.

Moses' song declares that God 'in thy mercy hast led forth the people which thou hast redeemed' (geʾalita), using the same kinsman-redeemer language to celebrate deliverance from Egypt—the archetypal redemption narrative.
Paul writes, 'Ye are bought with a price,' using redemption language (agorazō in Greek) that parallels the ransoming verb here—Christ purchases our freedom through his sacrifice.
Another psalm declares, 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy,' using geʾalah to describe God's ongoing role as covenant redeemer of Israel.

commentary.historical_context: The kinsman-redeemer system was central to ancient Israelite law and practice. The gōʾēl had specific rights and responsibilities: to buy back an impoverished kinsman's sold inheritance (Leviticus 25:25-26), to avenge the blood of a murdered kinsman (Numbers 35:19), and to marry the widow of a childless kinsman (Ruth 3-4). This legal institution encoded the principle of covenant solidarity—family members were bound together not by sentiment alone but by binding obligation encoded in law. A man without a gōʾēl was in extreme vulnerability. When the psalmist invokes this language toward God, he is claiming that God stands in this covenantal relationship to Israel: bound by the most intimate obligations of rescue and restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 2:3, Lehi speaks of 'the Lord God...by which ye shall be redeemed' (yadaʿta), using the language of covenant redemption. Alma 11:37 presents Jesus Christ as the ultimate redeemer who pays the ransom price ('he shall come down among the children of men, and shall redeem all those who believe on his name').
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:18-19 presents Christ's atonement as both kinsman-redeemer work ('Wherefore, I command you again to repent, lest I humble you with my almighty power') and ransom payment ('which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore'). The redemption imagery in Doctrine and Covenants 138:1-24 (President Joseph F. Smith's vision of the spirit world) frames Christ's work as the fulfillment of the kinsman-redeemer role for all humanity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The redemption language here resonates with temple covenant language. In the endowment, the candidate is presented as one who needs redemption and protection through covenants—brought into God's household, ransomed, and adopted into the family of Christ. The two verbs (geʾalah and pedah) correspond to both the mercy and justice aspects of covenant—God's gracious obligation (mercy) and the required payment (justice) that makes redemption possible.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse prefigures Christ's redemptive work with striking precision. Jesus is the ultimate gōʾēl—the kinsman-redeemer who, by incarnation, enters the human family and becomes bound by the law and by love to rescue us from captivity. He is also the ultimate ransom: 1 Timothy 2:6 explicitly calls Christ 'a ransom for all' (antilytron). His enemies (sin, death, the adversary) are defeated through his redemptive work. The phrase 'because of mine enemies' finds fulfillment in the cross: Christ's suffering and victory serve not merely his own vindication but God's triumph over all opposition to the divine will.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members live in the confidence that God acts as both kinsman-redeemer and ransom-payer. When facing opposition, mockery, or the sense of being trapped by circumstances, this verse invites us to appeal to God on both grounds: as covenant family (God has bound himself to us through baptism and the temple) and as the only power capable of purchasing our freedom. The phrase 'because of mine enemies' reframes personal struggle as a matter of divine honor—when we are oppressed, we can ask God to act not primarily for our sake but for his name's sake, that his enemies may not triumph. This does not mean God lacks concern for us, but rather that we can rest in the assurance that vindication serves God's purposes in the world. In our own Latter-day Saint context, this psalm validates both the language of covenant kinship ('saints,' 'chosen generation,' 'covenant people') and the language of purchased redemption ('bought with a price,' 'ransomed from death').

text_kjv: Thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour: mine adversaries are all before thee.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist now anchors his petition in a theological fact: God's all-seeing knowledge. Before requesting anything else, he establishes that God already knows the full extent of his humiliation. This is more than a complaint—it is an appeal to God's omniscience as the ground of both justice and hope. The accumulation of three shame words (cherpah, boshet, kelimmah) is deliberate, creating a crescendo of humiliation that cannot be dismissed or minimized. The psalmist does not ask God to learn about his suffering; rather, he asserts that God sees what enemies think hidden or trivial. The final line, 'all my adversaries are all before thee,' means that not a single enemy escapes God's notice. This formulation serves a dual rhetorical purpose: it comforts the sufferer (God sees injustice) and warns the oppressor (God sees your crimes). The repetition of 'all' (kol-tsoreray, all my adversaries) emphasizes completeness—nothing is obscured from divine vision.

word_study.meaning: Insult, reproach, disgrace, verbal abuse. The word carries the sense of contempt expressed through speech. It is the assault of words—mockery, scorn, defamation. Unlike physical injury, cherpah wounds through shame.
word_study.significance: Cherpah is frequently directed at God's people to undermine their faith (2 Kings 19:4, Isaiah 37:17). By invoking this word, the psalmist acknowledges that persecution is not mere circumstance but deliberate attack on his dignity and standing. God's awareness of cherpah validates that the spiritual and emotional dimensions of suffering matter to him.

word_study.meaning: Shame, dishonor, the state of being exposed or humiliated. Boshet describes the internalization of disgrace—when shame enters and colonizes the self. It is more internal than cherpah; it is what the sufferer feels when insulted.
word_study.significance: In Hebraic thought, shame is not merely emotional but a social and spiritual condition. To be ashamed is to lose standing in the community and before God. When God is asked to acknowledge boshet, the psalmist is asking God to restore what has been destroyed: social standing, honor, the ability to face others with dignity.

word_study.meaning: Humiliation, disgrace, reproach. Kelimmah often carries the sense of shame experienced before witnesses or a community. It is the public exposure of shame.
word_study.significance: The three words together form a progression: cherpah (the attack), boshet (internalized shame), kelimmah (public humiliation). By naming all three, the psalmist conveys that his suffering is complete—external, internal, and social. The Covenant Rendering's choice to render this cluster as 'insult, my shame, my humiliation' preserves the escalation.

word_study.meaning: Before you, in front of you, in your presence. The word negad carries both spatial ('in front') and epistemic ('in your awareness') meaning. It means 'visible to you' or 'known by you.'
word_study.significance: The statement 'all my adversaries are before you' does not merely mean they exist; it means they are transparent to God, visible in all their malice. Nothing is hidden. This formulation transforms God from a distant deity into an ever-present witness. It is comfort and warning combined.

cross_references.connection: Another lament psalm similarly catalogs God's knowledge of shame: 'All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant.' The pattern of invoking God's awareness as ground for appeal runs throughout the Psalms.

The servant of the Lord is 'despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief,' echoing the threefold shame language here—rejected (cherpah), sorrowful (boshet internally), and acquainted with grief (kelimmah socially).
Jesus 'endured the cross, despising the shame,' using the Greek equivalents of cherpah and kelimmah—Christ bore reproach and public humiliation, knowing that God saw every element of that suffering.

Nephi writes that God 'knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it,' affirming the omniscient knowledge the psalmist invokes here. The Book of Mormon reinforces that God's all-seeing nature is the basis for trust.

The great 'omniscience psalm' declares, 'Thou hast searched me, and known me...Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising,' establishing God's complete knowledge as the foundation for prayer in suffering.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, honor and shame were public commodities. An insult was not merely an emotional hurt but a legal and social injury. When an enemy publicly reproached you, they damaged your standing and your family's reputation. Courts could award damages for cherpah (verbal insult). The gravity with which the psalmist catalogs shame words reflects the social reality: his reputation has been systematically destroyed, and that destruction has real consequences for his standing in the community. In a shame-honor culture, to lose honor was to lose access to social resources, marriage prospects, business partnerships, and protection. God's acknowledgment of this shame (rather than dismissing it as merely spiritual or immaterial) reflects the ancient Israelite understanding that social humiliation is a genuine form of suffering that requires God's justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 12:24-27, Abinadi experiences intense reproach as the priests mock him, yet Abinadi maintains faith in God's knowledge. King Benjamin's discourse in Mosiah 2-3 emphasizes that God 'knoweth all things' and 'comprehendeth all things.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly asserts that God's omniscience is not distant but intimate—God knows the desires and thoughts of all people (Alma 18:32).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 137:6 presents a vision of Christ's knowledge: 'the Saviour has said, and I also say unto you, that inasmuch as you have done it unto one of the least of these, ye have done it unto me.' Christ's awareness of injustice and suffering parallels this psalm's invocation of God's omniscience. D&C 95:7-8 emphasizes that 'I have sworn in my wrath...if ye seek the pleasures of the world, ye shall lose the things which I have promised unto you.' God's knowledge encompasses not only suffering but judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the candidate is positioned as one whose struggles are witnessed and acknowledged by God and the heavenly powers. The temple drama affirms that no suffering, no injustice, no shame is hidden from heaven. This creates sacred space where the humiliated can find validation: God sees what the world has done, and God's judgment will supersede human judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's experience of reproach is the ultimate fulfillment of this verse. In the Gospels, Jesus endures all three forms of shame: cherpah (the soldiers mock him, 'Hail, King of the Jews,' Matthew 27:29), boshet (he is stripped naked before crowds, Mark 15:20), and kelimmah (he is hanged as a criminal between two thieves, Luke 23:32-33). Yet what distinguishes Christ's suffering is that he knows God sees. His cry from the cross, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1) expresses not the absence of God's knowledge but the agony of bearing shame while aware of God's presence. The resurrection declares that God's knowledge of injustice leads to vindication: Christ is justified, and his shame is transformed into glory.
commentary.application: This verse offers solace to modern covenant members experiencing public ridicule or social ostracism. The reassurance is not that suffering will be eliminated (Psalm 69 is not a prosperity gospel) but that it is known. God's omniscience means that no injustice escapes his notice. When colleagues mock your beliefs, when your family misunderstands your commitments, when you are laughed at for your convictions—God sees. Moreover, God sees your adversaries. The enemies of the righteous are fully visible to heaven; their malice is catalogued and witnessed. This formulation reframes persecution: it is not meaningless suffering but meaningful opposition in the presence of an all-seeing Judge. For members experiencing discrimination based on faith, this verse anchors hope in divine justice rather than human approbation.

text_kjv: Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none.

commentary.narrative: This verse descends from cosmological appeal (God sees all) to intimate confession: the psalmist's heart is broken, his body is sick, and he is utterly alone. The verb shavrah ('broken') suggests not a gradual fracture but a shattering blow—cherpah has struck with such force that the organ of emotion, will, and selfhood has been fractured. The verb va-anusah ('I am sick, I am incurable') moves from emotional devastation to physical illness, suggesting that prolonged reproach has manifested in bodily symptoms. The isolation then deepens: the psalmist looked for nud (sympathy, someone to witness his grief) and found no one. He sought menachamim (comforters, those who sit with the suffering) and found none. This is the depth of suffering: not only is the body ill and the heart broken, but there is no human companionship, no one to bear witness, no presence to mitigate the pain. The verse creates a portrait of complete abandonment—internal, physical, relational. This makes the earlier assertion that 'God knows' all the more poignant: if humans have abandoned him, God's knowledge may be the only knowledge that remains.

word_study.meaning: To break, to shatter, to fracture. When applied to the heart (lev), shavrah describes not a gentle weakening but a violent rupture. The word is used for breaking pottery (Jeremiah 19:10), breaking gates (Judges 5:8), breaking yokes (Leviticus 26:13). It is the language of destruction.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not say his heart is sad or troubled. He says it is shattered. The language reflects trauma: reproach has struck like a hammer, and the result is internal fragmentation. This is not sentimentalism but the description of a soul whose integrity has been assaulted.

word_study.meaning: To be sick, to be incurable, to be grievously ill. The root anush can also mean 'desperate' or 'hopeless'—a sickness from which recovery seems impossible. The verb form va-anusah ('and I am sick, and I grow sicker') suggests not a temporary illness but a chronic, worsening condition.
word_study.significance: The pairing of shavrah (broken heart) with anusah (incurable sickness) establishes the mind-body-spirit unity of Hebraic anthropology. Emotional trauma produces physical illness, and both remain incurable through ordinary means. This is the interior landscape of despair.

word_study.meaning: To shake, to wave, to make a gesture of sympathy or grief. The noun refers to someone who comes alongside the suffering to witness and acknowledge their pain through physical gesture—shaking the head in sorrow, waving in acknowledgment. To seek nud is to seek validation that one's suffering is real and deserves witnessing.
word_study.significance: Nud is relational—it requires a witness, someone present to acknowledge grief. The psalmist's inability to find nud means he cannot find even basic social recognition of his pain. He is isolated not merely physically but in terms of being seen and acknowledged.

word_study.meaning: Those who console, those who comfort. The root nacham refers to both physical comfort (bringing food, water, shelter) and emotional comfort (the presence that soothes grief). Menachamim are the community members who sit with the mourner in silence, who provide the material and emotional sustenance of consolation.
word_study.significance: In the biblical world, menachamim were essential to survival during grief. When Job's friends came to comfort him, they were fulfilling a sacred duty. The absence of menachamim means the psalmist has been utterly abandoned by the community. This is a particular cruelty: not only suffering, but suffering without witness or care.

word_study.meaning: The heart, the center of emotion, will, intellect, and moral consciousness in Hebrew anthropology. The lev is not merely the seat of feeling but the seat of the whole person—thought, decision, desire, covenant commitment, and the capacity for faith.
word_study.significance: When the psalmist says his heart is broken, the damage extends to his entire personhood. It is not a metaphor for sadness but a literal sense that his capacity for wholeness, for decision, for covenant relationship, has been fractured.

cross_references.connection: Another lament: 'I looked on my right hand, and beheld, but there was no man that would know me,' expressing the same isolation—no one recognizes the sufferer, no menachamim appear.
Jeremiah laments Jerusalem: 'all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they are become her enemies,' and 'she hath none to comfort her,' echoing the absence of menachamim described here.

Jesus in Gethsemane experiences a broken-hearted anguish: 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death,' and finds that even Peter, James, and John cannot stay awake to witness his agony—the absence of menachamim in his moment of greatest need.

Paul writes of 'the God of all comfort; who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble,' directly responding to the kind of isolation described here by offering God and the church as the true source of nachemim.

The Book of Mormon quotes Isaiah 53's prophecy of Christ: 'all we like sheep have gone astray...the Lord hath laid on him the iniquities of us all,' connecting Christ's isolation to this psalm's description of abandonment while bearing the suffering of others.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, to be without menachamim (comforters) was to be severed from the community. The duty of nud (showing sympathy) and nechamah (comforting) was not optional sentiment but a binding social obligation. When Job sat on the ash heap, his friends' duty was to sit with him—and the breakdown of that comforting presence marked the depth of his trial. Similarly, mourning rituals required the community to come alongside, bring food, and participate in lamentation. To suffer without comforters was to experience not merely individual pain but social death—the community had rejected the sufferer. This had practical implications: without social support, survival itself was jeopardized. A sick person without comforters would lack food, water, and care. A person in mourning without witnesses would have no one to testify to their loss or validate their grief. The psalmist's complaint is not sentimental but describes a crisis of community dissolution.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 8:4-14, Lehi experiences overwhelming despair—'I was overcome with fear' and 'I thought I saw'—suggesting a state of broken-hearted anguish. However, unlike the psalmist, Lehi is not left alone; he receives a vision and guidance. Alma the Younger's experience in Mosiah 27:28-32 presents the inverse: 'the very thought of coming into the presence of my God did rack my soul with inexpressible horror,' but ultimately he receives menachamim in the form of his father's prayers and the angelic visitation. The Book of Mormon suggests that isolation is not God's final word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:1-10 presents Joseph Smith receiving vision in the midst of anguish: 'he spoke not as he had done in past times, but gave counsel unto us concerning the visions.' The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that God provides guidance and comfort (nachamim) when human menachamim fail. D&C 121:7-9 contains Joseph Smith's anguished cry from Liberty Jail, expressing the weight of isolation: 'O God, where art thou?' Yet the response comes: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple experience includes the theme of affliction followed by comfort. The candidate moves through trials (represented symbolically) and is then received and comforted by those who represent the heavenly community. The endowment presents menachamim—those who comfort and uphold the faithful through their journey. This reverses the psalm's experience: where the psalmist found no comforters, the temple participant is promised that divine and communal support awaits.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse describes Christ's passion with profound precision. Christ's heart is broken—not figuratively, but in the garden of Gethsemane his soul is 'exceeding sorrowful, even unto death' (Matthew 26:38). He experiences sickness: 'His visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men' (Isaiah 52:14). He seeks comforters: 'Could ye not watch with me one hour?' (Matthew 26:40)—Peter, James, and John cannot stay awake to witness his anguish. He finds no menachamim among them. The disciples flee. Even God seems absent—'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' Yet the resurrection reveals that Christ's isolation was not eternal. God was present, witnessing and vindicating. Christ becomes the ultimate menachem (comforter): 'I will not leave you comfortless' (John 14:18).
commentary.application: This verse validates the reality of spiritual, emotional, and physical suffering integrated together, and it acknowledges the particular pain of isolation during trial. For modern members, this verse legitimizes the experience of loneliness during faith struggles. When doubt arises, when suffering seems meaningless, when the community seems indifferent, the psalm allows us to name this—not as lack of faith but as real human experience. The verse also indicts any Latter-day Saint community that fails to provide nachamim (comfort) to those in crisis. Our covenant duty includes sitting with the grieving, the doubting, the struggling; offering not answers but presence. Finally, the psalm ultimately insists that even if all human menachamim fail, God remains. The verse's isolation prepares us for verse 30's resolution: God will provide comfort. Modern covenant life includes the specific promise that the Holy Ghost is the Comforter (John 14:26)—when human menachamim are absent, the divine Comforter is available to those who seek him.

text_kjv: They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

commentary.narrative: The persecution here moves from psychological (reproach) and spiritual (isolation) to direct physical cruelty: the enemies actively work to increase the psalmist's suffering by poisoning what should sustain life. The enemies place rosh (a poisonous plant) in his bread, and when he is thirsty, they give him chomets (sour vinegar) instead of water. This is not accidental harm but deliberate mockery—the inversion of hospitality into torture. In the ancient world, bread and water were the basic elements of survival and the basic tokens of welcome. To poison bread and withhold fresh water was to transform the sustenance of life into instruments of death. The verse presents enemies who are not content with passive hostility but who actively scheme to intensify suffering. The verb form 'they gave me' (yadvakim, 'they put/gave to me') emphasizes deliberate action—this is not accidental poisoning but intentional mockery. This verse is historically significant because the Gospel writers see it as directly fulfilled in Christ's passion: the soldiers who offer Jesus vinegar on a sponge (Matthew 27:48, John 19:28-30) are identified as fulfilling this very verse. The psalmist's ancient complaint becomes a messianic prophecy when read through Christian interpretive tradition.

word_study.meaning: A bitter, poisonous plant (possibly hemlock or another toxic substance). Rosh is used in the Hebrew Bible for anything bitter or deadly. It can refer to venom (Deuteronomy 32:33), or metaphorically to idolatry and injustice (Amos 6:12, 'ye have turned justice into hemlock'). The KJV renders it 'gall' (which technically refers to bile), but the sense is 'poison.'
word_study.significance: That enemies put rosh in bread is not merely spoiling food but actively weaponizing it. Bread was the staff of life; bread poisoned is nourishment become instrument of harm. The word rosh carries covenantal overtones: those who break covenant by poisoning the covenant meal (bread and water are signs of covenant sustenance) prove themselves covenant-breakers.

word_study.meaning: My food, my bread, my sustenance. The term comes from bara (to eat) and refers to the basic provisions that keep one alive. Barut can also carry the sense of 'my portion'—what is mine by right.
word_study.significance: When enemies poison the psalmist's barut (food), they are attacking not merely at the level of the body but at the level of provision and belonging. In ancient society, to provide food was to covenant with someone; to poison their food was to radically violate that covenant.

word_study.meaning: Sour wine, vinegar, a fermented beverage. In the ancient world, vinegar was cheap, available to soldiers and the poor, often mixed with water to make a refreshing drink. However, it was not what the thirsty sought—fresh water was. To offer vinegar to one dying of thirst was to mock: yes, here is liquid, but it increases the burn in the throat rather than quenching.
word_study.significance: Chomets is not cruel because it is poison but because it is a mockery of relief. It presents the appearance of answering need (liquid for the thirsty) while actually intensifying suffering. It is cruelty disguised as mercy—'here, drink'—only to offer what torments.

cross_references.connection: The soldiers offer Jesus 'vinegar to drink,' which the Gospel writers explicitly identify as the fulfillment of this verse. The Psalmist's ancient complaint becomes the Gospel's prediction of Christ's passion.

John emphasizes that Christ 'saith, I thirst,' and the soldiers give him vinegar, noting that 'when Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished.' The offering of vinegar marks the moment of completion.

Moses' song describes apostasy: 'Their vine is of the vine of Sodom...their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps,' using the language of bitter/poisonous drink to describe covenant-breaking.

The wise woman says, 'Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts'—offering drink that comforts rather than torments, the opposite of this verse's cruelty.
Amos denounces: 'ye have turned judgment into hemlock, and the fruit of righteousness into rosh,' using the same word for bitter poison to describe the corruption of justice by covenant-breakers.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the poisoning of food and drink was a specific form of attack associated with covenant-breaking and profound betrayal. Archaeological evidence and literature from Mesopotamia and Egypt describe how enemies might poison the well or the feast. The taboo against poisoning food was severe because eating together created covenant bonds. To share bread and salt with someone created mutual obligation (the so-called 'bread and salt covenant'). Therefore, to poison that food was to commit not merely murder but sacrilege—the violation of the most sacred social bond. The offering of vinegar to the thirsty was also known: it was the drink of common soldiers and the desperately poor, the consolation drink of those who could afford nothing better. To offer it to someone of rank was either an insult or an act of mockery. The combination in this verse (poisoned bread + mocking vinegar) represents the complete inversion of hospitality and covenant. The enemy actively schemes not merely to refuse help but to pervert help itself into harm.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, persecution by mockery is frequent. The Nephites endure not merely attack but ridicule—enemies 'revile' and 'mock' (Alma 31:8, 38). Abinadi's martyrdom includes both physical cruelty and the taunt: the priests burn him after he has prophesied against them. The pattern suggests that the most intense persecution combines physical harm with spiritual mockery—the enemy tries to prove that God's people are wrong by making their suffering seem pointless.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 127:2 records Joseph Smith's reflection on persecution: 'having made a public disclosure of my situation...I have not as yet received the information relative to my family's condition, which I am anxious to receive...I am yet in bondage.' The pattern of persecution intensifying suffering (through isolation, through mockery) appears in Joseph Smith's journals and revelations. D&C 98:3 emphasizes that 'all they who suffer persecution for my name shall receive an hundredfold,' suggesting that God knows the specific character of persecution and will reward it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes representation of opposition and mockery. The candidate is tested and challenged by those representing the adversary. This ritual enactment validates the reality of persecution and frames it not as meaningless but as a test that leads to exaltation. The temple meal (the covenant feast in the celestial room, or the sacrament) stands in direct contrast to the poisoned food of verse 22: what the enemy tries to corrupt, God provides in sanctified form.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of this verse. In all four Gospels, Christ is offered vinegar at the moment of crucifixion (Matthew 27:48, Mark 15:36, Luke 23:36, John 19:28-30). But the Gospels explicitly frame this as fulfilling Psalm 69:21. Moreover, Christ's entire passion can be understood as the ultimate poisoning of what should sustain: the disciples who should have watched with him betray him; the bread and cup he instituted for covenant (the Last Supper) are rejected by those who condemn him; the water that should quench becomes vinegar. Christ's cry of thirst (John 19:28) echoes the psalmist's desperation. Yet the Gospels insist this is not meaningless suffering but redemptive—Christ's willingness to drink the cup of suffering (Matthew 26:39) becomes the basis for our redemption. His acceptance of vinegar, his willingness to be treated as the enemy deserves to be treated, becomes the means of our rescue.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse can validate the experience of having good intentions perverted or having offerings of help mocked. When testimony is dismissed as stupidity, when service is characterized as judgment, when genuine love is reinterpreted as arrogance—enemies are attempting the psalm's poisoning. This verse legitimizes anger at such perversion. It also, however, points to Christ's response: he does not fight back, does not demand that enemies stop, but accepts the suffering and thereby transforms it. For those in positions of leadership or influence, this verse warns against the specific cruelty of mocking others' faith or perverting their offerings. It calls for vigilance in maintaining covenantal integrity: never poison the meal of community, never mock what is offered in sincerity, never transform covenant bonds into instruments of harm. The verse ultimately points to the Atonement: Christ's willingness to drink poison so that we need not creates the path to redemption.

text_kjv: Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist now shifts from describing his suffering to pronouncing judgment on his enemies. This transition marks the beginning of the imprecatory section of the psalm—prayers for God to curse or punish enemies. The specific language inverts verse 22: where enemies gave him poisoned bread, now his prayer is that their own table become a snare. The shulchan ('table') represents both literal sustenance and metaphorically all that people build to support themselves: livelihood, reputation, family security, inheritance. The psalmist prays that what the enemies have built to secure themselves becomes the very instrument of their undoing. The 'snare' (pach) is a trap that catches animals unaware—suddenly, what seemed safe becomes deadly. Importantly, the psalmist is not wishing mere misfortune but a specific kind of justice: he wants the enemies to be caught in the consequences of their own hostility. This is the lex talionis (law of retaliation) applied as prayer. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:9-10, applying it to the hardening of Israel—the gospel of grace becomes a stumbling block to those who reject it. The theological weight here is that God's mercy can, for the unrepentant, become judgment; what should bring salvation can bring destruction.

word_study.meaning: Table, the place where food is set, the gathering place for community and covenant. The shulchan in biblical literature is where rulers display power (the royal table, 1 Kings 7:48), where family bonds are affirmed (the family meal), where covenants are ratified (eating bread together). The table is the place of hospitality and integration into community.
word_study.significance: When the shulchan becomes a pach (snare), the prayer is that the very place where the enemies' power and security are displayed becomes their downfall. What they have built in pride becomes the instrument of their judgment. In Paul's quotation in Romans 11:9, the table metaphorically refers to the spiritual 'table' of God's covenant—the gospel itself. For those who reject it, it becomes stumbling.

word_study.meaning: A snare, a trap, a hidden danger that catches the unwary. A pach is set covertly; the victim does not see it until it closes. The word is used throughout the Psalms for spiritual dangers and divine judgment (Psalm 91:3, 'surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler').
word_study.significance: The snare is not an obvious threat but a hidden one—justice catches suddenly, unexpectedly. The prayer is not for the enemy to be openly conquered but for them to be undone by forces they do not see coming, often by the very means they have employed.

word_study.meaning: Peace offerings, welfare, prosperity, well-being, all that contributes to wholeness and safety. Shelom (peace) in Hebrew includes material security, health, social harmony, spiritual wholeness. When someone prospers, we say shalom to them—wishing them everything that contributes to flourishing.
word_study.significance: The prayer inverts the natural order: what should bring shalom (wholeness, peace) becomes moqesh (trap). For the unrepentant, abundance becomes danger; security becomes liability. This is the psalmist's deepest prayer for justice: that God's judgment will show the enemies that what they thought was building their power was actually building their downfall.

word_study.meaning: A trap, a snare, a pit dug to catch prey. Similar to pach but often referring to a pit or deadfall trap. The moqesh is set in advance and disguised; the victim walks into it unknowingly.
word_study.significance: The pairing of pach ('snare') and moqesh ('trap') emphasizes the totality of judgment: the enemies are caught from every direction. There is no escape. The word is also used metaphorically for spiritual captivity and judgment.

cross_references.connection: Paul quotes this verse and verse 24, applying them to Israel's rejection of the gospel: 'Let their table become a snare...that their eyes should be darkened,' arguing that God's mercy becomes judgment for those who persist in unbelief.

Wisdom teaches that those who lay snares for others will be caught in their own traps: 'Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird. But these lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives.'—the principle that hostile intent returns to the hostile one.

Another lament-imprecatory psalm prays similarly: 'They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down...Let the mischief of their own lips cover them.' The pattern of praying that enemies be caught in their own schemes runs throughout the Psalter.
Paul warns that 'they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare (pach/pagida), and into many foolish and hurtful lusts,' applying trap language to spiritual danger and moral failure.

In the Book of Mormon, Alma warns the apostate Korihor that he is being caught in his own arguments: 'thy very words shall be used against thee at that day of judgment.' The enemy is caught in the consequences of his own words—a form of the snare/trap justice here invoked.

commentary.historical_context: The imprecatory psalms (prayers for God to curse enemies) were standard in ancient Near Eastern complaint literature. Ugaritic, Egyptian, and Babylonian texts all include prayers for divine retribution. However, the biblical imprecatory psalms have a distinctive character: they are not vendetta prayers (where the psalmist claims to act as executioner) but justice prayers (where the psalmist appeals to God as the righteous judge). The snare language is particularly apt for ancient context: traps for animals were common, and the idea that someone might be caught in their own trap was a proverbial expression for divine justice. The table reference would resonate in a culture where the king's table was a place of honor and power—to pray that the powerful one's table (their seat of authority and security) becomes a trap is to pray for a complete reversal of fortune. This kind of prayer assumes that God can overturn the social order and that divine justice sometimes works through poetic reversal: the proud are brought low, the mighty are rendered powerless through the very means of their pride.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently depicts enemies being caught in their own schemes. In Alma 30:60, Korihor 'was struck dumb, that he could not speak,' unable to continue the very arguments that had been his weapon. In Helaman 6:30, the wicked are described as being 'caught in their works.' The Nephite history illustrates the principle that opposition to God's people ultimately traps the opposer.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:23 presents a form of this justice: 'And your redemption cometh in and through the blood of the Lamb; and now I make an end of my sayings.' D&C 88:104-110 teaches that those who reject light and truth will have judgment upon them: 'Whatever principle of intelligence we attain unto in this life, it will rise with us in the resurrection.' The wicked are not freed by their opposition but trapped by it. The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that moral consequences are built into the cosmos.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes the principle of judgment—those who break covenant are denied access to the presence of God. In a sense, their own choice to reject covenant becomes the 'snare' that excludes them. Conversely, the faithful who keep covenants find their table (their sustenance from God) becomes security rather than danger.

commentary.christological_typology: In a complex way, Christ embodies both the psalmist and the subject of imprecation. Christ prays for those who persecute him: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' (Luke 23:34). Yet the Gospels also record that Christ's rejection becomes judgment: in John 3:16-18, those who 'believe not' are 'condemned already.' The cross itself becomes both the instrument of salvation for the believers and the basis of judgment for those who reject it. The 'table' of the Last Supper becomes, for Judas, the moment of betrayal—his participation in the covenant meal marks the moment his treachery is made manifest. In a sense, what should unite Judas with Christ becomes the snare that exposes his heart (John 13:18-30). Christ does not explicitly pray for enemies to be trapped, but his sacrifice makes it clear that those who persist in rejecting God's mercy will find that very mercy becomes judgment.
commentary.application: This verse presents a theologically complex challenge for modern Latter-day Saints. The principle of lex talionis—that justice often works through reversal, that the tools of oppression often become instruments of judgment—is biblical and important. However, the Christian teaching (especially from Christ) is not to pray for God to trap enemies but to pray for their repentance. The modern application might be this: (1) We can trust that God's justice is built into the moral universe—opposition to God is self-defeating; (2) We should not curse or manipulate, but can observe that enemies often fall through their own schemes; (3) We should pray for their repentance, not their judgment. The verse also warns those of us in positions of power: if we use our table (our security, our influence, our resources) to harm others, we are building the very snare that may catch us. The covenant principle is that those who bless shall be blessed, and those who curse shall be cursed—not through magic but through the operation of divine justice woven into reality. For modern members, this might mean vigilance: do not use resources, influence, or position to trap others, or those very things will become your own snare.

text_kjv: Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake.

commentary.narrative: The imprecation continues with two forms of incapacity: blindness and physical weakness. The prayer that enemies' eyes be darkened so they cannot see invokes darkness as judgment throughout the Hebrew Bible—blindness is both a condition of the body and a metaphor for spiritual obtuseness and moral confusion. To be unable to see is to be cut off from understanding, direction, and the ability to navigate reality. The prayer parallels Pharaoh's hardened heart—God 'darkened' Egypt in the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21-23), and later Israel's rejection of Jesus results in their spiritual blindness (Romans 11:8-10, where Paul again quotes this verse). The second curse—that their loins shake continually—moves from mental incapacity to physical symptom. The loins (matna) are the seat of strength and virility; to shake (hamʿad) is to tremble with fear, weakness, or infirmity. The psalmist prays not for momentary defeat but for chronic, unending instability. Together, the two curses describe complete incapacity: mental blindness paired with physical trembling creates a condition in which the enemy is both unable to understand and unable to act. The 'continually' (tamid) emphasizes that this is not temporary but ongoing, perpetual judgment. Paul again quotes this verse in Romans 11:10, applying it to Jewish rejection of Christ—the gospel becomes the very thing that blinds them to their need and weakens their ability to resist.

word_study.meaning: To be darkened, to become dark, to be obscured. The root chashak means 'darkness' and is used throughout Scripture for both literal darkness and spiritual blindness. When eyes are darkened, they lose the ability to perceive.
word_study.significance: Darkness in biblical thought is not neutral; it is the condition of judgment and separation from God (who is light). When God 'darkens' the eyes of enemies, it suggests not merely failing eyesight but a spiritual condition in which they are separated from truth and understanding. This connects to the imagery of being 'given over' to delusion (Romans 11:8, 2 Thessalonians 2:11).

word_study.meaning: To see, to perceive, to understand. In Hebrew, 'seeing' is not merely optical but epistemological—to see is to know, to understand, to perceive truth. The verb raah can mean visual perception but also spiritual sight (Proverbs 29:18, 'Where there is no vision [raah], the people perish').
word_study.significance: The prayer is not just for physical blindness but for spiritual confusion—the enemy will not be able to perceive the truth, will not understand the consequences of their actions, will wander in moral and spiritual darkness.

word_study.meaning: The loins, the lower back, the seat of strength, virility, and ability. In biblical anthropology, the loins are where power resides—to 'gird up one's loins' is to prepare for action (Isaiah 45:5). The loins are also the seat of fertility and procreation. To have weak loins is to be without strength or vigor.
word_study.significance: The prayer for shaking loins is a curse on the enemy's physical strength and stability. It echoes the curse formula in ancient Near Eastern curses: the enemy will become weak, unable to stand firm, unable to act decisively. In a secondary sense, weak loins can mean infertility or the failure of one's line to continue—a comprehensive destruction.

word_study.meaning: To shake, to totter, to become unstable, to quiver with fear or weakness. The verb maʿad describes the trembling of the earth (Psalm 60:2), the knees giving way (Isaiah 35:3), or the whole person becoming unstable. Tamid means 'continually' or 'perpetually.'
word_study.significance: The 'continual shaking' is not a single blow but an ongoing condition—the enemy is in perpetual instability, unable to find firm footing, trembling constantly. This echoes the curse in Deuteronomy 28:65-66 against covenant-breakers: 'And among these nations shall thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest...thy life shall hang in doubt before thee.'

cross_references.connection: Paul explicitly quotes verses 23-24, applying the darkening of eyes and shaking of loins to Israel's spiritual hardening. The apostle uses the imprecatory language to describe how rejection of Christ's gospel paradoxically leads to spiritual blindness and instability.

The ninth plague of Egypt: 'the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven; that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.' Pharaoh's hardness of heart results in darkness—the same judgment pattern as this psalm's prayer.

The covenant curse formula: 'The LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart...and thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness.' The psalmist's prayer echoes the standard covenant judgment against the unfaithful.

Jesus teaches that spiritual blindness is a form of judgment: 'I am come into this world...that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.' Those who reject truth are darkened in understanding.

Paul warns that in the last days, people 'shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.' The darkening of the eyes and ears is a form of judgment that comes through persistent rejection of truth.

commentary.historical_context: Curse formulas were common in ancient Near Eastern literature, particularly in curse sections of treaties (vassal treaties, royal inscriptions, tomb curses). Egyptian curse texts, Mesopotamian boundary stone curses, and Hittite treaty curses all included similar language: may the gods blind you, may you be weak, may you tremble, may your land be desolate. These curses were understood not as mere wishes but as invocations of cosmic or divine power. The curses were written or spoken as though reality itself would respond. In biblical context, the imprecatory psalms work similarly: the psalmist invokes divine judgment against those who have broken covenant with God and harmed his people. The specific language (darkness, trembling, weakness) reflects the understanding that covenant-breakers experience not only external judgment but internal corruption: their ability to perceive truth (eyes) and their ability to act effectively (loins) are damaged. The repeated 'continually' (tamid) reflects the view that divine judgment is not temporary; the covenant-breaker remains under judgment until he repents.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, spiritual blindness is repeatedly associated with rejection of truth. Alma 26:16-19 describes those who, despite direct witnesses, cannot see spiritual truth: 'they will not believe me.' In 2 Nephi 27:29, Isaiah's prophecy is quoted: 'the learned shall not read them, for they shall say, I am not learned.' The inability to perceive truth is presented as a form of judgment. Helaman 16:13-15 describes how signs are given, but some 'do harden their hearts, and do reject all the words which have been spoken by the prophets,' resulting in spiritual blindness that is characterized as their own choice leading to judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:76-80 presents the principle of judgment: those who reject the covenant 'shall be delivered up unto the buffetings of Satan unto the day of redemption, saith the Lord.' The physical trembling and weakness may be literal or metaphorical—the point is that covenant-breakers are in a state of instability and weakness. D&C 42:27-28 warns: 'keep yourselves unspotted from the world; for that which cometh from above is clean, and that which is down beneath is filthy.' Those who embrace darkness remain in it—their spiritual sight fails.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes stages of enlightenment and blindness. Before the full initiation, the candidate wears a blindfold, symbolizing spiritual darkness. This represents the condition of those outside the covenant. Those who accept the covenant are brought into light. The psalm's prayer that enemies remain in darkness contrasts with the promise that those who enter the temple move from darkness to light. The temple affirms both the possibility of seeing (through covenant) and the reality that some refuse to see.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's passion includes elements of this verse's imagery. In John 3:19-21, Jesus teaches that darkness is the condition of those who reject truth: 'light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.' The enemies who crucify Jesus are, in a sense, those with darkened eyes—they do not perceive that they are crucifying the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). Yet Christ does not curse them. Instead, he prays for their forgiveness. The Gospels indicate that some responded (the centurion, Nicodemus), while others remained hardened. For those who persist in rejecting Christ, the result is indeed spiritual blindness and instability (as Paul argues in Romans 11). However, the path to light is always open for those who turn. Christ does not want enemies to remain in darkness but offers light to all (John 12:46, 'I am come a light into the world').
commentary.application: This verse presents a sobering truth: persistent rejection of truth results in spiritual blindness and instability. For modern Latter-day Saints, this serves as both warning and clarification. The warning is directed inward: if we persistently ignore the still small voice, reject the counsel of prophets, harden our hearts against truth, we will find our spiritual vision dimmed and our foundation shaken. The Spirit's influence will withdraw (D&C 63:32). However, the verse should not be used to judge others or to invoke curse upon them. The Christian response (following Christ's example) is to wish for their repentance, not their judgment. For those who have experienced having their faith mocked or opposed, this verse validates that opposition to God's work is self-defeating—enemies of the gospel are, in a sense, already caught in its judgment through their own blindness and instability. They cannot ultimately prevail because their very opposition binds them to darkness. The verse also teaches that spiritual health requires maintaining open eyes (receptivity to truth) and firm loins (strength to act on truth). In modern context, this means cultivating humility, maintaining openness to new revelation, and grounding oneself in covenants. The 'shaking' that comes through trial or doubt is not judgment but invitation to strengthen one's foundation.

text_kjv: Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 69:25 marks the transition into the psalm's imprecatory section—prayers asking God to execute judgment against those who have persecuted the psalmist. This verse employs visceral imagery: God's fury is 'poured out' like a flood, and His anger 'overtakes' the enemies as if in relentless pursuit. The Hebrew shefokh ('pour out') deliberately echoes the deluge language of Genesis, where divine wrath is expressed through overflowing water. This is not merely emotional venting; it is a formal petition for divine justice delivered by someone who has exhausted human remedies. The parallelism of 'indignation' and 'wrathful anger' intensifies the prayer—the psalmist calls upon God's full arsenal of judgment.
commentary.narrative_para_2: In the ancient Near Eastern context, imprecatory psalms were understood as belonging to the covenant lawsuit genre (rib pattern). The victim of injustice has the right to appeal to God as the ultimate judge when human authorities fail. The psalmist is not acting as a private citizen seeking personal revenge; he is invoking God's name and justice. The verb yasigem ('overtake them') suggests that God's anger pursues the enemies as a hunter pursues prey—there is no escape, no refuge from divine judgment. This reflects the ancient belief that God's wrath is an active, pursuing force that cannot be outrun or hidden from.
commentary.narrative_para_3: For modern readers, this verse challenges us to understand the psalms as honest prayers that include anger, grief, and the cry for justice. Ancient and medieval commentators recognized imprecatory psalms as expressions of righteous indignation against those who actively oppose God's purposes. The Reformation translators and later scholars debated whether such prayers should be prayed by Christians, with some concluding they can be prayed only when the psalmist represents the cause of God against His enemies, not personal vengeance.

word_study.meaning: To pour, to pour out, to spill. Used for water, blood, and in this context, divine wrath. The Covenant Rendering notes the same 'pouring imagery' applied to flood waters (Genesis), now directed at enemies. The term carries the sense of abundant, unrestrained outpouring.
word_study.significance: This verb establishes God's wrath as an overwhelming force—not measured or restrained, but fully released. It suggests totality and finality in God's judgment.

word_study.meaning: Fury, indignation, wrath—specifically the wrath of God against those who defy Him. It carries a sense of divine displeasure at rebellion or injustice.
word_study.significance: Za'am is God's righteous response to wrongdoing, not mere anger but the just fury of a covenant God against covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: Burning of anger, burning wrath—literally 'heat of anger.' The noun charon ('burning') combined with af ('anger, nose') creates the image of nostrils flaring with divine heat.
word_study.significance: This doublet intensifies the previous term, adding the physical dimension of heat and intensity to divine judgment. It reflects anthropomorphic imagery common in Hebrew poetry.

word_study.meaning: To overtake, to reach, to capture, to pursue and catch. In context, it suggests pursuit and capture—the enemies cannot escape.
word_study.significance: This verb transforms wrath from a static quality into an active pursuit. God's anger is not passive; it actively hunts down those who oppose the psalmist and God's justice.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same Hebrew root for 'poured out' (shefakta) to describe God's wrath against Egypt: 'thou sentest forth thy wrath.' Both verses depict divine judgment as an overwhelming force directed against enemies.

Isaiah declares that God 'poured out upon him the fury of his anger,' using identical imagery (shefakh + za'am) for God's judgment. Both psalms and prophets employ the metaphor of divine wrath as a poured-out substance.

Paul cites Deuteronomy 32:35 ('Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord'), teaching that believers should not seek personal revenge but trust God's justice—directly addressing how to pray imprecatory psalms in the New Testament.
John's apocalypse describes angels 'pouring out' (ekcheo) the bowls of God's wrath upon the earth, drawing on the same pouring/judgment imagery found in Psalm 69:25.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern covenant texts and legal proceedings, wronged parties appealed to the gods (or to the suzerain in vassal treaties) for judgment against those who violated justice. The imprecatory psalms reflect this judicial prayer pattern. Archaeological and textual evidence from Hittite, Aramaic, and Egyptian sources shows that such formal curse-prayers were understood as legal petitions, not personal outbursts. The 'pouring out' imagery may also reflect ancient Mesopotamian divination practices where wrath was understood as a tangible, overpowering force. The Psalms present the psalmist as a covenant-keeper whose enemies are God's enemies, justifying the appeal for divine judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar imprecatory language in 2 Nephi 15:24-25 (Isaiah 5:24-25), where the Lord's anger is kindled against His people and His hand is stretched out to strike them. Like Psalm 69, this reflects God's role as divine judge who 'pours out' judgment against the covenant-breaker.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 19:15-17 presents Jesus Christ speaking of divine indignation poured out, establishing that God's wrath is real and purposeful. D&C 88:88 declares that 'the Lord shall come down in judgment upon Idumea, or the world.' These passages confirm that imprecatory prayers call upon real divine judgment, not abstract concepts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes a covenant dimension where the individual covenants to forsake evil and cleave to righteousness. Psalm 69:25 may be understood as calling upon God to separate the righteous from the wicked—a separation accomplished through the temple covenant and priesthood authority.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 69 is one of the most directly Christological psalms, with verses 4, 8-9, 20-21, and 25-29 applied to Christ's passion and betrayal in the New Testament. Verse 25 foreshadows the judgment upon those who reject or betray Christ. Christ bore the indignation that justly belonged to all humanity (D&C 19:18); imprecatory prayers ultimately point to His role as both judge and the one who absorbs the wrath that sinners deserve.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members should understand imprecatory psalms not as permission for personal revenge, but as expressions of submission to God's justice. When we pray Psalm 69:25, we are recognizing that we are not judges—God is. We release our anger and our demand for retribution to Him. This is particularly difficult when we have been genuinely wronged, which is precisely why these psalms exist: to give voice to the cry for justice while directing that cry toward God, not toward human vengeance. The prayer calls us to faith that God will ultimately judge all injustice, even when human courts fail.

text_kjv: Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents.

commentary.narrative: Verse 26 continues the imprecation by calling for the desolation of the enemies' dwellings. The word tirah ('encampment, fortress, dwelling') may suggest military encampments or fortified settlements, not merely private homes. The prayer is that these structures become neshamah ('desolate, devastated')—abandoned, uninhabited, bereft of life. This is not merely property damage in the modern sense; in the ancient world, a desolate dwelling place meant social death: family line severed, property forfeited, inheritance lost. The parallel 'let none dwell in their tents' reinforces the completeness of the desolation—not a temporary abandonment but permanent exclusion from habitation.
commentary.narrative_para_2: The significance of this image extends beyond military contexts. In the ancient Near East, the 'house' or 'tent' represented not just physical property but family continuity, blessing, and covenant status. To have one's dwelling made desolate was to be cut off from the land of the living, from inheritance, from the future. This verse may reflect the practice of herem ('devoted destruction') found in Joshua's conquest narratives, where entire cities and their structures were devoted to destruction as acts of covenantal judgment. The prayer asks that the enemies experience this same comprehensive removal from the land.
commentary.narrative_para_3: Peter's quotation of this verse in Acts 1:20 (applying it to Judas Iscariot's betrayal and death) demonstrates how the early Church understood imprecatory psalms as having prophetic significance regarding covenant-breakers. Judas's replacement was necessary because 'his habitation be desolate' (Acts 1:20, quoting Psalm 69:25). This apostolic application shows that the psalm was read as having layers of meaning: first, literal judgment against historical enemies; second, theological judgment against all covenant-breakers; and third, eschatological judgment in the final separation of righteous from wicked.

word_study.meaning: Encampment, fortress, dwelling place, settlement. Can refer to military camps, fortified cities, or established communities. The term carries connotations of protection and security.
word_study.significance: The desolation of tirah means the loss of security and shelter—a comprehensive removal from safety and community standing.

word_study.meaning: Desolation, devastation, ruin. Literally derived from root meaning 'to be desolate.' Describes a place emptied of life, stripped of inhabitants, abandoned to waste.
word_study.significance: This is not mere abandonment but active devastation—a place that has lost its vitality and purpose. The term emphasizes totality: nothing remains intact or functioning.

word_study.meaning: Tents—portable dwellings used by nomadic peoples, shepherds, and military forces. In biblical poetry, tents often represent family, household, and the dwelling place of the living.
word_study.significance: Tents are temporary structures, yet their desolation means the permanent loss of family continuity. The prayer asks that these dwelling places—symbols of security—become empty shells.

cross_references.connection: Peter directly quotes Psalm 69:25-26 in applying it to Judas Iscariot: 'Let his dwelling place be desolate, and let no one live in it.' This is the only explicit New Testament quotation of these verses, establishing their prophetic dimension.

Job's friend Eliphaz declares that the dwelling place of the wicked will be desolate ('the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate'), using similar language to describe judgment against the unfaithful.
Isaiah describes Judah's desolate cities and cottages burned with fire, using the imagery of abandoned dwellings as a sign of covenant judgment and abandonment by God.

The covenant curse formula includes: 'Cursed shalt thou be in the city, and cursed shalt thou be in the field' (with dwelling and harvest desolated). Psalm 69:26 invokes this same curse pattern against the enemies.
The account of Jericho's herem ('devoted destruction') shows the ancient practice of making cities desolate as acts of covenantal judgment—the model underlying imprecatory psalm language.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, desolation was understood as divine judgment on a community or individual. Archaeological evidence from the Levant shows destructions and abandonments attributed to divine punishment in ancient sources. The 'dwelling place' held profound significance: inheritance of land was central to covenant theology in Israel. To lose one's dwellings meant loss of covenant status, loss of inheritance, and loss of future generations. The image of desolate tents would have resonated powerfully with an audience familiar with nomadic life and the vulnerability of settlements to conquest and destruction. The practice of herem (devoted destruction) in Joshua's conquest involved not just killing but the total destruction and abandonment of cities—a precedent that makes the imprecation linguistically and theologically coherent.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's use of language in 2 Nephi 1:19-22 includes cursing language directed against those who break covenants ('cursed art thou because of thy hardness of heart'). Like Psalm 69:26, the Book of Mormon understands that covenant-breakers experience desolation from God's presence and blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 41:5 declares that the wicked 'shall be hewn down and cast into the fire,' suggesting total removal. D&C 101:23-24 uses the image of desolate fields and houses to describe judgment on the covenant-breaker. The principle of covenant consequence appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the righteous are gathered into Zion while the wicked are separated out. Psalm 69:26 foreshadows this separation—the righteous dwell in God's house (Psalm 23), while the covenant-breaker's dwelling becomes desolate. This is a fundamental temple principle: there is a place prepared for the faithful and a separation for the unfaithful.

commentary.christological_typology: Peter's application of this verse to Judas establishes that covenant-breakers (those who betray Christ) experience desolation. Christ Himself prayed in Gethsemane that His disciples be kept, while those who reject Him are separated out (John 17). The desolation of the enemies' dwellings prefigures the outer darkness where covenant-breakers are separated from God's presence.
commentary.application: For the covenant member, Psalm 69:26 teaches that there are real consequences to breaking covenants. Dwelling in God's house—whether the temple, the Church, or the faithful community—is a privilege that requires fidelity. Those who actively work against God's purposes and His covenant people face a kind of desolation: separation from the blessings of community, from God's presence, from inheritance in Zion. This verse invites us to reflect seriously on our covenant status and to recognize that 'no man taketh this honour upon himself' (Hebrews 5:4)—covenant standing is God's to grant and to withdraw.

text_kjv: For they persecute him whom thou hast smitten; and they talk to the grief of those whom thou hast wounded.

commentary.narrative: Verse 27 introduces a moral and theological complexity that distinguishes this imprecation from mere personal revenge: the enemies persecute someone whom God Himself has already struck down. The psalmist (or one he represents) is already suffering divine affliction, yet rather than showing compassion, the enemies add persecution to this suffering. This is not simply cruelty to an unfortunate person; it is kicking someone whom God Himself is judging. The Covenant Rendering brings out the sharp theological tension: 'For they persecute the one you have struck; they talk about the pain of those you have wounded.' The enemies 'talk about the pain' (yesapperu el makh'ov)—they discuss the victim's agony not with sympathy but as gossip, accusation, or mockery.
commentary.narrative_para_2: This verse reveals the theological logic of the imprecation: the psalmist is not asking God to punish innocent people but to judge those who abuse the already-afflicted. The phrase 'they persecute him whom thou hast smitten' suggests that the psalmist understands his suffering as divinely permitted or ordained. Rather than rescue him immediately, God allows the testing, but the enemies cross a moral line by adding their own cruelty to God's discipline. In the ancient Near Eastern legal context, this would be understood as compounding injustice: the victim suffers divine judgment, but justice would require that others not add insult or further injury. The prayer is not for God to afflict the innocent but to hold the enemies accountable for their abuse of the suffering.
commentary.narrative_para_3: The verb 'talk to the grief' (yesapperu el makh'ov) is particularly revealing. Rather than silence or sympathy in the presence of suffering, the enemies 'tell' or 'speak about' the pain—they narrate the victim's agony. This could mean they gossip about the victim's wounds, use his suffering as an occasion for mockery, or spread his pain as news. This transforms the enemies' action from violence to a kind of psychological torture: they take the victim's existing suffering and weaponize it as a subject of conversation. They treat sacred pain—the pain of one God has touched—as an occasion for casual talk or accusation.

word_study.meaning: To pursue, to hunt, to persecute. Literally means to run after or chase prey. In legal/moral contexts, it describes the active pursuit and oppression of a vulnerable person.
word_study.significance: This verb emphasizes active, relentless pursuit. The enemies do not merely dislike the victim; they actively hunt him down, adding their own violence to his existing affliction.

word_study.meaning: To strike, to smite, to wound. Used for God's judgment, punishment, or affliction. Indicates a blow already delivered by God.
word_study.significance: This verb establishes that the victim is already under divine judgment. The enemies are not striking the first blow; they are adding their violence to God's already-delivered strike.

word_study.meaning: Pain, ache, wound—the physical and emotional suffering that results from being struck. Carries the sense of lingering pain, not instantaneous injury.
word_study.significance: Makh'ov emphasizes the ongoing suffering of the afflicted one. The enemies talk about wounds that are still open, still painful—they weaponize the victim's ongoing agony.

word_study.meaning: To tell, to recount, to narrate, to spread word about. Can mean to gossip, to publicize, to tell stories.
word_study.significance: This verb suggests the enemies are not silently cruel; they actively spread news of the victim's suffering. They make his pain a topic of conversation, multiplying the wound through social humiliation.

cross_references.connection: After David's sin with Bathsheba, Nathan declares that the enemies of God 'laugh to scorn' the Lord by David's stumble—making the leader's shame a subject of mockery, paralleling how the enemies in Psalm 69:27 weaponize the victim's suffering.

The Servant (prophetically Christ) is 'despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.' Yet people 'esteemed him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted'—they treat his God-ordained suffering as an occasion for disdain, mirroring Psalm 69:27.

The suffering prophet in Lamentations 'giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him' and 'is filled with reproach.' Like Psalm 69:27, the victim suffers not only divine affliction but additional human cruelty and mockery.

Job laments that his kinfolk have withdrawn, his servants despise him, his wife abhors him—all while he suffers what he perceives as divine affliction. Job's friends add theological judgment (suggesting his suffering proves his guilt) to his physical agony, paralleling the enemies' behavior in Psalm 69:27.

At the crucifixion, enemies mock Jesus, 'wagging their heads' and 'saying, Thou that destroyest the temple'—treating His divinely-ordained suffering (Psalm 69 is applied to Christ's passion) as an occasion for public ridicule.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, one of the worst forms of social punishment was public mockery and shame. The 'public spreading' of one's suffering (yesapperu) would have been understood as a form of social death—not just injury but public humiliation. Additionally, the concept of someone already 'struck by God' carries religious weight: in ancient Israel, affliction could be understood either as punishment for sin or as a trial permitted by God to test faithfulness. Either way, adding human cruelty to divine affliction was seen as crossing a moral line. Ancient Near Eastern legal codes distinguish between striking an already-afflicted person and striking a healthy one—the former was often treated with greater severity, as it compounded an existing injustice. The verse reflects this legal and moral sensitivity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's experience in 1 Nephi 18:19-20 shows how Nephi is scourged while his own brothers 'did smite me with a rod,' then publicly mock him. Like Psalm 69:27, Nephi suffers both divine testing (in the form of his brothers' affliction upon him) and human cruelty that compounds his suffering. Nephi's response—to pray for them—models how to respond to this kind of doubled persecution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-9 presents a profound meditation on suffering that arises precisely when one is righteous. 'My soul has been sad because of war, and my heart has been pained because of all the tribulations of my people.'
