word_study.meaning: And they will inherit it, and they will possess it. From yarash, meaning 'to inherit, to take possession, to dispossess.' The word carries the sense of inheritance—not merely occupation but the fulfillment of a covenantal promise.
word_study.significance: Yarash connects this promise to Abraham's covenant: the land is an inheritance promised to the patriarchs, and the restored community will finally and fully possess it. This is not colonization or conquest but the fulfillment of divine promise.

cross_references.connection: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion...for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem—Isaiah's vision of Zion's restoration parallels this psalm's promise, showing the consistency of this hope across prophetic literature.

For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place...Jeremiah's promise to the exiles of restoration and return directly parallels the hope of verse 36.

But in the last days it shall come to pass, that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established in the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills...the law shall go forth of Zion—Micah's eschatological vision of Zion's ultimate exaltation and the nations flowing unto it extends the promise of verse 36.

Therefore, I send you again to the testimony which ye have already received, that you may know that my word is true...And his dominion shall be an everlasting dominion—D&C's teaching about Zion's gathering and the restoration of God's kingdom applies the principle of verse 36 to the restored Church.

And the Lord called his people Zion, because they were of one heart and of one mind, and dwelt in righteousness...And the Lord blessed the land, and they were blessed upon the mountains—Pearl of Great Price defines Zion in terms of spiritual unity and righteousness, showing how the promise of verse 36 is ultimately about the restoration of a covenant people.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 36 is widely understood by scholars as evidence of a post-exilic (or exilic) date for these concluding verses. The destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE, the Babylonian exile, and the subsequent return under Persian rule form the historical backdrop. The promise that God will "build the cities of Judah" would have been profoundly meaningful to exiles or those recently returned from exile. The specificity about Judah (rather than the northern kingdom, which had fallen in 722 BCE) reflects the historical reality of the post-exilic period: only the southern kingdom of Judah was restored. The theological framework—that exile is not punishment beyond redemption, but a trial that God will reverse—becomes central to post-exilic thought. The rebuilding of the Temple under Zerubbabel (c. 515 BCE) and the subsequent rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (c. 445 BCE) under Nehemiah are the historical events that fulfilled this promise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon applies this promise to the Americas. In 1 Nephi 13:37, it is declared that the Gentiles shall help God's covenant people by bringing them to the land. In Alma 9:24, the prophet teaches that Zion (the promised land) will be established. The gathering of the covenant people to a promised land is the overarching theme of the Book of Mormon, showing how the ancient promise of Zion's restoration is extended and fulfilled in the latter days. The righteous Nephites experience the temporary establishment of Zion in 4 Nephi, but the fall into wickedness shows the principle that Zion can only be maintained through righteousness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants extensively develops this promise in terms of the restored Church. D&C 97:18-21 teaches: 'Let the city Hiram be appointed a place of refuge. Let it be a place of safety for the saints of the Most High God...That the poor may receive the gospel in all their plainness...Zion must and will be built upon the principles of the law of the celestial kingdom.' D&C 45:66-67 promises: 'And it shall come to pass that your remnants shall be gathered unto one place upon the land of Zion.' The promise of verse 36 is fulfilled in the Restoration through the establishment of the New Jerusalem and the gathering of covenant Israel to Zion. D&C 84:2-3 identifies Independence, Missouri as the location of the New Jerusalem and the House of the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple stands as the center of Zion—the meeting place of heaven and earth where God dwells and where the covenants are sealed. The promise of verse 36 is ultimately about the restoration of the Temple and the covenant community gathered around it. In the Latter-day Restoration, the building of temples—from Kirtland to Salt Lake to temples throughout the world—represents the fulfillment of the promise that God will 'build the cities of Judah.' Each temple becomes a Zion, a place where the covenant people gather and dwell in the presence of God. The ultimate fulfillment is the New Jerusalem of D&C 45:66-67, where the Temple will be the center.

commentary.christological_typology: Zion ultimately points to Christ as the spiritual center toward which all covenantal hope converges. The New Jerusalem (Revelation 21-22) is described as descending from heaven, with Christ as its light and the Lamb as its temple. The promise that God will 'save Zion' is fulfilled in the Atonement and the establishment of Christ's kingdom. The 'cities of Judah' represent the scattered covenant people gathered by Christ into one. The restoration of Zion after exile prefigures the restoration of all things through Christ's Second Coming (Revelation 11:15). Christ himself is the foundation of Zion (Isaiah 28:16), and his sacrifice makes possible the spiritual restoration promised in verse 36.
commentary.application: This final verse moves the promise from personal deliverance to communal and national restoration, but also—through the Restoration—to spiritual restoration. The promise that 'God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah' applies to you not as an individual in isolation, but as a member of God's covenant people. Your personal redemption (verses 31-32) contributes to the building of Zion. Your praise (verse 35) participates in the cosmic restoration. This teaches a fundamental principle: your individual faithfulness matters not because it serves your private interests, but because it contributes to the gathering and building of God's covenant community. When you make covenants in the Temple, sustain the leaders of the Church, serve in your ward and stake, or invite others to the gospel, you are literally building Zion. When you endure trials with faith, as the psalmist does, you are helping to restore the vision of a covenant people dwelling together in unity and righteousness. This week, identify one specific way you can contribute to the building of Zion: it might be caring for the poor and needy (thus fulfilling verse 34's principle), strengthening your family (the basic unit of Zion), or serving in the Church. Let your personal faith become concrete action that builds the kingdom.

text_kjv: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 70 opens with a superscription that frames the entire composition. The Hebrew term lehazkir ('for remembrance') carries weight beyond simple notation—it suggests this psalm serves a specific liturgical function. In the Levitical system, the 'memorial offering' (azkarah) was the portion of a grain offering burned on the altar as a token, causing a pleasing aroma to ascend before the Lord (Leviticus 2:2). This superscription may indicate that the psalm itself functions as a verbal 'memorial'—a prayer presented before God with the expectation that it will be noticed, considered, and acted upon. The psalmist is not simply singing; he is depositing his petition in the divine audience chamber. This reflects a theology of prayer in which human speech is real, meaningful, and capable of moving God's attention and action.

word_study.meaning: For the director/leader of music; the preposition indicates this is a heading for performance or recitation. The root natzach carries the sense of 'to oversee, direct, make prominent.'
word_study.significance: This psalm is not a private meditation but a communal prayer, formatted for public worship under the direction of a skilled musician. The 'director' is responsible for ensuring this prayer reaches both the congregation and the throne room of heaven.

word_study.meaning: For remembrance; the infinitive construct of zakar, 'to remember.' The preposition le- indicates purpose or function: 'in order that [this prayer] be remembered.'
word_study.significance: This is not passive memory but active calling-to-mind. The psalmist asks God to remember—to bring the petition from the background of divine awareness into the foreground of divine action. As The Covenant Rendering notes, this may connect to the memorial offering, where a token is burned so the entire offering is remembered before God.

cross_references.connection: The memorial offering (azkarah) burned on the altar creates a pleasing aroma before God, paralleling how this psalm 'for remembrance' is presented before divine attention.
Both psalms use 'to bring to remembrance' in their superscript, indicating a shared liturgical category of prayer designed to capture God's focused attention.
In John's vision, the prayers of the saints are offered as incense before the throne, echoing the memorial offering theology embedded in the psalm superscript.
The Lord addresses His servants as those whom He will remember and call forth in the day of judgment, reflecting the theme of making one's petition memorable before God.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm superscripts were the ancient labels that designated how and when a psalm was to be used in Israelite worship. The notation 'for remembrance' likely belonged to a subset of psalms recited during specific festivals or offerings—possibly the Passover, Tabernacles, or at the daily memorial offering (minchah). Such psalms were believed to have particular efficacy in drawing God's attention. The psalmist operates within a cultic framework where prayer is not casual conversation but formal petition, shaped by liturgical protocol and designed for maximum spiritual impact. The superscript itself—not added by David but by later liturgical editors—transformed a personal lament into a communal resource, a prayer anyone facing persecution could inhabit.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon portrays prayer as a serious practice with real power to move heaven. Nephi's prayers (2 Nephi 33:3-4) and the prayers of the people in Alma 31 show prayer as an offering that God receives and acts upon—much like the memorial offering theology behind this psalm's superscript.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:23 teaches that 'there is no greater thing you can do than to preach the word of God,' but the principle extends to prayer itself. The superscript frames prayer as a formal act of worship—something 'chief musicians' direct and orchestrate. D&C 109 (the Kirtland Temple prayer) shows Joseph Smith crafting extensive prayers designed to be remembered before God, paralleling the memorial function of this psalm.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The memorial offering (azkarah) is fundamentally a temple rite. The notion that a prayer can function as a memorial—a way of calling God's name and drawing His memory—connects to covenant renewal and petition within the temple context, where names are written in the divine registry and souls stand before the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the fulfillment of what this psalm presumes: He is the perfect memorial offering whose name is always before the Father. His intercessory prayer in Gethsemane and His eternal priesthood ensure that the prayers of the saints are never forgotten but eternally presented before the throne of God.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members can take courage from this superscript's theology: prayer is not merely personal catharsis but formal petition presented before God. When you write in a journal, pray aloud, or kneel in a temple, you are placing your petition in the divine registry. God does not forget. Your name and your need are literally presented before Him. This truth should reshape how you pray—not as casual speech but as deliberate, serious, memorable offering.

text_kjv: Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD.

commentary.narrative: The psalm opens with two imperative commands joined by repetition: 'Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD.' The Hebrew verb chushah ('make haste, hasten, hurry') is not polite request but urgent demand. This is the vocabulary of emergency—someone in crisis pressing God to act without delay. The repetition is not rhetorical embellishment but intensification. The psalmist addresses God twice (Elohim in the first line, YHWH in the second), and twice uses the verb of speed, creating a rhythmic hammering of urgency. This is prayer in extremity, where politeness gives way to desperation. Yet even in desperation, the psalmist names God rightly and trusts that speed of response is within God's nature and willingness. The dual terminology—'deliver me' (hatzileni, 'rescue me from immediate danger') and 'help me' (ezrati, 'come to my aid')—shows the psalmist calling on God as both rescuer and helper, the one who removes threat and the one who sustains.

word_study.meaning: An imperative meaning 'hasten, hurry, be swift.' This verb carries urgency and demand, not polite petition. Used also in Psalm 22:20 ('make haste to help me'), 38:23, and 71:12—the standard emergency vocabulary.
word_study.significance: The verb embodies the theology of the psalm: God is not slow or indifferent but responsive to crisis. The psalmist does not doubt God's power, only God's speed of response. This is faith expressed as urgent demand, not resignation.

word_study.meaning: From natzal, 'to snatch away, rescue, save from peril.' The infinitive with preposition indicates purpose: 'in order to rescue/snatch me away.' Combined with the preposition to me (the suffix -ni), it is entirely personal: 'rescue ME.'
word_study.significance: Deliverance (hatzalah) is not generic blessing but specific rescue from active threat. The verb suggests being snatched from the jaws of danger—not a gentle release but an urgent extraction.

word_study.meaning: From azar, 'to help, aid, support.' The infinitive with le- again indicates purpose, and the suffix marks it personal: 'to come to my aid.' Ezrah ('help') often denotes God as an ally, a helper in battle.
word_study.significance: While hatzal stresses rescue from danger, azar stresses companionship in struggle. Together they portray God as both the one who removes threat and the one who stands alongside the sufferer.

cross_references.connection: Uses the identical verb chushah ('make haste') in the context of desperate prayer: 'But be not thou far from me, O LORD... make haste to help me, O LORD my salvation.'
Again employs chushah in distress: 'O God, be not far from me: O my God, make haste for my help.' The pattern across psalms establishes this as the language of covenant prayer in crisis.
Uses the same emergency verb in similar context: 'Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation,' showing the standardization of this phrase across the Psalter.
The Lord promises: 'I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left,' assuring that divine help is not distant or slow but present and engaged.

Nephi calls on the Lord to 'make haste to help' in his debate with the antichrist Jacob, using language that echoes Psalms 70 and shows the Nephite tradition holding fast to this vocabulary of urgent prayer.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern prayer literature (Ugaritic, Egyptian, Mesopotamian) frequently employs urgency language, especially in royal prayers and laments. The psalmist is not unique in demanding speed from the deity. However, Israel's covenant theology gives this demand a particular weight: the God of Israel has bound Himself by covenant to His people and has pledged swift response in distress. Deuteronomy 4:7 boasts, 'For what nation is there so great, who hath God so nigh unto them, as the LORD our God is in all things that we call upon him for?' This cultural confidence in divine accessibility—rooted in the Sinai covenant—underpins the psalmist's right to demand haste. The urgency is not disrespect but covenantal claim.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Enos's prayer (Enos 1:4) shows him 'crying unto the Lord in mighty prayer and supplication' until he receives an answer 'in the quiet of [his] soul.' The intensity of Enos's crying parallels the urgency of 'make haste' in Psalm 70:2—both show faith as active, demanding prayer, not passive resignation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1 records revelation to Joseph Smith: 'Hearken, O ye elders of my church, saith the Lord your God, who have assembled yourselves together, according to my commandments.' The Lord responds to covenant people who gather in His name, reflecting the same principle: God honors the urgent, covenantal appeal of His people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenant members speak divine names and make specific petitions, expecting God to hear and respond. The urgency of 'make haste' reflects the intensity with which temple prayer is offered—not as background meditation but as focused, directed petition.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ in Gethsemane exemplifies the prayer of Psalm 70:2. Though He asks the Father that 'this cup pass from me,' He also submits to the Father's will with urgency and intensity. His prayer in extremity models the trust embedded in the psalmist's demand: that God hears crisis and responds with compassionate speed.
commentary.application: When you face urgent need—financial crisis, health emergency, relational breakdown, spiritual wilderness—this verse gives you permission to pray with intensity and demand. Meek prayer has its place, but so does urgent supplication. The psalmist shows that calling on God's name with direct, repeated demand is faithful, not presumptuous. God's covenant binds Him to respond to His people's crisis. Speak your emergency plainly. Demand His haste. This is the language of trust.

text_kjv: Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt.

commentary.narrative: Having called on God to come with haste, the psalmist now describes what divine action should look like: the total reversal and public humiliation of those who seek his harm. Verse 3 employs four distinct verbs of shame and defeat, accumulating with mounting force: yevoshu ('let them be ashamed'), yachperu ('let them blush, be humiliated'), yissogu achor ('let them be turned back, retreat'), and yikkallemu ('let them be disgraced'). This is not a prayer for death but for defeat and shame. The enemies are identified by their intention: 'seekers of my life' (mevaqshey nafshi) and 'those who desire my harm' (chafetsey ra'ati). These are people actively working toward the psalmist's destruction. Yet the psalmist's prayer does not match their malice with a prayer for their death. Instead, it asks for their shame—their public humiliation before others. This reflects the ancient understanding that shame is a social death, a stripping of honor and standing within the community. In the psalmist's worldview, if God acts, the enemies will find themselves defeated, exposed, and disgraced in the eyes of all who witness. This is proportionate justice: they sought to destroy the psalmist's reputation; let their own reputation be destroyed.

word_study.meaning: From boshet, 'shame, disgrace.' As an imperative, 'let them be ashamed, let them feel shame.' The root carries both the emotion of shame and the social condition of being exposed as false or foolish.
word_study.significance: Shame in the Hebrew Bible is not mere internal feeling but public status. To be ashamed is to lose standing, credibility, and honor. The psalmist calls for the enemies to be stripped of their social dignity.

word_study.meaning: From chafar, 'to blush, be confused, be put to shame.' The verb carries the sense of social embarrassment and disorientation. As The Covenant Rendering renders it, 'let them be humiliated, let them blush.'
word_study.significance: Where boshet is public shame, chafar is the emotional accompaniment—the blushing, the confusion, the loss of composure. Together with the first verb, it paints a complete picture of social collapse.

word_study.meaning: From nagash (to drive back) with achor (backward). The verb indicates forced retreat, being driven back in defeat. In military contexts, it describes the retreat of a defeated army.
word_study.significance: This verb shifts from emotional to physical consequence: the enemies do not merely feel shame; they are actively driven back, defeated, forced to retreat. Their schemes come to naught.

word_study.meaning: From kalam, 'to be put to shame, be disgraced, bring shame upon.' The verb emphasizes the public and lasting nature of shame—disgrace that sticks, that defines the person going forward.
word_study.significance: This is the final verb of the sequence, and it brings the accumulation to its climax. The enemies will not merely feel shame momentarily; they will be marked by disgrace, their reputation permanently altered.

word_study.meaning: Mevaqshey ('seekers, pursuers') with nafshi ('my life, my soul, my being'). The phrase indicates not casual opposition but active, intentional pursuit of the psalmist's destruction. Nafshi carries the sense of the whole person, the animating life-force.
word_study.significance: This identifies the enemies not as mere critics or rivals but as predators actively stalking the psalmist. Their malice is not passive but dynamic. This justifies the intensity of the prayer for their reversal.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same vocabulary of enemies' shame: 'Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul,' showing this as a standard prayer against predatory enemies throughout the Psalter.
Another imprecatory psalm that prays for enemies to be clothed with shame and confusion, demonstrating the broad use of shame-language in psalms of lament and divine judgment.
The righteous are bold as a lion, but the wicked flee when no one pursues them—reflecting the same theology that evildoers' own fear and shame will drive them back.
The Lord promises His servants that their enemies 'shall be turned back because of their shame,' echoing the exact prayer of Psalm 70:3 and showing God's commitment to defending the righteous.
The people of Noah, who sought the life of Abinadi, are themselves turned back and confounded, fulfilling in real time the prayer pattern of Psalm 70:3.

commentary.historical_context: Shame and honor were the primary social currencies in the ancient Near East, more significant than guilt and innocence in some contexts. To be publicly shamed was to lose one's standing in the community, to be marked as false or wicked. The psalmist's prayer reflects this cultural reality: he does not ask for the enemies to be privately punished in some hidden judgment but to be publicly reversed and humiliated before the community that witnesses their threat. The accumulation of four shame-verbs in rapid succession echoes the rhetorical patterns of covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:15-68), where punishment is portrayed as an avalanche of reversals and humiliations. The psalmist is essentially invoking the covenant curse against those who violate the covenant by threatening a covenant member.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 30:50-60 describes Korihor's judgment: he becomes dumb, unable to speak, reduced to begging for bread—a graphic fulfillment of being 'ashamed and confounded.' The prayer pattern of Psalm 70:3 is enacted in history, showing God's faithfulness to turn back those who seek to harm His people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 110:7 records that angels will be sent to 'war against those nations, kingdoms, and people, who shall rise up against the Church of the Lamb of God.' The principle of divine defense against enemies is explicit in latter-day revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, covenants include the explicit recognition that covenant breakers will face divine judgment. The prayer of Psalm 70:3 aligns with the temple theology that God defends and vindicates those who keep their covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ, pursued by enemies and plotters throughout His ministry, embodies the psalmist's condition. His prayer for His enemies ('Father, forgive them') transforms the prayer of Psalm 70:3 into something higher—not asking for shame but for forgiveness and transformation. Yet Christ's enemies were indeed 'turned backward' and 'confounded' by the Resurrection, their plot to destroy Him utterly reversed by God's power.
commentary.application: This verse permits you to pray for God's judgment on those who actively seek to harm you—not from personal revenge but from covenant trust. When someone pursues you with malice, when predatory enemies stalk your family or reputation, you can bring that reality into prayer and ask God to expose them, turn them back, and strip away their power. This is not petty malice but covenantal justice. At the same time, this verse calls you to examine whether you yourself are a 'seeker of someone's life'—whether you pursue another's destruction. If so, the warning is implicit: you will be turned back and confused.

text_kjv: Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 narrows the focus and intensifies the mockery. Those identified in verse 3 by their predatory intent are now identified by their contempt: 'they that say, Aha, aha.' The exclamation he'ach he'ach ('Aha! Aha!') is not a neutral vocalization but a taunt of gloating malice. It is the sound of an enemy laughing at the psalmist's suffering, finding delight in his misery. To mock the suffering is to compound the injury—it transforms mere attack into contempt. The enemies do not simply wish the psalmist harm; they savor it, they exult in it. The prayer therefore asks for a precise reversal: 'Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame.' The word 'reward' (agam, from the verb 'to pay, repay, reward') suggests repayment in kind. The enemies who gloated at the psalmist's shame will themselves be repaid with shame. Their taunt will rebound on them. This is poetic justice at its most precise. The mockers will be mocked. The gloaters will experience the humiliation they wished for another. The verse embodies the principle of measure-for-measure judgment: you receive according to your actions.

word_study.meaning: An exclamation of triumph, mockery, or gloating. Often associated with contemptuous laughter or jeering. The doubling (he'ach he'ach) intensifies the malice.
word_study.significance: This is not casual speech but deliberate, contemptuous mockery. To say 'Aha!' in the context of another's suffering is to take delight in destruction. The psalmist marks the enemies not merely as those who harm but as those who revel in harm.

word_study.meaning: From the verb shakam or agam, 'to repay, reward, requite.' The noun means 'recompense, reward, repayment.' In this context, it indicates justice that is repaid—what one sows, one reaps.
word_study.significance: This word transforms the prayer from mere wishful thinking into an appeal to divine justice. The enemies will not simply be defeated; they will be paid back according to their deeds. Their own mockery becomes their recompense.

word_study.meaning: From nagash, 'to be driven back, forced to retreat.' The same verb appears in verse 3, showing continuity and accumulation of judgment.
word_study.significance: Repetition of this verb across verses 3 and 4 makes the point unmistakable: the enemies will not stand. They will be driven back. Their advance will be halted and reversed.

cross_references.connection: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.' The principle of retaliation that finds expression in Psalm 70:4 is enshrined as moral law in wisdom literature.

Describes enemies who mock and make light of the psalmist's suffering: 'They did tear me, and ceased not... with hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.' Shows the same dynamic of contemptuous enemies.

The prophet grieves that enemies have heard of Jerusalem's suffering and rejoice: 'They have heard that I sigh: there is none to comfort me.' The combination of suffering plus enemy gloating is a particular aggravation.
Describes the Lord's judgment of the wicked: their mockery and contempt toward the righteous will be their own condemnation. God's judgment is precisely calibrated to the offense.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern accounts of war and judgment frequently portray conquerors gloating over the defeated. Assyrian annals boast of humiliating conquered peoples. Egyptian records mock defeated enemies. The taunt ('Aha! Aha!') is the signature sound of the victor's contempt. In Israel, by contrast, covenant theology insisted that God would not tolerate permanent mockery of the righteous. The taunt would rebound. The gloaters would face their own humiliation. This reflects a unique moral confidence: the God of Israel guarantees that arrogant mockery will not have the last word. Justice will reverse it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Laman and Lemuel, who mock Nephi and his faithfulness, are themselves confounded and driven back by an angel (1 Nephi 3:29-31). Their taunts give way to fear and flight. The pattern of Psalm 70:4—mockers repaid with shame—is enacted repeatedly in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:23 warns: 'Cursed are all those that shall lift up the heel against mine anointed, saith the Lord, and cry they have sinned when they have not sinned before me, saith the Lord, but have done that which was meet in mine eyes, and all this that they may be found spotless before the bar of my judgment—and this shall be their lamentation in the day that they are judged.' Mockery of the righteous specifically invokes divine judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenant keepers are warned against those who would mock their covenants. The prayer of Psalm 70:4 aligns with the temple principle that God defends those who keep sacred vows against the contempt of the wicked.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ was mocked on the cross, and soldiers said 'Aha!' as they pierced Him. Yet His Resurrection and Ascension reversed their mockery entirely. Their gloating did not endure; Christ's vindication and glory lasted forever. Psalm 70:4 finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ's triumph over those who mocked Him.
commentary.application: When you are mocked for your faith, for your efforts to do right, or for your covenant keeping, this verse assures you that God sees the taunt and will answer it. The mockers do not have the final word. Bring the mockery into your prayers—name the specific contempt you face—and ask God to turn back those who gloat at your struggle. At the same time, examine whether you yourself taunt others. To laugh at another's suffering, to 'Aha!' their misfortune, is to invite the precise retaliation this verse describes. The mockers will be mocked.

text_kjv: Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified.

commentary.narrative: The psalm concludes with a stunning reversal. Verses 3-4 poured out prayers against enemies who seek the psalmist's harm and who mock his suffering. Verse 5 pivots to those who seek God Himself—not the psalmist's enemies but God's friends, those whose orientation is toward divine salvation rather than against human suffering. The structure of verse 5 directly mirrors the structure of verse 3: both begin with those who 'seek' (mevaqshey), but in opposite directions. Verse 3 condemns 'seekers of my life'; verse 5 blesses 'all who seek Thee.' This is not accidental parallelism but theological intentionality. The psalm sets before the reader two kinds of seekers: those seeking destruction and those seeking God. One will be ashamed; the other will rejoice. The two joy verbs—yasisu ('let them be joyful, exult') and yismechu ('let them be glad, delight')—directly match the two shame verbs of verse 3, creating a perfect structural and theological balance. For every curse on the wicked, a blessing on the righteous. The psalm concludes with its truest note: those who love God's salvation (yeshuatekha) will continually say, 'God is great!' This is not occasional praise but continuous (tamid) proclamation. The righteous do not merely celebrate a moment of deliverance; they embed praise into the rhythm of their lives, making the magnification of God their constant refrain.

word_study.meaning: From baqash, 'to seek, search for, desire, inquire of.' The plural form mevaqshekha refers to 'those who seek Thee.' This is the same verb root used in verses 3-4 ('seekers of my life'), but now redirected toward God.
word_study.significance: The word choice creates intentional irony: just as enemies actively 'seek' the psalmist's destruction, the righteous actively 'seek' God. Both are pursuits, but one leads to shame and one to joy. Your seeking defines your destiny.

word_study.meaning: Yasisu from sus, 'to be joyful, exult, delight.' Yismechu from samach, 'to be glad, rejoice, be happy.' Together, they constitute fullness of joy—internal delight and external expression.
word_study.significance: These are the same emotions the psalmist will feel when God delivers him. By praying that all who seek God experience this joy, the psalmist binds his own deliverance to the larger pattern of God's faithfulness to all the righteous.

word_study.meaning: Ohavey from ahav, 'to love, delight in, hold dear.' Yeshuatekha from yeshuah, 'salvation, deliverance, victory.' The phrase identifies the righteous not merely as those who want to be saved but as those who love God's saving action itself.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, this distinction is crucial. The righteous love not just their own safety but God's redemptive power. Their joy is not selfish survivalism but delight in God's mighty acts. They are covenant-lovers, not merely self-preservationists.

word_study.meaning: An adverb meaning 'continually, always, perpetually, without ceasing.' Often used to describe perpetual worship, constant praise, or enduring conditions.
word_study.significance: The righteous do not praise God once and then move on. Their magnification of God is built into the structure of their lives—constant, recurring, habitual. Praise becomes the grammar of existence.

word_study.meaning: From gadal, 'to be great, grow large, become mighty.' As a Pual form, it means 'let it be made great, let it be magnified.' This is a passive construction—God's greatness does not depend on human magnification, but human speech confirms and proclaims what is eternally true.
word_study.significance: The magnification of God is the psalmist's ultimate prayer—not 'Save me so I can live,' but 'be magnified, be exalted, be recognized as supreme.' The personal deliverance is ordered toward the larger goal of God's glory.

cross_references.connection: Uses nearly identical language: 'But let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, The LORD be magnified.' Shows this as a refrain embedded in multiple psalms.

Another parallel: 'Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the LORD be magnified.' Again demonstrates the standardization of this conclusion across the Psalter.

Paul writes: 'According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death.' The magnification of God through the faithful covenant-keeper is both Old and New Testament theme.

Describes the glory of the righteous: 'And now, after all these testimonies, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!' The continual testimony of the saved is that God is magnified through His redeeming work.

Ammon declares: 'Therefore, let us glory, yea, we will glory in the Lord; yea, we will rejoice, for our joy is full; yea, we will praise our God forever.' Echoes the pattern of Psalm 70:5—joy expressed as continual praise.

commentary.historical_context: The final verse of many psalms shifts from lament or imprecation to praise, a pattern called the 'turn' or 'pivot' in Hebrew poetry. This was not abrupt mood-swinging but theological intentionality: the resolution of prayer is always the magnification of God. Even in distress, the psalmist orients toward praise as the ultimate goal. In Israelite worship, such concluding praise would be sung or recited aloud, involving the whole congregation. The 'they' of 'let them rejoice' was not theoretical but actual—real worshipers in the sanctuary who would embody the praise being called for. This made the psalm not merely an individual's prayer but a communal resource that shaped collective identity around the magnification of God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:9-11 describes the power of small and simple things: through them 'great things are brought to pass.' The righteous, though small in number, magnify God through their continual praise. Abinadi's magnification of God before King Noah (Mosiah 12-13) exemplifies the pattern of verse 5—even before enemies, the covenant-keeper's ultimate commitment is to declare God's greatness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:104 teaches: 'Cease to find fault one with another; cease to sleep longer than is needful; retire to thy bed early, that ye may go to your labors early. Organize yourselves; prepare every needful thing; and establish a house, even a house of prayer, a house of fasting, a house of faith, a house of learning, a house of glory, a house of order, a house of God.' The entire structure of Zion exists to magnify God continually through unified commitment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the ultimate 'house of magnification'—the place where God is exalted and praised. Covenant members who engage in temple worship embody Psalm 70:5, participating in the continual magnification of God in a space set apart for that purpose.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ, at His Resurrection, became the ultimate object of continual praise. The righteous in all dispensations magnify God through Christ. Hebrews 1:3 describes Christ as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.' When the righteous magnify God, they are magnifying the God revealed through Christ. The last prayer of the psalm—'Let God be magnified'—is ultimately a prayer that Christ, God's supreme revelation, be exalted.
commentary.application: The psalm ends where it began: with seeking and remembrance. You began by asking God to remember your petition. You conclude by committing yourself to perpetual remembrance of God—to the continual magnification of His name. This is the resolution of all faithful prayer: from 'remember me' to 'I will magnify You.' In your own life, build the habit of tamid ('continually') magnifying God. Not once a week in church, but woven into daily life. Morning and night, in success and struggle, let your speech and thought continually testify that God is great. This is not rote repetition but the deep conviction that shapes every other commitment. When you seek God—not your enemy's shame or your own comfort, but God's kingdom—you will rejoice and be glad. This is the promise of Psalm 70:5.

text_kjv: In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 71 opens with a plea for refuge that deliberately echoes the opening of Psalm 31:2—a liturgical resonance that would have been immediately recognized by Israel's worshippers. The psalmist is not attempting originality but rather claiming tested words, prayers that have already proven their power in the community's worship. This choice is theologically significant: by quoting established liturgy, the psalmist places his personal crisis within a larger stream of faith. He is saying, in effect, 'I am not the first to need refuge, and I will not be the last. But I speak the words that saints have spoken before me.'

The verb 'put my trust' (chasiti, from chasah) carries a concrete, physical weight. To 'take refuge' in ancient Hebrew imagery is not a passive or merely emotional act—it is to flee actively, to run toward a stronghold, to hide in the shadow of a rock or fortress. The psalmist is vulnerable, but he is not helpless. He moves toward God with intentionality. The second clause intensifies the stakes: 'let me never be put to confusion' (shame) suggests that abandonment by God would not merely be painful—it would be a public humiliation, a sign that the psalmist's trust was misplaced. To be shamed is to be exposed as foolish before the watching community. The prayer thus stakes everything on God's faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: to take refuge, to flee for shelter, to hide. The root carries the image of running toward a protective fortress or hiding place. It implies both vulnerability (the need for shelter) and active agency (the choice to flee toward God rather than remain exposed).
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves the past tense—'I have taken refuge'—emphasizing that this act has already happened. The psalmist's trust is not something he is attempting to muster but something he has already done. This grounds his later petitions in an already-established relationship.

word_study.meaning: to be put to shame, to be confounded, to be exposed as foolish. In a communal context, shame is not merely private embarrassment but public humiliation before the watching community.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's prayer against shame reflects the ancient Israelite understanding that faith is not a solitary, interior matter but a public witness. To be abandoned by God would be to be exposed as one who trusted in a lie.

cross_references.connection: The opening of Psalm 31 reads 'In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be ashamed'—nearly verbatim repetition, indicating the psalmist's deliberate use of established liturgical language.
Another petition against shame coupled with trust in God: 'O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me.'
The Servant of the Lord declares, 'For the Lord GOD will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded'—the same word for shame used in a messianic context.
Alma, in his spiritual crisis, calls upon God: 'O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me'—echoing the pattern of seeking refuge in God's name during extremity.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the concept of 'refuge' or 'asylum' was both metaphorical and literal. Cities of refuge existed in Israel's law (Numbers 35), but the language of taking refuge in God represents a spiritual internalization of that legal practice. The psalmist speaks as one whose actual life circumstances—perhaps exile, persecution, or illness—have created a genuine need for protective shelter. The public dimension of shame was also deeply embedded in ancient honor-shame cultures; to be abandoned by one's God was not merely a private loss but a visible, communal disgrace.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of taking refuge in God during persecution appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma and his followers flee 'into the wilderness' and find refuge in God's protection (Alma 24:28–30). The phrase 'put my trust' echoes Nephite language of faith in times of extremity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 6:34 promises, 'Fear them not, for I am with thee'—God's presence functioning as refuge. The concept of being gathered as a refuge appears in D&C 29:8, 'Wherefore, I am the same that leadeth men to all good.'

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist seeking refuge in God prefigures the believers' ultimate refuge in Christ. Hebrews 6:18 states that believers 'have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us.' Jesus Himself becomes the 'strong habitation' (cf. verse 3) to which His followers flee for safety.
commentary.application: Modern readers in crisis often delay turning to God, waiting until they have exhausted other options. This verse invites a different posture: immediate, active flight toward God as refuge. The connection to established liturgy suggests that when our own words fail, we can draw on the tested prayers of the faithful tradition. In covenant community, our personal faithfulness has a public dimension—our shame or vindication affects our witness to others.

text_kjv: Deliver me in thy righteousness, and cause me to escape: incline thine ear unto me, and save me.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 escalates from a general cry for refuge (verse 1) to a specific petition grounded in a theological claim: the psalmist asks God to deliver him *in Your righteousness*. This is crucial to understanding how ancient Israel understood divine righteousness. The tsidqah of God is not abstract moral perfection or a distant attribute—it is active, saving intervention. To pray 'deliver me in Your righteousness' is to say: Your own character, Your own integrity, demands that You act. God's righteousness is not separate from His willingness to save; rather, righteousness *is* the saving action itself.

The verse then piles three imperatives upon God: 'deliver me' (tatssileni), 'rescue me' (tefalleteni), and 'save me' (hoshieni). The multiplication of commands reflects increasing desperation, but it also reflects faith—the psalmist speaks to God with the familiarity of one who believes he will be heard. The bracketing phrase 'turn Your ear toward me' personalizes this appeal. The psalmist is not asking for an abstract divine response but for God's *attention*—for God to bend down and listen to this particular voice. This intimate language suggests that the psalmist knows God personally, not merely as a cosmic principle.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, saving action. In the Psalms, tsidqah refers not to an abstract moral quality but to God's active intervention to vindicate and deliver those in the right. It is forensic and relational—God acts rightly by delivering the one who trusts Him.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not base his petition on his own merit but on God's character. This reframes the prayer: it is not 'Save me because I deserve it' but 'Save me because saving me is what Your righteousness requires.'

word_study.meaning: To cause to escape, to pull out, to extract from a tight or dangerous space. The image is of extraction from a trap, a collapsing structure, or a compressed hiding place. Implies being wrenched free from danger.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'rescue' captures the forceful sense better than 'cause me to escape.' The psalmist is not asking to slip away quietly but to be actively pulled to safety.

word_study.meaning: To turn one's ear, to incline toward listening, to give attention. The verb natah suggests bending or turning toward the speaker. It is an intimate gesture of listening, often used of a king turning his attention to a subject.
word_study.significance: This phrase personalizes the prayer. The psalmist asks not merely for rescue but for God's personal, attentive listening. It assumes familiarity and a relationship that has been established.

cross_references.connection: Nearly identical phrasing: 'Deliver me in thy righteousness... Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily.' The literary parallels suggest these were established liturgical formulas.
A prophecy of salvation: 'Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness'—God's righteousness as an active, descending force.
Paul echoes this Hebraic understanding: 'The righteousness of God... which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe'—righteousness as saving action.
Jacob teaches of 'the righteousness of God' as the power that 'shall sweep away the wicked off from you,' echoing the psalmist's sense of God's righteous action as deliverance.

Christ declares to the faithful: 'Hearken unto my voice, and go forth in my name, and do whatsoever I have commanded thee.' God's attentive hearing and personal direction parallel the psalmist's petition.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, righteousness (tsidqah in Hebrew, sedu in Akkadian) was often understood as relational and dynamic rather than abstract. A righteous king was one who 'saves' his people; a righteous judge delivers those in the right. The petitioner's appeal to God's 'righteousness' as grounds for deliverance reflects this understanding. The phrase 'incline thine ear' draws on courtroom or royal audience imagery—the speaker addressing a powerful figure in a position to grant or deny requests. The accumulation of imperatives ('deliver,' 'rescue,' 'save') was a stylistic feature of both Israelite and broader Near Eastern prayer texts, conveying urgency without disrespect.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The appeal to God's righteousness as grounds for deliverance appears in 1 Nephi 17:35, where Nephi declares that God 'loveth those who will have him to be their God.' The concept of God's saving righteousness—active intervention on behalf of the faithful—is central to Book of Mormon soteriology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 45:3-5 presents the risen Jesus as the one who 'answereth unto all things whatsoever the Father hath asked of him.' God's righteousness is fulfilled through Christ's willingness to listen and answer.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies God's righteousness in action. In 1 Corinthians 1:30, Paul writes that Christ is made unto believers 'righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption'—the active, saving righteousness for which the psalmist appeals. Christ is God's ear turned toward humanity and God's hand extended for rescue.
commentary.application: When facing difficulty, believers often worry that they lack sufficient merit to deserve God's help. This verse reframes the petition entirely: we appeal not to our worthiness but to God's character. God's righteousness requires Him to deliver those who trust in Him. In covenant practice, this suggests that bearing testimony of God's faithfulness—speaking of rescue already experienced—can be a form of prayer, inviting God to listen and act again in new circumstances.

text_kjv: Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress.

commentary.narrative:
In verse 3, the psalmist transforms the abstract concept of refuge into a dwelling place. He asks God to become a 'rock of refuge, a stronghold to enter continually' (tsur maon, labo tamid). The shift from momentary rescue (verses 1-2) to permanent habitation is theologically sophisticated. The psalmist is not asking for a one-time intervention but for an ongoing relationship in which he can repeatedly return to God's presence for protection. The phrase 'to enter continually' suggests habit, routine, and the formation of spiritual practice. Each time danger approaches, the psalmist has a place to go.

A remarkable claim follows: 'You have given commandment to save me' (tsivvita lehoshieni). The psalmist treats salvation not as a future possibility dependent on his petition but as a standing order already issued by God. This reflects a theological audacity grounded in past relationship. If God has already commanded his deliverance, then the psalmist is not begging for an unpromised favor but calling God to fulfill an already-established decree. The verse closes with a double assertion: 'for thou art my rock and my fortress.' The repetition of titles—rock and fortress, strength and refuge—is not poetic redundancy but accumulating certainty. Each name for God's protection reinforces the reality of his security.

word_study.meaning: A rock formation that serves as both fortress and dwelling. The image is of a cave or cliff dwelling carved into stone—protected by geography itself. Maon carries the sense of refuge, hideaway, and habitation combined.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering reads 'rock of refuge' rather than the KJV's 'strong habitation,' preserving the concrete geological image while maintaining the sense of shelter. The word maon appears in the Song of Moses (Exodus 15:13) to describe God's leading the redeemed people to His 'holy habitation.'

word_study.meaning: To enter repeatedly, habitually, without interruption. Tamid appears frequently in the Psalms to express the constancy of God's care or the psalmist's perpetual need for refuge.
word_study.significance: This phrase shifts the metaphor from a one-time hiding to a pattern of spiritual practice. The psalmist envisions himself as one who habitually returns to God's presence. This suggests spiritual discipline and the formation of rhythmic trust.

word_study.transliteration: tsavah (to command, decree) + yasha (to save, deliver)
word_study.meaning: You have given a command, issued a decree, that I be saved. Tsavah is the verb used for royal or divine decrees. It places salvation in the category of something already ordered, not something still uncertain.
word_study.significance: This is theologically daring language. The psalmist speaks as if salvation is not contingent on his current worthiness but is already divinely ordained. It reflects confidence born of relationship.

word_study.meaning: Rock emphasizes the natural, solid, unmovable quality of God's protection. Fortress emphasizes constructed defense—walls, parapets, strategically positioned fortification. Together they cover both natural and human means of security.
word_study.significance: The doubling reinforces the comprehensiveness of God's protection. Whether thinking of geological security or military fortification, God provides both.

cross_references.connection: Nearly identical: 'Be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me... Thou art my rock and my fortress.' The literary connection confirms the liturgical tradition underlying Psalm 71.

Moses' song declares, 'He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.' The rock metaphor for God's unchanging character.
David seeks refuge from Saul by going 'unto the hold' (metsudah)—the same word for fortress used here, showing the connection between political asylum and spiritual refuge.

Jesus teaches that one who hears His words and acts on them 'is like a wise man which built his house upon a rock: and the rain descended... but it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.' God's protection is unshakeable.

The Lord promises the faithful, 'Therefore, let your heart be comforted; fear not; what I have said, I have said.' God has already decreed the salvation of the faithful, echoing the psalmist's claim of a standing commandment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Judah, both the fortress city and the rock outcropping were real features of survival. Jerusalem itself was built on rocky terrain with natural water sources (the Gihon Spring). During times of unrest, people literally fled to fortified cities and rock caves (cf. 1 Samuel 13:6). The cave of Adullam, mentioned in 1 Samuel 22:1, was where David gathered his followers. The psalmist's language reflects this historical reality: refuge was not merely spiritual but geographical. A fortress provided actual defense; a cave provided actual shelter. The theological language thus grounds itself in lived experience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 5:12 contains a striking parallel: 'Remember that it is upon the rock of our Redeemer, who is Christ... that ye must build your foundation; that when the devil shall send forth his mighty winds... it shall have no power over you... because ye are built upon the rock.' The rock of Christ as both protection and foundation echoes verse 3.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 states, 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me; ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.' The repeated invitation to approach God reinforces the 'enter continually' theme.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple serves as the modern psalmist's 'rock and fortress'—the habitation to which one continually returns for spiritual refuge and renewal. The pattern of regular attendance echoes 'lavo tamid,' entering continually.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the rock of refuge. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:4 that the Israelites 'drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.' Christ is both the unchanging foundation and the source of perpetual spiritual sustenance.
commentary.application: Modern believers sometimes approach prayer as crisis management—turning to God only when problems become acute. This verse invites a different spiritual architecture: building a regular, habitual practice of entering God's presence. For Latter-day Saint readers, this might find expression in temple attendance, morning prayer, scripture study, or other spiritual disciplines that create a 'place' to which one continually returns. The claim that God has already 'commanded' our salvation should produce not passivity but grateful assurance that undergirds our efforts in covenant-keeping.

text_kjv: Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked, out of the hand of the unrighteous and cruel man.
text_kjv_alternate: Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked, out of the hand of the unrighteous and cruel man.

commentary.narrative:
After the theological assertion of verses 1-3, verse 4 returns to the concrete reality that necessitates these prayers: the psalmist faces actual enemies. The 'hand' of the wicked represents not mere hostility but active, pressing danger. To be 'in the hand' of an enemy is to be within their grasp, subject to their power. The verse does not describe the enemies in abstract theological terms but through a cascade of specific moral descriptors: they are 'rasha' (wicked), 'me-avvel' (unjust), and 'chomets' (ruthless, sour, oppressive).

The three-fold characterization creates a portrait of enemies whose corruption is comprehensive. They are not accidentally or temperamentally wicked; their character has been shaped by moral fermentation. The word 'chomets,' literally 'sour' or 'leavened,' carries an image of corruption that has permeated their entire being—like dough that has been exposed to unclean yeast. The repetition of 'hand' emphasizes the immediacy and intimacy of the threat. This is not distant, abstract evil but enemies whose hands are ready to strike. The psalmist's petition thus moves from theological principle (God's righteousness, established refuge) to visceral, embodied reality: fear of being crushed by those who wish him harm.

word_study.meaning: Wicked, guilty, one who acts contrary to law or justice. In biblical usage, wickedness is not merely a private moral failing but a violation of the social and divine order that affects others.
word_study.significance: The rasha represents not just moral evil but someone whose actions disrupt the community. The psalmist's petition against the wicked is thus a prayer for justice, not mere personal revenge.

word_study.transliteration: avvil (from avil, to act unjustly, to do wrong)
word_study.meaning: Unjust one, wrongdoer, one who perverts justice. The root avil carries the sense of twisting, bending, or distorting what should be straight and true.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves 'unjust' to capture the legal/judicial dimension. These enemies are not just personally cruel but corrupt in their treatment of justice.

word_study.transliteration: chometz (from cham, to be hot, sour, fermented)
word_study.meaning: Ruthless, sour, oppressive, one whose character has fermented into cruelty. The image is of something leavened, spoiled, or fermented to the point of being bitter and unusable. It suggests a person whose nature has been corrupted through and through.
word_study.significance: This rare word creates a visceral image of spiritual corruption. The enemy is not just a momentary threat but someone whose very essence has become corrupted. This reflects the psalmist's sense that the opposition is not accidental but rooted in the enemies' fundamental character.

cross_references.connection: Another prayer against enemies: 'Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the violent man.' The same language of 'hands' represents the active threat.

Peter describes the devil as 'as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist stedfast in the faith.' The enemy as active predator seeking to consume corresponds to the psalmist's portrayal of hands ready to strike.
Alma asks the faithful, 'Can you withstand the temptations of the devil?' echoing the Psalms' concern with rescue from active moral and spiritual enemies.

The Kirtland Temple prayer asks that God's people 'be delivered from the hands of our enemies, that we may stand independent above all other creatures beneath thy celestial throne.' The petition for deliverance from enemies' hands appears in LDS liturgy.

commentary.historical_context: Psalm 71 likely emerges from a period of political turbulence or personal persecution. The 'wicked' and 'unjust' enemies may refer to political rivals, religious opponents, or those seeking the psalmist's death. In ancient Israel, such threats were real and immediate—not metaphorical. Kings and prophets faced assassination attempts (2 Kings 6:8-10). The legal language ('unjust') suggests that the enemies were perhaps perverting justice itself to harm the psalmist, turning legal structures toward unrighteous ends. The prayer for deliverance thus addresses both the external threat and the injustice of the system that should have protected the psalmist.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently depicts the righteous as facing enemies who embody comprehensive moral corruption. The Lamanites, when influenced by Amalickiah, are portrayed as 'wicked and perverse' (Alma 51:21). However, the solution is always God's power, not the righteous' own strength—precisely the psalmist's posture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:28-29 describes the wicked as those who 'received not the testimony of Jesus in the flesh, but received it not.' The comprehensive rejection of truth corresponds to the psalmist's three-fold characterization of enemy wickedness.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ faced enemies who sought His death—'the hands of the wicked' came against Him in Gethsemane and at Calvary. Yet His response was not to call for their destruction but for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34). The psalmist's prayer for deliverance from enemies anticipates not merely physical rescue but the ultimate victory of Christ over spiritual wickedness through redemption rather than retaliation.
commentary.application: Modern believers face less obvious but no less real enemies: the 'wicked' and 'unjust' forces that attempt to derail faith and corrupt justice. This verse invites honest acknowledgment that such opposition exists and is not merely internal struggle but external reality. However, the cure is not defensive aggression but appeal to God's greater power. For those who face actual persecution (which many members in the worldwide Church do), this verse validates their experience and directs them toward the source of true deliverance.

text_kjv: For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 5, the psalmist begins the autobiographical turn that will become increasingly prominent in verses 5-6. This verse is transitional: it returns from the external threat (verse 4) to internal theological grounding. The psalmist declares that God is his 'hope' (tiqvah) and his 'trust' (mivtach), but with a temporal expansion: these are not recent developments born of current crisis. Rather, they stretch back to 'my youth' (mineuray).

This historical dimension is theologically potent. The psalmist is essentially arguing: 'I have had decades—my entire lifetime—of experience with God's faithfulness. If God is now abandoning me, He would be contradicting His own established pattern.' This is not the prayer of someone making a desperate leap toward an unknown God but the prayer of someone who knows God's character through long experience. The use of the covenant name 'Adonai YHVH' ('Lord GOD') signals solemnity and invokes the full weight of the covenant relationship. The conjunction 'for' (ki) connects this autobiographical claim to the petitions that precede: the reason God should deliver the psalmist is that God's faithfulness has already been established across a lifetime. Past grace becomes the basis for present petition.

word_study.meaning: Hope, expectation, something waited for. The root suggests both the state of waiting and the object of that waiting—what one hopes for. In biblical usage, hope is not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in God's character.
word_study.significance: Tiqvah appears frequently in Psalms as a steadfast conviction rather than mere optimism. The psalmist's hope is not that his circumstances will improve but that God will remain faithful. This is hope grounded in covenant.

word_study.transliteration: mivtach (from batach, to trust, to feel secure)
word_study.meaning: Trust, confidence, security. It describes both the act of trusting and the object of trust—God as the one who provides security. The noun form emphasizes the stability and reliability of the trust.
word_study.significance: Unlike chasah (refuge, shelter), which emphasizes fleeing toward protection, mivtach emphasizes resting secure in an established relationship. It is trust as ongoing confidence rather than crisis response.

word_study.meaning: This pairing combines the title of sovereignty (Adonai) with the covenant name (YHVH). It invokes God both as Master and as the one bound by covenant relationship.
word_study.significance: The doubling is relatively rare in the Psalms and signals particular solemnity. The psalmist is making an appeal to the full reality of God: both ultimate ruler and covenant partner.

word_study.meaning: From my youthful days, from childhood, from as long as I can remember. The temporal marker extends the psalmist's knowledge of God backward through his entire conscious life.
word_study.significance: This phrase is crucial to the psalmist's rhetorical strategy. The longer the relationship with God, the stronger the claim that God should not abandon him now.

cross_references.connection: Another psalmist recounts God's care 'from the womb': 'thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts.' The theme of lifelong divine care.

God declares through the prophet, 'For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end' (tiqvah in Hebrew). God's hope/expectation for His people.
Train up a child in the way he should go... reflects the biblical understanding that spiritual formation from youth establishes patterns that persist through life.
Nephi begins his account by noting his 'goodly parents' and the teaching he received 'in the learning of my people'—establishing that spiritual identity is formed from youth.

The Lord commands, 'And again, inasmuch as parents have children in Zion... they shall teach them to understand the doctrine of repentance, faith in Christ the Son of the living God.' This echoes the biblical pattern of lifelong spiritual formation beginning in youth.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the transition from youth (ne'urim) to old age (ziqnuth) was a recognized and significant life passage. The psalms often evoke this progression to invoke continuity with God's care. An elderly person recounting youth is, implicitly, someone with deep credentials to speak about God's faithfulness. The convention of beginning with youth also reflects a society where oral tradition and personal testimony were crucial to transmitting faith. The psalmist's recollection of his entire life becomes a form of instruction to others.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's account emphasizes that his faith was formed through 'goodly parents' who taught him 'the learning of my people' (1 Nephi 1:1). Alma the Younger's dramatic conversion leads him to teach from his youth (Mosiah 26:36). The pattern of lifelong faith formation characterizes Book of Mormon spirituality.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-8 contains the Lord's promise: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment... if thou knowest that thou hast kept my covenants thou shalt triumph.' The appeal to a history of covenant-keeping as grounds for present comfort echoes verse 5.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's own trust in God the Father, established from His youth and unshaken throughout His ministry and passion, exemplifies the kind of enduring faith to which the psalmist testifies. Hebrews 5:7-8 notes that Christ 'in the days of his flesh... was heard in that he feared; Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered.' His hope and trust were refined through trial.
commentary.application: This verse invites reflection on the arc of one's own spiritual journey. Conversion is not merely a moment but a lifetime of growing in relationship with God. For those nearing the end of life or facing significant trial, the memory of God's faithfulness across decades becomes a powerful resource. For younger members, consciously forming habits of hope and trust creates spiritual capital for future crisis. In covenant community, bearing testimony about lifelong faith—how God has been faithful 'since my youth'—becomes a form of strengthening others.

text_kjv: By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 pushes the timeline of God's care back beyond conscious memory to the moment of birth itself. The psalmist declares that he has been 'upheld' by God not just since youth (verse 5) but 'from the womb' (mibeten). This extension to birth represents the ultimate claim to God's foundational care. The psalmist did not choose God in youth; rather, God chose and sustained him from his very emergence into life.

The clause 'You drew me out from my mother's body' employs the rare word gozi (from gazah, 'to cut'), which likely refers to the cutting of the umbilical cord at birth. God is presented not merely as a distant guardian but as the intimate presence at the moment of birth itself—the midwife who severs the psalmist from the womb and brings him into independent life. This is intensely personal theology: God's care is not abstract or theoretical but grounded in the most vulnerable, foundational moment of human existence.

The consequence of this lifetime care is worship: 'My praise shall be continually of You.' The phrase 'tehillati tamid' (my praise is continual) echoes back to verse 3's 'lavo tamid' (to enter continually). Just as the psalmist habitually returns to God's refuge, so also his praise becomes a constant practice. The logic is complete: a lifetime of experience with God's faithfulness, grounded in care from before consciousness, naturally overflows in perpetual worship. The psalm moves from petition (verses 1-4) through testimony (verses 5-6) to the promise of perpetual praise. This is the trajectory of true faith: from crisis prayer to established confidence to continuous thanksgiving.

word_study.transliteration: samach (to support, to uphold, to lean upon)
word_study.meaning: I have been supported, upheld, sustained. The verb samach describes both physical support (being held up) and emotional/spiritual reliance (leaning upon someone). The niph'al form emphasizes the passive reception of support.
word_study.significance: The past tense 'I have been upheld' implies that the upholding is not hypothetical but proven through experience. The psalmist is not hoping for support but confirming support already received.

word_study.transliteration: beten (womb, belly, the internal space of pregnancy)
word_study.meaning: From the womb, from before birth, from the time of gestation. Beten describes the physical location of the developing fetus, hence the earliest possible moment of human existence.
word_study.significance: By anchoring God's care in beten, the psalmist makes the strongest possible claim to foundational divine relationship. This is not a faith chosen in adulthood but a reality established before consciousness.

word_study.term_english: took me out / drew me out
word_study.transliteration: gazah (to cut, to sever, to draw out)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'my cutter' or 'the one who cut me out.' This rare form likely refers to the cutting of the umbilical cord, making God the midwife who brings the child from womb to independent life. Some scholars debate the word's origin, but the context of birth imagery (beten, me'ei immi) strongly supports this reading.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'drew me out' captures the action while avoiding the medical specificity of 'cut the umbilical cord,' which might seem anachronistic. Yet the underlying image is of God's hands present at the most vulnerable moment of transition from protected womb to exposed world.

word_study.meaning: The internal organs, specifically the womb. The word me'im appears in contexts of deep emotion ('moved in his bowels,' i.e., moved with compassion) and in contexts of birth. Here it refers to the physical location of gestation.
word_study.significance: The visceral language—'bowels,' 'womb'—grounds theology in embodied reality. This is not abstract belief but lived, physical experience.

word_study.transliteration: tehillah (praise, song of praise) + tamid (continually, perpetually, without ceasing)
word_study.meaning: My praise is continuous, uninterrupted, perpetual. Tehillah describes both the act of praising and the hymn or song that expresses praise. Tamid emphasizes that this praise is not occasional but constitutive of the psalmist's ongoing existence.
word_study.significance: The promise of perpetual praise is the logical outcome of perpetual care. A life of continuous trust produces a life of continuous thanksgiving.

cross_references.connection: A parallel expression of care from the womb: 'But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts.' The same pattern of foundational divine care from birth.
God speaks to Jacob: 'Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the womb... Fear not, O Jacob, my servant.' God's forming and care from the womb as grounds for confidence.
God says to Jeremiah, 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee.' God's knowledge and consecration precede conscious existence.
Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, recognizes the unborn John the Baptist moving in her womb. The womb becomes a location of spiritual awareness and God's presence.

Nephi declares, 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them.' God's foundational care and preparation parallel the psalmist's experience from the womb.

The Lord states, 'And in that day the enmity of man, and the enmity of beasts, yea, the enmity of all flesh, shall cease to be, as it has been so it shall be; and our earth shall be as the Garden of Eden.' God's care extends from the beginning to the consummation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the survival of childbirth was not guaranteed. High maternal and infant mortality meant that successful birth was viewed as a divine miracle and blessing. The family and extended kin group would gather at birth; older women (like Elizabeth, John the Baptist's mother) would serve as midwives. The fact that the psalmist reaches old age (implied by his retrospective of a lifetime) is itself evidence of God's faithfulness from the beginning. The image of God as 'the one who cut me free' echoes not only the medical reality of childbirth but also covenantal language: separation from Egypt, circumcision as covenant marking, the ritual severing of the Passover lamb. To be 'cut free' is to enter a new state of existence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma describes his dramatic conversion in language that echoes birth into new life: 'I was racked with eternal torment... Behold, I am born of the Spirit' (Alma 36:17-23). The Nephite understanding of spiritual rebirth—being 'born of God,' becoming a 'new creature'—parallels the psalmist's sense of God's foundational care as a kind of spiritual birthing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 45:3 states that Christ 'receiveth not the things of this world, neither the honors of the world.' Yet in verses preceding, Christ is shown as one 'filled with the love of God, with fervent charity, as the very heart of love.' God's love for His children begins before they are born and continues perpetually. The concept of 'being born again' in D&C 20:37 and throughout Restoration texts echoes the psalmist's sense of God's care at the threshold of life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple language of 'newness of life' and covenant rebirth—being 'born again' through ordinances—parallels the psalmist's experience of God as the one who 'drew him out' from the womb. Baptism and endowment involve passage through new thresholds of divine relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's birth narrative in Luke and Matthew emphasize God's providential care over the miraculous conception and vulnerable infant. The angel at His birth declares, 'Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21)—affirming that even in infancy, Christ is bound by divine covenant to save. Christ's entire earthly life, from conception through resurrection, displays God's continuous care.
