Moreover, Christ's perpetual intercession (Hebrews 7:25) corresponds to the psalmist's promise of 'continually' praising God.
commentary.application:
Modern believers often locate their faith primarily in choices they consciously made—the moment they were baptized, married in the temple, served a mission. This verse invites recognition that God's care predates conscious choice. Parents and grandparents who prayed for children yet unborn, God's covenant promises that extend to generations, and the Church's theology of premortal existence all underscore a truth the psalmist grasps: we are known and upheld by God from before memory.

For those facing significant life changes—aging, loss of former strength or capacity, approaching death—this verse offers profound consolation. The God who upheld me from the womb is upheld me through every transition. The promise of 'continual praise' transforms hardship into worship: even the losses of aging, the pains of illness, the approach of mortality can become occasions of praise for a God whose faithfulness extends from womb to tomb and beyond.

text_kjv: I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist opens this section with a profound theological tension. His life—marked by suffering and visible affliction—has become a public spectacle, an interpretive text that others read and judge. The Hebrew word mofet (sign, wonder, portent) is deliberately ambiguous. It can denote a miraculous sign of God's favor (as in the Exodus plagues), but here it carries the weight of ambivalence: the psalmist's suffering makes him an object lesson, perhaps a cautionary warning, possibly a sign of divine rejection. This is the experience of the afflicted in any age—their pain becomes commentary, their body becomes text.

Yet the adversative 'but' (ve-attah) that opens the second line pivots the entire verse theologically. The psalmist does not deny his visible affliction or the interpretations others draw from it. He concedes the fact of his suffering and its public visibility. What he refuses to concede is its theological meaning. Regardless of what observers conclude, the psalmist knows something they do not: God remains his strong refuge (machasi oz). The phrase machasi-oz combines machseh (shelter, refuge, hiding place) and oz (strength, might, fortress). God is not distant or indifferent; He is the psalmist's active shelter and strength. The verse thus models a spiritual practice: holding fast to God's protective reality even when external circumstances invite a different narrative.

word_study.meaning: A sign, portent, or wonder. Can denote miraculous signs (as in Exodus 7:3 for the plagues) or ominous portents and objects of judgment (Deuteronomy 28:46, 'a sign and a wonder' referring to curses). The word carries inherent ambiguity—it is a phenomenon that demands interpretation. In this context, the psalmist's affliction has become publicly visible and is being read as evidence against him.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that mofet is 'charged'—the psalmist's suffering is not merely personal but has become a public text being misread. The psalmist's body and circumstance are being interpreted by observers as proof that God has rejected him. This captures the existential weight of public suffering: not only pain, but the burden of others' judgments upon that pain.

word_study.meaning: A compound construction: machsei (shelter, refuge, hiding place; from chasa, to seek refuge, to take shelter) + oz (strength, might, fortress). The combination emphasizes God as both a place of safety and an active source of protective strength. Machseh appears throughout the Psalter as a refuge from enemies (Psalm 2:12, 'Blessed are all they that put their trust in him'; Psalm 36:7, 'How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God').
word_study.significance: This is not passive safety but active fortress-protection. The psalmist's claim is that despite appearing abandoned by observers, his refuge is both real and strong—a sheltering place that actively fortifies him against the threats closing in.

word_study.meaning: Conjunction + pronoun: 'and you' or 'but you.' The emphatic second-person pronoun (attah) with the conjunction creates an adversative force—'but you,' marking a sharp theological reversal or contrast. This construction carries weight when it pivots from a negative clause to an affirmation of God's character or action.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this 'but' carries 'the entire theological weight of the verse.' It is not merely a grammatical connector but a theological statement: whatever others say about the psalmist's condition, whatever interpretation they draw, God's protective presence remains the counter-reality. The adversative 've-attah' is a recurring device in the Psalter for asserting God's faithfulness against apparent abandonment.

cross_references.connection: God tells Moses that he will multiply His 'signs and wonders' (otot umofetim) in Egypt. The word mofet in Psalm 71:7 echoes this miraculous meaning, but the psalmist applies it to his own suffering—inviting us to read affliction as a sign that God is at work, not absent.

The curses of the covenant will 'be upon thee for a sign and for a wonder' (le-ot ve-le-mofet)—here mofet denotes judgment and divine action against the disobedient. The psalmist's awareness of this usage deepens the interpretive crisis: observers are reading his suffering as a curse-sign, but he protests that God remains his refuge.

Another suffering psalm where the taunt rings out: 'He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him' (implying that God has not). Psalm 71:7 shares this pattern—the psalmist's visible affliction invites enemies to conclude that God has abandoned him.
Celebrates God's lovingkindness and the shadow of His wings as a refuge (machseh). Psalm 71:7 echoes this trust in God as an active shelter despite visible circumstances.

Ammon declares that he is 'a sign...unto those people,' having been given power to work among the Lamanites. Like the psalmist, those engaged in covenant work may become signs—examples whose afflictions and faithfulness become instructive to observers.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, physical affliction was often read as a sign of divine disfavor or curse (as seen in Job's comforters' reasoning). The sufferer bore not only pain but also social shame—the assumption that God had withdrawn His blessing. Old age compounded this vulnerability; an aging person without active family protection faced abandonment or exploitation. The psalmist's situation—visible suffering and the public's negative interpretation of it—reflects the real social dynamics of the ancient world. His defiant claim that God remains his refuge directly contradicts the visible 'proof' that others see in his suffering.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's experience in Alma 36 parallels this verse: he too became a sign to many (his conversion and subsequent missionary work becoming an interpretive text read by others), yet he maintained unshakeable confidence in God's redeeming power. The pattern appears again in Moroni's closing testimony—the book of Mormon itself becomes a 'sign and wonder' to the world, subject to interpretive dispute, yet ultimately a vehicle of God's protecting truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 31:9 speaks of persecution and shame that will come upon the faithful, yet promises: 'I am in your midst.' Like the psalmist, the Lord assures His covenant people that regardless of outward appearances of abandonment, His protective presence is active and real.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language of 'refuge' (machseh) and 'strong fortress' (oz) appears in temple liturgy and covenant language. To take refuge in God is to enter into the protection of the covenant—a sheltering that is both intimate ('my refuge') and mighty ('strong').

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's suffering that makes him a 'sign to many' prefigures Christ, who became the ultimate interpretive text. His crucifixion was read by observers as proof of divine rejection ('if thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross'—Matthew 27:40), yet it was the supreme act of God's protective love. Christ became a 'sign and wonder' (mofet) in the fullest sense—a phenomenon that demanded interpretation and revealed the observer's spiritual state. Those who trust God see His redemptive power; those without faith see only defeat.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the spiritual experience of visible suffering. When our afflictions become public—illness, grief, loss, struggle—others will interpret them. Some may conclude that God has abandoned us. The psalmist invites us to hold two truths simultaneously: (1) acknowledge the reality and visibility of our suffering, and (2) refuse to let others' interpretations of that suffering determine our theology. God's protective presence is not suspended when we are weakened or visible. Our calling is to know this reality ourselves and, in due time, to become a sign of God's faithfulness to observers who are watching how we bear affliction.

text_kjv: Let my mouth be filled with thy praise and with thy honour all the day.

commentary.narrative:
This verse shifts from petition to declaration of intent. The psalmist does not ask God to fill his mouth; he wills it. This is not passive waiting for inspiration but active disciplined speech—a spiritual practice of filling one's mouth with praise and glory despite the afflictions just named. The parallelism pairs tehillateka (Your praise) with tif'artteka (Your splendor, glory, beauty). Praise here is not mere thanksgiving but declaration of God's magnificent character. It is the public proclamation of who God is, not merely gratitude for what He does.

The phrase 'all day long' (kol hayyom) signals perpetuity. This is not momentary enthusiasm or crisis-driven piety but habitual, intentional speech throughout the day. The Covenant Rendering notes that this phrase 'echoes verse 24 and creates a frame of perpetual worship,' suggesting that the entire psalm is structured around this commitment to continuous praise. The paradox is striking: the psalmist has just described being a spectacle of suffering, enemies conspiring against him, and the threat of abandonment. Yet his response is to resolve that his mouth will be the instrument of praise. This reveals a fundamental spiritual posture: the decision to speak God's reality rather than circumstance, to voice His splendor rather than one's own pain.

word_study.meaning: Praise, song of praise, hymn. From hallel (to praise, to celebrate). The word denotes not merely appreciation but active celebration and vocal declaration of God's greatness. Tehillim (Psalms) is the plural form—a collection of praises. Tehillah can be intensely personal ('my praise is of thee'—Psalm 22:25) or communal.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not pray for contentment or acceptance of affliction. He commits to vocal, active praise—the deliberate declaration of God's character. This is not emotional piety but disciplined speech that counters the alternative narratives circulating (that God has abandoned him).

word_study.meaning: Beauty, splendor, glory, adornment. From pa'ar (to glorify, to adorn). The word conveys both aesthetic majesty and active magnificence. In the Psalter, tif'eret often describes the visible manifestation of God's power and beauty (Psalm 26:8, 'the beauty of the Lord'; Psalm 90:16, 'thy work...thy glory'—using tif'ar).
word_study.significance: Paired with tehillah, tif'eret emphasizes that praise declares not God's benefits to us but His inherent majesty. The psalmist's mouth will pour forth the splendor—the magnificent beauty—of God's being. This is God-centered rather than self-centered worship.

word_study.meaning: All the day, throughout the day, the whole day long. A phrase that signals continuity and constancy. Kol means 'all, whole, every'; yom means 'day.' The phrase captures perpetual practice across the span of waking hours.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's note that this 'echoes verse 24' is significant—the framing of the psalm around 'all day' worship suggests that continuous praise is not an occasional practice but a fundamental orientation. Even in suffering, the psalmist commits to this vocal, daily discipline.

cross_references.connection: The final verse of Psalm 71 echoes this language: 'My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long.' The repetition of 'all day' frames the entire psalm as a commitment to perpetual praise despite affliction.

'LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.' Like Psalm 71:8, this verse celebrates the beauty (tif'eret—honor, glory) of God's presence and commits to dwelling there through praise.

'And my tongue shall speak of thy righteousness and of thy praise all the day long.' This verse uses identical language to Psalm 71:8, establishing a theme: the afflicted saint commits to vocal witness and praise despite circumstances.

'Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.' Paul echoes the psalmist's call to continuous praise—not as emotional denial but as spiritual discipline that reorients the soul toward God's reality.

'And let all thy doings be in the name of the Lord, and thy designs shall be established, and thy plans shall be made known.' The principle of constant reference to God's character and purpose, living with intentional awareness of His majesty, parallels the psalmist's commitment to fill his mouth with praise all day long.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern worship, the recitation of divine praise and the declaration of God's attributes were central liturgical practices. Psalms were sung in temple worship and at gatherings. The psalmist's commitment to 'fill his mouth' with praise reflects a culture in which vocal, public declaration of God's greatness was both spiritual discipline and communal witness. Praise was not private sentiment but public speech—a proclamation that shaped how community members understood ultimate reality. In a context where suffering tempted observers to conclude that God had abandoned the afflicted, the psalmist's determination to proclaim God's splendor was a counter-narrative, a refusal to let circumstance define theology.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:35-36 presents a similar pattern: despite tribulation and opposition, Alma declares, 'I will glory in my Jesus; for he hath redeemed my soul from hell.' The commitment to vocal praise and declaration of God's greatness characterizes the Book of Mormon's most powerful witnesses. Nephi's psalm (2 Nephi 4:15-35) employs identical language about filling the soul with praise despite affliction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 19:37 instructs: 'Let thy words condescend upon the people as the dews upon the tender grass.' The principle is that the mouth becomes an instrument of spiritual power and witness. Psalm 71:8's commitment to praise connects to the principle that 'the tongue of the righteous is choice silver' (Proverbs 10:20), shaping reality through words.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language of 'filling the mouth' with praise connects to covenantal speech and testimony. In temple contexts, the mouth becomes sanctified for witness and declaration. Psalm 71:8 reflects this principle: the psalmist's speech becomes an instrument consecrated to God's glory.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's mouth was 'filled' with a different kind of declaration—not boastful praise but the patient proclamation of God's kingdom, even when it led to His suffering. Yet the Psalter finds its fullest interpretation in Christ's resurrection and exaltation, where His mouth indeed proclaims God's splendor 'all the day' (eternally). The psalmist's discipline of filling his mouth with praise anticipates the way Christ's glorified voice will celebrate the Father's majesty forever.
commentary.application: This verse invites us into a spiritual discipline: intentional, deliberate speech that proclaims God's character and majesty. Not as denial of real suffering, but as an active choice to let our words reflect ultimate reality. In an age of complaint, negativity, and the amplification of grievance through social media, this verse calls us to a countercultural practice: let your mouth be filled with praise 'all the day'—in your conversations, your thoughts, your witness. This is not suppression of pain but the refusal to let pain have the final word. What we say shapes what we believe, and what we believe shapes how we persevere.

text_kjv: Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth.

commentary.narrative:
This verse is the emotional and theological center of Psalm 71. The raw vulnerability here cuts through any remaining distance between reader and psalmist. The verb tashlikeni ('cast me off, throw me away') is violently physical—it describes discarding something no longer useful, like a broken tool or a worn garment thrust aside. The psalmist does not ask for healing or restoration; he asks for presence. The phrase 'in the time of old age' (le-et ziqnah) names what the psalmist fears most—not death itself, but abandonment before death, rejection when he is most vulnerable and most needy.

The parallel line deepens the plea: 'when my strength is spent, do not abandon me' (kikhlot kochi al ta'azbeni). Kiklot kochi literally means 'when my strength is finished'—the psalmist does not deny physical decline or try to pretend it is not happening. He acknowledges directly that his power is waning. The theological argument implicit here is devastating in its clarity: weakness is not grounds for divine rejection. This contradicts a widespread ancient (and modern) assumption that God's favor is proportional to one's utility or strength. The psalmist argues the opposite: covenant love must be precisely most present when strength fails.

The Covenant Rendering notes that 'This verse has no parallel in Psalm 31, confirming that Psalm 71 is not merely a copy but an original composition shaped by the experience of aging.' This detail is crucial: the psalmist is not recycling ancient formulas but speaking from the particular ache of old age. And the plea against abandonment in old age is 'theologically distinctive in the Psalter'—few other psalms name aging as a spiritual crisis point in quite this way. The verse honors old age not as a season of rest and reward but as a time of maximum vulnerability when covenant fidelity is tested most severely.

word_study.meaning: Cast, throw away, hurl forth. From shalachim (to throw, to cast out). The verb conveys violent rejection and discarding. It is used elsewhere for casting out demons (Luke 9:42 in LXX contexts), for abandoning things no longer needed, for military throwing of spears. It is not gentle separation but forceful rejection.
word_study.significance: The psalmist chooses a word that emphasizes the violence of potential abandonment. He is not asking God to maintain a distant benevolence but to refrain from active rejection. The intensity of the verb matches the intensity of the fear.

word_study.meaning: Old age, the time of being old. From zaqen (to be old, to grow old, to become aged). The noun denotes a life stage characterized by diminished physical capacity. In Levitical law (Leviticus 19:32), elders are to be honored; in wisdom literature, age brings counsel and authority. Yet ziqnah also appears in contexts of decline and vulnerability.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translator notes emphasize that in 'a culture that honored elders (Leviticus 19:32), the fear of being cast off in old age represents a profound social and theological crisis.' Aging in the ancient world was not a secure season but one fraught with risk—economic dependence, physical vulnerability, social marginalization. The psalmist's plea is rooted in the real dangers of aging without family or divine protection.

word_study.meaning: Strength, power, ability, vigor. From a root meaning to be strong or mighty. Koach denotes physical strength, military power, and vital capacity. When koach fails, the ability to work, defend oneself, and maintain independence is compromised.
word_study.significance: The psalmist uses a term that encompasses not merely physical vigor but the capacity for effective action and autonomy. When koach is finished, the psalmist faces not only physical weakness but loss of agency and independence.

word_study.meaning: Do not abandon me, do not leave me, do not forsake me. From azab (to abandon, to leave, to forsake). The negative imperative 'al ta'azbeni' is the parallel structure to the opening 'al tashlikeni'—both are pleas against different forms of divine rejection.
word_study.significance: While tashlikeni suggests violent casting out, ta'azbeni suggests withdrawal or passivity—leaving the psalmist alone. Together, the two verbs cover the full range of possible divine rejection: either active throwing out or passive abandonment. The psalmist is asking God to do neither.

cross_references.connection: 'Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man.' The law commands honor for the aged. Psalm 71:9 assumes this cultural norm and argues that if human society must honor elders, surely God must not abandon them—making the psalmist's plea not merely personal but covenantally grounded.

A parallel lament: 'Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am in trouble...my soul and my belly'—expressing physical distress. Though Psalm 31 does not focus on aging as specifically as Psalm 71:9, both psalms plead against divine abandonment during affliction.

'And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.' This prophetic promise directly addresses the psalmist's fear, assuring that God does not abandon in old age but actively 'carries' the aged.

Nephi speaks of his own struggles and declares: 'My spirit hath had no space to expand itself, because of the narrowness of the way...Notwithstanding the Lord hath been merciful in keeping me that I have not been carried away.' The pattern of pleading for God's protective presence despite affliction and weakness appears in Book of Mormon scripture.

In the midst of Joseph Smith's persecution and imprisonment, the Lord assures: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul...the integrity of your heart...shall make you more precious than fine gold.' The psalmist's plea not to be cast off in weakness is answered by this covenant promise that weakness does not diminish divine regard.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, aging without family protection was catastrophic. The extended family or kinship network provided economic security, care, and social standing in old age. To be abandoned in ziqnah meant economic destitution, physical vulnerability to exploitation or abuse, and social shame. The Israelite law codes reflect this reality—parents were to be honored and cared for (Exodus 20:12, 'Honour thy father and thy mother'). The psalmist's fear of being cast off in old age is not abstract anxiety but grounded in social reality. His appeal to God is ultimately an appeal for what human society is mandated to provide: honor and protection for the aging. If family fails (which the context suggests they have), God remains the last recourse.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes God's covenant promise to never leave or forsake the righteous. Nephi's personal psalm (2 Nephi 4) echoes Psalm 71 in structure and theology—a cry of affliction coupled with a reaffirmation of God's protective covenant. The principle that age does not diminish God's regard appears in the accounts of aged leaders like Alma and Lehi, who received visions and guidance in their final years.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 teaches: 'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.' The promise to those of little strength is that they need not be abandoned if they maintain faith. D&C 121, written by Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail during profound affliction, reframes the logic of Psalm 71:9—abandonment by enemies does not mean abandonment by God. The psalmist's fear finds its answer in restored covenant theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant renewed in temple worship is precisely a covenant against abandonment. The endowment teaches that God's protective presence accompanies the faithful through every stage of life, including aging and infirmity. The language of 'forsaking' appears in temple contexts as the supreme test of faith—will we maintain loyalty even when God's presence seems withdrawn?

commentary.christological_typology: Christ, in His suffering on the cross, cries out with language echoing this verse: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). Yet Christ's cry is answered not by rescue but by resurrection—the Father does not 'cast off' the suffering Son but vindicates Him through exaltation. The psalmist's plea against abandonment in old age finds its ultimate answer in Christ, who descended into death (the ultimate aging and weakness) and was not left there but was raised. Christ's resurrection proves that weakness and aging do not trigger divine abandonment but divine redemption.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to one of modernity's deepest anxieties: the fear of irrelevance and abandonment as we age. A culture that values productivity and youth often casts the elderly as burdensome—used up, no longer useful. Psalm 71:9 rejects this logic utterly. The psalmist argues that covenant love does not fluctuate with utility. As we ourselves age or watch parents and mentors enter old age, this verse calls us to a radical commitment: to honor and care for the aging precisely because they are weaker, not in spite of it. And for those entering old age, it invites trust—not denial of physical decline, but confidence that declining strength does not trigger divine abandonment. God's covenant is most radiant when ours is most dim.

text_kjv: For mine enemies speak against me; and they that lay wait for my soul take counsel together,

commentary.narrative:
The verse shifts focus from the psalmist's internal plea to the external threat: enemies are conspiring. The phrase 'lay wait for my soul' (shomrei nafshi) describes predators watching for the moment of vulnerability. They are not merely hostile; they are strategic and patient. The phrase nafshi (my soul, my life) uses a word that encompasses both one's physical life and one's essential being. The enemies do not seek mere defeat; they seek to destroy the psalmist's very being.

The phrase 'take counsel together' (noa'atzu yachd) indicates collaborative conspiracy. This is not random hostility but organized plot. The verb noa'atz (to take counsel, to consult together) appears in contexts of deliberate strategy. The enemies have conferred and settled on their course of action. What makes their conspiracy particularly effective is its timing: they wait for the moment when the psalmist's strength is spent, precisely as verse 9 has just named. Old age, which makes the psalmist vulnerable, also makes him vulnerable to enemies who perceive his weakness.

The theological structure of Psalm 71 is now becoming clear: the psalmist faces a perfect storm. Internally, he confronts his own aging and the terrifying prospect of divine abandonment. Externally, he faces enemies who, perceiving his weakness, plot his destruction. Neither threat is imaginary; both are real and acute. The verse does not minimize the danger but names it with precision. Enemies speak, watch, consult, and conspire. They are coordinated and patient predators.

word_study.meaning: Those who watch for my life, those who lie in wait for my soul. Shomer means watcher, guard, or sentinel; nafshi means soul, life, self, being. The phrase describes predators watching for the right moment to strike—hunters tracking prey, military scouts watching for an opening, enemies waiting for vulnerability.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that they 'are not merely hostile; they are strategic, waiting for the right moment to strike—and old age provides it.' The phrase captures the calculated patience of malice, not merely immediate attack but deliberate timing to maximize the victim's vulnerability.

word_study.meaning: They took counsel together, they consulted with one another, they plotted collectively. Noa'atz (from ya'atz, to give counsel, to advise, to plot) in the Niphal form means to deliberate or take counsel. Yachd (together, collectively) emphasizes unified action. The phrase denotes organized conspiracy, not sporadic hostility.
word_study.significance: The enemies have coordinated their strategy. This is not random attack but deliberate, collaborative effort. In the Psalter, this phrase appears in contexts where multiple antagonists unite against the righteous (Psalm 2:2, 'The kings of the earth set themselves...against the LORD'; Psalm 83:5, 'they have consulted together with one consent').

word_study.meaning: They said, they spoke, they declared. From amar (to say, to speak, to declare). The verb is simple but denotes the power of speech to shape reality. In Hebrew thought, words are not merely descriptive but performative—they enact what they declare.
word_study.significance: The verse begins with enemies' speech, suggesting that their words are a weapon as significant as any physical action. They do not merely hate the psalmist; they speak against him, using language to demean, to spread suspicion, to turn community against him.

cross_references.connection: 'The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD.' The same language of coordinated conspiracy appears in the context of opposition to God's anointed. Psalm 71:10 applies this cosmic pattern to the personal level—enemies organize against the vulnerable.

'For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee.' Again, the language of 'counsel together' (ya'atz) describes organized opposition. The pattern is repeated throughout the Psalter: enemies do not act randomly but deliberately coordinate their hostility.

'A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.' The enemies' speech (verse 10) is a weapon that divides and destroys community. Their words 'speak against' to create social isolation around the psalmist.

'Now the chief priests, and elders, and all the council, sought false witness against Jesus, that they might put him to death.' The enemies' conspiracy against Jesus follows precisely the pattern of Psalm 71:10—they 'take counsel together' and 'speak against' the righteous one they wish to destroy.

Zeezrom, perceiving the weakness in Alma's explanation, 'began to contend with him, seeking to trip him up, that he might commit himself and thus render himself an easy prey to his destruction.' The enemies' strategy of waiting for vulnerability and then striking—exactly as Psalm 71:10 describes—appears in the Book of Mormon.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern contexts, conspiracy and coordinated opposition were real social dangers. The weak or marginalized (particularly aging individuals) were especially vulnerable to organized hostility. The psalmist's reference to enemies who 'lay wait' (watching for vulnerability) reflects the actual social dynamics of ancient communities where reputation, patronage, and protection networks determined survival. An aging person without active protectors or family support would indeed be prey to those who sought advantage. The reference to coordinated counsel suggests that the enemies have publicly discussed and agreed upon their course—making the threat both external and social, a matter of public knowledge that further isolates the psalmist.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly documents organized opposition to righteous figures. Alma faces enemies who 'sought to destroy him' (Alma 6:6). Nephi confronts Laman and Lemuel, who conspire against him. The pattern recurs: the righteous are vulnerable, enemies perceive the vulnerability, and they coordinate their opposition. This theological pattern—that enemies will test the righteous—is a constant in restored scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 3:7 warns: 'Behold, I say unto you, that you are chosen out of the world to declare my everlasting gospel...but the world receiveth you not.' The promise of the gospel is not protection from enemy conspiracy but faithful witness despite it. D&C 31:9 addresses persecution: 'Do not be afraid of your enemies, for I have decreed in my heart to support you; therefore, what have they against you?' The perspective shifts from enemy strategy to God's protective decree.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment teaches that opposition is inevitable and that the faithful must pass through trials—including organized opposition—with steadfast faith. The language of enemies 'taking counsel together' resonates with temple symbolism of the adversary's coordinated opposition to covenant-making.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 10:8-10 predicts the wicked one who 'sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor.' This describes the strategy of enemies 'laying wait' as in Psalm 71:10. Jesus embodies the vulnerable righteous one hunted by coordinated enemies. The Gospels record the conspiracy of chief priests, elders, and rulers—precisely as Psalm 71:10 predicts the vulnerable righteous face. Yet Jesus' vulnerability becomes the means of redemption.
commentary.application: This verse acknowledges a hard reality: the righteous often face organized opposition. Not every conflict is a sign of spiritual failure; some enmity is simply the cost of faithfulness. The verse invites us to name opposition clearly—to see it not as random hostility but as organized threat—and to respond not with denial but with clear-eyed spiritual preparation. Like the psalmist, we can be honest about enemies while refusing to let them define our reality. The specific mention of enemies watching for vulnerability in old age (following verse 9) reminds us that those who care for aging parents, grandparents, or vulnerable community members must sometimes protect them from predators who perceive their weakness. This verse calls us to vigilance on behalf of the vulnerable.

text_kjv: Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him.

commentary.narrative:
Now the psalmist reveals the precise content of the enemies' conspiracy: they spread the taunt that God has abandoned him. This is the psychological weapon; the claim that the psalmist lacks divine protection. The enemies' theology is their strategy—if they can convince the community (and the psalmist himself) that God has forsaken him, then he has no refuge, no ultimate protection, no reason for others to aid him. The taunt 'God hath forsaken him' ('Elohim azabo') is not merely blasphemy; it is psychological warfare designed to isolate the victim.

The command that follows—'Persecute and take him'—flows logically from the declaration of abandonment. If God has indeed forsaken him, then he is fair game. There is 'none to deliver him' (en matzil)—neither divine rescue nor human intervention. The logic is ruthlessly consequential: abandonment by God equals defenselessness before enemies. This is the precise counterclaim to the psalmist's assertion in verse 7 that 'Thou art my strong refuge.' The enemies deny it; they argue that this refuge is illusory. They attempt to replace the psalmist's theology with their own.

The Covenant Rendering notes that 'The enemies' statement mirrors the taunt against the sufferer in Psalm 22:9' and other passages—'the recurring claim that God has withdrawn.' This pattern is not unique to the psalmist but recurring. The psalmist must contend not only with his enemies' actions but with their theology, their attempt to rewrite reality by claiming that the most fundamental promise (God's protective presence) has been revoked. This is why verse 8's commitment to praise is not optional piety but essential spiritual warfare—the psalmist's words declaring God's splendor are directly opposed to the enemies' words declaring God's withdrawal.

word_study.meaning: He forsook him, he abandoned him, he left him. From azab (to leave, to abandon, to forsake). This is the same root as the 'al ta'azbeni' (do not forsake me) of verse 9, but here the enemies claim it is already accomplished. The verb azab denotes both permanent withdrawal and active abandonment.
word_study.significance: The enemies' taunt uses the exact language of the psalmist's deepest fear. In verse 9, the psalmist pleaded, 'do not abandon me.' Now the enemies declare that this abandonment is already fact. Their theology mirrors the psalmist's fear—the difference is that they accept what he resists.

word_study.meaning: Pursue, chase, persecute. From radaf (to pursue, to chase as a hunter pursues prey, to persecute). The verb conveys active, ongoing hostility—not a single blow but sustained pursuit.
word_study.significance: The enemies' conspiracy moves from word (the taunt) to action (persecution). The verb radaf (pursue) echoes verse 10's image of enemies 'laying wait'—now they move from watching to active hunting.

word_study.meaning: Seize him, take him captive, grasp him, lay hold of him. From taphas (to grasp, to seize, to capture). The verb denotes physical seizure and control.
word_study.significance: The progression from pursuit (radfu) to seizure (tif'su'u) completes the imagined trajectory—from speaking against to hunting to capturing the defenseless prey.

word_study.meaning: No one who rescues, no deliverer, none to save. From natzal (to rescue, to snatch away, to deliver from danger). The phrase denies the possibility of rescue from any quarter—neither divine nor human.
word_study.significance: The enemies' claim is comprehensive: no one can save the psalmist. This is the spiritual logic behind their confidence—they have declared him abandoned by God and helpless before them. The phrase 'matzil' (rescuer, savior) ironically anticipates the recognition of God as the ultimate matzil—yet the enemies' words seek to negate this.

cross_references.connection: 'He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him.' The taunt here mirrors the enemies' sarcasm in Psalm 22—the claim that God has withdrawn His favor. The pattern appears across multiple psalms of lament.

'Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God.' The enemies' theological claim—that God will not save—is a recurring weapon against the righteous. The psalmist responds not by denying the claim but by reaffirming faith in God's protective reality.

'He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.' The Gospels record the exact taunt against Jesus at crucifixion—enemies mock the claim of divine protection, arguing that God's silence proves abandonment. Like the psalmist, Jesus faces the enemy's claim that he has been forsaken.

Korihor argues: 'Ye look forward and expect to be exalted; but behold, we know that all is vain and foolish...there is no God; for if there were a God he would make himself known unto us.' Like the enemies of Psalm 71:11, Korihor's argument is theological—he denies divine protection and presence to undermine the righteous.

The description of the sons of perdition: 'These are they who are cast down to hell and are not redeemed from the devil's power by any means...their sins...are not remitted unto them.' The ultimate abandonment—the denial of redemption—is the fate of those who deny God's protection. The verse implies that refusing the matzil (rescuer) has cosmic consequences.

commentary.historical_context: The enemies' taunt represents a form of psychological warfare common in ancient Near Eastern contexts. To claim that a person was abandoned by their deity was not merely an insult; it was a claim with social and religious consequences. In honor/shame cultures, such a public declaration of divine abandonment would be profoundly isolating. Other community members, hearing that the gods had withdrawn favor, would distance themselves (no one would wish to be contaminated by association with the cursed). The taunt was thus a multileveled weapon: psychological (attacking the victim's faith), social (isolating the victim from community support), and practical (authorizing persecution by claiming the victim lacked divine protection).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar attempts by enemies to undermine faith through theological claims. Korihor's arguments (Alma 30) attempt to convince believers that God does not protect or deliver. The counterclaim of Mormon and Alma—that God does deliver the righteous—directly answers this enemy tactic. In Alma 36, Alma's account of his conversion includes his rescue from despair and destruction, providing personal testimony that God does indeed deliver.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 addresses this exact vulnerability: 'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.' The Lord's command is precisely what Psalm 71 models—maintaining faith in divine protection despite enemies' claims to the contrary. D&C 121:7-8, Joseph Smith's prayer during persecution, reframes the enemies' taunts: 'thy integrity of heart shall make thee of more worth than fine gold,' inverting the enemies' claim of worthlessness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes a test where the adversary's representative mocks the covenant and claims that God will not protect those who make covenants. This reflects the ancient pattern of Psalm 71:11—enemies attempting to undermine faith by claiming God has abandoned His people. The covenant response is to stand firm despite the taunt.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the supreme matzil (deliverer, rescuer). The enemies' taunt in Psalm 71:11—'there is no deliverer'—is answered by Christ, whose resurrection proves that God does indeed rescue and deliver. Christ experiences the enemies' exact claim at His crucifixion ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'), but this moment of apparent abandonment becomes the doorway to resurrection. The psalmist's faith that God remains his refuge, despite enemies' claims to the contrary, is vindicated in Christ, who is rescued from death itself by the Father's power.
commentary.application: This verse acknowledges the power of lies to shape spiritual reality—or to try to. Enemies who declare that God has abandoned us may be articulate, organized, and convincing. They may point to our afflictions as 'proof' of divine withdrawal. Yet the psalmist invites us to resist this interpretive capture. We do not deny that the enemies speak; we deny that they speak truth. The practical application is this: when facing organized hostility, do not let the enemies' theology colonize your own thinking. They will attempt to convince you (and others) that God has withdrawn. Your task is to hold firm to the reality of God's protective presence, even when all visible evidence (circumstances, enemies' words, isolation) seems to contradict it. This is not denial but faith—a spiritual discipline of insisting on the deepest truth even when the surface tells another story.

text_kjv: O God, be not far from me: O my God, make haste for my help.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist responds to the enemies' taunt with an urgent prayer. The structure is striking: having named the enemies' claim that God has forsaken him (verse 11), the psalmist immediately pivots to direct address of God (verse 12). The enemies' theology is countered not by theological debate but by prayer—by the psalmist's insistent reorientation toward God's presence. The first plea, 'Do not be far from me' ('Al tirchaq mimeni'), directly negates the enemies' central claim. The enemies said God has abandoned him; the psalmist says, 'Do not be far.' The second plea, 'My God, hurry to help me' (chushah le-ezrati), names the urgency of the situation.

The verb chushah ('hurry, hasten') conveys desperation—the situation is not merely difficult but urgent and potentially fatal. Delay could mean death. This is not philosophical prayer but the cry of someone in immediate peril. Yet notice what the psalmist does not do: he does not argue with the enemies or defend his claim that God is his refuge. He does not engage in debate. Instead, he prays. His response to the enemies' false theology is not better theology (though verse 7-8 have provided this already) but direct invocation of God. The prayer is performative—it embodies the faith that the enemies deny.

The Covenant Rendering notes that this verse 'echoes Psalm 22:12 and 22:20, reinforcing the literary connections between these psalms.' This connection is significant: Psalm 22 is the supreme psalm of divine abandonment ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'), yet it too resolves into trust and the calling of God as 'my God.' The pattern recurs: crisis of confidence, enemies' taunt, and the psalmist's ultimate response—not denial of the crisis but an urgent appeal to the God who remains his God. The use of two different names for God ('Elohim' and 'Elohay') adds weight: God in His power and justice (Elohim) and God in His personal covenant relationship (Elohai, 'my God') are both invoked.

word_study.meaning: Do not distance yourself from me, do not go far from me, do not withdraw from me. From rachaq (to be far, to distance oneself, to withdraw). The phrase uses negative imperative with directional language—'not be far'—making it the direct opposite of withdrawal or distance.
word_study.significance: This phrase directly contradicts the enemies' claim in verse 11 ('God hath forsaken him'). The psalmist's prayer assumes the possibility of God's presence and prays against its withdrawal. The verb rachaq (to distance) is the opposite of karav (to draw near), capturing the poles of divine relationship.

word_study.meaning: My God, my divine protector. The possessive form of Elohim (God), emphasizing personal covenant relationship. This is not God in abstract but God in relationship—'my' God, the God of covenant and protection.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'O God' ('Elohim') in the first line to 'O my God' ('Elohay') in the second line deepens the intimacy and the claim of relationship. The psalmist is not addressing an abstract deity but the God with whom he stands in covenant.

word_study.meaning: Hurry, hasten, make haste. From chush (to hurry, to move quickly, to act with urgency). The verb conveys not merely request but urgent pleading—the situation is dire and delay could be fatal.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this verb 'conveys desperation.' This is not a polite or patient prayer but an urgent cry. The verb appears in contexts of crisis: 'Make haste to help me' (Psalm 22:20, 'Be not far from me: O my strength, haste thee to help me'); 'Hurry and deliver me' (Psalm 31:2, 'Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily'). Chushah is the language of someone whose life hangs in balance.

word_study.meaning: Help, aid, assistance. From azar (to help, to aid, to support). The word denotes active, practical intervention—not mere sympathy but actual aid.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not ask for God's distant blessing or theoretical protection. He asks for 'ezrah'—actual help, intervention, practical aid. This is prayer grounded in real need and expecting real response.

cross_references.connection: 'Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help me.' The verse echoes Psalm 71:12 almost verbatim, establishing a literary and theological pattern across the psalms of lament.

'Deliver my soul from the sword...Save me from the lion's mouth.' The same language of urgent appeal—the Covenant Rendering notes this connection explicitly, noting that Psalm 71:12 'echoes Psalm 22:12 and 22:20.'

'Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me.' Like Psalm 71:12, Psalm 31 combines the appeal for God not to be far with the plea for speedy help, grounding both in relationship ('my God') and need.
'Forsake me not, O LORD...Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation.' The structure parallels Psalm 71:12—the plea against abandonment followed by the plea for speedy intervention.

'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not...Cast all your cares upon me; for I am your God.' The Lord's response to the psalmist's plea is to teach the pattern of verse 12—turning attention toward God and casting concerns upon His care, trusting in His speedy help.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern prayer, urgent appeals to the deity often employed the language of distance and proximity. To be 'far' from one's god meant to lack protection and presence; to draw 'near' meant to receive active aid. The psalmist's prayer reflects cultural and theological assumptions about divine presence and absence. The urgency conveyed by chushah ('hurry') reflects the real peril—in the ancient Near East, vulnerable individuals (especially the aging) could face rapid deterioration or attack. The prayer is not leisurely meditation but a cry from someone in immediate danger.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly records prayers following the pattern of Psalm 71:12—urgent appeals to God not to withdraw but to act. Alma's prayer in Alma 34 ('O Jesus, thou Son of God...thou canst not hide thyself from us') follows this structure: addressing God directly, reminding Him of covenant relationship, and pleading for immediate intervention. Nephi's psalm (2 Nephi 4:25) similarly voices urgent prayer when danger threatens.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 teaches: 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me.' The principle is reciprocal—the psalmist's prayer to draw God near is met by God's promise to draw near to those who seek. D&C 81:3 assures: 'Be faithful and diligent in keeping the commandments of God, and I will encircle thee in the arms of my love.' The psalmist's fear of distance is answered by God's commitment to proximity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple worship often employs language of drawing near to God's presence. The temple represents the place where God is not far but near, where the covenant relationship is most vividly enacted. Psalm 71:12's prayer to not be far from God is answered in temple covenant—a ritual assurance of proximity and protection.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ on the cross cries out with language echoing Psalm 71:12: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1, which shares the structure of verse 12). Yet Christ's cry is answered by resurrection—God does not remain far but acts with salvific power. Christ's resurrection proves that the distance implied by crucifixion is overcome; God does indeed 'make haste' to help. The psalmist's prayer finds its ultimate answer in Christ, who experiences the depth of separation ('My God, why hast thou forsaken me?') only to be rescued and exalted by the Father's power.
commentary.application: This verse invites us into the posture of urgent, honest prayer. When facing crisis—whether the slow crisis of aging, the acute crisis of enemies' opposition, or any real threat to our wellbeing—this verse gives permission and language for desperate prayer. We do not need to be calm or composed; we do not need to philosophize or theologize. We can cry out: 'Do not be far. Hurry to help.' The verse also models the movement from acknowledgment of crisis (verses 7-11 have named suffering, enemies, taunt, abandonment) to prayer (verse 12). We do not overcome crisis by denying it or by intellectual argument. We overcome it by turning directly to God and calling upon His name. The prayer is an act of faith—not a guarantee of immediate rescue but an assertion that God can and does hear and act. In our modern context of increasing secularization and the subtler abandonment of those deemed no longer productive, this verse calls us to voice the ancient prayer: 'God, do not be far from me. Hurry to help.'

text_kjv: Thy righteousness also, O God, is very high, who hast done great things: O God, who is like unto thee!

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist's personal experience of divine rescue now opens onto a cosmic perspective. After pages of complaint, complaint, and petition, the author suddenly shifts register — from 'help me' to 'who is like You?' This is the language of incomparability, the recognition that God's character transcends all human categories. The righteousness of God is not merely a private transaction (God rescued me) but a universal reality extending 'to the heights' — filling the heavens, ordering the cosmos. The rhetorical question 'mi kamokha' ('who is like You?') echoes Exodus 15:11, sung by Israel after crossing the Red Sea, and its presence here connects the psalmist's deliverance to the foundational redemptive narrative of Israel. There is no answer to the question because none exists.

The phrase 'Thy righteousness...is very high' (tsidqatcha ad-marom) is crucial: God's justice and faithfulness extend beyond what the psalmist can see or measure. In Hebrew thought, 'height' is not mere spatial distance but moral and spiritual elevation — the realm where God dwells in absolute otherness. The psalmist who began in the dust, begging for help, now sees that the dust-level problem he was suffering was always held within a framework of cosmic, unchanging divine righteousness. What felt like abandonment was never abandonment at all; it was the working out of God's justice in ways the sufferer could not initially comprehend.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, faithfulness, vindication. In Hebrew thought, tsidqah is not abstract moral rectitude but relational rightness — God's unwavering commitment to covenant, to the restoration of order, to the vindication of the oppressed. It is what God does, not merely what God is.
word_study.significance: This is the keyword of Psalm 71 (verses 2, 15, 16, 19, 24). The psalmist's entire journey has been waiting for tsidqah — for God to act justly on his behalf. The repetition makes clear: righteousness is not a philosophical concept but the divine power that sustains and redeems.

word_study.meaning: To the heights, to the high place, upward to heaven. Marom can mean both literal height and the realm of the divine. The preposition ad means 'as far as,' suggesting extension or reach.
word_study.significance: God's righteousness does not remain localized to the psalmist's deliverance but extends upward and outward — it is cosmic in scope. The TCR rendering ('reaches to the heights') captures the sense of extension and reach that the KJV's 'is very high' may miss. This is about God's character filling all of reality.

word_study.meaning: A rhetorical interrogative expressing incomparability. 'Who is like You?' expects no answer — it is a declaration that none exists. This formula appears throughout Israel's worship literature (Exodus 15:11; Psalm 35:10; Isaiah 40:25).
word_study.significance: The phrase is not philosophical monotheism (declaring that only one God exists) but experiential monotheism — no other power has done what this God has done, no other being has proven as reliable, as mighty, as just. It is worship language, not dogmatic language. The TCR translation preserves this by rendering it as direct address: 'who is like You?' rather than 'who is like thee.'

cross_references.connection: The original 'mi kamokha' declaration after the crossing of the Red Sea. The psalmist consciously echoes Israel's foundational redemption narrative, claiming that his personal deliverance participates in that same pattern of divine incomparability.
Another instance of 'to whom then will you liken Me, or shall I be equal?' — the language of incomparability appears in Isaiah's declaration of the Lord's sovereignty and power over all creation.

Another 'mi kamokha' declaration: 'Who is like unto Thee, which deliverest the poor from him that is too strong for him, yea, the poor and the needy from him that spoileth him?' The same formula used to celebrate God's justice on behalf of the oppressed.
A parallel declaration: 'O LORD God of hosts, who is a strong LORD like unto thee?' Again, the incomparability formula celebrating God's covenant faithfulness and power.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'mi kamokha' is among the oldest liturgical formulas in Hebrew scripture. Exodus 15:11 is often dated to the 12th century BCE, making it one of the earliest hymnic compositions in the Hebrew Bible. By the time of the Psalter (likely post-exilic, though many individual psalms are older), this language would have carried centuries of accumulated meaning — every Israelite who sang it would have been conscious of connecting to the foundational story of liberation. The 'heights' (marom) reflects both mythological imagery (the heavenly palace) and the concrete geography of Jerusalem, where the temple stood on the height of Zion. For an exiled or displaced community, declaring that God's righteousness reaches 'to the heights' would have been an affirmation that even when Jerusalem lay in ruins, God's justice and power had not been diminished.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3 echoes this movement from personal deliverance to cosmic perspective: 'I do know that whosoever shall put their trust in God shall be supported in their trials, and their troubles, and their afflictions.' The principle of extending personal experience to universal principle appears in Book of Mormon theology as well.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:39-44 teaches that God's light 'proceedeth forth from the presence of God to fill the immensity of space' — a modern revelation that echoes the psalmist's vision of God's righteousness extending to the heights. This is the Restoration's version of tzidqah ad-marom.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the ascent through different degrees of glory and the vision of God's majesty reflects this same movement from personal petition to cosmic awareness of God's righteousness. The temple experience invites the covenant member to participate in this enlargement of vision.

commentary.christological_typology: The question 'Who is like unto Thee?' finds its answer in the Restoration: Jesus Christ is the express image of God's person (Hebrews 1:3), the embodiment of divine righteousness and justice. His redemptive work—purchasing us with His blood (1 Peter 1:18-19)—makes Him the ultimate answer to the psalmist's declaration: God's incomparability is most fully revealed in Christ's atoning sacrifice, which extends righteous judgment and mercy to all who believe.
commentary.application: When circumstances make you question whether God sees you or cares about your suffering, this verse invites an enlargement of perspective. The psalmist's breakthrough came not when the external circumstances fully changed, but when he suddenly recognized that his small crisis was held within a framework of infinite, unchanging divine righteousness. In modern covenantal life, this means learning to trust that God's character — His justice, His faithfulness, His power — is constant and cosmic, even when His actions toward us remain hidden or confusing. The question 'Who is like God?' is not meant to be answered intellectually but to be lived — to move your faith from demanding understanding to resting in incomparability.

text_kjv: Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist now directly addresses God with a bold confession: 'You have shown me great and bitter troubles.' The Hebrew word for 'troubles' (tsarot) can mean distress, affliction, or siege — the sense is of being surrounded by calamity. The psalmist is not denying the reality of suffering or suggesting it never happened; rather, he is acknowledging that God allowed him to experience it, and now — in the same breath — he declares that God will 'quicken' (revive, bring back to life) him from the depths.

The second half of the verse is resurrection language, though we must be careful not to over-read Christian theology into it. 'Bring me up again from the depths of the earth' (tehomot ha-arets) evokes Sheol, the realm of the dead, the place of no return. The psalmist is saying: I was as good as dead, I descended to the threshold of the grave, and You brought me back. The verb techayyenu ('You will revive us/me') is the same root used in the Ezekiel valley-of-dry-bones passage (Ezekiel 37:5), making it resonant with images of resurrection. For an elderly person facing enemies who declare him abandoned (as we saw in verses 10-11), being 'brought up from the depths of the earth' means not only survival but restoration to the living community, to dignity, to remembered history.

word_study.meaning: Plural of tsar, meaning trouble, distress, adversity, siege. Tsarot can refer to enemies pressing in, circumstances pressing down, or abstract affliction. The plural suggests multiplicity — not one trouble but many layered troubles.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not minimize his suffering; he fully acknowledges its weight and complexity. Yet in acknowledging it, he also places it in God's hands, as if to say: 'God, You allowed this; now act on my behalf.'

word_study.meaning: To make alive, to revive, to restore to life. In biblical usage, this verb can mean literal resuscitation or metaphorical restoration to wholeness, dignity, and function. The root is chai (life, living).
word_study.significance: This is covenant language. God 'quickens' those who are His. The Masoretic Text reads 'us' (techayyenu), suggesting that the psalmist's personal revival is bound up with the community's restoration. In the LDS tradition, this language of 'quickening' connects to D&C passages about resurrection and the quickening power of God.

word_study.meaning: The depths, the abyss, the realm beneath the earth. 'Tehom' is the primordial waters, the chaos beneath the created order. In Psalm 71 context, it refers to Sheol, the place of the dead.
word_study.significance: The psalmist uses the language of descent and ascent — the cosmic drama of falling into chaos and being lifted back into the light and order of the living. The TCR captures this movement with 'from the depths of the earth / You will bring us up again' — vertical movement from below to above, from death to life.

cross_references.connection: The valley of dry bones: 'Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord GOD, thou knowest...Prophesy...saying, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live.' The same language of chayah (quickening/reviving) and restoration.
Hannah's song: 'The LORD killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up.' The pattern of descent and ascent, death and life, attributed to God's sovereign power.
New Testament parallel: 'Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more. Death hath no more dominion over him.' The psalmist's hope for revival anticipates Christ's resurrection.

Another thanksgiving psalm with similar language: 'I will extol thee, O LORD; for thou hast lifted me up...O LORD my God, I cried unto thee, and thou hast healed me. O LORD, thou hast brought up my soul from the grave.'

commentary.historical_context: The imagery of 'depths of the earth' draws on ancient Near Eastern cosmology, where the underworld (Sheol in Hebrew, Irkalla in Mesopotamian, Duat in Egyptian thought) was understood as a real place beneath the earth, a realm of darkness and silence where the dead existed in a diminished state. Descent to Sheol was irreversible in ancient thought — which makes the psalmist's confidence that God will 'bring him up' all the more striking. It represents faith in God's power over the boundary between life and death, visible and invisible, hope and despair. For a community facing exile or displacement, this language would have been deeply resonant — Jerusalem itself seemed to have 'descended' into the hands of enemies; the psalmist's personal revival becomes a type of national restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-22 describes Alma's spiritual death and resurrection: 'And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God...And as my soul could find no rest, behold, I desire to visit them.' The movement from depths of despair to revival through the power of Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:26: 'And again, verily I say unto you, that on the day of judgment, all those who are found upon my left hand shall be cast down into outer darkness; there is a weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth; and these are they who shall go away into the lake of fire and brimstone, with the devil and his angels.' Yet D&C 76:81-90 describes the redemption of those who rise from the depths. God controls both descent and ascent.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ritual enacts the pattern of descent into the depths (entering the terrestrial room, symbolic of mortality and separation from God) and ascent to the celestial room (symbolic of resurrection and reunion with God). This verse's language of being brought up from the depths maps directly onto temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's descent to the depths and return to life prefigures Christ's descent into the grave and His resurrection on the third day. More profoundly, Christ's Atonement is the ultimate 'quickening' — the power that revives all humanity from spiritual death (separation from God) and physical death (the grave). His willingness to descend into the depths of suffering and death is what gives power to His ascent and glorification.
commentary.application: In seasons when you feel you have descended into depths — grief, failure, despair, isolation — this verse teaches that descent is not permanence. It is a moment in a larger pattern that God controls. The psalmist does not say 'I will lift myself up' or 'circumstances will improve'; he says 'You will revive me.' This is a call to shift your locus of hope from external improvement to divine power working within and through your circumstance. The deepest spiritual work often happens in the depths, not on the surface. Trust that being 'brought up' by God is not only rescue but transformation.

text_kjv: Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side.

commentary.narrative:
The movement continues: from cosmic righteousness (verse 19) to restoration from the depths (verse 20) to restoration of personal dignity and standing (verse 21). The Hebrew word gedullatai means 'my greatness,' 'my honor,' 'my dignity,' 'my status.' For an elderly person whom enemies have declared abandoned and worthless (verse 10-11: 'God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him'), the promise that God 'will increase my greatness' is not vanity — it is the restoration of his human dignity and his standing in the community.

The second half of the verse — 'comfort me on every side' — uses the verb tissov, which literally means 'turn around' or 'surround.' The TCR rendering 'You will turn to comfort me' captures the sense that God, who seemed distant or hidden, will return with comfort. But the image also suggests being surrounded with comfort — comfort pressing in from all sides, comfort that is inescapable and total. The elderly psalmist who feared isolation now looks forward to being enveloped by divine comfort. This is concrete: he will be vindicated; his honor will be restored; he will be surrounded by support and solace.

word_study.meaning: Greatness, honor, majesty, dignity, exalted status. From the root gadal (to grow, to become great, to be magnified). The word can refer to objective status or to the quality of being esteemed.
word_study.significance: In the context of an aged person facing mocking and abandonment, this is not about arrogance but about restoration to honored status. The promise to 'increase' gedullatai means God will not merely restore what was lost but will enhance it — the vindication will be public and obvious.

word_study.transliteration: tissov (from sabab, 'to surround, to go around, to turn') + tenchhameni (from nacham, 'to comfort, to console')
word_study.meaning: Tissov = 'You will turn, You will go around, You will surround.' Tenchhameni = 'to comfort me, to console me.' Nacham carries the sense of a parent consoling a child, of restoration to wholeness after loss.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering ('You will turn to comfort me') emphasizes the turning—God's return. But the verb sabab also suggests surrounding, being enclosed. The image is of comfort approaching from all directions, inescapable and total. This is intimate comfort, not distant assurance.

cross_references.connection: Similarly, David promises: 'Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me...Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies.' Comfort and honor in the face of opposition.
A promise to Zion: 'For the LORD shall comfort Zion...and he will make her wilderness like Eden.' The verb nacham (comfort) paired with restoration and increase.

Another aged person's testimony: 'I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul shall make her boast in the LORD.' The restoration of dignity and public vindication.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern cultures, honor and shame were not primarily psychological states but social realities. To be declared abandoned by God was to be stripped of honor and left vulnerable to mockery. Conversely, to be vindicated by God was to have one's place in the community restored and often elevated. The enemies' taunt — 'God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him' (verse 11) — is an attempt to perform a social execution, to remove the psalmist from the honored community. God's promise to 'increase his greatness' is therefore not merely comforting words but a promise of public reversal of fortune. The comfort ('nacham') that God offers is similarly not private sentiment but the restoration of the elderly person to honored status within the community — to be surrounded by people who now acknowledge God's vindication of him.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:18-19 describes the reversal of the righteous: 'And lo, he cometh to redeem those who will be baptized unto repentance, through faith on his name...Therefore, blessed are they...for they shall cry mightily unto the Father in that day.' The increase of honor for those who are righteous.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45-46: 'Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men...then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.' The promise that righteousness leads to increased standing and honor.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the covenant member moves progressively from outer to inner rooms, each transition representing an increase in standing, honor, and proximity to God. The promise to 'increase my greatness' echoes this progression toward exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's humiliation (descent, rejection, crucifixion) is followed by His exaltation (resurrection, glorification, ascension). The psalmist's pattern of anticipated vindication and increase of honor mirrors Christ's vindication. In the Atonement, Christ takes upon Himself the shame of human sin and death, submits to the depths of suffering, and is then exalted to the right hand of God — His greatness increased eternally.
commentary.application: If you are in a season where your status, reputation, or sense of honor has been diminished—whether by age, circumstance, false accusation, or actual failure—this verse offers a different timeline than the world's. The world says: once your status is gone, it is gone. God says: I will increase your greatness. This does not mean you should be passive about your circumstance or arrogant about your vindication, but it does mean you can trust that your ultimate honor and standing are in God's hands, not the world's. The comfort that surrounds you comes not from external affirmation but from the quiet certainty that God sees you, knows your heart, and will vindicate you—either in this life or in the life to come. Let that be enough.

text_kjv: I will also praise thee with the psaltery, even thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist has moved from petition to praise, and now he makes a vow of future worship. He will respond to his vindication and restoration not with silence or private gratitude, but with public, artistic, instrumental worship. The nevel (psaltery/harp) and kinnor (harp/lyre) are the instruments of David (1 Samuel 16:23), the instruments that would have been played in the temple, the instruments of Israel's highest worship.

Crucially, the object of the psalmist's praise is not merely the deliverance itself but 'Your truth' (amitteka). The Hebrew word emet (truth) in biblical usage means not abstract philosophical truth but concrete fidelity, reliability, faithfulness. It is the quality of being trustworthy, of keeping covenant, of being the same yesterday, today, and forever. The psalmist celebrates not that the crisis has ended, but that God's character has proven reliable. This is the deepest kind of praise—praise for who God is, not merely what God has done.

The title 'Holy One of Israel' (Qedosh Yisrael) appears here in a psalm context where it is rare. It is primarily an Isaianic title, appearing frequently in Isaiah 1:4, 5:19, 10:20, and elsewhere. Its presence in Psalm 71:22 connects the psalmist's personal experience to the prophetic tradition, to Israel's larger story of covenant and redemption. The psalmist is saying: 'The God who stands apart, who is utterly holy and other, who is the Holy One of the entire nation Israel—this God is my God, and I have experienced His reliability.'

word_study.meaning: A stringed instrument, likely a type of angular or vertical harp, larger than the kinnor. Used in temple worship and royal courts.
word_study.significance: The nevel was not a private instrument but a public, formal instrument. To praise with the nevel is to commit to public worship.

word_study.meaning: Truth, reliability, faithfulness, fidelity, constancy. In Hebrew, emet is not primarily propositional truth but relational truth—the quality of being faithful to a covenant, being dependable.
word_study.significance: The psalmist has learned that God's emet is the deepest reality. Not only does God act; God is faithful. This is what deserves celebration and worship.

word_study.meaning: A stringed instrument, smaller than the nevel, a lyre. Associated with David (1 Samuel 16:23) and Apollo in Greek tradition. Used in both public worship and intimate musical expression.
word_study.significance: The kinnor was the instrument of David, Israel's ideal king. To play the kinnor is to place oneself in the lineage of David and to participate in the kingdom's worship.

word_study.meaning: The Holy One of Israel. Qadosh means holy, set apart, radically other. The title combines God's transcendent otherness with His covenantal relationship to Israel. It is primarily an Isaianic title.
word_study.significance: This title emphasizes both God's otherness (God is not like any earthly power) and God's particularity (God has chosen Israel and bound Himself by covenant). For the psalmist to invoke this title is to acknowledge that his personal deliverance is part of Israel's larger redemptive story.

cross_references.connection: David played the kinnor to soothe Saul: 'And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed.' The psalmist's promise to play the same instrument connects him to David.

The first appearance of 'Holy One of Israel' in the prophetic corpus: 'Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity...they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger.' The title appears in Isaiah in contexts of both judgment and covenant renewal.
Another rare appearance of 'Holy One of Israel' in the Psalter: 'Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel.' Again, a note of covenant accountability.

The New Testament's echo: 'And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways.' The pattern of instrumental and vocal praise for God's character.

commentary.historical_context: Temple worship in ancient Israel involved levitical musicians playing nevel and kinnor alongside singers. Psalms like Psalm 71 were often inscribed with notations indicating which instruments should accompany the singing—'to the chief Musician upon Neginoth' (stringed instruments). The psalmist's vow to praise 'with the psaltery and harp' would have been understood not as a private promise but as a liturgical commitment—a pledge to participate in temple worship and to lead others in celebration. The use of the Isaianic title 'Holy One of Israel' suggests that this psalm may have been revised or repurposed in post-exilic settings when the prophetic books were gaining authority. The psalmist is intentionally placing his testimony within the framework of Israel's prophetic tradition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:8-9: 'And I have been supported under trials and troubles of every kind, yea, and in all manner of afflictions; yea, God has delivered me from prison, and bonds, and death; yea, and I do put my trust in him, and he will still deliver me.' Then verse 12: 'Now when our hearts are sorrowful, we turn to our music and our poetry and our hymns to lift our souls unto God.' The Book of Mormon explicitly connects deliverance with musical praise.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 25:12: 'For my soul delighteth in the song of the heart; yea, the song of the righteous is a prayer unto me, and it shall be answered with a blessing upon your heads.' The Lord explicitly declares that praising with instruments and voice is a form of prayer.
