restoration_lens.temple_connections: The musical instruments used in temple worship are literal and symbolic—they represent the harmony and order that covenant creates. The promise to play them in worship is a promise to participate in Zion's song, the gathering of the righteous in praise.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfiller of the covenant's music and worship. He is the 'David' who plays the kinnor of perfect obedience; He is the 'Holy One of Israel' incarnate. His Atonement is the ultimate occasion for the song of praise. In Revelation 5:9-10, the redeemed sing a 'new song' to the Lamb. The psalmist's vow to praise with instruments anticipates the eternal worship that Christ makes possible.
commentary.application: Praise is not something to reserve for moments when everything is resolved. This verse teaches that praise—particularly praise for God's faithfulness and character—should be offered even while you are still in the middle of your trial or vulnerability. Public worship (the nevel and kinnor) is a way of testifying both to God and to your community that you trust God's faithfulness. When you sing or play music in worship, you are not merely expressing feeling; you are making a covenant commitment. Consider: What would it mean for you to offer God praise not for the outcome you want, but for the character you have come to know—His faithfulness, His truth, His otherness and power? That is the deepest kind of worship.

text_kjv: My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing unto thee; and my soul, which thou hast redeemed.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist moves from the instruments to the voice and body. 'My lips shall greatly rejoice'—the mouth, the lips, will be the vehicle of joy and worship. The verb ranan (to shout, to cry out in jubilation) suggests not quiet satisfaction but exuberant, audible joy. The phrase 'when I sing unto thee' (ki azammera lakh) uses the imperfect tense—when I make music to You (future or habitual)—suggesting that the singing is ongoing, not a one-time event.

Then comes the profound summary statement: 'my soul, which thou hast redeemed.' The Hebrew word padah (redeemed) is the language of payment and liberation. To redeem means literally to buy back, to pay a price in order to free someone from bondage. The word is used in Isaiah 52:3 for redemption from exile: 'Thus saith the Lord, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.' The psalmist's 'soul' (nephesh—his entire self, his life force, his person) has been purchased back from the grip of death, enemies, despair, and abandonment. Redemption is not a metaphor; it is an economic and legal transaction in which God has paid the price to restore him.

This is the climax of the psalm's movement: from a person begging not to be cast off in old age (verse 9) to a person who understands that his very soul has been ransomed. He will not merely survive; he will be restored to his whole self, his nephesh, his essential humanity and dignity.

word_study.meaning: To shout for joy, to cry out in jubilation, to sing loudly, to resound. The root suggests vocal intensity—not quiet contentment but audible exultation.
word_study.significance: This is embodied joy. The lips will not merely think happy thoughts; they will shout and sing. The TCR rendering 'will shout for joy' captures the intensity that the KJV's 'shall greatly rejoice' hints at.

word_study.transliteration: azammera (from zamar, 'to sing, to make music')
word_study.meaning: To sing, to make music, often specifically with instruments. The root is the same as mizmar (psalm). To zamar is to participate in the musical and poetic expression of praise.
word_study.significance: This is participatory worship—the psalmist will not merely listen to others worship but will actively create music. This connects to his promise in verse 22 to praise with instruments.

word_study.meaning: Soul, self, life, person, breath, living being. Nephesh is the animating principle of life—what makes a human alive rather than merely flesh. It can refer to the emotional, volitional, and spiritual center of a person.
word_study.significance: When the psalmist says 'my soul, which thou hast redeemed,' he is saying: the very core of who I am—not just my circumstances, but my essential humanity—has been ransomed. To lose the nephesh is to be diminished as a person.

word_study.meaning: To redeem, to ransom, to buy back, to liberate by paying a price. Padah is a commercial and legal term—it describes the transaction of paying money to free someone from captivity or debt.
word_study.significance: This language is central to the Atonement theology. Christ's sacrifice is a redemption—a ransom paid to buy back the souls of humans from death, sin, and separation from God. The psalmist's language of being padah (redeemed) becomes, in Christian context, a prefigurement of the Atonement. In LDS theology, redemption (the power by which Christ's sacrifice frees us) is one of the central concepts of the restored Gospel.

cross_references.connection: A parallel use of padah in a context of divine restoration: 'Thus saith the Lord, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.' The same language of redemption/ransom applied to liberation.

Another psalmist's vow of public praise: 'My soul shall make her boast in the LORD: the humble shall hear thereof, and be glad. O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together.' The connection between personal redemption and public worship.

New Testament use of redemption language: 'Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold...But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish.' The fulfillment of the psalmist's redemption in Christ's sacrifice.
Elihu's statement: 'He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light.' The pattern of redemption from the depths and restoration to light.

commentary.historical_context: The language of redemption (padah) in ancient Israel is bound up with concrete legal and economic practices. A person sold into debt slavery could be redeemed—bought back—by a kinsman redeemer (go'el). The most famous instance is in the Book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as go'el for Ruth and Naomi. The psalmist's use of padah to describe God's action is therefore not metaphorical but liturgical—it places God in the role of kinsman redeemer, the one who has the power and the will to buy back the psalmist's life from bondage. In exile theology (which likely influenced the final editing of the Psalter), this language would have resonated powerfully—Israel had been 'sold' into captivity; God would 'redeem' the nation and restore it to the land.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:25-26: 'And now, behold, I say unto you, my brethren, you that belong to this church, have you sufficiently retained a remission of your sins?...Or have ye forgotten what he said, saying that he came to redeem those who believe on his name?' The language of redemption through Christ is central to Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:69: 'These are they whose bodies are celestial, whose glory is that of the sun, even the glory of God the highest of all.' The redeemed inherit the glory of the redeemed. D&C 138:19: 'I beheld that the faithful elders of this dispensation, when they depart from mortal life, continue their labors in the preaching of the gospel in the Spirit world.' Redemption is ongoing, involving the whole self—body, spirit, and mission.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony involves the restoration of the soul to its full status and standing before God. The psalmist's redemption prefigures the covenant member's restoration through endowment and sealing.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's redemption is a type of Christ's redemptive work. The ransom paid to buy back the psalmist's soul is fulfilled in Christ's blood shed for the redemption of all souls. In Matthew 20:28, Christ teaches that He came 'to give his life a ransom for many' (lytron = redemption price in Greek). The psalmist's future joy in singing becomes, through Christ, the eternal joy of all the redeemed before God's throne (Revelation 7:9-10).
commentary.application: The phrase 'my soul, which thou hast redeemed' invites you to consider: Has your soul been redeemed? Not in some distant abstract sense, but in your actual lived experience? The psalmist understood that redemption is not merely doctrinal—it is personal. Your soul has been redeemed if you have allowed God to buy back your deepest self from the grip of sin, despair, meaninglessness, or self-hatred. The price has been paid (Christ's blood). The transaction is complete. Your response—like the psalmist's—should be public, audible joy and praise. Let your lips shout for joy. Let others see and know that something real has happened in you. Do not contain the redemption; express it.

text_kjv: My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long: for they are brought to shame, for they are confounded, that seek my hurt.
text_kjv_extended: My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long: for they are brought to shame, for they are confounded, that seek my hurt.

commentary.narrative:
The psalm ends where it began—with the word 'righteousness' (tsidqah). The first verse prayed 'In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust...let me never be put to shame: deliver me in thy righteousness.' Now, in the final verse, the psalmist declares that his tongue will 'talk of thy righteousness all the day long'—the entire day, continuously, obsessively, like someone who cannot stop thinking about something. The verb tehgeh ('will murmur, will meditate aloud') is the same verb used in Psalm 1:2 to describe meditating on Torah 'day and night.' It suggests a low, continuous, almost involuntary recitation—the psalmist will not be able to stop speaking about God's righteousness because his mind will not be able to leave it.

The final two lines provide the completion of the narrative arc: 'for they are brought to shame, for they are confounded, that seek my hurt.' The enemies have been shamed and disgraced—the two verbs boshu ('they are ashamed') and chafru ('they are disgraced') form a standard Hebrew word pair for total social humiliation. The psalmist who began in fear of being put to shame (verse 1) now sees that the shame has been transferred to his enemies. Their theology was wrong. They declared that God had abandoned the psalmist—a public declaration designed to shame him and strip him of standing in the community. But time, God's action, and the vindication have proven them wrong. They are the ones who are now shamed.

This is not revenge fantasy or vindictive gloating. It is the resolution of a covenant lawsuit. The enemies charged God with injustice (by claiming He abandoned the righteous); God's vindication of the psalmist proves God's character and proves the enemies wrong. The psalmist's continuous speaking of God's righteousness is therefore not merely personal testimony—it is the execution of a legal verdict. Every time he speaks, he is reaffirming that God is just, and by implication, that those who accused God of injustice are now revealed as false witnesses.

word_study.transliteration: tehgeh (from hagah, 'to murmur, to meditate, to utter')
word_study.meaning: My tongue will murmur, will speak aloud, will meditate. Hagah is a verb that suggests continuous, often involuntary utterance—like the murmuring of water or the continuous low sound of someone thinking aloud.
word_study.significance: The verb's presence in Psalm 1:2 ('his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night') suggests that the psalmist's continuous speech about God's righteousness is similar to constant meditation on Torah. His mind and mouth have been re-centered on God.

word_study.meaning: God's justice, faithfulness, vindication power. Tsidqah appears at the beginning of Psalm 71 (verse 2) and at the end (verses 19, 24)—it is the bookend and the core of the entire psalm.
word_study.significance: That the psalm begins and ends with tsidqah shows that the psalmist's entire journey has been one of learning to trust in God's righteousness—not his own, but God's unwavering justice. The word has shifted meaning through the psalm: it began as something the psalmist needed (verse 2, 'In thy righteousness deliver me'); it became something cosmic (verse 19, 'Thy righteousness...is very high'); and it ends as something the psalmist will proclaim continuously.

word_study.term_english: all the day long / every day
word_study.meaning: All day, the whole day, continuously throughout the day. Kol = all, totality. Hayom = the day.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests an all-consuming focus. The psalmist will not merely mention God's righteousness occasionally; it will be his constant refrain. This is obsessive meditation born from genuine encounter with the divine.

word_study.transliteration: boshu (from bosh, 'to be ashamed') + chafru (from chafar, 'to dig, to burrow, to be disgraced')
word_study.meaning: Boshu = they are ashamed, they are put to shame. Chafru = they are dug down, they are disgraced, they are brought low. The pairing is a standard formula for total public humiliation.
word_study.significance: These two verbs working together create an image of being thoroughly exposed and diminished. The enemies' attempt to shame the psalmist has been reversed. The TCR rendering 'have been shamed and disgraced' captures the comprehensiveness of their downfall.

word_study.transliteration: mevaqqeshei raati (those who seek/require my evil/hurt)
word_study.meaning: Those who seek my harm, those who desire my evil, those who pursue my destruction. Mevaqqesh = to seek, to require, to demand. Ra = evil, harm, hurt, misfortune.
word_study.significance: The enemies are not merely hostile; they are defined by their seeking of harm. Their entire identity is wrapped up in their intention to destroy the psalmist. The irony is that they have been destroyed instead.

cross_references.connection: The same verb tehgeh (meditate, murmur) appears: 'But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.' The psalmist's continuous speech about God's righteousness mirrors the righteous person's meditation on Torah.

The psalm's opening and closing are bookended by tsidqah (righteousness): 'In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust...Deliver me in thy righteousness...Bow down thine ear to me; make haste to deliver me: be thou my strong rock, for an house of strength to save me.' What was petitioned at the beginning becomes proclaimed at the end.

A different kind of victory and vindication: 'And it came to pass, when they brought out those kings unto Joshua, that Joshua called for all the men of Israel...Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings. And they came near, and put their feet upon the necks of them...And afterward Joshua smote them, and slew them.' The psalmist's verbal vindication contrasts with Joshua's military vindication, but both involve the overturning of the enemies' power.

A New Testament echo: 'Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more. Death hath no more dominion over him.' The principle that what was meant to destroy is itself destroyed, what was meant to shame is itself shamed.

A similar theme of overcoming: 'For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith. Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?' The faith that the psalmist has learned is the same faith that overcomes.

commentary.historical_context: The concept of being 'brought to shame' (boshu) has concrete social consequences in honor/shame cultures. Public humiliation was a real social death—to be shamed was to lose standing, to be excluded from community participation, to have one's testimony declared false. The enemies who 'seek the psalmist's hurt' were not merely hostile; they were engaged in a formal accusation designed to strip him of honor. By declaring that God had abandoned him, they were performing a social execution. The reversal at the end—where they are shamed instead—is therefore not petty gloating but the restoration of social and legal order. The psalmist's continuous testimony about God's righteousness is the mechanism by which this restoration is maintained. Every time he speaks, he reaffirms: 'My testimony is true. Their testimony was false. God's character has been vindicated.'

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:27-29: 'And I have been supported under trials and troubles of every kind, yea, and in all manner of afflictions; yea, God has delivered me from prison, and bonds, and death; yea, and I do put my trust in him...Now when our hearts are sorrowful, we turn to our music...to lift our souls unto God.' The pattern of vindication leading to continuous praise is echoed in Alma's testimony.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:23-24: 'Therefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth his brother the offences which he hath committed against him shall be forgiven of the Heavenly Father; and ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.' The principle that God vindicates the righteous and judges the wicked.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the covenant member stands before God with cleared conscience and vindicated standing. The psalmist's final proclamation of God's righteousness is the temple member's constant refrain—the acknowledgment that God's judgment is just and that the faithful will be vindicated.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate vindicated sufferer. Falsely accused, mocked, shamed, crucified—He was brought to the depths of ignominy. Yet His resurrection and exaltation reversed every charge against Him and revealed the justice of God. The psalmist's pattern of being shamed and then vindicated prefigures Christ's Passion and Resurrection. In Hebrews 12:2, Christ is described as 'despising the shame' yet now sitting at the right hand of God. The psalmist's continuous proclamation of God's righteousness becomes, in Christian understanding, the Church's proclamation of Christ's vindication: He is risen, He is exalted, His accusers are proven wrong.
commentary.application: The final verse teaches that vindication, when it comes, should produce testimony. You do not vindicate yourself through counter-attack or self-justification; you vindicate yourself through continuously, devotionally proclaiming God's righteousness. Let your tongue work all day long, telling the story: 'God is just. God is faithful. God sees the hidden. God acts on behalf of the righteous.' This is not boasting about your own righteousness; it is declaring God's. The enemies of truth and goodness will indeed be shamed—not by your condemnation, but by the steady, relentless, audible proclamation of a higher standard and a higher judge. Your continuous testimony is the proof that God's righteousness has vindicated you. Do not hide your light. Do not minimize your deliverance out of false humility or fear of appearing boastful. Let your tongue speak. Let others know what God has done. In doing so, you participate in the work of declaring God's justice and making it visible in the world.

text_kjv: Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 72 opens with a superscription identifying it as either a psalm 'of' or 'for' Solomon, and the opening petition immediately establishes the theological framework for what follows: the king's authority is not autonomous but derivative. David (or the psalmist) asks God to grant the king His own judicial attributes—not power for its own sake, but the capacity to render decisions that mirror God's own character. The phrase 'judgments' (mishpat) refers not to abstract legal principles but to concrete verdicts rendered at the gate—decisions about property, disputes, grievances. The prayer asks that these rulings flow from God's righteousness (tzedaqah), a righteousness that is both relational (right relationship with God) and restorative (justice that restores right order to society).

The parallelism 'the king' / 'the king's son' is significant. If this is indeed David's prayer for Solomon, it reflects the transition of power from one generation to the next. But it also establishes a principle: the son inherits not the throne's symbols but its moral burden. He is granted God's judgments and righteousness not as decoration but as the very tools he will need to rule justly. The Covenant Rendering's rendering—'Of Solomon'—emphasizes the personal, specific nature of this petition: a named son is the subject of a father's intercession.

word_study.meaning: Judgment, justice, verdict, the practical execution of justice. Mishpat is not abstract legal theory but concrete judicial decisions rendered at the city gate—who wins the case, who receives restitution, whose claim is upheld. The word carries the sense of 'what is due' or 'what is right' in a particular situation.
word_study.significance: The psalmist asks that the king's rulings—the thousands of individual verdicts he will render—align with God's own sense of what is just. This is the operational heart of righteous governance: not grand proclamations but daily decisions that protect the vulnerable and uphold what is true.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, right relationship. Tzedaqah encompasses both moral uprightness and the active restoration of right order. In the Psalms, it frequently refers to God's covenant faithfulness—His commitment to honor His promises and protect His people, especially the vulnerable.
word_study.significance: The king is asked not merely to be well-intentioned but to embody a righteousness that is fundamentally relational: right standing with God that overflows into right treatment of others. This is the antidote to tyranny—a ruler whose power is tethered to God's character.

cross_references.connection: David's final words describe the ideal ruler as one who 'rules in the fear of God,' bringing light to his people just as the sun brings light at morning—echoing the rain imagery of Psalm 72:6.
A king who judges the poor with faithfulness establishes his throne, a principle that Psalm 72:4 elaborates through the specific promise to 'vindicate the afflicted.'

The revelation on priesthood authority teaches that power becomes persuasive through 'virtue garnished with thy thoughts unceasingly'—paralleling the psalmist's conviction that the king's authority flows from God's righteousness, not from force.

King Benjamin's instruction that judges should be chosen by the people to judge in righteousness illustrates the Nephite application of the principle that kingly authority serves justice, not oppression.

The messianic king 'shall judge...with righteousness' and 'shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth'—language that directly echoes Psalm 72 and suggests the psalm was read as a messianic prophecy.

commentary.historical_context: The superscription 'of Solomon' (le-Shlomoh) is ambiguous in Hebrew—it could mean 'by,' 'for,' 'to,' or 'concerning' Solomon. Ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions often celebrate a king's justice and benevolence toward the poor as a sign of divine favor. The image of the king as the executor of divine will appears in Egyptian pharaonic theology and in the Hammurabi stele, where the law code is presented as delivered by the sun-god Shamash to the king. However, the explicit focus on the 'afflicted' and 'poor' as primary beneficiaries of the king's justice is distinctive to Israel's covenant theology. In ancient Near Eastern context, the king might show mercy to the poor, but in Psalm 72, the poor are not an afterthought but the direct focus of royal justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's address in Mosiah 2-4 articulates the same principle: royal authority is a stewardship from God, not an entitlement. The king is accountable to God for how he treats his people, particularly the poor. Alma's teachings on priesthood in Alma 13 similarly emphasize that authority granted by God must be exercised in righteousness or it becomes a curse rather than a blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:34-37 directly addresses the principle that priesthood or authority (which kings exercise) cannot be maintained 'by the virtue of the priesthood' alone; it requires righteousness, gentleness, meekness, and love. This is the modern covenant language for what Psalm 72 asks the king to embody.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The king as mediator between God and people parallels the role of temple ordinance workers and priesthood holders—those who stand in authority to bless others must do so with godly attributes. The prayer for the king to embody God's judgments and righteousness mirrors the endowment's emphasis on receiving divine attributes through covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 72 is a portrait of ideal kingship that no earthly king fully realized. In Christian and early Jewish tradition, it was read as a messianic psalm—a description of the king of the age to come. In Latter-day Saint theology, Jesus Christ is the ultimate king who perfectly embodies God's judgments and righteousness. He judges not by outward appearance but by perfect knowledge of hearts (Alma 12:15). His entire ministry demonstrates the principle of this verse: authority granted by God, exercised for the relief of the afflicted, the vindication of the wronged, and the destruction of oppressive power.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse reframes authority and stewardship. If you hold any form of authority—as a parent, leader, employer, teacher—the psalm asks whether your daily decisions in those roles mirror God's character or merely your own preferences. The question is not merely 'Am I competent?' but 'Do my judgments protect the vulnerable? Do my decisions reflect God's righteousness or my own agenda?' The prayer also invites us to petition God for leaders and authority figures, asking that they be granted godly wisdom, not merely intelligence or charisma.

text_kjv: He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment.

commentary.narrative:
The second verse deepens and clarifies the prayer of verse 1 through explicit parallelism. The king's judicial function is restated, but now the object of that judgment becomes more specific and more urgent: 'Your people' and 'Your afflicted ones.' The parallelism is not synonymous (saying the same thing twice) but rather progressive or emphatic—it moves from the general (all Your people) to the particular (the most vulnerable among them). This is a deliberate rhetorical strategy to direct the reader's attention: yes, the king judges all the people, but pay special attention to what happens to the poor.

The phrase 'Your afflicted ones' (aniyyekha) identifies the poor not as a social category to be managed but as God's particular possession and concern. Throughout the Psalter, the aniyyim (afflicted, poor, humble) are portrayed as those whom God hears, defends, and vindicates. They are not peripheral to God's justice; they are central. This verse therefore makes a radical claim: the measure of a king's success is not his military victories or economic expansion but how he treats those least able to defend themselves. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'afflicted ones' preserves the Hebrew sense of those who have been pressed down, oppressed, and weakened by circumstance.

word_study.meaning: To judge, render judgment, arbitrate. In this context, the verb carries the sense of vindicating or establishing justice for someone who has been wronged or oppressed.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the judgment theme from verse 1 now shows its practical outworking: the king's judgments (mishpat) must include a specific commitment to the poor. Justice is not neutral; it actively defends the defenseless.

word_study.meaning: Poor, afflicted, humble, oppressed. The word describes those who are economically vulnerable, socially marginalized, and often unable to advocate for themselves. In Hebrew thought, aniyyim are frequently the recipients of God's special protection and vindication.
word_study.significance: The appearance of aniyyim here signals that the psalm is not simply describing royal prerogative but articulating a covenant obligation. The king's power over the poor must be exercised as protection, not exploitation.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, right order. Tzedek emphasizes the state of being in right relationship and right standing. When paired with judgment, it means judgments that restore what is right.
word_study.significance: The king judges 'with righteousness'—meaning his verdicts must be animated by a commitment to restore justice, not merely to render a decision. This is the antithesis of corruption, favoritism, or selective enforcement.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist directly calls on God and judges (elohim) to 'defend the poor and fatherless' and 'deliver the poor and needy'—the same mandate applied here to the earthly king as God's representative.
An exhortation to 'open thy mouth for the dumb...for the rights of all such as are appointed to destruction'—the same priority given to advocating for those unable to advocate for themselves.
The prophet calls Israel to 'seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow'—the exact social responsibilities Psalm 72:2 places upon the king.

Alma teaches that mercy must take effect 'upon the terms of the law' so that 'justice is not denied'—the Book of Mormon's way of articulating that true judgment must serve the vulnerable while upholding justice.

King Benjamin teaches that 'ye should succor those that stand in need of your succor' and be 'judge[s] of this people'—showing that the royal mandate to judge in righteousness extends to all covenant members.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the king was ideally the last court of appeal for those unable to obtain justice through normal channels. Inscriptions from Egyptian pharaohs, Babylonian kings, and Hittite rulers all celebrate their role as defenders of the weak and dispensers of justice. The Code of Hammurabi (18th century BCE) presents itself as a gift from the sun-god Shamash to the king for the express purpose of establishing justice and protecting the widow and orphan. However, the gap between ideal and practice was often vast. Prophetic books in the Hebrew Bible frequently condemn kings and judges for perverting justice and oppressing the poor (Isaiah 3:14-15, Jeremiah 22:13-19). Psalm 72 articulates the ideal as a prayer and aspiration, acknowledging that even a king as renowned for wisdom as Solomon sometimes failed to embody it (see 1 Kings 12).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The entire framework of Book of Mormon kingship assumes this principle. When Nephi establishes himself as king, his concern is explicitly stated as judgment and justice (2 Nephi 5:10-11). When Mosiah abolishes kingship, he does so because no mortal king perfectly embodies this ideal—only Christ can (Mosiah 29). The aniyyim of Psalm 72 appear throughout the Book of Mormon as the 'humble followers' of Christ whom He personally serves and whom the righteous are constantly urged to succor.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:42 commands the Saints to 'remember in all things the poor and the needy, the sick and the afflicted.' This is the same mandate Psalm 72 places on kings, now extended to all covenant members. Authority within the Church is explicitly framed as stewardship for others' benefit (D&C 104:11-12).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes explicit commitments to care for the poor and afflicted. The washing and anointing, the clothing in the robes of priesthood, and the final oath all reinforce the principle that those who receive power and authority in God's presence are bound to use it for others' benefit, especially the vulnerable.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the king who perfectly judges 'the poor with judgment.' His ministry began with a proclamation of good news to the poor (Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61:1) and consistently prioritized those society had marginalized: tax collectors, prostitutes, the sick, the demon-possessed. His final judgment scene (Matthew 25:31-46) makes clear that the measure of all judgment is how one treated 'the least of these'—the hungry, the stranger, the prisoner. In this sense, Psalm 72:2 is a direct prophecy of Christ's character and method.
commentary.application: This verse challenges any holder of authority—whether in family, workplace, civic office, or church—to measure their success by how they treat the vulnerable, not by their popularity or power. What specific decisions this week did you make regarding those with less power than you? Did you advocate for them, or did you remain neutral? Did you use your position to disadvantage them, however subtly? The psalm suggests that godly authority means consciously tilting toward those who have been 'pressed down' by circumstance or injustice.

text_kjv: The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 shifts from explicit judicial language to vivid natural imagery, yet the theological content is continuous. The mountains and hills are called upon to 'bear' or 'carry' peace for the people—a verb (yis'u) that typically describes bearing a physical burden or producing fruit. This is one of the most evocative images in the psalm: the earth itself, through the rule of a just king, becomes productive of peace. The phrase 'by righteousness' indicates that this peace is not accident or fortune but the inevitable result of righteous governance.

The choice of mountains and hills is deliberate within the geography and theology of ancient Israel. Mountains in the Psalms and Prophets often represent stability, permanence, and God's presence (Psalm 48:1, Isaiah 2:2). The image suggests that from the highest places down to the humblest terrain, the entire land will experience the peace (shalom) that flows from righteous rule. Shalom here is not mere absence of war but the presence of right order, wholeness, and well-being. The Covenant Rendering's rendering of yis'u as 'bear' (like bearing fruit or bearing a burden) preserves the sense that peace is a productive yield, something the land actively generates under the conditions of righteousness.

word_study.meaning: To lift, carry, bear, produce. The verb can mean to physically bear a burden, to produce or yield (as in bearing fruit), or to carry/take up a responsibility. Here it captures both ideas: the mountains 'carry' or 'produce' peace as a burden they bear and a fruit they yield.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that peace is not imposed from above but emerges from the land itself when righteousness is established. This is the vision of a flourishing creation—mountains and hills cooperating in the production of human flourishing.

word_study.meaning: Peace, wholeness, completeness, harmony, well-being. Shalom encompasses not merely the absence of conflict but the presence of right relationship, justice, health, and flourishing. It is a state in which creation is functioning as it should.
word_study.significance: The use of shalom rather than merely saying 'the king will establish order' or 'the king will bring stability' indicates that righteous rule produces not just order but genuine flourishing—the healing of social fractures and the restoration of creation to wholeness.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, vindication. Tzedaqah is both a moral quality (being righteous) and a dynamic action (establishing justice, vindicating the oppressed). Here it is the animating force that causes peace to emerge.
word_study.significance: Righteousness is not a passive virtue but an active principle that reshapes reality. When a king rules with tzedaqah, the natural result is shalom—the landscape itself becomes fruitful in justice.

cross_references.connection: The prophet describes the future restoration: 'the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing'—echoing Psalm 72:3's vision of creation itself responding to righteous rule.
A parallel image: 'Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other'—the same pairing of tzedaqah and shalom that Psalm 72:3 presents as the fruit of just kingship.

The messianic vision depicts the 'mountain of the Lord's house' established in the latter days, from which instruction goes forth and 'nation shall not lift up sword against nation'—the eschatological fulfillment of Psalm 72's vision.

The revelation envisions a day when 'the earth shall be in travail, and all the elements shall be shaken' but eventually 'the mountains shall be made low' and 'the valleys...exalted,' reflecting the restoration theology that ties earthly and cosmic order to righteousness.

King Benjamin promises that those who keep God's commandments 'shall have eternal life...and shall dwell with him in a state of never-ending happiness'—the covenant promise of shalom through righteousness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite thought, the land itself was covenantal—it responded to the people's obedience or disobedience (Deuteronomy 28, Leviticus 26). Fertility, rain, and abundance were God's rewards for righteousness; famine, drought, and desolation were the consequences of injustice. The metaphor of mountains and hills bearing peace assumes this covenantal relationship between moral order and natural order. The ancient world generally believed that cosmic harmony flowed from a righteous ruler—this appears in Egyptian theology, Babylonian kingship ideology, and throughout the ancient Near East. However, Israel's distinctive contribution is the explicit connection between justice for the poor and land prosperity: the land flourishes not when the king is powerful but when he is righteous.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The covenant land—the Americas—responds to the righteousness or unrighteousness of its inhabitants (Alma 36:30, Ether 9:16). When the Nephites are righteous, the land becomes fruitful; when they embrace injustice, the land itself becomes their adversary. This principle, central to Book of Mormon theology, is the exact dynamic Psalm 72:3 describes: righteousness produces flourishing, not just socially but cosmically.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:3-4 teaches that the earth and its bounty are given to 'the obedient and the righteous,' and D&C 38:39 commands care for the poor, linking these two principles. The Restoration teaching is that the earth and its resources belong to God and are meant to be stewarded justly; peace and abundance flow from righteous stewardship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple cosmology envisions a restored creation where all elements are in harmony—the waters are separated properly, the earth brings forth vegetation, and all things are consecrated to righteous purposes. Psalm 72:3's vision of the earth itself producing shalom prefigures the temple's vision of a restored creation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ, as the righteous king, is the one through whom creation itself will be restored to shalom. Romans 8:19-21 teaches that 'the creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.' Christ's rule will eventually extend to a cosmic restoration where righteousness produces universal peace. Psalm 72:3 is a vision of that future reality—the Revelation's promise of a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with humanity and all things are made new.
commentary.application: This verse invites contemplation of how your own sphere of influence—your home, your workplace, your community—either flourishes or withers based on the presence or absence of justice and righteousness. If you govern any realm (as parent, manager, leader), consider whether that realm is becoming more peaceful and fruitful, or more fractious. The psalm suggests that justice and peace are not separate from productivity and flourishing but inseparable from it. Injustice always breeds chaos; righteousness always produces flourishing.

text_kjv: He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 returns to explicit judicial language, but now with intensified action verbs that move beyond judgment to vindication and destruction. The focus narrows sharply to the poor and needy—their condition is not incidental to the king's role but central. The parallelism articulates a three-part action: the king vindicates (yishpot) the poor, rescues (yoshia) the needy, and crushes (vidakke) the oppressor. This is not passive justice but active intervention. The verb yoshia (save, rescue, deliver) suggests that the needy are in mortal danger and require rescue, not merely fair adjudication.

Most strikingly, verse 4 does what verses 1-3 have prepared: it places the oppressor in the crosshairs. The king does not merely judge neutrally between all parties; he specifically targets those who exploit the vulnerable. The verb 'break in pieces' (vidakke) is violent—it is the same language used for crushing enemies in battle. This is a crucial theological point: the king's justice is not abstract neutrality but active hostility toward injustice. There is no ambivalence about oppression in this psalm. The vision of peace and flourishing in verse 3 requires the destruction of those who profit from exploitation. The Covenant Rendering preserves the force of this language: 'crush' (not merely 'restrain' or 'limit') the oppressor.

word_study.meaning: To judge, render judgment, vindicate, establish justice. In this context, the verb specifically means to advocate for or vindicate someone who has been wronged—to render a judgment in their favor.
word_study.significance: The king's judgment is not neutral arbitration but active vindication of the wronged. Justice is partisan—it takes the side of those who have been treated unjustly.

word_study.meaning: To save, rescue, deliver, help. The verb implies that someone is in mortal danger or distress and requires forceful intervention to preserve their life or wellbeing.
word_study.significance: The needy are not merely waiting for a fair hearing; they are in genuine danger and require active rescue. This elevates the king's responsibility from adjudication to intervention.

word_study.meaning: To crush, break, shatter, oppress. The verb describes violent destruction—like crushing something under a heavy weight. It can also mean 'to oppress' when used of the oppressor, but here it describes what happens to the oppressor himself.
word_study.significance: The language is unambiguous: the oppressor is not reformed, managed, or limited but actively destroyed. There is no redemptive arc for those who systematically exploit the vulnerable. Justice requires their undoing.

word_study.meaning: Oppressor, one who practices extortion or exploitation. The noun describes someone who uses power to take advantage of those weaker than themselves—to crush them, extract from them, deny them what is rightfully theirs.
word_study.significance: The oppressor is not a category but a type of person defined by their actions toward the vulnerable. The king's primary adversary in this psalm is not a foreign enemy but the domestic exploiter.

cross_references.connection: The Lord 'executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed'—the divine action that the human king is meant to mirror.
'Rob not the poor, because he is poor...For the LORD will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them'—God Himself becomes the vindicator when human oppressors act with impunity.

Isaiah condemns judges who 'slay the righteous' and 'take reward against the innocent,' then promises that when Zion is redeemed, her judges will be restored to the original righteousness—precisely the vision Psalm 72 articulates.

Alma's judgment of Corianton combines rescue of the sinner with severity against the sin itself, illustrating the principle of active vindication of the wronged paired with opposition to the wrongdoer.
Christ says 'the wicked shall not stand in that day'—the eschatological fulfillment of Psalm 72:4's vision that oppressors will be broken in pieces in the day of righteous judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The image of a king as the active protector of the poor against exploitation would have resonated powerfully in a agrarian, honor-based society where land dispossession and debt slavery were constant threats. Archaeological evidence from ancient Israel shows that small landholders were frequently dispossessed by larger landowners through legal manipulation, usury, and coerced debt slavery. The prophets consistently condemned this practice (Amos 2:6-7, Micah 2:1-2). The ideal king, in this context, is not merely someone who holds court but someone who actively intervenes to prevent exploitation. The language of 'breaking in pieces' is severe, but it reflects the seriousness with which ancient Israelite theology regarded oppression—it is not a minor social problem but a cosmic injustice that merits divine destruction.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Noah's oppression of the Lamanites, Amalickiah's manipulations, and the robbers of Gadiantion all represent the 'oppressor' condemned in Psalm 72:4. Conversely, Captain Moroni's military strategy explicitly prioritizes defending the poor and vulnerable (Alma 48-49), embodying the spirit of verse 4. The Book of Mormon consistently shows that oppression ultimately leads to the oppressor's destruction (Alma 37:13-14).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:77-80 teaches that the wicked should be removed from among the righteous, paralleling Psalm 72:4's vision of breaking the oppressor. D&C 121:22 warns that 'it is the nature and disposition of almost all men...to exercise unrighteous dominion'—addressing the very impulse that oppression represents and that a righteous king must oppose.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple oath includes a covenant against exploitation and a commitment to protect the vulnerable (implied in the commitment to become as God—who defends the fatherless and widow). The sacred name itself connects the covenant maker to God's character as the one who crushes injustice.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the king who 'came to set at liberty them that are bruised' (Luke 4:18). His opposition to the moneychangers in the temple (Matthew 21:12-13) directly enacts Psalm 72:4—driving out those who exploit the vulnerable through commercialized religion. His promise to come again 'in judgment' (Revelation 19:11-16) is painted in imagery of righteous violence against oppression. The Book of Mormon's description of Christ as 'mighty God' and 'Mighty One' emphasizes not passive forgiveness but active power exercised on behalf of the oppressed.
commentary.application: This verse requires honesty about complicity. In a complex economy, most of us benefit, directly or indirectly, from systems that exploit the vulnerable. The question is not whether you are absolutely innocent of participation in oppressive systems (likely impossible in modern society) but whether you actively work to dismantle them or passively profit from them. What injustices in your immediate sphere have you actively opposed? Where have you remained silent when your voice might have made a difference? The psalm calls for more than neutral fairness; it calls for active advocacy and opposition to exploitation.

text_kjv: They shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure, throughout all generations.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 shifts grammatical subject and temporal scope. The focus moves from the king's actions to the people's response ('they shall fear You') and from the present rule to perpetual and universal reverence ('as long as the sun and moon endure, throughout all generations'). This is the longest temporal formula in the poem, suggesting a timelessness that no merely human kingdom could achieve. The verb 'fear' (yira'u) in Hebrew religious context encompasses not mere dread but reverence—respect, awe, recognition of authority rooted in divine character.

Crucially, the object of fear shifts from the king to God: 'they shall fear You'—addressing God, not the king. This subtle shift is theologically significant. The king's just rule is so effective that it produces not fear of the king but fear of God. The people see the king's justice and infer the character of the God behind it. In other words, effective human justice points people beyond the human ruler to the divine ruler. The temporal language—'as long as the sun and moon endure'—echoes covenant language (Genesis 9:16, Psalm 89:37) and suggests an everlasting rather than provisional rule. Yet no historical monarch's reign actually lasts through all generations, which intensifies the eschatological or messianic character of this vision.

word_study.meaning: To fear, revere, respect, stand in awe. In Hebrew religious context, 'fear of God' is not mere terror but reverence—the recognition of God's authority and the desire to maintain right relationship with Him.
word_study.significance: The fear produced by a just king is not the fear of the oppressed for the tyrant but the reverence of those who recognize divine order. The king's justice teaches the people what God is like—strong, just, and protective.

word_study.term_original: יִרְאוּ עִם־שָׁמֶשׁ (yira'u im shamesh) + וְלִפְנֵי יָרֵחַ (lifnei yarach) — 'as long as the sun' and 'before the moon'
word_study.meaning: Sun and moon represent the celestial order, the cosmic constants. 'As long as the sun endures' is a standard Hebrew idiom for perpetuity or the longest conceivable duration.
word_study.significance: The comparison to celestial bodies suggests that the king's rule will be as permanent and regular as the movements of the cosmos. This language signals either hyperbole (which any historical monarchy would be) or messianic expectation (which would be fulfilled only in Christ).

word_study.meaning: Generation by generation, age after age, perpetually. The double phrase emphasizes continuous succession and longevity.
word_study.significance: The vision extends not merely through one lifetime but through the succession of generations—something only possible if God Himself sustains the rule or if the rule is transferable through a dynasty that maintains the same principles.

cross_references.connection: God's covenant with David is described in nearly identical language: 'his seed also will I make to endure for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven...his throne shall endure as the sun before me...and as a faithful witness in heaven'—Psalm 72:5 applies this covenant promise to an ideal king.
The rainbow is God's covenant sign 'for an everlasting covenant,' using the phrase 'throughout all generations'—the same phrase Psalm 72 uses, linking the king's just rule to God's covenant promises.

The messianic vision of one 'like the Son of Man' receiving 'dominion...that shall not pass away' and 'a kingdom...which shall not be destroyed'—language that echoes Psalm 72's vision of an everlasting rule.
The vision of exaltation describes those who receive God's glory as having 'received of his fulness'—echoing the principle that recognizing just rule leads to recognizing divine order.
'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever'—the fulfillment of Psalm 72's vision in the ultimate reign of Christ.

commentary.historical_context: The language of eternal kingship was a staple of ancient Near Eastern royal ideology. Pharaohs claimed to reign eternally; Babylonian kings claimed perpetual legitimacy; Hittite kings styled themselves as eternal representatives of the gods. However, the reality was always different—dynasties fell, kingdoms collapsed, rulers were displaced or died. The Davidic dynasty itself, for which this psalm was likely written, lasted about 400 years before the Babylonian exile destroyed it. This tension between the rhetoric of everlasting rule and the historical reality of political collapse is part of what drove messianic expectation in Judaism. If the psalm is a prayer for Solomon or any historical king, it expresses hope that exceeds historical possibility—which is precisely why the Early Church and the Latter-day Saint tradition read it as ultimately fulfilled only in Christ.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records periods when just rulers brought the people to 'fear God' (Mosiah 1:17, Alma 23:4-6). These periods of righteousness are described in language very similar to Psalm 72—the land flourishes, the people prosper, and the next generation inherits both the physical and spiritual benefits. However, each generation must choose to maintain righteousness; the automatic transmission of justice through generations ultimately requires each person's covenant commitment, which the Book of Mormon shows repeatedly fails.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 110 records that Christ appeared in the Kirtland Temple and stated 'I have accepted this house'—establishing a stake of Zion for the latter days. The vision extends the Davidic covenant promise into the restoration era, suggesting that Christ's rule will eventually be established 'in all the earth' (D&C 87:8, D&C 45:56-60).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple sealing ordinances are meant to bind families 'for time and all eternity'—reflecting the covenant principle that righteous rule (beginning in the family) can extend through generations. Parents who teach their children God's law can hope that their posterity will also 'fear God' and maintain the covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ's rule is the only one that will genuinely endure 'as long as the sun and moon endure.' Latter-day Saint theology teaches that Christ's reign began spiritually at His resurrection and will culminate in a literal thousand-year reign (D&C 29:11, D&C 88:96). Psalm 72:5's vision of perpetual, universal reverence finds its ultimate fulfillment in the universal acknowledgment of Christ's lordship (Philippians 2:9-11). The fact that no human king or dynasty has ever achieved what Psalm 72 promises is powerful evidence that the psalm points to a being beyond human limitations—the eternal king, Jesus Christ.
commentary.application: Consider what kind of influence you want to have across generations. What will you teach your children, students, or those you mentor about justice, God's character, and the fear (reverence) of the Lord? The challenge of verse 5 is that it calls for a kind of excellence that transcends your own lifetime—you are building something meant to extend through your children's children. What values are you establishing that could outlast you? What example are you setting? The verse reminds us that the most lasting influence is not power or wealth but the living example of someone who reverences God and treats the vulnerable with justice.

text_kjv: He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 is among the most beautiful and precisely crafted images in the Psalter. The king is compared to rain—the most precious and life-giving resource in an arid climate. But the comparison is not generic; the poet specifies that this is rain falling on 'mown grass'—freshly cut, seemingly destroyed, vulnerable, utterly dependent. The image suggests restoration after apparent loss, life after cutting, growth after devastation. The poetic effect is profound: a king is not likened to a storm-god (the typical warrior imagery) but to gentle, nourishing water.

The second line reinforces the image with rare, onomatopoetic language: 'showers that drench the earth' (zarzifim zarzip eretz). The Covenant Rendering's rendering of zarzif as 'dripping' preserves the sound-sense of the Hebrew word—it literally sounds like water dripping and splashing. The cumulative effect is to suggest a king whose reign feels like relief from oppressive heat, whose presence is gentle rather than terrorizing, whose rule produces not fear but flourishing. This verse recalls 2 Samuel 23:4, David's final testament, which compares a good ruler to the morning sun breaking through clouds. The emotional shift from the stern language of verse 4 (breaking the oppressor in pieces) to the tender image of rain on mown grass suggests a complete vision of kingship: severity toward injustice, gentleness toward the vulnerable.

word_study.meaning: To descend, come down, go down. The verb pictures the king's approach as a descent from a higher place, like rain falling from the sky.
word_study.significance: The verb subtly establishes the king's relationship to those below him—a descent, a movement toward those who need him, rather than a movement upward or away. Authority moves downward to serve.

word_study.meaning: Rain, the water that falls from heaven. In an arid land, rain is the most precious commodity, the difference between life and death, flourishing and famine.
word_study.significance: The comparison to rain (rather than to a river, a well, or a fountain) emphasizes that the king's benefits flow from above, are not merely humanly generated, and are essential to survival. In the ancient Near East, rain was a divine gift; a king compared to rain is compared to one through whom divine blessing flows.

word_study.meaning: Mown grass, freshly cut hay, a meadow that has been harvested. The word paints a picture of a field that has been cut and lies vulnerable, exposed, needing moisture.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'mown grass' rather than simply 'grass' or 'field' is crucial. Mown grass has been stripped, harvested, made vulnerable. Rain on gez is the image of renewal after cutting, life after apparent destruction—suggesting that the king's rule restores what has been damaged or depleted.

word_study.meaning: Showers, drops of rain, drizzle. The word suggests not a deluge but gentle, consistent moisture.
word_study.significance: Revivim (plural) suggests multiple, gentle showers rather than a single downpour. This is the king's benevolent rule conceived as consistent, gentle, life-giving rather than overwhelming or destructive.

word_study.meaning: To drip, splash, sprinkle; the noun zarzip means drops or dripping. The word is onomatopoetic—it literally sounds like dripping water.
word_study.significance: The rare word choice is deliberate poetic artistry. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'drench' captures the sense better than 'water alone.' The word creates an auditory image—you almost hear the gentle splashing of water.

cross_references.connection: David's final words: 'The God of Israel said...one that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. And he shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth'—the same image of benevolent, life-giving rule as Psalm 72:6, presented as the ideal of kingship.

Moses describes his teaching as falling like rain: 'My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew'—using the same rain imagery to suggest that true instruction is gentle, nourishing, and life-giving.

The prophet compares God's word to rain that waters the earth and produces fruit: 'as the rain cometh down from heaven...so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth'—establishing the metaphor that divine blessing flows like rain from above.
'He shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth'—using the same metaphor to describe God's returning favor and restoration to His people.

The revelation describes the work of bringing people to repentance as preparing them to receive the Lord's 'bounteous mercy'—the principle that God's blessing flows like rain upon those prepared to receive it.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, particularly in the Levant, rain was both precious and unpredictable. The region experiences a Mediterranean climate with a brief rainy season (November-March) followed by a long dry season. Failure of the rains meant crop failure, famine, and death. The image of a king as rain would have carried profound emotional and economic weight. Unlike Egypt, which had the Nile's predictable inundation, Israel's prosperity depended on seasonal rain. A king who brings fertility to the land—who is, in effect, a conduit of divine blessing—would be seen as supremely valuable. The metaphor transcends mere political ideology; it is deeply rooted in agricultural necessity. Archaeological evidence shows that Bronze and Iron Age kingdoms that managed water resources effectively (through cistern construction, terrace agriculture, and canal systems) prospered, while those that did not often failed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:26 uses water imagery when King Benjamin teaches that the Saints should 'succor those that stand in need of your succor' and be 'judge[s] of this people,' suggesting that kindly rule toward the vulnerable is as essential as rain to a parched land. Alma 32:28-43 develops the metaphor more explicitly, comparing God's word to a seed that grows like a plant when watered—suggesting that spiritual nourishment, like physical sustenance, requires gentle, consistent care.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:24 describes Christ's blessing as 'light and truth...that shineth in darkness,' and D&C 88:11 promises that 'the light which is in all things...giveth life to all things'—Latter-day Saint cosmology reframes the rain metaphor as light, suggesting that the king's (or Christ's) blessing flows through the natural world itself.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Water is a central symbol in temple ordinances. The washing and anointing, the font, the water under the floor of the temple—all symbolize the flow of cleansing and life-giving divine power. The king in Psalm 72:6, like the priesthood holder in temple covenant, is a conduit through which blessing flows to others. The 'waters of life' promised in Revelation 21:6 and referenced in Latter-day Saint theology (D&C 63:23, D&C 88:61) echo this same metaphor.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate rain upon the earth. John 7:37-39 records Christ's invitation: 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink' and promises that 'out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water'—adapting Psalm 72:6's rain imagery to Christ's ministry. The imagery of Christ's gentleness is fundamental to New Testament Christology: He came not to condemn but to save (John 3:17), not to break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax (Matthew 12:20, quoting Isaiah 42:3). Christ's kingdom, paradoxically, combines the severity of verse 4 (He will judge and break the oppressor) with the gentleness of verse 6 (He is rain upon the parched ground). Revelation 22:1 describes the river of water of life flowing from God's throne in the new creation—the eschatological fulfillment of Psalm 72:6's vision.
commentary.application: This verse invites reflection on how you exercise any form of authority or influence. Is your leadership—whether of a family, organization, or group—experienced by others as a blessing, like rain on parched ground? Or do those under your care experience you as demanding, extractive, or indifferent to their flourishing? The verse challenges you to consider whether your leadership style serves others' growth or merely your own agenda. Moreover, it asks whether you yourself are allowing God's gentle, life-giving influence (the 'rain') to soften your heart and restore areas where you have been 'mown down' by disappointment, grief, or failure. Are you prepared to receive God's blessing as gentle restoration?

text_kjv: He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the needy.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the shift from the king's justice in the courts (verses 1-4) to his active compassion for the vulnerable. The Hebrew verb yachos ('he will have pity') describes not mere legal fairness but emotional identification with suffering. The king does not merely rule over the poor; he *feels* for them. This is covenant language — the king's heart is bound to the condition of his most defenseless subjects.

The repetition of 'needy ones' (evyonim) in a single verse is emphatic and driving. The KJV translates this as 'the poor and needy' in the first clause and 'the needy' in the second, but the Hebrew repeats the same word to intensify the point: the needy, the needy, the needy. They are not an afterthought to royal justice; they are the measure of it. The verb 'save' (yoshia) carries the sense of deliverance from danger or oppression — this is soteriological language applied to the king's role.

word_study.meaning: To have compassion, spare, show pity; an emotional response of compassion that moves one to action. The root suggests a feeling that leads to restraint from harm and active protection.
word_study.significance: This is not detached judgment but felt compassion. The king's heart is moved toward the poor. In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the king's role was often limited to punishment of wrongdoing; here, the royal virtue is active identification with suffering. The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'have pity' — an interior disposition, not merely external behavior.

word_study.meaning: The destitute, the poorest of the poor; those who lack basic necessities. Distinct from dal ('poor'), evyonim emphasizes absolute poverty and helplessness. In covenant language, they are the primary recipients of God's justice.
word_study.significance: The repetition of evyonim within verse 13 is not accident — it drives home the king's central responsibility. In biblical ethics, the evyonim are the measure of covenant faithfulness. God identifies with them; the king must too.

word_study.meaning: To save, deliver, rescue from danger or oppression. The root carries the sense of making wide, giving space, freeing from constraint. In theological contexts, it refers to God's deliverance of Israel.
word_study.significance: Here, the king takes on a divine function — yoshia is the language of God's redemption applied to the monarch. The king does not merely rule; he rescues. This foreshadows messianic expectation: the ultimate king will be the ultimate savior.

cross_references.connection: The charge to speak for the voiceless and judge fairly for the poor and needy mirrors the psalmist's description of ideal kingship.
The messianic king 'shall judge the poor with righteousness' — a direct echo of Psalm 72's royal ideal applied to the eschatological king.

King Benjamin teaches that the wealthy must 'retain a remission' of their sins by 'distributing to the poor,' reflecting the covenant principle that the king (and all leaders) must actively protect the vulnerable.

In the Lord's covenant with the Saints, 'it is his will that you shall live together' and 'he that hath sufficient shall not bestow upon him who hath not sufficient' — the principle that covenant community must be ordered toward the care of the needy.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, royal inscriptions from Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Levant regularly claimed that the king 'judged the widow and orphan' and 'heard the cry of the oppressed.' However, these claims were often formulaic and disconnected from actual practice. Psalm 72 may be understood either as an idealization (what kingship *should* be) or as a description of an actual justice system (possibly associated with Solomon's early reign, 1 Kings 3:16-28). The emphasis on *feeling* (yachos) for the poor distinguishes this from mere bureaucratic justice — it insists that royal virtue requires emotional solidarity with suffering.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's address in Mosiah 4 repeatedly returns to the responsibility of the righteous to save the poor and needy. Benjamin teaches that God's covenant people must 'succor those that stand in need of your succor' (Mosiah 4:26) — language that echoes Psalm 72:13's yoshia ('save'). The righteous king and righteous people are bound together by a commitment to active deliverance of the vulnerable.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:24-27 establishes the Lord's law for Zion: 'Thou shalt not be idle; for he that is idle shall not eat the bread nor wear the garments of the laborer.' This is not mere prohibition of idleness but the principle underlying Psalm 72: covenant community is structured to ensure that everyone has what they need. The covenant that binds a community binds the strong to active care for the weak.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple covenant, one covenants to 'succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees' (adapted from D&C 81:5). The king's compassion for the poor in Psalm 72 reflects the covenantal obligation to care for those bound to us by the eternal covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist describes an ideal king who 'saves' (yoshia) the poor through felt compassion. In the Gospels, Jesus is repeatedly moved with compassion (Greek: splagchnizomai, which parallels yachos) at the sight of suffering crowds (Matthew 9:36, 14:14). His miracles of healing and feeding are acts of yoshia — saving deliverance. The Atonement itself is the ultimate saving act of the ideal King. Psalm 72 describes what messianic kingship looks like: the king's heart is fused with the condition of the powerless, and his power flows toward their rescue.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern covenant members with a standard: to what extent does our felt compassion for the poor move us to actual deliverance? The Hebrew yachos is not mere sympathy or agreement that poverty is bad; it is an emotional response that compels action. The king's justice is not punitive but liberatory — he rescues. In Relief Society, priesthood quorums, and ward communities, are we identifying with the needy in our midst, and are our hearts moved to save? This verse asks whether our covenant commitment to 'succor the weak' (D&C 81:5) is driven by genuine compassion or mere duty.

text_kjv: He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 14 deepens the portrait of royal justice by naming the two primary forms of oppression that destroy the poor: fraud (tokh, 'oppression' or 'deceit') and violence (chamas). The king's role is not merely to comfort the suffering but to *redeem* them — to use the specific legal-familial mechanisms available to him to buy back what has been stolen, to restore what has been seized, to avenge what has been violated.

The most powerful phrase appears at the verse's end: 'their blood will be precious in his eyes.' This is devastatingly simple. In the ancient world, the blood of the powerless was routinely spilled without legal consequence. A master could kill a slave without facing execution; the wealthy could murder the poor and face only fines. Psalm 72 makes the radical claim that under just rule, the life of the poorest person is *valuable* — their blood is yaqar (precious) in the king's sight. This transforms the poor from invisible to sacred.

word_study.meaning: To redeem, buy back, reclaim; the action of the go'el (kinsman-redeemer). The go'el was responsible for buying back family members sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47-49), reclaiming family land (Leviticus 25:25), and avenging murdered kin (Numbers 35:19). It is a relationship of intimate responsibility.
word_study.significance: When the king 'redeems' (yig'al) the poor, he takes on the role of go'el for the entire nation. He is no longer distant ruler but family member responsible for their welfare. This is covenant language — it binds the king to the poor with ties as strong as kinship. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this by using the language of redemption rather than mere 'salvation.'

word_study.meaning: Oppression, exploitation, or deceit. The root meaning is uncertain, but in context it describes how the powerful systematically wrong the weak — through fraud, manipulation, and coercive extraction of resources. It is the invisible violence of exploitation.
word_study.significance: Paired with chamas (overt violence), tokh represents the full spectrum of harm: the violence you see coming (chamas) and the harm you don't immediately recognize (fraud, false dealing). The king must counteract both.

word_study.meaning: Violence, outrage, wrongdoing; the overt, brutal harm perpetrated by the strong against the weak. Chamas appears frequently in prophetic literature as the sign of a society's covenant unfaithfulness.
word_study.significance: The pairing of tokh and chamas in verse 14 is significant: oppression (hidden) and violence (visible). The king must address both the systemic and the spectacular forms of harm.

word_study.meaning: Precious, valuable, costly; that which is honored and esteemed. In the context of 'blood,' it means that human life — specifically the life of the poor — is valued, protected, honored.
word_study.significance: This single word overturns the entire social order of the ancient world. In societies where status determined the legal value of blood, Psalm 72 insists that under God's just rule, even the poorest person's blood is precious. Their life has worth because the king values them — his eyes see their worth.

cross_references.connection: Boaz acts as go'el for Ruth and Naomi, redeeming them through covenant responsibility — the same relational dynamic the psalmist envisions for the king's relationship to the poor.
The law of the go'el establishes that a family member must redeem a poor kinsman sold into slavery — the legal precedent for the psalmist's vision of the king as universal go'el.

When 'truth faileth' and righteousness is gone, the Lord himself takes on the role of redeemer: 'He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore his arm brought salvation unto him' — the divine redeeming the human when human kings fail.
Amulek teaches that no man can redeem another's sins 'except it be by the atonement of Christ the Lord' — the ultimate redemption (yig'al) of all humanity, fulfilling the kingly role of go'el.

In the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple, the Lord is addressed as 'thou who hast paid the price of blood' — a covenantal affirmation that the precious blood of the redeemed is valued by the Divine King.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern law codes, the legal penalties for killing or harming someone varied dramatically based on social status. Hammurabi's Code (c. 1750 BCE) prescribed different penalties for harming a 'man' (awilu, the free upper class) versus a 'commoner' (mushkenu) versus a 'slave.' The life of an upper-class person was worth more; the life of a slave was valued minimally. Psalm 72 implicitly rejects this graduated valuation of human life. The covenant God makes with Israel establishes that all bearers of the divine image have equal dignity and inviolable worth. This is not a claim the ancient world would readily accept; it represents the theological revolution of biblical ethics.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's sermon to Zoramites in Alma 32-34 repeatedly emphasizes that God 'doth not cast out any who come unto him' — that the poor and despised are precisely those God seeks to redeem. When Alma teaches that 'ye are all precious unto me' (Alma 34:3 in the larger context of his ministry), he is articulating the principle Psalm 72 asserts: the king (and by extension, all who hold authority) must regard the poor as precious in their sight.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 123:13-14 teaches that 'it is an imperative duty that we owe to all the frailties of our nature' and that every Saint should work 'to redeem Zion.' The language of redemption (yig'al) connects to the Doctrine and Covenants' vision of a community of mutual covenant care where no one is disposable and all are valued as sacred.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant to 'bear one another's burdens' (Mosiah 18:8-9) and 'comfort those that stand in need of comfort' reflects the go'el principle: one is bound by sacred covenant to act as kinsman-redeemer for one's covenant family.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate go'el — the kinsman-redeemer. He enters into covenant kinship with humanity, assumes responsibility for our redemption from sin and death, and 'redeems their soul' (yig'al nafshan) through his atoning blood. In Isaiah 59:16, when no human redeemer appears, the Lord himself becomes the redeemer. In Psalm 72, the ideal king foreshadows the one who would actually accomplish what all earthly kings could only approximate: universal redemption through the spilling of precious, covenant blood. Revelation 5:9 celebrates Christ as the one 'slain from the foundation of the world,' whose blood is indeed precious — the price of universal redemption.
commentary.application: This verse asks believers to examine whether they regard the poor and vulnerable as precious. In a world that constantly assigns differential value to human lives based on wealth, status, and visibility, Psalm 72:14 insists that covenant community must reverse this logic. Every member of the body of Christ is precious in the Father's sight. When a sister is exploited by a false friend (tokh) or harmed by domestic violence (chamas), does our community recognize her blood as precious and act to redeem her? Do we regard the homeless person, the refugee, the immigrant, the abuse survivor as precious in our sight? The covenant of discipleship binds us as go'el to those who suffer.

text_kjv: And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold of Sheba: prayer also shall be made for him continually; and daily shall he be blessed.

commentary.narrative:
The focus shifts now from the king's actions toward the poor to the people's response to such a king. 'May he live' is the prayer of a grateful nation — they pray for the king's long life and flourishing because his justice sustains their own flourishing. The mention of 'gold from Sheba' evokes the visit of the Queen of Sheba to Solomon (1 Kings 10:2, 10), suggesting that this ideal king will receive tribute and honor from distant nations. This is not mere materialism; in ancient Near Eastern thought, a king who receives tribute is a king whose justice has earned him international respect and blessing.

But the most significant image here is ceaseless intercession: 'may prayer be offered for him continually; may he be blessed all day long' (The Covenant Rendering's rendering of tamid kol hayyom — 'continually, all day long').
