The people do not merely obey this just king; they hold him up in prayer without ceasing. Their constant blessing of the king is their way of asking God to sustain him in the hard work of justice. This is the covenant relationship made visible: the people pray for their ruler as their ruler cares for them.

word_study.meaning: May he live, may his life be sustained; the jussive form expressing a prayer or wish for the king's long life and vitality.
word_study.significance: In covenant perspective, to pray 'may he live' is to recognize that even the king's continuation depends on the Lord's grace. The people's prayer is not command but petition — they ask God to sustain their ruler, understanding that true justice flows from divine blessing.

word_study.meaning: To pray, intercede, make supplication; the reflexive form suggests deliberate, sustained prayer-making.
word_study.significance: The people's intercession for the king is not ceremonial but sacrificial — they invest their spiritual energy in his continuation and his ability to do justice. This reflects a theology where prayer for leaders is itself a form of supporting justice.

word_study.meaning: Without interruption, perpetually, at all times; the combination emphasizes unceasing, relentless prayer throughout the entire day.
word_study.significance: This is not halfhearted or occasional intercession. The people's commitment to praying for their just king is as constant as the sun (which itself appears in the next verse as a symbol of permanence). Their prayer is ceaseless because justice is never finished; it must be renewed and upheld daily.

word_study.meaning: May he be blessed, may blessings be pronounced over him; the causative form suggests the people actively calling down blessing upon the king.
word_study.significance: The people do not wait for blessings to come to their king; they pronounce blessings themselves. This reflects a theology where the people's words have creative power — their blessings literally sustain the king's ability to do justice.

cross_references.connection: The Queen of Sheba brings gold to Solomon, and his fame is associated with his wisdom and justice — the historical background for the reference to Sheba's gold as a sign of a just king's honor.

Paul urges prayers and intercessions to be made for all people, especially for 'kings, and all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life' — the principle that prayers for rulers sustain just governance.

The Lord teaches the Saints to 'give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me; for his words ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth' — affirming that sustained support for righteous leadership flows from covenant commitment.

The sons of Mosiah 'had waxed strong in the knowledge of the truth' because they 'had prayed much and labored exceedingly' — showing the connection between persistent intercession and spiritual sustenance for those called to lead.

commentary.historical_context: Sheba (modern Yemen/southwestern Arabia) was famous in the ancient world for its wealth in incense, spices, and precious materials. The Queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon (1 Kings 10) is one of the Bible's most famous international encounters and signifies Solomon's prestige and power. By invoking Sheba's gold, Psalm 72 suggests that a just king will gain international respect and tributary relationships. However, the deeper point is theological: a nation that prays for its king, that invests its spiritual energy in his success, binds itself to him and him to justice. Intercession is not passive; it is the people's active participation in sustaining righteous governance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 29, after King Benjamin's death, the people desire to install one of his sons as king, but the Lord forbids hereditary kingship and establishes a system of judges instead. Alma becomes the chief judge, and the text repeatedly emphasizes that the people's spiritual covenant sustains the judges' ability to judge righteously. When the people are righteous and prayerful, the judges judge justly; when the people transgress, the judges fail. The principle in Psalm 72:15 — that the people's prayers sustain just leadership — is central to the Book of Mormon's political theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:1-6 establishes the Saints' covenant to sustain Church leadership through prayer and support. The principle of 'sustained prayer' (tamid) for leaders appears throughout modern revelation. Doctrine and Covenants 109 records the Saints' intercessory prayers at the Kirtland Temple dedication — public, sustained prayer for the establishment of Zion.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, covenants are made to sustain righteous leaders and to build up God's kingdom. The idea of 'sustaining' (through covenant commitment and prayer) those who lead in righteousness is central to temple theology and the Latter-day Saint understanding of covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one for whom 'prayer is made continually' (tamid). Hebrews 7:25 affirms that Christ 'ever liveth to make intercession for us' — he is both the king for whom prayers are continually offered and the one who himself makes perpetual intercession. Just as the people in Psalm 72 sustain their just king with ceaseless prayer, the Church sustains Christ as King through prayer, worship, and covenant commitment. The reference to gold from Sheba foreshadows the gifts brought to the infant Jesus by the Magi (Matthew 2:11), though Matthew's Magi come from the east, connecting to the Arabian world known for precious materials.
commentary.application: Latter-day Saints covenant to 'sustain' Church leaders — not through blind obedience but through deliberate, sustained prayer and support. This verse asks: How consistently do we pray for those called to lead? The phrase 'continually, all day long' (tamid kol hayyom) suggests that sustaining leaders in prayer is not an occasional duty but a daily practice. When we encounter news about bishops, stake presidents, general authorities, or civic leaders, do we pause to pray for them, asking that God grant them wisdom and strength to do justice? The covenant to sustain is active prayer, not passive agreement.

text_kjv: There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 16 describes the material and spiritual prosperity that will flourish under just rule. This is visionary language — the psalmist is describing not merely political justice but eschatological abundance, a restoration of Eden-like fertility. The image of grain growing on mountaintops is deliberately impossible under normal conditions; mountaintops are too high, too cold, too exposed for grain cultivation. Yet under this king's reign, even the impossible becomes real. The grain waves 'like Lebanon' — a reference to the magnificent cedars of Lebanon, whose size and beauty were legendary in the ancient world. This is supernatural fecundity.

The final phrase — 'they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth' — extends the blessing from rural fields to urban centers. Cities are not typically described as places of natural flourishing, yet the psalmist envisions even urbanites prospering 'like grass.' This is comprehensive abundance: rural fields overflow, cities flourish, and the poor (now cared for by the just king) share in the general plenty. The theological claim is profound: covenant justice produces not merely moral improvement but material transformation. A society ordered by righteousness experiences tangible blessing.

word_study.meaning: Handful, cake, or abundance; the exact meaning is debated by scholars. In context, it likely means 'abundance' — a measure of grain so great it seems almost impossible.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering and most modern commentaries render this as 'abundance,' emphasizing the eschatological superabundance rather than the literal 'handful.' The point is that grain will be so plentiful it overflows all normal containers.

word_study.meaning: To wave, shake, quiver; the movement of grain fields in the wind, a sign of their fullness and health. The word can also mean 'to tremble' or 'to resound.'
word_study.significance: The grain does not merely grow; it moves visibly, palpably present. The earth itself becomes vocal in its fruitfulness — it shakes with the weight of blessing.

word_study.meaning: To bloom, flourish, shoot up; the verb of budding, sprouting, coming to visible life. It emphasizes the dynamism and visibility of growth.
word_study.significance: The people in the city are not merely surviving; they are visibly, abundantly alive. Covenant justice produces visible, tangible flourishing.

cross_references.connection: The Garden of Eden's abundance — trees 'pleasant to the sight, and good for food' — parallels the eschatological abundance Psalm 72 envisions; both represent God's original covenant intention for creation.

In the eschatological vision, 'the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands' — creation itself responds with joy to covenant restoration.

In the restoration, 'the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt' — eschatological abundance flowing from covenant restoration.

In the Book of Mormon account of Jaredite civilization, when righteousness prevails, 'they did have flocks of herds, and silks, and fine-twined linen; and they did work in all manner of craftsmen's work' — material prosperity flowing from covenant obedience.

The Lord promises Zion's establishment: 'And it shall be called the New Jerusalem, a land of peace, a city of refuge, all the faithful of the Lord shall be gathered there' — the gathering into covenant blessing produces material and spiritual abundance.

commentary.historical_context: The reference to Lebanon's cedars connects this vision to ancient royal ideology. Lebanon's great forests were the resource base for Solomon's building projects (1 Kings 5:6-10). Cedar was the marker of royal magnificence and stability. When the psalmist says the grain will 'shake like Lebanon,' he is evoking both the natural beauty of the cedars and their association with royal stability and divine blessing. The image of grain on mountaintops is also connected to the temple theology — the temple mount was understood as the cosmic axis mundi, the place where heaven and earth met. Eschatological abundance flows from covenant renewal centered on the temple.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:27-30, Alma describes the state of the Church when righteousness prevails: they 'were exceedingly prosperous and waxed strong in the land.' The connection between covenant obedience and material abundance is consistent throughout the Book of Mormon. When the Nephites keep their covenants, 'all manner of good' flows to them. When they break covenant, famine and distress follow.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:17-20 establishes the Lord's will for Zion: 'For if you will that I give unto you a place in the celestial world, you must prepare yourselves by doing the things which I have commanded you and required of you.' The promise of eschatological abundance in Zion is conditional on covenant faithfulness. Zion itself becomes the realization of Psalm 72's vision.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place of covenant restoration and abundance. In temple theology, the endowment recapitulates the Fall and Atonement, moving from the Garden (abundance) through transgression and redemption toward covenant restoration. Psalm 72:16's vision of Eden-like fertility is the temple's promise of what covenant community can become.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the source of all true abundance and blessing. In Matthew 6:11, he teaches us to pray for 'our daily bread' (arton hemeras), connecting sustenance to covenant prayer. In John 6, he identifies himself as the 'bread of life' — the true source of all nourishment and flourishing. The eschatological vision of grain covering mountaintops finds its fulfillment in the messianic reign, where Christ's redemption restores all creation to Edenic abundance. Revelation 22:1-2 describes the heavenly city where the river of life flows and the tree of life bears 'twelve manner of fruits' — the eschatological abundance that Christ's reign produces.
commentary.application: This verse connects covenant righteousness to concrete, material blessing — not merely spiritual benefit but tangible prosperity. For modern covenant community, this means that communities ordered by justice, integrity, and mutual care do experience measurable flourishing: better mental health, stronger families, more resilient institutions. Conversely, societies marked by corruption and injustice experience measurable deterioration. This is not a prosperity gospel claim that righteousness automatically produces wealth for individuals; it is a claim about collective flourishing. When a ward or community practices covenant justice, mutual care, and honest dealing, it experiences a different quality of life — what Psalm 72 calls 'abundance.' The question for each community is: Are we willing to practice the kingdom justice Psalm 72 describes in order to experience its promised flourishing?

text_kjv: His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and men shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 17 is the theological pivot point of Psalm 72. The language shifts from the king's earthly reign to the eternal, messianic significance of his name and his blessing. The verb yinnon ('may his name flourish, may it generate offspring') is rare and carries profound resonance. The Hebrew root nin means 'offspring' or 'posterity,' so yinnon suggests that the king's name does not merely survive but produces new life, new generations, new meaning. His name is generative — it continues to give birth to blessing across time.

The phrase 'all nations shall find blessing in him' (veyitbarekhu vo kol goyim) is the critical echo of the Abrahamic covenant. In Genesis 12:3 and 22:18, God promises Abraham that 'all nations shall be blessed in him/by you.' Psalm 72:17 applies this exact phraseology to the king, making an explosive theological claim: the Davidic king *is* the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham. The universal scope of blessing — not limited to Israel but reaching all nations — positions this king not as a merely political figure but as the messianic conduit through whom God's covenant blessing flows to all humanity. The Talmud recognized this and listed Yinnon as one of the names of the Messiah (Sanhedrin 98b).

word_study.meaning: May it flourish, may it propagate, may it beget; a rare verbal form related to nin ('offspring, posterity'). The name does not merely endure but generates new life and meaning across generations.
word_study.significance: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) lists Yinnon as one of the possible names of the Messiah, based on Psalm 72:17. This is not merely a name that survives; it is a name that generates blessing in perpetuity. The connection to Abraham's covenant (Genesis 12:3, 22:18) makes Yinnon the quintessential messianic title — the name that brings blessing to all nations.

word_study.meaning: May they be blessed, may they bless themselves; the reflexive form suggests that all nations actively participate in receiving blessing through this figure.
word_study.significance: The word yitbarekhu is the exact form used in Genesis 12:3 and 22:18 to describe the Abrahamic promise. By employing this same verb, Psalm 72 makes the explicit connection: this king fulfills what God promised to Abraham.

word_study.meaning: May they call him happy, may they pronounce him blessed; to declare someone's blessedness or good fortune. The verb carries the sense of public recognition and acclamation.
word_study.significance: This is not hidden blessing but proclaimed, public acclamation. All nations will openly declare this king's blessedness. This is universal acknowledgment of messianic status.

word_study.meaning: Sun; the celestial body that marks time and order. The sun symbolizes permanence, constancy, and divine blessing in ancient Near Eastern thought.
word_study.significance: To say the king's name endures 'as long as the sun' is to anchor his significance in cosmic permanence. This is not merely political but cosmic theology — the king's blessing is woven into the fabric of creation itself.

cross_references.connection: God's promise to Abraham: 'in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed' — the foundational covenant that Psalm 72:17 claims the king fulfills.
After the binding of Isaac, the Lord reiterates: 'in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed' — the messianic promise that the Davidic line fulfills.
Nathan's prophecy to David: 'his kingdom shall be established for ever' — the eternal establishment of David's line that Psalm 72 portrays.

Alma quotes Isaiah and connects the messianic expectation to Christ: 'as the Lord God liveth, surely a prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto his people' — identifying Christ as the fulfillment of the promised king.

The Lord speaks of the eternal light and glory: 'the light which shineth, which giveth you light, is through him who enlighteneth your eyes' — identifying Christ as the eternal light that sustains all blessing.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, kings were understood to provide blessing to their realms — through their justice, through their relationship with the gods, and through their own person. However, the claim in Psalm 72:17 that *all nations* will be blessed through this king exceeds typical royal ideology and ventures into messianic eschatology. The Talmudic recognition of Yinnon as a messianic title shows that Jewish interpretive tradition understood Psalm 72:17 as explicitly messianic rather than merely descriptive of an ideal earthly ruler. The echo of the Abrahamic covenant makes clear that the psalmist is claiming continuity between God's promise to Abraham and the promise inherent in the Davidic dynasty.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Nephi's vision (1 Nephi 11-12), Nephi sees Christ 'descend out of heaven' and his 'name should be Jesus Christ' — establishing that this name, like Yinnon, will generate blessing for all people. Alma's prophecy in Alma 7:9-10 identifies Christ as the one 'after whom this land is named' and through whom 'all nations shall come unto him' — echoing Psalm 72's claim of universal blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:24 identifies Christ as 'the Son of the Living God' whose name is 'Jesus Christ' — a name that, like Yinnon, is eternally generative. D&C 88:1-13 portrays Christ as the light of creation, the source through whom all things are blessed and sustained — the cosmic dimension of the messianic blessing Psalm 72 envisions.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the center from which blessing flows to all the earth. In temple theology, Christ is the source of all covenant blessing, and the temple is the place where that blessing is transmitted. Psalm 72's vision of universal blessing flowing through the king finds its temple expression in the concept of endowment — the transmission of divine blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 72:17 is overtly messianic and explicitly points to Jesus Christ as the one whose name (Yinnon, but also Jesus, meaning 'Savior') endures forever and through whom all nations are blessed. Revelation 5:13 depicts the heavenly vision where creation itself 'saith, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever' — the ultimate fulfillment of all nations pronouncing blessing upon the messianic king. In Philippians 2:9-11, Paul teaches that 'God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow' — the universal acclamation of the king that Psalm 72:17 prophesies.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse affirms that blessing does not flow exclusively through institutional channels or geographic boundaries. Christ's name and blessing reach 'all nations' — transcending culture, ethnicity, and nationality. For Latter-day Saints, this has profound implications for missionary work, humanitarian service, and inter-faith engagement. The kingdom of Christ is not tribal or sectarian but genuinely universal. Furthermore, the generative nature of Yinnon's name suggests that the blessing of the gospel multiplies and expands rather than depletes. Each act of faith, each sharing of testimony, each living of the gospel adds to the blessing flowing outward. Members are not merely recipients of blessing but participants in its propagation across all peoples.

text_kjv: Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 72 concludes with a formal doxology — a statement of praise and blessing directed toward God. This doxology is not unique to Psalm 72; it marks the end of Book II of the Psalter. The five books of Psalms are each concluded with a doxology (41:14 ends Book I; 89:53 ends Book III; 106:48 ends Book IV; and 150 serves as the doxology for Book V). The placement of this doxology after Psalm 72's vision of ideal kingship affirms that all earthly kingship — even the most perfect — ultimately exists in service of God's sovereignty and wisdom.

The statement 'who only doeth wondrous things' (oseh nifla'ot levado) positions God, not the king, as the ultimate source of all blessing and justice. The Hebrew nifla'ot (wonders, wondrous deeds) refers to divine acts that exceed human understanding or power — miracles, cosmic acts, the manifestations of God's character. By concluding Psalm 72 with this affirmation, the psalmist reminds the reader that even the most just and compassionate human king operates within the sphere of God's wonders. The justice described in verses 1-17 is only possible because God empowers it; the abundance described in verse 16 depends on God's sustaining hand; the universal blessing described in verse 17 flows from God's eternal covenant. This doxology is not anti-climactic but foundational — it grounds the entire vision of the psalm in theocentric rather than anthropocentric reality.

word_study.meaning: Blessed, praised, honored; the opening word of a formal doxology or hymn of praise. Baruk directs attention upward, toward God, in recognition of divine character and acts.
word_study.significance: This is the language of covenant affirmation — the people bless God in response to recognizing God's character and covenant faithfulness. The doxology is not flattery but acknowledgment of reality.

word_study.meaning: Wonders, wondrous deeds, things that are wonderful or miraculous; divine acts that exceed normal expectation and reveal God's power and character.
word_study.significance: The term nifla'ot appears frequently in the Psalter in connection with God's mighty acts — the exodus, the sustaining of creation, the protection of Israel. By using this term to close Psalm 72, the psalmist affirms that the justice and blessing described throughout the psalm are themselves manifestations of divine wonder.

word_study.meaning: Alone, only, exclusively; emphasizing that this quality or action belongs uniquely to God.
word_study.significance: By affirming that God 'alone' does wonders, the psalmist asserts monotheistic conviction. No human king, no earthly power, no foreign deity can accomplish what God accomplishes. The king's justice is derivative; God's justice is primordial.

cross_references.connection: The identical doxology appears at the end of Book I, affirming the same theocentric foundation: 'Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.'

The Song of the Sea asks: 'Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?' — identifying God's wonder-working as the foundation of Israel's covenant.
The final Psalm affirms: 'I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works' — making nifla'ot (wonders) central to covenant praise.

Moroni invites the reader to 'ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, if these things are not true; and if ye shall ask with a sincere heart, with real intent, having faith in Christ, he will manifest the truth of it unto you, by the power of the Holy Ghost' — the wonders (nifla'ot) of the Spirit manifesting truth.
The Lord teaches: 'All things must come to pass in their time' — affirming that the accomplishment of all covenant promises rests in God's hands and wisdom, not in human agency alone.

commentary.historical_context: The five-fold division of the Psalter into five books (mirroring the five books of Torah) and the placement of doxologies at the end of each book suggest that the Psalter was edited as a complete theological work rather than a mere collection of individual poems. The doxology at Psalm 72:18 affirms that all earthly kingdoms, no matter how just or glorious, exist within the sphere of God's ultimate sovereignty. In the context of post-exilic Judaism (when the Psalter reached its final form), this affirmation was especially significant: Israel no longer had a king, yet the covenant relationship with God endured. The doxology affirms that God's wonder-working does not depend on human kingship but on God's own character and faithfulness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 2, King Benjamin delivers his final address and affirms that his kingship is itself a covenant responsibility from God: 'the substantial meaning of that which hath been spoken by our fathers are fulfilled, in this our time' (Mosiah 1:16). Benjamin acknowledges that the wonders of God — the covenant, the sustenance, the redemption — exceed any earthly king's powers. This is the same theocentric foundation Psalm 72:18 affirms.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:21 teaches: 'In nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things, and obey not his commandments' — affirming the theocentric vision that all blessing, all power, all wonder flows from God's hand, and all human responsibility consists in recognizing and aligning with God's character.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The doxology of Psalm 72:18 appears in the temple context as a fundamental acknowledgment that all covenant work is done in the presence of God and under God's direction. The temple is not a monument to human achievement but a house of the Lord where God's wonders are made manifest.

commentary.christological_typology: The doxology concludes by affirming God's ultimate sovereignty and wonder-working. In Christ, God's wonders reach their highest expression. Colossians 1:15-17 describes Christ as 'the image of the invisible God' and 'by him were all things created' — the ultimate revelation of God's character and power. Hebrews 1:3 affirms that Christ 'is the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power' — God's wonder-working made incarnate and visible. When the psalmist affirms that God 'alone doeth wondrous things,' the Christian reader understands that these wonders are most fully revealed in the incarnation, atonement, and resurrection of Christ.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this doxology is a corrective to two errors: (1) the error of assuming that human institutions, leaders, or programs are ultimately responsible for covenant blessing, and (2) the error of despair when human institutions fail or disappoint. Psalm 72:18 places all ultimate power and blessing in God's hands. Church leaders, no matter how faithful, are human and limited. The justice system, no matter how righteous, cannot ultimately redeem humanity. Families, communities, and nations, no matter how well-ordered, cannot sustain themselves without God's sustaining grace. The doxology calls us to look beyond human achievement to divine character. When we encounter injustice or suffering in the world, Psalm 72:18 does not minimize it but redirects our faith: the ultimate remedy lies not in human effort alone but in God's wonders. This cultivates both humility before God and courage in covenant work — we labor knowing that our efforts are participation in God's redemptive purposes, not autonomous human achievement.

text_kjv: And blessed be his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 72 concludes with a magnificent doxology that shifts from petition to proclamation. After sixty-eight verses of royal prayer, the psalmist ends not with a whispered hope but with a bold declaration: God's name and glory will fill the entire earth. The double 'Amen, and Amen' is not casual repetition but a solemn seal—the congregation's corporate affirmation that transforms individual prayer into communal covenant. This verse reflects the Israelite understanding that God's 'glory' (kavod) is not abstract or distant but manifest, weighty, and earth-filling. It echoes Isaiah 6:3, where the seraphim declare that 'the whole earth is full of his glory'—suggesting that what the prophet glimpsed in the heavenly temple is here affirmed as an eschatological promise and present aspiration.
commentary.narrative_continued: The structure reveals theological depth: the prayer does not end with 'let the king reign' but with 'let God's glory fill all the earth.' This reorientation is critical. The Davidic king is not the ultimate subject of the psalm; he is an instrument through whom God's justice and mercy flow. The doxology essentially says: 'All the petitions for the righteous king serve one purpose—the manifestation of God's glory throughout creation.' The psalmist prays not for the king's power but for the king to be so just and righteous that his reign becomes transparent to God's own character. When we 'bless' God's glorious name, we are affirming His reputation, His standing in the world, His undeniable presence.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The Hebrew shem kevodo—rendered by The Covenant Rendering as 'the name that is His glory'—carries weight beyond simple translation. In Hebrew thought, a name is not mere label but reveals essence. To bless His 'glorious name' is to bless the totality of who He is as it becomes known and experienced. This prepares us for understanding why the Restoration emphasizes the significance of God's name in covenants and temples. The prayer that His glory fill the earth is simultaneously an acknowledgment of present reality (His glory does sustain all things) and an eschatological promise (the day when all creation will recognize and experience that glory).
commentary.narrative_continued_3: The double Amen seals the Second Book of the Psalter (Psalms 42–72). In Hebrew worship, Amen was the community's response—'let it be so, let it be established.' By saying 'Amen and Amen,' the congregation doesn't merely approve the prayer; they stake their own covenant identity on it. They say: 'We align ourselves with this vision. We commit to living toward this reality. May God's glory fill the earth through our righteousness, our justice, our faithfulness.' This is why the doxology appears here—not as addendum but as the culmination of the Second Book's entire theological arc.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently emphasizes that God's glory will fill the earth in the last days. In 1 Nephi 14:15, Nephi sees 'the beauty and goodness and glory of the sanctified world,' and in Alma 26:35, Alma testifies that 'the Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and kindred, to teach his word, yea, in wisdom, all that he seeth fit that they should have.' The Nephite tradition inherits and sustains the psalmist's vision that God's glory—manifested through righteous teaching and covenant community—eventually fills the earth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly echoes this psalm's vision. D&C 101:16 teaches that 'the fulness of the earth is yours' when the Saints covenant with God. D&C 38:27 affirms that 'the fulness of the earth is the Lord's,' and those who are faithful will inherit it. Most powerfully, D&C 76:24 declares that the glory of the celestial kingdom is 'incomparable'—suggesting that the full manifestation of God's glory awaits those who keep their covenants and become worthy to dwell in His presence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the earthly manifestation of the vision that God's glory fills a sanctified space. In the Latter-day Saint temple, the Endowment teaches that creation itself is progressing toward a state where God's glory and order permeate all things. The prayer circle and the sealing power directly connect to this psalm's petition: that God's name and glory be established and sealed throughout creation. The temple is where individual covenants participate in the cosmic reality that God's glory fills all things.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 72 itself is understood in Christian tradition as Messianic—a prayer for the ultimate King whose justice and reign will extend to all nations. Verse 19's affirmation that God's glory will fill the earth through a righteous king points typologically to Jesus Christ. His kingship is not political but spiritual and eternal; His reign establishes God's justice, mercy, and glory throughout creation. The doxology affirms that Christ's coming and covenant work fulfill the psalmist's deepest prayer—that God's character and presence become unmistakably evident and transformative throughout all creation. In the Latter-day Saint understanding, Christ is the prototype of the righteous king, and the sealing of ordinances in His name extends His glory-manifesting power into the present and future.
commentary.application: For modern covenant holders, this verse invites us to examine whether our own lives and choices bless God's glorious name and allow His glory to manifest through us. The question is not 'Am I admired?' but 'Am I transparent to God's character?' When we act justly, show mercy, teach truth, and keep our covenants, we become vessels through which God's glory becomes evident to others. The corporate 'Amen' reminds us that our righteousness is not private; we affirm together that we belong to a covenant community whose purpose is to let God's name and glory fill the earth. In practical terms, this means: Do our families reflect God's glory? Do our communities demonstrate His justice and mercy? Are we using our talents and influence to reveal—not ourselves—but God's character? The double Amen seals our commitment to answer these questions with faithful action.

cross_references.connection: The seraphim's declaration that 'the whole earth is full of his glory' directly parallels this verse's prayer. The psalmist echoes the heavenly vision and makes it a covenant petition for earthly fulfillment.
God's own oath: 'As truly as I live, all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD.' This verse affirms that the psalmist's prayer is aligned with God's own declared purpose and covenant.

In the vision of the degrees of glory, the statement 'Now this is the gospel, the glad tidings which the voice out of the heavens bore record unto us' connects to the theme of God's glory being revealed and experienced. The Restoration emphasizes that understanding God's glory is central to salvation.

King Benjamin teaches that those who keep God's commandments are blessed 'in all things.' This reflects the same principle that righteousness (whether of a king or a people) allows God's glory to manifest and bless the land.
The Lord's promise that Zion will 'be the glory of the whole earth' echoes this psalm's eschatological vision. God's covenant people become instruments through which His glory fills the earth.

commentary.historical_context: The doxology of Psalm 72:19 belongs to a genre of liturgical praise found throughout the ancient Near East. However, the theological focus is distinctly Israelite: the psalmist does not celebrate the king's power for its own sake but subordinates royal authority to God's purposes. Ancient Near Eastern royal ideology typically positioned the king as the primary mediator between heaven and earth. The Israeli psalmist inverts this hierarchy—the king is blessed only insofar as he becomes transparent to God's justice and glory. The double Amen reflects liturgical practice in Second Temple worship, where the congregation's corporate affirmation was essential to prayer. Archaeological evidence from synagogue inscriptions and prayer texts shows that Amen was recited by the assembled community in response to blessings and prayers, making prayer a covenantal act involving both leader and people.

word_study.meaning: From a root meaning 'to kneel' or 'to bless,' baruch carries the sense of praise, adoration, and the acknowledgment of someone's worth or power. In covenantal context, to bless God is to affirm His character and covenant faithfulness. The passive form here ('blessed be') invokes a blessing upon God's name—though paradoxically, God as infinite being is not 'increased' by our blessing; rather, our blessing aligns us with reality.
word_study.significance: This same term appears in the Beatitudes ('Blessed are the poor in spirit') and throughout the liturgical language of prayer. The psalmist uses it not as casual praise but as a formal affirmation of God's worthiness to be praised across all generations.

word_study.meaning: The phrase combines two theologically rich terms: shem ('name,' which in Hebrew denotes essence and character) and kevodo ('His glory,' from a root meaning 'to be heavy or weighty'). The Covenant Rendering's interpretation—'the name that is His glory'—captures the sense that God's glorious name is not separate from His weighty, undeniable presence. His reputation in the world IS His glory.
word_study.significance: In Latter-day Saint theology, the concept of God's name and glory is central to temple covenants and the New and Everlasting Covenant. To make covenants 'in the name of Jesus Christ' and to seek to 'build the kingdom in His name' is to align ourselves with His glory and character. The psalmist's prayer that God's glory fill the earth is a covenant prayer—a petition that God's character and justice become manifest throughout creation.

word_study.meaning: Derived from a root meaning 'to be heavy or weighty,' kavod denotes God's substantive, undeniable presence and character. It is not merely 'honor' in the abstract but the manifest weight and reality of God's being. When God's glory fills the earth, creation becomes saturated with His presence, as when the glory of the LORD filled Solomon's temple.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's note that 'God's glory is His weight—His substantive, undeniable presence in the world' is profound. This connects directly to LDS concepts of God's substance and presence. The entire creation is filled with His glory; the prayer is that all creatures recognize and respond to that reality. The vision anticipates the Restoration teaching that truth and light are the substances from which creation is formed and that God is not distant but densely present throughout His creation.

word_study.meaning: From a root meaning 'to be firm, steadfast, true,' Amen signifies affirmation, confirmation, and the sealing of an oath or prayer. It is spoken by the congregation in response to a prayer or blessing, declaring 'Let it be so, let it be established.'
word_study.significance: The double 'Amen and Amen' is not redundancy but emphasis and solemnity. It appears in the doxologies closing each book of the Psalter, serving as a liturgical seal. In Latter-day Saint usage, the sealing power and the covenant language of 'so mote it be' and 'selah' carry similar force—the community's ratification of sacred words.

text_kjv: The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended.

commentary.narrative: This final verse is not a prayer but a colophon—an editorial note marking the conclusion of the Second Book of the Psalter. The phrase 'The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended' (Hebrew: kallu tefilot David ben Yishai) serves as a formal closure. The Covenant Rendering's rendering—'Here conclude the prayers of David, Jesse's son'—clarifies that this is not a statement about David's historical prayers being finished, but rather the editors' declaration that this particular collection is complete. The specific naming of David as 'Jesse's son' echoes the genealogical formula used in ancient Near Eastern texts and the Samuel narrative (1 Samuel 16:1), grounding the psalms in the historical David while simultaneously marking this as a literary artifact.
commentary.narrative_continued: The appearance of this colophon reveals the hand of the post-exilic editors who shaped the Psalter into its five-book structure. The First Book (Psalms 1–41) and Second Book (Psalms 42–72) both end with formal doxologies (41:13 and 72:18–19) followed by editorial notes (41:13b and 72:20). The placement of this colophon signals that the editors distinguished between the collected prayers and the framing doxology—Psalm 72:19 is the prayer-community's affirmation; Psalm 72:20 is the editors' signature. This is crucial for understanding how the Psalter was transmitted and treasured. The ancient Jewish and Christian communities recognized that the psalms they prayed were carefully curated and organized by wise editors who understood their spiritual power and theological direction.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The word kallu—'are ended, are completed, are finished'—carries a sense of finality and fullness. In Hebrew, this root (kalah) can mean 'to complete,' 'to finish,' or 'to come to an end,' but in covenantal context it often implies 'to fulfill' or 'to accomplish.' The editors are not saying David's prayers failed or were abandoned; they are saying the collection is whole, fulfilled, and sealed. This reflects the ancient practice of closing a scroll or codex with a formal statement, ensuring that readers understood: 'You have received the complete text; nothing essential is missing.' For a community dependent on oral transmission and hand-copied texts, such assurance was vital.
commentary.narrative_continued_3: The theological significance of closing the Second Book with this colophon is profound. By distinguishing between the prayers themselves (ending with Psalm 72:19's Amen) and the editorial framework (the colophon of verse 20), the ancient editors affirmed a crucial principle: the prayers are sacred speech, but the collection is a human responsibility. The editors do not claim to be prophets but rather stewards and scholars. They have gathered the prayers, organized them, and sealed them—inviting future generations to pray them, learn from them, and add their own Amens. This model of sacred tradition—where human faithfulness preserves and transmits divine truth—is foundational to Latter-day Saint understanding of scripture and revelation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon employs a similar editorial technique. Nephi records his visions and teachings, then affirms their completion and authenticity. The pattern of individual prophet-seers contributing to a larger, divinely guided record mirrors how the post-exilic editors gathered Davidic psalms into a unified, covenant-affirming collection. The Nephite emphasis on keeping records 'for the welfare of our souls' (Jacob 3:14) reflects the same stewardship consciousness evident in the Psalter's editors.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The concept of sealing appears throughout D&C revelation. When the Lord commands Joseph Smith to translate, correct, and publish texts, He is establishing divine authorization for the transmission of sacred words. D&C 21:4-5 emphasizes that the Church president (or in this case, the editors) receives revelation 'as he receiveth them'—acknowledging that human responsibility and divine guidance work together. The sealing of the Psalter and the sealing of scripture in the Restoration both reflect this principle: humans participate in preserving and transmitting revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Psalter functions in the temple tradition as a liturgical text—psalms are sung and recited in temple worship, just as they were in the Second Temple period. The colophon's affirmation that the collection is complete and sealed invites each covenant holder to treat the psalms as a finished, authoritative guide for temple prayer and meditation. The relationship between the editor's seal and the sealing power of the priesthood is subtle but real: both affirm that sacred speech and sacred action, when properly transmitted and received, bind heaven and earth together.

commentary.christological_typology: While verse 20 is primarily an editorial note rather than a prayer, it carries typological significance in affirming that the Davidic tradition—culminating in Jesus Christ—is preserved and transmitted faithfully. The colophon witnesses to a pattern of covenant stewardship: David's psalms are not lost or corrupted but sealed and delivered to future generations, just as Christ's doctrine and power are sealed and delivered to His covenant people. The naming of David as 'Jesse's son' traces the lineage that leads to Jesus, called 'the son of David' in the New Testament. The editors' careful preservation of the Davidic psalms prefigures the Church's role in preserving and transmitting Christ's teachings to all generations.
commentary.application: For covenant holders today, this verse offers a teaching about scripture, tradition, and stewardship. Just as ancient editors recognized that they were custodians of sacred texts—not authors, but faithful arrangers—modern readers must approach scripture with similar humility and trust. We receive the psalms as a completed, sealed collection, yet we are invited to pray them as if they were spoken today. This paradox—receiving ancient words as eternally living—mirrors how we engage with all scripture in the Restoration context. Additionally, verse 20 reminds us that community matters: the prayers collected here are communal, liturgical, and meant to be prayed together. Our personal spirituality is deepened when we remember that we are part of a covenant line stretching from David through Christ to ourselves, and onward to future generations. If we are stewards of scripture and tradition, we must ask: What are we preserving and transmitting? Are we, too, sealing truths and prayers that will bless those who come after?

cross_references.connection: The doxology closing the First Book: 'Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting: Amen, and Amen.' This parallel structure shows that each book of the Psalter follows the same editorial pattern: prayers + doxology + colophon.

Samuel is sent to anoint David, called 'Jesse's son.' The genealogical formula in the colophon echoes this foundational text, rooting the psalms in David's historical narrative and covenant anointing.

The Lord's direction to the Church regarding revelation: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' This reflects the principle that revealed and transmitted texts are received as a stewardship—parallel to how the editors stewarded the Davidic psalms.

Moroni's promise that one can 'know the truth of all things' through the Holy Ghost parallels the ancient editors' trust that the collected psalms, when received with faith, carry spiritual power and authenticity beyond their literary form.

The opening of the Second Book begins a new collection. The colophon of verse 20 marks the boundary between the First and Second Books, affirming that the Psalter is deliberately structured in distinct units, each with its own theological voice.

commentary.historical_context: The colophon of Psalm 72:20 is one of the clearest pieces of internal evidence for the Psalter's editorial history. Ancient scholarship has long recognized that the five-book structure of the Psalter mirrors the five books of Torah (Genesis through Deuteronomy), suggesting an intentional theological architecture. The colophons marking the end of Books I and II reveal the hand of post-exilic Jewish editors—likely from the Persian or early Hellenistic period (5th–3rd centuries BCE). These editors were not merely collecting texts; they were constructing a theological statement: that the covenant tradition of David continues in the worship life of the restored community. The genealogical reference to 'Jesse's son' ties the psalm collection to the Davidic dynasty, which had been terminated by the Babylonian exile. By attributing the psalms to David and organizing them into a coherent collection, the editors affirmed that the Davidic covenant promise—that David's throne would be established forever (2 Samuel 7:16)—was being realized spiritually through the prayer life of the post-exilic community. Ancient Near Eastern textual practice included such colophons to certify the completeness and authenticity of a work. The formula 'here end the prayers of [name]' appears in other ancient texts and served as a seal of authenticity and finality.

word_study.meaning: From a root meaning 'to judge' or 'to intercede,' tefilot denotes formal, structured prayers—not casual requests but covenantal intercessions. In the plural, the term acknowledges the psalms as a collected body of prayer-speech, each distinct but forming a unified liturgical corpus.
word_study.significance: The use of the plural tefilot rather than a singular reference underscores that the Second Book is not a monolithic work but a treasury of diverse prayers—lament and praise, petition and thanksgiving, individual and communal. Yet they are bound together by the editors' affirmation that they all belong to the Davidic tradition and serve the covenant community.

word_study.meaning: From the root kalah, meaning 'to complete, finish, accomplish, or consume.' In this context, it denotes the completion or fulfillment of the collection. The Covenant Rendering's note that the word carries 'a sense of finality and completion' is exact.
word_study.significance: The choice of kallu rather than simpler terms like 'stopped' or 'ceased' suggests theological intentionality. The prayers are not abandoned but fulfilled—their purpose accomplished. In Latter-day Saint parlance, this parallels the concept of sealing: the collection is sealed and complete, ready to bless future generations.

word_study.meaning: A formal genealogical designation invoking David's lineage. The phrase 'son of Jesse' connects to the Samuel narrative and David's anointing (1 Samuel 16). It is not a casual aside but a deliberate anchoring of the psalms in Davidic history and legitimacy.
word_study.significance: This phrase affirms that the psalms, though compiled long after David's era, claim descent from the Davidic tradition. It is simultaneously a historical claim (these prayers reflect Davidic piety) and a literary convention (like 'Book of David' or 'Davidic Psalter'). For LDS readers, this recalls the Restoration emphasis on lineage and covenant descent—the psalms belong to the covenant line that flows from David through Christ.

text_kjv: To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of Asaph.

commentary.narrative: This superscription identifies the psalm's liturgical setting and musical tradition. Jeduthun (also spelled Ethan) was one of three chief musicians appointed by David to oversee the temple worship (1 Chronicles 25:1-6). The phrase 'according to Jeduthun' likely indicates either that the psalm was sung to a tune associated with Jeduthun's musical guild or performed in the manner characteristic of his tradition. Asaph, identified as the composer, was himself a Levitical musician and seer appointed by David. The dual attribution—a psalm 'of Asaph' performed 'according to Jeduthun'—suggests this was a communal liturgical piece, not private meditation. Understanding this context matters: the psalm that follows is not merely personal anguish but corporate worship, performed in the temple before the congregation of Israel.
commentary.narrative_continued: The superscription also tells us that what follows—even a psalm of profound doubt and spiritual crisis—was considered appropriate material for public worship. This legitimizes lament as a valid form of prayer within the covenant community. The fact that Israel preserved and performed psalms expressing doubt and confusion about God's faithfulness indicates that faith includes wrestling with God, not just praising Him. For modern readers, this superscription opens permission: our own seasons of questioning and distress are not failures of faith but may be the substance of genuine prayer.

word_study.meaning: The word derives from natzach ('to shine, to endure, to set over'). As a musical term, it refers to the director or conductor—the one who oversees the performance. Some scholarship suggests it may also mean 'to make victorious' or 'to make endure,' giving the psalm a secondary sense of 'dedicated to victory' or 'for enduring triumph.'
word_study.significance: This is not a passive liturgical note but a claim about the psalm's purpose: it is meant to be conducted, performed, and perhaps most importantly, to lead the worshiper toward endurance and God's ultimate victory, even though the psalm itself begins in despair.

word_study.meaning: A proper noun referring to one of David's three chief musicians (alongside Asaph and Heman). The name may derive from a root meaning 'to praise' or 'to confess.' Jeduthun's guild is mentioned repeatedly in Chronicles as overseeing temple worship, suggesting an established musical and prophetic tradition.
word_study.significance: By associating this psalm with Jeduthun's tradition, the superscription connects it to an established lineage of Levitical worship and prophecy. The reader is invited to understand this as part of a continuous tradition of seeking God through music and lament.

word_study.meaning: From the root zamar ('to sing, to make music'). A mizmor is a song, particularly one accompanied by stringed instruments. It implies both musical performance and spiritual intention.
word_study.significance: This designation tells us the psalm is meant to be sung, not merely read. The melody, the communal voice, the embodied act of singing together—these are not incidental but central to how this prayer works. Distress expressed in song becomes distress witnessed and carried by the community.

cross_references.connection: Names Jeduthun (also called Ethan) as one of David's three chief musicians appointed to prophesy with harps, psalteries, and cymbals in the temple worship.
Describes Asaph as a chief musician and seer left by David to minister continually before the ark of the covenant, establishing the prophetic character of Israel's temple music.
Paul instructs believers to teach and admonish one another with psalms, songs, and spiritual hymns, affirming that lament-psalms like this one serve a formative purpose in corporate worship.

The Lord commands Emma Smith to make a selection of hymns and to prepare them for publication, establishing that music and singing are central to covenant worship, echoing the role of Asaph and Jeduthun in Israel.

commentary.historical_context: The three chief musicians—Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun—are well-documented in the Chronicles narratives as professional Levites whose guilds maintained distinct musical and liturgical traditions. Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that Levitical musicians held prophetic authority in ancient Israel; they were not merely entertainers but spiritual guides whose music accompanied divine revelation. The superscriptions of Psalms often reference these guilds, indicating that the psalms were associated with specific musicians' traditions and performed according to their characteristic modes. This psalm's attribution to both Asaph (the primary musician) and the tradition of Jeduthun suggests it may have been widely performed across multiple Levitical communities, marking it as particularly valued in Israel's worship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon preserves similar attitudes toward communal lament. In Mosiah 21:14, the people of King Noah cry out to God in distress: 'And they did cry mightily to the Lord their God for their deliverance.' The legitimacy of desperate prayer within the covenant community is a consistent theme across restored scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 25:11-12 establishes that hymn-singing is central to Restoration worship. D&C 128:22 speaks of 'the sound of the trump' and the voice of prophecy, connecting the Restoration understanding of musical worship to prophetic utterance, much like the ancient role of Asaph and Jeduthun.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple context of Asaph and Jeduthun's music connects this psalm to the covenant worship setting. Like the music that accompanied the dedicatory ordinances of Solomon's Temple (2 Chronicles 5:12-13), this psalm is meant to be performed in a setting of covenant remembrance and renewal.

commentary.christological_typology: While the superscription itself is not typological, the role of Asaph and Jeduthun as prophetic musicians prefigures Christ as the true director (menutzéach) of worship. In Hebrews 2:12, Christ identifies Himself as singing praises to the Father in the midst of the congregation—He is the true musician and conductor of God's people. The psalmist's desperate cry prefigures the cry of Christ in Gethsemane and on the cross (Matthew 26:39, Luke 22:44), where even the Son of God experiences the apparent absence of comfort and must learn obedience through suffering (Hebrews 5:8).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members may recognize in this superscription an invitation to bring our whole selves—including our doubts, fears, and deepest struggles—into communal worship. Like Asaph, we are not meant to suffer alone but to give voice to our distress within the company of believers. The designation 'according to Jeduthun' reminds us that there are spiritual traditions and practices (prayer, fasting, studying scripture, singing hymns) through which others before us have sought God. When we participate in these traditions, we join a lineage of seekers. Additionally, the fact that this psalm is titled 'A Psalm of Asaph' but performed 'according to Jeduthun' suggests that our individual experience of faith exists within corporate and communal structures. The leader (Asaph) may express the anguish, but the tradition (Jeduthun) provides the framework and community through which that anguish is held and transformed.

text_kjv: I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me.

commentary.narrative: The psalm opens with an act of crying out (tsa'aq) to God—not a whisper, not a private meditation, but a loud, urgent vocalization of distress. The repetition 'unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice' intensifies the plea through parallelism. In Hebrew poetry, repetition is not mere emphasis but a way of dwelling in the reality being expressed. The psalmist is hammering on heaven's door, repeating the address to God as if the first plea might not have reached Him. This is the vocabulary of emergency: the same verb tsa'aq is used in Exodus 2:23 for the Israelites' cry under Egyptian slavery—it is the cry of the oppressed calling to a superior power for deliverance.
commentary.narrative_continued: Yet the verse ends with a surprising confidence: 'and he gave ear unto me' (or 'may He hear me,' depending on how one reads the Hebrew verb form). The Covenant Rendering captures the ambiguity well: 'may He hear me!' This captures the tension at the heart of the psalm. The psalmist cries out with desperate force, but then what? The answer seems simultaneously assured ('He gave ear') and pleading ('may He give ear'). This is the peculiar honesty of biblical lament: the speaker wants to believe God hears and yet has seen no evidence of it. The repetition of 'my voice' also emphasizes the physicality of prayer—this is not abstract theology but the psalmist's own embodied cry. In a covenant with a God who hears, the capacity to speak and be heard is a fundamental sign of relationship.

word_study.meaning: A verb specifically denoting the loud, urgent cry of one in distress calling to a superior for help. It is not prayer in general but prayer in emergency. The root conveys both the involuntary nature of the cry (it comes from desperation, not deliberation) and its intensity (it must be heard).
word_study.significance: By using tsa'aq rather than a more formal prayer vocabulary, the psalmist grounds his prayer in raw, embodied distress. This is prayer that cannot be polite or measured. It is the prayer of the sufferer who has reached the limit of what can be borne.

word_study.meaning: Sound, voice, call. In biblical usage, qol can refer to the actual sound of a person's voice, but also to one's testimony, reputation, or the effect one has in the world. 'Lift up your voice' means to make your reality known.
word_study.significance: The doubled 'my voice' (qoli...qoli) emphasizes both the physical act of crying and the insistence that the psalmist's reality be acknowledged. Repetition of qol stresses that this is not an internal struggle but something that must be heard externally, audibly, by God.

word_study.meaning: From the root azan ('ear'); the hiphil verb form means 'to cause to hear, to give ear to, to listen.' It emphasizes the active choice to attend to and give weight to what is being communicated.
word_study.significance: In covenant theology, God is characterized as one who 'hears' the cries of His people. This verb captures not mere passive hearing but active attention—God bends toward the cry, makes it His concern. Yet the ambiguity of the verb form in context creates tension: is this a statement of fact (God has heard) or a hopeful plea (may God hear)?

cross_references.connection: Uses the same verb tsa'aq to describe Israel's cry under slavery: 'And the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up unto God by reason of the bondage.' God's hearing of the desperate cry is the prelude to deliverance.

Declares that 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry'—affirming that God's capacity to hear is an essential attribute of His covenantal relationship with His people.
Applies Psalm 34:15 to New Testament believers, emphasizing that God's ears remain open to the cry of the righteous in all dispensations.
Amulek teaches that the poor and afflicted can cry unto God and be heard, that God will hear their cry and deliver them—echoing the same confidence in God's responsive attention to the desperate.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern religious literature, the cry (or prayer-petition) to a deity typically followed a formulaic pattern: identification of the petitioner's distress, appeal to the deity's power and righteousness, and request for intervention. The Psalms often preserve this pattern. The verb tsa'aq was used specifically for the cry of the oppressed or enslaved—those at the absolute limit of their resources. This was not polite prayer but the last resort of one who had no other recourse. The emphasis on 'voice' (qol) also reflects ancient Near Eastern understanding that the spoken word had power and that being heard was itself a form of vindication. In the courts of ancient kings, the right to be heard was a fundamental right of petitioners. Israel's claim that God hears the cry of the afflicted was a radical statement: it meant that even the powerless, the enslaved, the marginalized had direct access to ultimate authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that the Lord hears the cries of the afflicted. Helaman 7:14 records Nephi's prayer: 'O Lord, wilt thou hearken unto me...O Lord, turn thine ear unto me.' Alma 26:16 celebrates: 'Now when our hearts were depressed, and we were about to turn back, behold, the Lord comforted us, and said: Go amongst thy brethren, the Lamanites, and bear with patience thine afflictions.'

Notably, in the Book of Mormon, the cry of the afflicted becomes a basis for God's intervention in history. The repeated pattern is: covenant people cry out → God hears → God delivers. This establishes a covenantal expectation that what the psalmist hopes for is indeed reliable.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 presents Joseph Smith in the dungeon of Liberty Jail, crying out with language echoing this very psalm: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion of thy hiding place? How long shall thy hand be stayed?' The revelation that follows (D&C 121:7 onward) affirms that God has heard even this cry from the depths and is about to answer. The Restoration teaches that God's attentiveness to the cry of the afflicted continues in the present dispensation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the plea 'O God, hear my prayer' becomes a central motif. The temple is understood as the place where heaven and earth meet, where the cry of the faithful is most directly heard. The Restoration reestablishes the practice of ritual petition in sacred space, following patterns evident in ancient Israelite temple worship.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's cry prefigures Christ's cry on the cross. In Matthew 27:46, Jesus cries out (using the Greek equivalent of tsa'aq), 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' Yet this cry is itself heard: Christ rises from the dead, demonstrating that even the cry of apparent abandonment is heard and answered. Hebrews 5:7 describes Christ in His earthly ministry as praying 'with strong crying and tears,' showing that the embodied, vocalized cry is central to Christ's own intercession. His cry is the ultimate tsa'aq—the desperate plea of one entirely dependent on the Father's hearing.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites honest acknowledgment of spiritual struggle. The psalmist does not spiritualize his pain or pretend it away; he gives it voice. Moreover, the doubled 'my voice...my voice' suggests that being heard matters—that the reality of our experience deserves witness and attention. In a world that often demands we hide suffering or 'keep a stiff upper lip,' the psalm grants permission to cry out. The verse also teaches an important lesson about prayer: it is not primarily about getting the words right or achieving the correct emotional state, but about pressing our need before God with our whole selves. Finally, the ambiguity at the end of the verse ('and he gave ear unto me / may he give ear to me') captures the truth of faith in difficult times: we do not always have certainty that God has heard, but we continue to cry out in the faith that He will.

text_kjv: In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted.

commentary.narrative: Verse 3 deepens and extends the crisis. 'In the day of my trouble' (beyom tsarati) marks the specific moment of rupture—not a chronic low-grade anxiety but an acute crisis that precipitates urgent seeking. The verb 'sought' (darashti) suggests not a casual prayer but persistent, diligent searching—the kind of seeking that involves the whole person. The Covenant Rendering's phrasing 'my hand was stretched out at night without rest' transforms the KJV's cryptic 'my sore ran in the night' into a vivid image of all-night prayer, hands raised toward heaven in supplication. The image of hands extended throughout the night emphasizes both the physical posture of prayer and its unbroken continuation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse climaxes in a devastating confession: 'My soul refused to be comforted' (me'anah hinnachem nafshi). This is not the happy ending we want prayer to have. The psalmist prayed all night—intensely, desperately, without ceasing—and received no relief. The soul (nafshi, often translated as 'life' or 'self') actively rejected comfort, suggesting that comfort offered without addressing the underlying crisis would itself be a betrayal. The structure of the verse moves from crisis to response to devastating silence: crisis → seeking → all-night prayer → refusal of empty comfort. This is the voice of someone who cannot be placated with platitudes, who will not accept a cheap resolution. The honesty is bracing.

word_study.meaning: From tsara (distress, trouble, siege). The 'day' marks a specific moment of acute suffering, often associated with military siege or external attack. In Psalm 77, the specific nature of the trouble is not mentioned; only its reality and intensity matter.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'day' (yom) rather than 'season' or 'time' emphasizes the acute, identifiable nature of the crisis. This is not vague unhappiness but a specific moment when the psalmist's world fractured.

word_study.meaning: To seek, to inquire, to search diligently. The root conveys active pursuit and investigation. When Israel 'seeks the Lord' (darash et-YHWH), it implies turning from other pursuits and redirecting one's whole attention toward God.
word_study.significance: This is not passive hoping but active seeking. The psalmist does not merely wait for God to act; he actively searches for God, turning toward Him in desperate supplication.

word_study.meaning: The Covenant Rendering reads this as 'was stretched out' rather than 'ran.' The Hebrew is difficult and has generated various interpretations. Some texts suggest it means 'was poured out' (tears flowing) or 'streamed' (hands extended). The Masoretic pointing supports a reading related to 'stretching out' or 'extending.'
word_study.significance: Whether the image is of tears flowing or hands extended in prayer throughout the night, the effect is the same: embodied, continuous distress without relief. The night-long vigil shows how consuming the crisis is.

word_study.meaning: From tapug, meaning 'to be slack, to flag, to become numb.' The negative (lo) reverses this: the hands did not go slack, did not become numb, did not flag. It conveys both physical persistence (the body's capacity to continue despite pain) and spiritual determination (the will not to relent).
word_study.significance: This captures the relentless nature of desperate prayer: the psalmist does not allow himself the relief of giving up or falling asleep. His hands remain raised all through the night.

word_study.meaning: From ma'an (to refuse) and nacham (to comfort, console). The passive form of nacham (hinnicham) suggests 'to be comforted' or 'to accept comfort.' The soul (nafshi) actively refuses this comfort. The refusal implies that offered comfort is insufficient or inappropriate to the depth of the crisis.
word_study.significance: This is a rejection of false comfort—the kind that minimizes genuine suffering or pretends the crisis is not as severe as it is. The psalmist will not be consoled until the actual problem is addressed.

cross_references.connection: Job similarly 'refuses to be comforted,' declaring that he will not accept platitudes because his suffering is real and his integrity requires honest acknowledgment of it.
Depicts Rachel refusing to be comforted for her children, establishing refusal of comfort as a legitimate spiritual response to genuine loss.
Speaks of desolation and destruction overwhelming the land—'none to comfort thee'—suggesting that sometimes comfort is genuinely unavailable and only God's restoration can address the loss.
Paul identifies God as 'the God of all comfort,' suggesting that only God's authentic intervention (not human platitude) can truly comfort in deep suffering.

The Lord tells Alma's people that He will ease their burdens, but only after they have 'submitted cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord'—comfort comes not through avoiding suffering but through genuine transformation of the crisis.

commentary.historical_context: The night-long prayer vigil appears in other ancient Near Eastern literature and in biblical narrative. The practice of spending entire nights in prayer or petition is documented in both Jewish and surrounding Near Eastern religious traditions. The raising of hands in prayer is an almost universal sign of supplication in ancient Mediterranean religion—it is the posture of one who has no resources of their own and must appeal to a superior power. The Hebrew phrasing 'my hand was stretched out at night' may also evoke the practice of temple night-vigils, where the faithful kept watch through the night seeking divine encounter or revelation. The psalmist's refusal of comfort is also culturally significant: in ancient Mediterranean society, comfort was often offered through the consoling presence of family, community, or hired mourners. The psalmist's rejection of these suggests he is utterly alone with his crisis.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon provides powerful parallels to this experience of seeking God without receiving immediate comfort. In Alma 36:18-21, Alma describes his spiritual crisis as consuming him: 'And now, for three days and three nights was I racked, even with the pains of a damned soul.' Like the psalmist, Alma 'sought for mercy,' and his seeking was all-consuming, not casual. The account suggests that genuine seeking sometimes involves extended suffering without immediate relief. Only later does comfort come. Similarly, Nephi in 2 Nephi 4:17-35 expresses distress ('O wretched man that I am!'), yet continues to seek God even when confidence is not immediately restored.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 presents Joseph Smith in profound spiritual crisis: 'O God, where art thou?' His seeking is not answered with immediate comfort but with further instruction about the nature of trials and God's character. The revelation teaches that seeking without immediate comfort is part of the covenant path: 'The ends of the earth shall inquire after thy name' (D&C 109:26). D&C 88:15 affirms that the Lord's 'voice is as the voice of many waters' (overwhelming, not gentle), suggesting that God's response to seeking may not be what the sufferer expects.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The practice of all-night prayer vigils connects to temple worship in both ancient Israel and the Restoration. Early Church members reported spending nights in prayer in the temple. The temple is the place where the barrier between heaven and earth is understood to be thin, where seeking is most likely to be answered. Yet even in the temple, the answer may not be immediate comfort but deeper understanding or spiritual endurance.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's all-night prayer in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41-44) directly parallels the psalmist's night-long seeking. Luke's account notes that Christ 'prayed more earnestly,' suggesting intensification rather than ease. The Gospel accounts indicate that Christ did not receive comfort in the garden but rather a strengthening to continue toward the cross. His prayer of seeking ends not with comfort but with resignation to the Father's will: 'Not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42). This suggests that the deepest prayer may lead not to the removal of the crisis but to transformation of the one who prays. Christ's refusal of the offered comfort (the wine mixed with myrrh, Mark 15:23) parallels the psalmist's refusal of empty consolation.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to anyone who has experienced the particular desolation of praying without receiving the comfort they desperately need. Modern members sometimes expect that consistent prayer will bring immediate peace. This verse authorizes a deeper, more honest spirituality: sometimes prayer intensifies rather than resolves the crisis. The all-night prayer image also speaks to the reality of spiritual struggle—it is not resolved in a convenient timeframe but consumes entire seasons of our lives. Moreover, the psalmist's refusal of false comfort is spiritually important. In a therapeutic culture that often seeks to minimize suffering or move quickly to 'solutions,' this verse affirms the integrity of acknowledging that genuine loss cannot be easily mended. The application is not to despair but to refuse platitudes and to insist that only authentic intervention—not mere words—can address what has been broken. For leaders and friends of the suffering, this verse teaches the danger of offering comfort before the crisis is truly acknowledged.

text_kjv: I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 marks a turn in the emotional geography of the psalm. The psalmist remembers God—zakartī Elohīm—and yet this remembrance does not bring comfort but distress ('and was troubled'). The Covenant Rendering reads 'I think of God and I groan,' capturing the involuntary sound of pain that accompanies the thought of God. This is deeply paradoxical: the one action that should bring peace (remembering God, calling God to mind) produces anguish instead. Why? The answer lies in the contradiction between who God is (the psalmist's memory of God's faithfulness) and what God appears to be doing (or not doing) in the present crisis. The gap between the remembered God and the apparently absent God produces a groan—an involuntary, wordless cry of dissonance.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse continues: 'I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed.' The verb 'complained' (sichah) can mean 'to meditate, to muse, to converse with.' It is related to prayer and reflection but here carries a tone of complaint or remonstrance. The subject is now the spirit itself: it 'was overwhelmed' (wrapped, enveloped, smothered—ataf). The progression from thinking about God to groaning to complaining to being smothered traces a deepening paralysis. The psalmist moves from active seeking (verse 2) through desperate prayer (verse 3) to a state where even thinking about God produces despair rather than hope. The addition of 'Selah' (a pause, a moment of silence) suggests that the psalmist stops here—lets the weight of this confusion settle. There is nowhere further to go in this line of thought; only silence.

word_study.meaning: To remember, to recall, to bring to mind. In biblical usage, 'to remember' is not merely a mental act but a relational one—it involves turning toward someone with intention, invoking their presence or their name. When God 'remembers,' it triggers action (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24).
