commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate fulfillment of verse 9. He is God's word speaking shalom—the Word made flesh who proclaims peace to all who will hear. His Sermon on the Mount is, in a sense, the content of what God speaks: blessed are the merciful, the peacemakers, those who hunger for righteousness. His crucifixion and resurrection enact the shalom He announces. The warning against returning to folly is the call to discipleship—to follow Him and not return to the reliance on self that characterized life before covenant with Him.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 9 invites a shift from constant petitioning to attentive listening. We are taught to pray, to ask, to seek—but equally important is the capacity to be still and know that God is God, to listen for His voice through scripture, through the Holy Ghost, through worthy leaders, through the still small voice of conscience. The application is a question of balance: Are we willing to stop talking long enough to listen? And when we do listen for God's word, what do we expect to hear? This verse suggests we should expect peace—not the world's peace, but the shalom that comes from right relationship with God and obedience to covenant. The warning against returning to foolishness is equally important: listening to God's shalom is not passive acceptance but active commitment to avoid the patterns that caused previous separation.

text_kjv: Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 begins the unfolding of what God speaks—the vision of restoration that fulfills every petition raised in verses 1-8. The word 'Surely' (Ak) signals confidence: what follows is not speculation but certainty rooted in God's character. Salvation is qarov ('near, close, at hand') to those who fear Him. The fear of God here is not terror but reverent awe—the orientation of those who stand in covenant relationship with Him. The word qarov establishes proximity: salvation is not distant or eschatological (purely future) but near, immediately available. In the historical moment of this psalm, when the people have experienced withdrawal and discipline, nearness is everything. God has not abandoned them; His deliverance is close.

But the purpose statement is what transforms this verse from comfort into vision: lishkon kavod be-artsenu ('so that glory may dwell in our land'). The verb shakan ('to dwell, to tabernacle, to take up residence') is the root of Shekhinah—God's manifest, localized presence. The ultimate goal of salvation is not merely the absence of judgment but the return of God's visible, glorious presence to the land. Kavod ('glory') in Hebrew denotes the weight or substance of something's nature—the visible manifestation of God's power and majesty. In the exodus narrative, kavod appears as fire, cloud, and radiance. Here, the psalmist envisions kavod dwelling (shakan) in the land, not just visiting or appearing but making permanent residence. This is restoration at the deepest level: the land, the people, and God's manifest presence reunited in stable, enduring communion.

The shift from plural 'them that fear him' to plural 'our land' shows that individual salvation and communal restoration are inseparable. Those who fear God experience individual nearness to salvation, but the ultimate goal is collective: God's glory dwelling not in private hearts but in the shared land, the common space of the people's existence.

word_study.meaning: salvation, deliverance, rescue; the state of being safe, whole, and restored
word_study.significance: As in verse 8, salvation encompasses both spiritual reconciliation with God and concrete, historical restoration of the people's condition.

word_study.meaning: near, close, at hand; describes spatial or temporal proximity
word_study.significance: The word conveys immediacy and accessibility. Salvation is not promised for some distant future but is ready at hand for those who fear God. This was particularly important for a post-exilic community recovering from long separation.

word_study.meaning: to fear, to stand in awe, to revere; to orient oneself toward God with reverent submission
word_study.significance: The fear of God is not cowering terror but the foundational posture of covenant relationship—recognition of God's absolute authority and worthiness of obedience.

word_study.meaning: glory, weight, substance, honor; the visible manifestation of God's power and majesty; that which gives something its essential worth
word_study.significance: Kavod is not abstract; it is the palpable presence of God that can be seen and felt. Its dwelling in the land means God's manifest presence will be constant and localized, not withdrawn or distant.

word_study.meaning: to dwell, to inhabit, to take up residence; used of God's presence in the tabernacle/temple
word_study.significance: This verb is the root of Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence. It suggests permanence and intimacy—not a fleeting visitation but a stable, covenantal presence.

cross_references.connection: 'Then a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle'—the original historical fulfillment of the promise that God's glory would dwell among His people.
'LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth'—the psalmist's deep love for the place where God's glory is manifest.

'Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee...For, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth...but the LORD shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee'—the eschatological promise of God's glory dwelling on His people and land.
'Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them'—the ultimate fulfillment of this vision in the renewed creation, where God's presence is perpetually with His people.

The vision of the Savior and Moses in the Kirtland Temple, with the appearance of 'the glory of God in the house'—modern revelation's affirmation that God's manifest presence can dwell among His people when they build sanctuaries in His name.

commentary.historical_context: For post-exilic Israel, the absence of God's visible presence was an acute theological problem. The first temple had housed the Ark of the Covenant and been filled with God's glory (2 Chronicles 5:13-14). But when the Babylonians destroyed the temple, the Ark disappeared and the visible manifestation of God's presence vanished. The rebuilt temple lacked the Ark and, according to rabbinic tradition, lacked the Shekhinah glory. Verse 10 expresses the deepest longing of post-exilic Judaism: restoration not just of the building or the sacrificial system, but of God's manifest presence. The word 'land' (artsenu) is particularly significant; it encompasses the whole people's territory, not just the temple. The vision is of a land healed and reconciled with God, not just a shrine restored.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly references the manifest presence of God (kavod) dwelling among a righteous people. 3 Nephi 9:1-2 records Jesus's appearance following His resurrection, and 3 Nephi 17-26 describes His extensive ministry among the Nephites—the fulfillment of the promise that God's glory will dwell with His people. The Restoration itself represents a renewal of this promise: the temple is again a place where God's glory is made manifest.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:15-16 speaks of the temple as the place where God's glory dwells: 'And inasmuch as my people build a house unto me in the name of the Lord, and do not suffer any unclean thing to come into it, that it be not defiled, my glory shall rest upon it.' The building of temples in the Restoration is the modern enactment of verse 10's vision—places where God's glory dwells among His covenant people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is precisely the place where God's glory is understood to dwell. In Latter-day Saint theology, the temple is where heaven and earth meet, where God's presence is most fully manifest. The endowment and other ordinances enact the restoration vision of verse 10: a people brought into full communion with God and the manifest blessing of His presence.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate embodiment of this verse. John 1:14 declares 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father), full of grace and truth.' In Christ, God's kavod—His glory and essential nature—dwells in human form among His people. He is salvation made near and tangible. The ascension and the promise of the Comforter (John 14:16-17) extend this presence: 'He dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.' Through the Holy Ghost, Christ's glory continues to dwell with the redeemed.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse invites reflection on where God's glory dwells in our lives and communities. Is the temple—that unique place where God's presence is most fully manifest in our dispensation—central to our spiritual experience? Do we approach it with the reverence suggested by 'fear of God'? But equally, the verse speaks to a personal level: the salvation God promises is near, not distant; it is available to those who fear Him. The question is whether we recognize that nearness and position ourselves to receive it. This might mean regular temple attendance, daily scripture study, prayer, and seeking for the subtle manifestations of God's spirit in our lives. The ultimate application is this: Is God's glory dwelling in my heart? In my home? In my community? The restoration vision is not only eschatological but present and immediate for those who align themselves with God's will.

text_kjv: Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

commentary.narrative:
This verse is the visionary center of Psalm 85 and one of the most luminous passages in the entire Hebrew Bible. It resolves in poetic language what seems theologically irresolvable: the relationship between God's justice and His mercy, between His demand for righteousness and His offer of peace. The verse is built on personification and the language of intimate encounter. Chesed ve-emet nifgashu: 'Faithful love and truth have met.' The verb nifgashu (Niphal of pagash, 'to encounter, to meet, to come face to face') describes two parties coming together after separation. In the broken world of verses 4-8, chesed (God's loyal love) and emet (His truth and reliability) seemed divided. How could God be both faithful in covenant love and true in His judgment? How could He both forgive and hold people accountable? The verse declares: they meet. They encounter each other and discover they are not in conflict.

Then the parallel: Tsedeq ve-shalom nashqu: 'Righteousness and peace have kissed.' The verb nashqu ('kissed') carries even more intimacy than 'met'—these are not strangers acknowledging each other but lovers embracing. Righteousness, which demands accountability and justice for wrongs, and peace, which desires harmony and restoration, do not oppose each other. They embrace. In fallen, broken reality, we experience these as in tension: justice demands punishment while mercy desires reconciliation; righteousness demands punishment while peace desires healing. But the psalm declares that in God's restored vision—and ultimately in His character—these attributes kiss. They are united, not sundered.

The stunning insight is that this reconciliation is not a future eschatological event but God's eternal character becoming visible. God is not choosing between justice and mercy in our case; He is revealing Himself as the one in whom both are perfectly unified. The crucifixion of Christ becomes the ultimate explanation of how these attributes kiss: in the atonement, justice is satisfied (Christ bears the penalty), mercy is extended (we are forgiven), righteousness is upheld (God's moral order is honored), and peace is restored (we are reconciled to God).

word_study.meaning: loyal love, faithful love, covenant mercy; persisting commitment that outlasts offense; the adhesive force of covenant relationship
word_study.significance: Chesed is the quality that makes forgiveness possible and restoration inevitable. It is God's commitment to His people that does not depend on their performance but is rooted in His own character and covenant oath.

word_study.meaning: truth, faithfulness, reliability, firmness; what is solid and trustworthy; derived from aman ('to be firm, to be reliable')
word_study.significance: Emet is not merely intellectual truth but the reliability and solidity of God's word and character. It is paired with chesed throughout the Hebrew Bible (chesed ve-emet, 'faithful love and truth') to describe the double anchor of God's covenant identity.

word_study.meaning: to meet, to encounter, to come face to face; Niphal form suggests mutual meeting rather than one pursuing another
word_study.significance: The verb implies that chesed and emet were separated but are now coming back together. The Niphal form suggests this is not one forcing the other but a mutual recognition.

word_study.meaning: righteousness, justice, right order, conformity to what God requires; the quality of doing what is morally right and demanded by covenant
word_study.significance: Tsedeq encompasses both the quality of being right and the action of bringing things into right order. God's tsedeq demands that wrongs be addressed and that the moral order be upheld.

word_study.meaning: peace, wholeness, completeness, well-being, right relationship; the state where nothing is broken or lacking
word_study.significance: Shalom is the comprehensive well-being that flows from right relationship with God and neighbor. In the context of this verse, it is the restored harmony that results when justice is satisfied and mercy is extended.

word_study.meaning: to kiss, to press lips to lips; to show affection, respect, or intimate greeting
word_study.significance: The verb elevates the relationship between righteousness and peace from mere coexistence to intimate union and affection. These are not reluctantly cooperating but lovingly embracing.

cross_references.connection: 'Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face'—another expression of how God's justice and mercy are unified foundations of His throne.

'Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness...let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together'—the same vision of cosmic reconciliation where righteousness and salvation emerge together.

Paul's explanation of the atonement: 'Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation...to declare his righteousness...that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus'—the theological explanation of how God's justice and mercy kiss in Christ.

Alma's explanation to Corianton: 'Now repentance could not come unto men except there were a punishment...But God did call on men, in the name of his Son...to repent and believe in his name...And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice'—the Book of Mormon's articulation of how mercy and justice are reconciled.

'These are they who have received of his fulness, and of his glory'—the promise that those who receive God's fullness receive the unified expression of all His attributes, including the balance of justice and mercy.

commentary.historical_context: This verse likely originates in wisdom literature or prophetic tradition, reflecting deep theological wrestling with theodicy—the question of how God can be both just and merciful in a world filled with suffering and injustice. The personification of abstract attributes was common in Near Eastern wisdom literature (see Proverbs, where wisdom and folly are personified). However, the Hebrew Bible's approach is distinctive: these are not impersonal forces but attributes of the living God whose character is unified, even when human experience seems to divide them. The post-exilic setting of Psalm 85 suggests this verse addresses the particular anguish of a people who had experienced God's judgment (exile) and were waiting for God's mercy (restoration). The verse insists that judgment and mercy are not God's alternating moods but unified expressions of His character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 42:1-31 provides the most extended theological explanation in the Book of Mormon of how mercy and justice can be reconciled. Alma explains that through the atonement of Christ, mercy can satisfy the demands of justice without God being unjust. The whole chapter is essentially an expansion of the principle declared in Psalm 85:11. See especially Alma 42:15: 'And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:10 presents a related principle: 'And the Lord's disciples and the prophets, the peaceable followers of Christ, as are recorded in the book of Mormon and the New Testament, shall be errors, but none of the residue shall be errors, inasmuch as they receive not of the fulness of my gospel.' Though the language differs, the principle is that God's restored gospel harmonizes principles that seemed in conflict.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The atonement of Christ, which is the central theme of temple ordinances, is the perfect expression of verse 11. In the temple, mercy and justice are understood to work together in the plan of salvation. The endowment portrays how God's justice is satisfied and mercy is extended through Christ's infinite atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is perhaps the deepest typological prophecy of the atonement in the Old Testament. Christ's death and resurrection are the event in which mercy and righteousness kiss, where justice is satisfied and peace is restored. The crucifixion is the place where God's righteous judgment on sin is carried out (Christ bears the penalty) while mercy is extended to the sinner (we are forgiven). 2 Peter 3:9 speaks of Christ as the fulfillment of this reconciliation: 'His divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue.' The incarnation, atonement, and resurrection are the means by which the attributes of God are made visible as unified rather than divided.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound comfort to anyone wrestling with the tension between God's justice and His mercy—a tension felt acutely in times of personal sin or communal suffering. It invites us to trust that God is not arbitrarily choosing between these attributes but that they are perfectly unified in Him. For our personal lives, it means we can confess sin with confidence: God's justice demands accountability, but His mercy extends forgiveness, and both are fully satisfied in our repentance and Christ's atonement. We do not have to choose between fearing God's justice and trusting His love; we can do both because they kiss. For our communal lives, it means we need not fear that God's judgment disqualifies His blessing: He can both hold us accountable and restore us. The deepest application is this: Can you trust that God is more wise and loving than you can comprehend, that the apparent contradictions in His character are actually expressions of perfect unity? This verse invites us to expand our understanding and rest in the paradox.

text_kjv: Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven.

commentary.narrative:
The vision of verse 11 expands into cosmic restoration. The meeting and kissing of divine attributes is not confined to the abstract or spiritual realm but reverberates through creation itself. Verse 12 presents a picture of heaven and earth in dialogue, with creation itself participating in restoration. Emet me-erets titsmach: 'Truth springs up from the earth.' The verb titsmach ('springs up, sprouts, grows, breaks forth') is agricultural language. Truth grows from the ground like a plant. The image is startling: truth is not imposed from outside but is something the healed earth produces naturally. When the land is restored, truth is its natural and abundant yield. This suggests that truth is not alien to creation but inherent in a properly ordered world—that the earth, when it is whole and right, testifies to truth simply by being what it is meant to be.

The parallel is equally vivid: Tsedeq mi-shamayim nishqaf: 'Righteousness from heaven looks down.' The verb nishqaf ('looks down, peers, gazes, surveys') places righteousness in heaven, observing and assessing the earth. The image suggests a benevolent oversight rather than condemning judgment—righteousness gazing down with satisfaction upon a restored creation. Heaven and earth are brought into relationship: truth rises from below, righteousness descends from above, and they meet in the middle. The cosmic breach is healed. Creation and Creator are no longer in conflict.

This vision is both personal and cosmic. Individually, each believer is 'earth'—physical, material, mortal. From such earth, truth should spring up. Righteousness from heaven (from God, from the transcendent realm) looks down upon us with approval when we align ourselves with truth. Communally, the people are the earth; God in heaven is righteousness. Together, they are restored to proper relationship. Theologically, the verse declares that the final state of things will be one in which creation itself is healed, in which the laws and order that govern the cosmos are fully manifest both upward (truth springing from earth) and downward (righteousness descending from heaven), creating a seamless harmony between material and spiritual, human and divine, temporal and eternal.

word_study.meaning: truth, faithfulness, firmness, reliability; what is solid, trustworthy, and enduring
word_study.significance: As noted in verse 11, emet is not merely intellectual accuracy but the reliability of God's word and the solidness of right order. That truth springs from the earth means that a restored creation naturally produces and witnesses to what is trustworthy and real.

word_study.meaning: to sprout, to spring up, to grow; to bring forth vegetation
word_study.significance: The agricultural metaphor is crucial: truth is not forced but grows organically. This suggests that when creation is healed, truth is its natural and abundant produce, not an external imposition but an expression of the creation's restored nature.

word_study.meaning: righteousness, justice, right order; conformity to what is morally and spiritually required
word_study.significance: Righteousness gazing down from heaven represents God's benevolent oversight and approval—not a condemning judgment but a satisfied observation of creation restored to right order.

word_study.meaning: to look down, to peek, to gaze, to survey; to oversee from above
word_study.significance: The verb conveys both oversight and observation—a benevolent looking down, as of a caregiver watching over what is being restored.

word_study.meaning: heaven, the sky, the expanse above; the realm of God and the divine order
word_study.significance: Heaven is the dwelling place of righteousness, the source of divine order and blessing. That righteousness looks down from heaven to meet truth springing from the earth represents the healing of the cosmic divide between the transcendent and the material.

cross_references.connection: 'Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness; let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together: I the Lord have created it'—nearly identical imagery and the same vision of cosmic restoration where heaven and earth work together.

'He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass...In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth'—another image of blessing from heaven meeting and producing abundant growth on earth.

Paul's vision of creation itself being redeemed: 'For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now...waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body'—the New Testament parallel to the vision that creation itself will be restored.

'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away...And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes'—the eschatological fulfillment of verse 12's vision of the cosmic breach healed.

The vision of the celestial kingdom: 'Then shall they be gods...and the earth shall be sanctified even as I stand upon it...wherefore the property of the earth shall pass into the hands of the righteous'—the Book of Doctrine and Covenants' articulation of creation restored and ruled by righteousness.

commentary.historical_context: The agricultural imagery would have resonated powerfully with an ancient Near Eastern people whose survival depended on the earth's fertility. The prophetic vision of truth and righteousness flowing between heaven and earth would have been understood as a promise not just of spiritual restoration but of cosmic renewal affecting harvests, weather, prosperity, and the land's fruitfulness. In the ancient Near East, a land's fertility was understood as a sign of divine favor and the presence of the god (or gods). An infertile land was cursed. Israel's experience of exile and return involved precisely this: the land suffered under divine judgment and would flourish again under divine blessing. Verse 12 expands this logic: when righteousness is restored (God's rule is acknowledged), the earth naturally produces truth and blessing. The psalmist is envisioning not merely spiritual renewal but cosmically integrated restoration where the material world fully expresses the divine order.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 13:37 speaks of the restoration: 'And the angel said unto me: These last records...shall establish the truth of the first, which are of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, and shall make known the plain and precious things which have been taken away from them.' The Book of Mormon, as a text arising from the earth (discovered buried in the earth), is portrayed as truth springing from the earth in the Restoration. More broadly, the vision of a restored earth (3 Nephi 8-9) where Christ comes in glory is the Book of Mormon's version of verse 12's cosmic restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:86-92 contains Joseph Smith's vision of creation restored: 'And the righteous shall be gathered on my right hand unto eternal life; and the wicked on my left hand will I be ashamed to own before the Father; Wherefore I say unto you, that ye shall have fulfilment of all things which I have caused to be spoken concerning that generation, in the incoming of the fulness of the times.' The whole Doctrine and Covenants is framed by the promise that God will gather all things in Christ (D&C 27:13), which is the ultimate expression of verse 12's vision.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment portrays the restoration of creation in sacred drama. The Creation scene at the beginning of the endowment, the fall, and the promise of redemption all lead to the vision of a restored humanity in a restored creation. The celestial room of the temple represents the state described in verse 12: a place where heaven and earth meet, where righteousness dwells, and truth flows in all directions.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of verse 12's vision. He is truth incarnate ('I am the way, the truth, and the life,' John 14:6) who sprung from the earth through His incarnation, becoming fully human. He is also righteousness from heaven, as the Son of God whose rule descends to earth. His resurrection and ascension complete the vision: a human body (earth) transformed and glorified in heaven, and from that glorified state (heaven), righteousness descends to establish His kingdom. In Revelation 22, John envisions the ultimate fulfillment: 'And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him' (Revelation 22:3)—the complete union of heaven and earth, of divine rule (righteousness from heaven) and human flourishing (truth from the earth).
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 12 invites a vision of integrated wholeness—not a divorce between spiritual and material, heavenly and earthly, but their reconciliation and cooperation. In our individual lives, this means seeking to let truth grow from the earth of our physical, daily existence. Our actions, words, relationships, work, and care of creation should naturally produce truth—not truth imposed from above but genuinely expressed through how we live. Simultaneously, we seek righteousness from heaven—the divine perspective, God's standards, the transcendent order that gives meaning and direction. The application is this: Am I seeking integration of my faith and my daily life? Do I live as though heaven and earth are separated, or as though they kiss and dance together? Do I trust that when I align my earthly existence with heavenly righteousness, truth naturally springs forth? The verse also speaks to community and creation care: as we work toward justice and right order in society, as we steward the earth with wisdom and care for its flourishing, we are participating in the vision of verse 12—allowing righteousness to look down from heaven upon an earth that produces truth. This is not escapism into the next life but engagement with this life, this world, this creation, trusting that God will ultimately perfect what we begin.

text_kjv: Yea, the LORD shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 85:13 is the triumphant conclusion to a psalm of restoration and divine reconciliation. The entire psalm has traced a movement from lament (the people crying out over past judgment) through confession and petition, arriving finally at confident assertion: the covenant promises will be fulfilled. This final verse moves from abstract theological vision to concrete, material reality. The psalmist is not speaking of ethereal spiritual blessings alone, but of actual harvest, genuine abundance, and the restoration of the land itself. This is covenant theology made tangible—when right relationship with God is restored, the physical creation participates in that restoration. The structure is elegant: 'The LORD shall give... and our land shall yield...' God's gift from above meets the earth's responsive abundance from below. The parallelism suggests that divine blessing and natural fruitfulness are not separate categories but interlocking realities.

word_study.meaning: The good, the beneficial, that which is advantageous and wholesome. In Hebrew covenant language, 'the good' encompasses material blessing, right relationship, shalom, and divine favor. The definite article 'ha' (the) suggests not abstract goodness but the specific, covenantal good promised to faithful Israel.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering preserves this by rendering it 'what is good' with the definite article intact. This is not random blessing but the promised reward of the covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: To give, to provide, to grant. The verb appears twice in this verse—YHWH gives (yiten) and the land gives (titen). Both are volitional actions: the land does not grudgingly produce but actively yields, as if responding to restoration.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the root natan creates a theological mirror: divine giving meets terrestrial giving. This reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that blessing flows downward from the divine realm and manifests in the material realm when covenant is honored.

word_study.meaning: Produce, harvest, the yield of the land. From the root ybl, it specifically refers to agricultural bounty. This is not metaphorical but literal—grain, fruit, oil, wine. The word grounds theology in survival and sustenance.
word_study.significance: As the TCR notes, this moves the psalm from 'cosmic abstraction to agricultural reality.' Ancient Israel understood that covenant faithfulness had material consequences. The land's fertility was not separate from God's favor—it was God's favor made visible. Drought meant judgment; abundance meant blessing.

word_study.meaning: Our land, our territory. The possessive form emphasizes covenant relationship—this is not just 'land' in abstract but the land given to the covenant community, the fulfillment of the promise to Abraham.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'He' (God) to 'we' (our land) includes the people in the blessing. The land itself is part of the covenantal family, responsive to the restoration of right relationship with God.

cross_references.connection: This passage details the blessings promised for covenant obedience, including abundant harvest and productive land. Psalm 85:13 is the fulfillment of these material blessings.
Isaiah describes how God's word goes forth to accomplish its purpose and returns with results—paralleling the downward movement of divine blessing and its manifestation in harvest.
The covenant law connects obedience to abundant harvest: 'Then I will give you rain in due season, and the land shall yield her increase.' This is the same promise the psalmist celebrates.
The Lord promises to 'hear' the heavens, which will 'hear' the earth, which will 'hear' the grain and wine—a cosmic chain of responsive giving that mirrors Psalm 85:13's structure.
Modern revelation confirms that the earth yields its increase by the power of God when used with gratitude and according to divine law, echoing the ancient covenant promise.

commentary.historical_context: This psalm likely originates from the period of Judah's restoration after exile (6th-5th century BCE), when the community faced the question: Has the covenant promise been restored? The land had been devastated; the temple had been destroyed and rebuilt; trust needed to be reestablished. The psalmist's vision of the land yielding its harvest would have been a profound affirmation that despite past judgment, the curse had been lifted and blessing restored. In the ancient Near Eastern context, a king's legitimacy was measured partly by agricultural abundance—the gods' favor was visible in full granaries. For a restored but vulnerable Judah, this promise of divine provision was both theological and deeply practical. The agricultural imagery would have resonated with a population whose survival depended on the season's yield.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 10:11-12 describes the Son of God preparing the land before coming to it—a reversal where the land itself is sanctified. The Book of Mormon concept of a covenant land (2 Nephi 1:5) that yields or withholds its increase based on righteousness directly parallels the Psalm 85 theology. Helaman 12:15 specifically states that the land obeys God's word, fulfilling the principle that land responsiveness is tied to covenant faithfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:3-4 teaches that the earth is the Lord's and He gives it to mankind, but 'it is contrary to the heart of God' when it is used without gratitude. Section 110 (dedicatory vision of the Kirtland Temple) shows the Lord's willingness to return and dwell with His people, which carries implicit promise of covenant restoration and blessing. The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly affirms that obedience brings material blessing and disobedience brings withholding of increase.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The restoration of the land's fertility mirrors the restoration of the temple as the dwelling place of God's presence. Both represent the re-establishment of covenant relationship after judgment and exile. The temple is where God's giving meets humanity's response—the altar where offerings are brought, the place where covenant is renewed. When the psalmist speaks of the land yielding, he speaks of the entire social and spiritual order being restored to its proper alignment with heaven.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of the promise that God will 'give what is good.' In the Incarnation, the Lord Himself enters the land and becomes the source of all true blessing. The feeding of the five thousand (John 6:11) echoes this promise—Christ Himself becomes the one through whom the land yields its increase. More fundamentally, in resurrection theology, Christ's conquered death means that curse is lifted from all creation. Romans 8:20-22 describes creation itself waiting for redemption from corruption—a redemption accomplished through Christ. The ultimate fulfillment of Psalm 85:13 is not merely restored harvest in ancient Judah but the renewal of all things through Christ's atonement and resurrection.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges a spiritualized reading of blessing that ignores material reality. God cares about actual abundance, actual nourishment, actual flourishing of His people and His creation. When we honor our covenants—through integrity, sacrifice, and consecration—we can expect God's blessing to manifest in concrete ways: health, sustenance, provision for family, resources to serve. Conversely, covenant carelessness has real-world consequences. But equally important: this verse teaches us to see the land itself as part of the covenant community. How we treat creation—whether we use it with gratitude and sustainability, or exploit it—is a measure of covenant faithfulness. The land will yield when we remember that all belongs to God and we are stewards, not owners. In practical terms: faithful tithing, honest work, wise stewardship of resources, gratitude for harvest (whether literal or metaphorical), and recognition that abundance is God's gift—not merely the reward for personal effort.

text_kjv: Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 86 opens with David's fundamental posture before God: a request for God to bend down and listen. The verb 'bow down' (hatteh in Hebrew) is visceral—it depicts God lowering His ear from heaven to hear a voice from below. David immediately establishes the theological reality underlying the entire psalm: the vast distance between God's transcendence and human weakness. This is not David the king speaking; this is David identifying himself as 'poor and needy' (ani ve-evyon), using the language of the destitute throughout the Psalter. The TCR rendering captures this movement precisely: 'Bend down Your ear, O LORD, and answer me.' The request for God's ear and God's answer are paired—hearing and responding are inseparable in David's theology.

What makes this opening remarkable is that David does not argue his case based on his status as anointed king. Instead, he strips away all earthly dignity and appeals on the only ground that matters before God: his absolute need and God's willingness to stoop. This establishes the genre and tone of the entire psalm—not a petition from strength or entitlement, but a cry of dependence. The ancient reader would recognize this as the language of covenant appeal: God has bound Himself to hear those who are vulnerable and call out to Him.

word_study.meaning: To incline, bend, turn, bow down. The Hiphil form means 'cause to bend' or 'incline toward.' It creates an image of condescension—God voluntarily lowering Himself to hear.
word_study.significance: This verb is not about David bowing before God (though that happens elsewhere), but God bowing toward David. It reverses the expected power dynamic. David is asking the transcendent God to close the distance. The word appears in Exodus 8:10 (plagues bowing), Isaiah 37:17 (God bending His ear), and throughout the Psalter as the standard verb for requesting God's attentive listening.

word_study.meaning: Ani ('afflicted, poor, humble') and evyon ('needy, destitute, one lacking necessities'). Together, they describe someone without resources or standing.
word_study.significance: This pair is not metaphorical for David. While he is king, he experiences himself as spiritually poor—without resources before God except God's grace. The TCR rendering 'afflicted and needy' captures the existential dimension. These same words describe the widow, the orphan, and the refugee throughout Scripture. By using them, David identifies with the most vulnerable and claims standing before God not through merit but through need.

cross_references.connection: Uses the identical phrase ani ve-evyon ('I am poor and needy'), showing this self-identification is David's consistent posture of dependence before God.
Hezekiah uses the same verb hatteh ('bow down Your ear') in a time of crisis, demonstrating this was the traditional language of covenant emergency appeal.
God's self-revelation of mercy and forgiveness will be directly quoted in verse 5 of this psalm, establishing that David's plea is grounded in God's own words about Himself.
Book of Mormon language of God not forgetting those who are weak and afflicted resonates with David's identification as vulnerable and in need of God's remembrance.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the image of a god bending down to hear a human prayer was known from Mesopotamian and Egyptian sources. However, the Israelite innovation was radical: the covenant God *chooses* to hear the cry of the lowest. David's identification as 'poor and needy' despite being king reflects a theological category, not a social reality. The poorest in ancient Israel had no standing before courts or councils, but the Psalter repeatedly asserts that such persons have standing before God. This psalm would have been sung by individuals of all social stations, each able to identify with the vulnerability David expresses. The title 'A Prayer of David' (Psalm 86:1 heading) signals this as a prayer form meant for communal use, even though it voices an individual's plea.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 31:26, Alma prays, 'O God, thou Mighty One, I pray come and visit my people, and bring them again unto thee.' The same posture—a leader identifying with the people's need and asking God to bend down in mercy—appears throughout Book of Mormon prayers, particularly among those facing persecution or spiritual weakness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:1 records: 'Hearken, O ye people of my church, saith the voice of him whose eyes are upon all things, whose arm is stretched out all the day long.' The image of God's attentive ear (Psalm 86:1) and stretched-out arm (D&C 29:1) convey the same truth: God is engaged and responsive to covenant people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The posture of lifting one's soul (verse 4) and bowing one's ear (verse 1) frame the entire dynamic of temple worship: the ascending and descending of heaven and earth, God coming down to meet His people in sacred space.

commentary.christological_typology: David's posture of absolute dependence and his appeal for God to stoop down prefigures Christ's incarnation—God bending down infinitely to meet humanity where it is weakest and most needy. Christ is the ultimate answer to this prayer: God has permanently bent His ear toward creation through the Atonement.
commentary.application: Before attempting to address God with our concerns, this verse calls us to recognize our spiritual poverty and need. We do not approach God as entitled or self-sufficient, but as those who depend entirely on His willingness to hear. This is the proper psychological and spiritual stance for prayer: an honest acknowledgment that without God's grace, we have no standing. Modern covenant members often rush into petitions; Psalm 86:1 teaches that the first act of authentic prayer is this humbling recognition.

text_kjv: Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 presents a theological claim that can initially confuse modern readers: David says 'I am holy' (chasid ani) immediately after calling himself poor and needy. The TCR rendering clarifies: 'Guard my life, for I am devoted to You.' This is not moral perfection but covenantal loyalty. The Hebrew word chasid describes someone bound by chesed—faithful love, covenant commitment. David claims not to be sinless but to be faithful, to be devoted to God's covenant. This reframing is crucial: David's worthiness to be heard rests not on his personal righteousness but on his covenantal relationship with God.

The verse then moves to a self-designation that will become the refrain of the entire psalm: 'Your servant' (avdekha). David appears as a king, yet he calls himself God's servant. This is not diminishment; it is the highest honor in Israel's theology. To be God's servant means to be commissioned, protected, and accountable directly to God. The final phrase—'the one who trusts in You'—anchors David's appeal: his request for salvation rests on his trust (batach) in God. He is not asking to be saved because he deserves it, but because he has placed his faith entirely in God's character and willingness to deliver.

word_study.meaning: One who is devoted, faithful, pious, bound by covenant love. The root chesed means 'faithful love, mercy, covenant loyalty.' A chasid is not primarily morally perfect but covenantally loyal—one who practices chesed.
word_study.significance: This word recalibrates what holiness means. In modern English, 'holy' often connotes moral perfection or separation from sin. The Hebrew chasid is relational—it describes the person bound in faithful relationship to God. This is why David, who has committed serious sins (as recorded in 2 Samuel 11), can still call himself chasid. He is devoted to God, committed to the covenant, and his ultimate allegiance is to God's law and character. The TCR's 'devoted to You' captures this perfectly.

word_study.transliteration: shamrah (feminine form, or possibly 'guard!' as imperative)
word_study.meaning: To keep, guard, watch over, preserve. Often used for God's protection of His people or covenant.
word_study.significance: The verb shamrah appears throughout the Psalter as a request for divine protection. In Genesis 2:15, Adam is called to 'keep' (shammar) the garden. Here David asks God to keep his life as a shepherd keeps sheep or a guardian keeps something precious. The request assumes vulnerability and the need for external vigilance.

word_study.meaning: A servant, slave, or subordinate. In the royal context, it can mean a minister or official. Here it is a self-designation of radical submission.
word_study.significance: The word avdekha appears four times in Psalm 86 (verses 2, 4, 16, and implied in verse 12). This repetition establishes David's entire persona in the psalm: he is not a king demanding, but a servant petitioning. In the ancient Near East, a king calling himself a god's 'servant' was acknowledging divine sovereignty over his own rule. For David to use this term is to place himself under God's authority, not above it. This is covenantal language—the servant is protected and sustained by the master.

word_study.meaning: To trust, rely upon, be confident in. The participle boteach describes an ongoing, habitual stance of trust.
word_study.significance: Trust (batach) is the cognitive and emotional foundation of David's prayer. He is not asking God for mercy as a last resort, but as the natural expression of his trust. The present participle 'the one who trusts' indicates that this is not a momentary trust but David's characteristic posture. This trust is not naive optimism but informed by God's historical revelation—by the exodus, by God's covenant with David's house, by God's known character.

cross_references.connection: Similarly identifies the faithful as 'the pious ones' (chasidim), showing that this term describes the community of the devoted to whom God listens.
God says to David, 'Shall you build me a house to dwell in?' establishing that David's role is to be God's servant in building the kingdom, not his own empire.
Contrasts trust in oneself with trust in the LORD, illustrating that batach ('trust') in the Wisdom literature is foundational to right living.
Ammon declares he is 'a servant of God' and that his strength comes from trust in God, echoing David's identification as God's servant whose power is not his own.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, particularly in Mesopotamian and Egyptian royal inscriptions, kings often called themselves servants of the god(s)—but this was often a performative claim. In Israel's covenantal theology, the claim is radical and non-performative: a king who truly submits his authority to God's authority is describing a real relationship, not a political formula. David's claim to be chasid ('devoted') despite his failures would have resonated powerfully with the later Israelite community, particularly those experiencing exile or oppression, who felt they could not be holy by works but only by covenantal attachment. The term chasid later became the name for the 'Hasidim' (the devoted ones), a renewal movement in Second Temple Judaism.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 26:33, Alma teaches that God will remember His covenant 'with all the people who have left a residue of their seed.' The idea that God's protection rests not on perfection but on covenantal devotion appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Nephi calls himself 'a faithful servant' (1 Nephi 21:15 in the Isaiah quotation), establishing that this language of servant-devotion is woven through the Restoration scriptures.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 11:29 states: 'And thy life shall be preserved unto the obtaining of the ends which God hath purposed in thy heart.' This echoes Psalm 86:2—God guards (shamrah) the life of His servants for the sake of covenant purposes. The servant who trusts is the servant whose life is guarded.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The designation of David as God's servant connects to the temple concept of priesthood—all covenanted members become 'servants in the Lord's house,' participating in His work. The trust required in verse 2 is the same trust that grounds covenant making in sacred space.

commentary.christological_typology: David's self-identification as God's devoted servant (chasid) and his plea to be preserved points to Christ, who is the perfect Chasid—the One absolutely devoted to God's will, whose trust in the Father was unwavering even unto death. Christ's life was preserved through the Resurrection, the ultimate answer to the prayer of Psalm 86:2.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern covenant members to reassess what holiness means. We are not holy because we are sinless; we are holy because we are devoted to God and bound by covenant. The recognition that God guards the lives of those who trust in Him should reframe how we approach personal struggles. Our worth before God rests not on our perfection but on our loyal attachment to Him through covenants. When we identify ourselves as God's servants, we paradoxically gain freedom—freedom from the burden of self-justification and freedom into a life of purpose aligned with God's designs.

text_kjv: Be merciful unto me, O Lord: for I cry unto thee daily.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 shifts the address from YHWH ('the LORD,' the covenant name) in verse 1 to Adonai ('Lord,' the title of authority and mastery). This shift is deliberate: David moves from appealing to God's covenant identity to appealing to God's absolute authority and power to bestow grace. The Hebrew verb chonneni ('be gracious to me, show me favor') asks for undeserved kindness—not justice, but grace. This is the language of desperate appeal throughout the Psalter, used by those who have nowhere else to turn.

The phrase 'all day long' (kol ha-yom) is crucial. David is not praying once, then hoping for the best. He is praying continuously, persistently, without ceasing. This reflects the reality of his situation: the need is not momentary but ongoing. The TCR rendering makes this clear: 'for to You I call all day long.' This is not a single petition but an all-consuming orientation of his life toward God. The verb 'cry' (qara) suggests not quiet contemplation but urgent vocalization—David's distress is real and expressed openly before God. What makes this plea powerful is its constancy: day after day, David turns to God and calls out for grace.

word_study.meaning: To show favor, be gracious, bestow grace. The root chanan is the verb behind the noun 'grace.' It describes undeserved kindness given by one with power to one without standing.
word_study.significance: This verb appears frequently in the Psalter as the cry of the vulnerable. Unlike 'mercy' (which responds to suffering), 'grace' (chanan) is about favor given to one who has no claim upon it. David does not ask for justice (he would lose such a case); he asks for grace. The imperative mood ('be gracious to me!') is bold—David is commanding the Lord to act, not timidly requesting. This is the confidence of covenantal relationship: one can speak to God with intensity.

word_study.meaning: To call out, cry aloud, invoke. Often used for crying out to God in distress or need.
word_study.significance: The verb qara is not a gentle request but an urgent vocalization. In Genesis 4:10, Abel's blood 'cries out' (qara) from the ground. In Exodus 3:7, God hears the 'crying out' (qara) of Israel in Egypt. David is using language of absolute necessity, not polite petition. His prayer is not rationalized or controlled but is the raw expression of his condition.

word_study.meaning: All the day, the entire day, continuously. A temporal marker indicating ongoing or habitual action.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes constancy and persistence. David is not a sometimes-pray-er; he is someone whose life is oriented toward calling on God. The phrase 'all day long' parallels the earlier 'all day long' in verse 3 of many Psalms (e.g., Psalm 25:5, 71:8), establishing that those who trust God maintain constant spiritual awareness and communication.

cross_references.connection: Also uses 'hear my cry' (shme'u qoli) in the same posture of persistent petition, showing this is David's characteristic prayer stance.
Uses the same phrase 'all day long' (kol ha-yom) to describe the crying out of Jerusalem in distress, indicating this language belongs to the vocabulary of lament and urgent appeal.
God says to Moses, 'I will show grace (chanan) to whom I will show grace.' This is the same verb David uses—he is invoking God's stated willingness to show undeserved favor.

The Book of Mormon teaches 'come unto Christ and be perfected in him...deny yourselves of all ungodliness.' The grace David calls upon in verse 3 is the grace Moroni describes—undeserved favor that transforms the one who receives it.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Levantine world, a person in distress would cry out for help—sometimes to a god, sometimes to a king or ruler. The Psalter Davidicizes this universal human experience: the person in distress cries to God as the ultimate authority who can grant grace. The address to Adonai ('Lord' as master) rather than YHWH (the covenant name) in verse 3 may reflect moments when David is not sure of his covenantal standing but appeals to God as the ultimate judge who has the power to grant grace. The constancy of prayer ('all day long') was an attainable ideal in an ancient Mediterranean or Near Eastern context where individuals might spend significant time in worship spaces or engage in contemplative prayer practice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Ether 3:2, the Brother of Jared 'cried unto the Lord' continually while climbing the mountain to create the stones. Like David in Psalm 86:3, the Brother of Jared's spiritual strength comes from unceasing prayer. The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches that continuous calling upon God is the mark of a covenant person (Alma 34:27).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 62:1 states: 'Behold, I say unto you, that ye shall let your minds stay upon me, O ye inhabitants of Zion.' The 'all day long' prayer of Psalm 86:3 is the scriptural precedent for the D&C teaching that one's mind (and heart) should be continuously oriented toward God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The persistent calling upon God ('all day long') connects to the temple covenant language of continual spiritual awareness and the daily recommitment of temple practice in restored theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, which involved anguished crying out to the Father, fulfills the archetype of the one who calls upon God in desperation and appealing for grace. Christ's entire earthly ministry was 'all day long'—continuous orientation toward God's will and toward the salvation of those who call upon His name.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often compartmentalize prayer into specific times and places. Psalm 86:3 challenges this: the pattern of continuous spiritual awareness—calling upon God 'all day long'—should characterize the devoted person. This does not require constant formal prayer but rather a constant orientation of the heart and mind toward God. When facing ongoing challenges (chronic illness, family conflict, financial strain), this verse teaches that persistent appeal for grace is not weakness but the proper posture of trust. David teaches us that we are not simply to pray and then wait; we are to maintain a stance of constant communication with God.

text_kjv: Rejoice the soul of thy servant: for unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 pivots from plea to aspiration—David moves from asking God to hear him to asking God to give him joy. The TCR rendering makes this movement precise: 'Gladden the soul of Your servant, / for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul.' This is not David presuming happiness will come; rather, he is asking God to cause joy (sammeach is a Piel imperative—'cause to be joyful'). This is a theologically loaded request: David acknowledges that joy is not something he can manufacture but something only God can grant. Even in his affliction, David's hope is anchored in God's power to gladden.

The second line employs the phrase 'lift up my soul' (nafshi essa), which echoes Psalm 25:1 verbatim. To lift one's soul is to offer one's entire inner life upward to God as a gesture of submission and surrender. This is not a casual prayer but an act of total dedication. The pairing of verse 4—asking God to gladden David's soul while David simultaneously lifts his soul to God—describes the double movement of prayer: the downward descent of God's grace and the upward ascent of human devotion. David is completely vulnerable, with his inner self extended toward God, and he trusts that God will meet him with gladness. This is the essence of childlike faith in the Psalter.

word_study.meaning: To make joyful, cause to rejoice, brighten. The Piel form is causative—it means to cause someone else to be joyful, not merely to be joyful oneself.
word_study.significance: David does not ask to become joyful; he asks God to cause him to be joyful. This is significant because it acknowledges the bondage of depression, affliction, or despair—David cannot simply will himself into joy. Only God can cause the transformation. The Piel form emphasizes God's agency. This echoes throughout the Psalter (e.g., Psalm 100:2, 'Make a joyful noise unto the Lord'), where joy is not a psychological state David manufactures but a gift God bestows.

word_study.meaning: To lift, raise, elevate. The verb nasa can mean to carry, bear, take up, or raise up. Here it describes the action of lifting one's soul upward.
word_study.significance: This phrase is a verbatim quotation of Psalm 25:1. By repeating it, David signals that this is his foundational gesture of prayer. To lift the soul is an act of offering—it is as if David is extending his deepest self upward to God. In ancient Levantine worship, lifting one's hands or eyes to heaven was a physical gesture; here, the entire soul is lifted. This is total devotion. The verb nasa is also used in the phrase 'lift up one's face' (nasa panav), which means to look toward someone in confidence or hope. When David lifts his soul to God, he is turning his entire being toward God with the expectation of meeting God's gaze.

word_study.meaning: Soul, life, self, person, breath. The nephesh is the animating life force, the seat of emotion and desire, the whole person.
word_study.significance: Throughout Psalm 86, nephesh ('soul') appears repeatedly (verses 2, 4, 14)—it is the locus of David's entire being that he extends toward God. The nephesh is not merely the spiritual component; it is the whole integrated self, including emotions, desires, and will. When David asks God to gladden his nephesh and lifts his nephesh to God, he is offering his complete person.

cross_references.connection: Contains the identical phrase 'unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul' (nafshi essa elekha), establishing this as David's foundational prayer posture of total offering.
States 'the joy of the Lord is your strength,' expressing the same idea that God's gift of gladness (sammeach) becomes the source of endurance and strength.
Paul's 'Rejoice in the Lord alway' echoes the Hebrew tradition of joy (sammeach) as coming from God's presence and character.
States 'be of good cheer; for I have overcome the world,' capturing the same promise that God causes gladness in those who surrender their souls to Him.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern worship, the lifting of hands, eyes, or the entire person toward heaven was a standard prayer gesture, documented in Egyptian tomb paintings and Mesopotamian seals. The phrase 'lift up the soul' represents the internalization of this gesture—it is not merely physical posture but the orientation of one's entire being. The request for God to 'cause joy' (sammeach) reflects the ancient understanding that joy is not a natural state in a world of hardship but a divine gift, particularly granted in the context of worship and encounter with the divine. The Psalter's repeated requests for God to gladden suggest that the post-exilic community experienced genuine suffering and depression, and their prayers express the confidence that God's presence can transform internal states.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 41:10, Alma teaches about the 'restoration of the soul,' describing spiritual transformation through alignment with God's will. David's lifting of his soul and asking for gladness is this restoration in action—the soul returns to God (nasa, lifting) and is made whole (sammeach, gladdened).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:11–13 describes a time when God will 'gladden' (D&C language) the souls of the faithful. The verse echoes this promise: God's fundamental work is to cause the souls of His covenant people to rejoice. Section 101:36 ('be of good cheer') carries the same Davidic promise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The lifting of the soul to God (verse 4) is the theological foundation of temple worship—the ascent of the soul from the terrestrial to the celestial, the presentation of the whole self before God in sacred space. The gladness promised is the joy of divine presence in the holy place.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ, in the Garden of Gethsemane, lifted His soul to the Father ('O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt,' Matthew 26:39). Christ is the perfect expression of Psalm 86:4—the one whose soul is totally lifted to God, and whose ultimate gladness comes through His resurrection and the Father's affirmation of His work.
commentary.application: This verse confronts the modern assumption that joy is something we produce through positive thinking or self-care. David teaches that authentic joy—especially in the context of affliction—comes from God. The practice of 'lifting one's soul' is an act of vulnerable offering: we extend our emotional and spiritual selves to God with the trust that He will respond with gladness. In modern covenant practice, this means that when we are depressed, anxious, or emotionally depleted, we are called not merely to manage our emotions but to lift our souls to God and trust that His grace can transform our inner state. This is not toxic positivity; it is the realistic hope that God's presence has the power to cause joy even when circumstances are unchanged.

text_kjv: For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 is the theological hinge of the entire psalm. Up to this point, David has made his petitions; now he states the reason why God will answer: because of who God is. The TCR rendering is luminous: 'For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, / abounding in faithful love to all who call on You.' This verse is structured as a self-contained statement of God's character, drawing directly from Exodus 34:6, where God reveals Himself to Moses after the golden calf incident. David does not merely hope God is forgiving; he knows it from the tradition, from Scripture, from covenant theology. When God's goodness (tov) is mentioned first, it becomes the foundation for all His other attributes. God is good—not as a feeling or inclination, but as His essential nature.

The word translated 'ready to forgive' (sallach) is exceptionally rare in Hebrew Scripture, appearing only in Psalm 86:5 and Nehemiah 9:17. This rarity makes it special: when the Bible describes God with this word, it is employing language reserved for the divine alone. God's forgiveness is not grudging or conditional but His characteristic response to those who call. The final phrase—'to all who call on You'—is universalizing: this mercy is not restricted to the elite or the righteous but is offered to all who approach God in prayer. The qualifier 'all who call' (le-khol qore'ekha) makes the offer unrestricted, yet it still requires the act of calling—one must approach God for the mercy to be received. This is the balance of biblical theology: grace is freely offered, but it must be appropriated through prayer and faith.

word_study.meaning: Good, pleasing, beautiful, beneficial. The root encompasses moral goodness, aesthetic beauty, and practical benefit.
word_study.significance: Tov is the first word used to describe creation in Genesis 1 ('God saw that it was good'). When David says God is tov, he is anchoring God's character in the fundamental ordering principle of creation. God's goodness is not sentimental; it is the expression of His creative power and moral order. In the Psalter, tov is often the reason given for praising God or approaching God in prayer.

word_study.meaning: To forgive, pardon, allow to pass by. It means to refrain from exacting punishment for wrongdoing.
word_study.significance: This verb appears almost nowhere in the Hebrew Bible outside Psalm 86:5 and Nehemiah 9:17. Its rarity makes it extraordinarily special—when Scripture uses sallach, it is describing a unique divine prerogative. The word suggests that God does not simply overlook sin; God actively, deliberately chooses to allow it to pass by. The adjective form here ('ready to forgive') suggests that this is God's standing disposition, not something God must be persuaded into. God is habitually forgiving, characteristically gracious. The contrast with God's justice (mishpat) is deliberate: God could exact justice, but God chooses to forgive those who call.

word_study.transliteration: rav chesed (great in faithful love, abundant in covenant loyalty)
word_study.meaning: Rav ('much, great, abundant') + chesed ('faithful love, mercy, covenant loyalty'). Together: overflowing with covenant faithfulness.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'abounding in faithful love' captures what the Hebrew communicates: God's chesed is not measured or limited but is vast, overflowing. Chesed is the core covenantal attribute—it is the faithful love God keeps with His people. Exodus 34:6 uses the exact phrase 'rav chesed' ('abundant in faithful love') to describe God's self-revelation. When David uses this phrase, he is quoting God's own words about Himself. He is saying, 'You are exactly what You claimed to be.' This is not David's opinion; this is David's knowledge grounded in Scripture.

cross_references.connection: God's self-revelation to Moses: 'The LORD...merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,' the foundational statement of God's character that David draws upon in this verse.
Uses the same rare verb sallach ('ready to forgive') in Israel's corporate prayer of remembrance, showing that acknowledging God's forgiving character is essential to covenant restoration.

Calls the unrighteous to return to God 'for he will abundantly pardon' (sallach), using the same vocabulary to assure that God's forgiveness is not restricted but is offered abundantly to all who return.

Amulek teaches 'Behold, he [God] sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them,' expressing the same universality and abundance as Psalm 86:5's 'rav chesed...to all who call.'

commentary.historical_context: The rarity of the verb sallach in the Hebrew Bible makes this verse extraordinary. While other verbs for forgiveness appear throughout Scripture, sallach is reserved for God's character in Psalm 86:5 and referenced in Nehemiah 9:17 during the post-exilic renewal. This suggests that sallach may have been preserved and emphasized in Israel's liturgy for particularly profound moments of forgiveness—moments when God's characteristic mercy needed to be affirmed. The echo of Exodus 34:6 in verse 5 is deliberate: David is reminding God and himself of God's self-revelation at a moment when forgiveness was most needed (after the golden calf). The universalizing language—'to all who call on You'—would have been particularly meaningful in the post-exilic period when Israel was reconstituting itself and needed to be reassured that God's forgiveness extended to all Israel, not just the elite.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 26:33 teaches 'he [God] has promised through his prophets that he shall take away the sins of those of his children who believe on his name.' This directly parallels Psalm 86:5—God's character is to forgive those who call upon Him. The Book of Mormon makes explicit what the Psalter assumes: the atonement of Christ is the mechanism through which God's forgiving character is expressed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:96 states God is 'merciful and compassionate,' drawing on the same vocabulary as Psalm 86:5. Section 1:31–32 reveals: 'I, the Lord, am merciful and gentle...nevertheless, he that has sinned against the light and knowledge of God is not excused.' The verse asserts both God's abundant mercy and the reality of moral accountability—consistent with Psalm 86:5's insistence that mercy is for 'those who call on You.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The assurance of God's readiness to forgive (sallach) is foundational to temple worship and covenants. The endowment structure—which moves from transgression to atonement—is built on the confidence that God is characterized by forgiveness toward those who approach Him through proper channels.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 5 is a prophecy that finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ. God's characteristic readiness to forgive (sallach) is realized through Christ's Atonement, which makes it possible for God's forgiveness to be extended to all who call upon Christ. Christ is the embodiment of God's 'rav chesed'—His covenant loyalty expressed in flesh, shedding His blood for the remission of sins. The Atonement is God's 'good' (tov) work of redemption.
commentary.application: Psalm 86:5 is a verse to memorize and recite when one is tempted toward despair about forgiveness. Modern members sometimes assume they have committed sins too grave for God's forgiveness, or they wrestle with whether God 'really' forgives. This verse settles the question: God is characteristically forgiving (sallach), characteristically abundant in faithful love (rav chesed), and this forgiveness is not restricted to a few but is offered 'to all who call.' The condition is calling—approaching God in genuine repentance and prayer. This verse is a corrective to both legalism (which suggests God is hard to appease) and antinomianism (which suggests God does not care about sin). God cares deeply about sin, but God is fundamentally disposed toward forgiveness of those who turn to Him.

text_kjv: Give ear, O LORD, unto my prayer; and attend to the voice of my supplications.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 returns from the statement of God's character to a direct petition, echoing the opening movement of verse 1 but with intensified language. The TCR rendering is: 'Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; / attend to the voice of my pleas for mercy.' Where verse 1 asked God to 'bend down Your ear,' verse 6 asks God to 'give ear'—the request is repeated, reinforced, emphasized. This repetition is not redundancy; it is the intensification of prayer through the psalm. The doubling of verbs—'give ear' (ha'azinah) and 'attend' (haqshivah)—creates a two-fold call: God must not only listen passively but must pay attention actively. The verb haqshivah carries the sense of 'lean in,' 'focus,' 'listen carefully.' David is asking God to filter out all other voices and focus entirely on his prayer.

The phrase 'my supplications' (tachanunot from the root chanan, 'show grace') is particularly evocative. These are not formal requests but desperate pleas, the language of begging. The term 'the voice of my pleas for mercy' emphasizes that David is not speaking with composure but with urgency and vulnerability. His voice—the actual sounding of his prayer—is what he is offering. This is why verse 6 is so powerful: it takes the inner reality of desperation and brings it into audible expression. David is saying, 'God, hear not just my words, but the voice beneath the words—the cry that comes from my situation of need.' This final petition before the psalm pivots (in verse 7) to address God's power to deliver completes the structure: David makes known his need (verses 1–3), reveals his hope (verse 4), grounds his hope in God's character (verse 5), and then makes his final urgent plea (verse 6).

word_study.meaning: To give ear, pay attention, listen. The Hiphil form is causative, meaning 'cause your ear to listen' or 'direct your ear to hear.'
word_study.significance: The verb 'azan appears in the Psalter specifically in the context of urgent prayer (e.g., Psalm 80:1, 'Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel'). The Hiphil imperative is bold and commanding—David is not timidly requesting but authoritatively directing God's attention. This is the confidence of covenantal prayer: David can address God with intensity because the covenant relationship allows such directness.

word_study.meaning: To listen attentively, pay attention, incline the ear. The verb suggests active, focused listening, not mere hearing.
word_study.significance: The verb qashav involves more than passive reception; it requires active concentration. When combined with ha'azinah ('give ear'), the two verbs create a full call for God's attention: first, God must direct His ear; then, God must focus His mind. This is the language of one who is aware that God could be distracted by other concerns and therefore emphasizes the urgency of His own plea.

word_study.meaning: Pleas for mercy, supplications, entreaties. The root is chanan ('show grace, be gracious'). These are not formal requests but desperate, grace-seeking appeals.
word_study.significance: The word tachanunot embeds the concept of grace within the very word for prayer. These are not prayers of thanksgiving or praise but prayers of desperation, prayers from those without standing who must appeal to grace. The plural form (tachanunot) suggests multiple layers or repeated pleas—David is not praying once but bringing his sustained cry of need to God. This term connects back to verse 3 where David described 'crying unto thee daily' (qare'u)—these tachanunot are the substantive content of that daily crying.

word_study.meaning: Voice, sound, noise. It can refer to an audible sound, the tone or quality of speech, or metaphorically to someone's testimony or witness.
word_study.significance: By emphasizing 'the voice of my pleas,' David is highlighting that his prayer is not merely mental or internal but is expressed in sound, in actual vocalization. In the ancient context, prayer was often spoken aloud, not silent. David is asking God to hear the sound of his distressed voice—his cry, his tone, his emotional state expressed in sound. This adds a dimension often lost in modern silent prayer: the physical, embodied reality of prayer.

cross_references.connection: Opens with similar language of lifting one's soul to God, establishing this as a foundational prayer posture that David repeats across his psalms.
Opens identically: 'Hear the right, O LORD, attend unto my cry,' showing that the double petition ('hear'/'attend') is David's characteristic prayer opening.
Hezekiah uses nearly identical language: 'Incline thine ear, O LORD, and hear,' demonstrating that this is the traditional language of kingly petition for divine intervention.

Amulek teaches to 'let your hearts be purified...and let all your doings be done with prayer,' echoing David's model that all of life should be oriented toward calling upon God with desperate sincerity.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Levantine context, audible prayer was the norm. The voice of prayer was understood not as a mere vehicle for words but as itself carrying spiritual significance—the tone, the urgency, the very sound of the prayer was part of what was being offered to God. This makes verse 6's emphasis on 'the voice of my pleas' meaningful: David is not asking God merely to read his thoughts but to hear his actual prayer as it is spoken. The repetition of petition ('give ear...attend') is also a feature of ancient prayer style—repetition was not viewed as redundancy but as emphasis and intensification. The use of imperatives (ha'azinah, haqshivah, attend) reflects a form of prayer that was bold and direct, characteristic of the lament psalms where the speaker addresses God with urgency and even intensity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 1:15, Lehi 'cried unto the Lord' in his prayer, and the Book of Mormon emphasizes that the Lord heard his voice. Similarly, Nephi prays throughout 1 Nephi with this same confidence that his voice reaches God.
