The Book of Mormon sustains the Davidic model that God attends to the actual voice and cry of His covenant people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 teaches: 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me.' The promise embedded in verse 6 is that when David calls out with urgency ('give ear...attend'), God responds by drawing near. The D&C affirms this reciprocal dynamic.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The petition to have God 'give ear' and 'attend' to one's voice connects to temple prayer, where the covenant member's voice is lifted in sacred space with the confidence that God attends. The temple is the place where God's attention is most assured, where His 'ear is ever open' to the petitions of His people.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's prayer in Gethsemane ('O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,' Matthew 26:39) embodies the desperate, vocal plea of Psalm 86:6. Christ's voice crying out in prayer, asking the Father to attend to His petition, is the ultimate expression of this Davidic prayer posture. The Father's response to Christ's prayer—answering through the angel who strengthened Him (Luke 22:43)—is the perfect fulfillment of the promise implicit in verse 6: when one calls with true desperation, God attends.
commentary.application: In modern covenant practice, where prayer is often silent and individualistic, Psalm 86:6 invites reconsideration of the power of vocal prayer. While silent prayer is valuable, there is something spiritually significant about giving voice to one's petitions—about letting the cry of one's heart be audible. In private personal prayer, speaking aloud, even quietly, can deepen the experience. More broadly, this verse teaches that when we pray, we should not assume God is distracted or unaware; rather, we should call upon God with the confident urgency that He is attentive and His ear is open. The double imperative ('give ear...attend') should instill in us the confidence to pray with intensity and directness, not with timidity or hedging.

text_kjv: In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me.

commentary.narrative:
David opens this section with a declaration grounded not in hope but in certainty. The phrase "in the day of my trouble" (yom tsarati) is not hypothetical—it describes the actual moment when the psalmist's resources are exhausted and only God remains. The Covenant Rendering captures something the KJV masks: the confidence embedded in "for you will answer me" is not a plea but an assertion of trust so deep it becomes declarative. David does not call hoping God might answer; he calls knowing God will answer. This is not naive optimism but covenant memory—the recollection of past deliverances that grounds present trust.

The "day of distress" is a recurring theme throughout the Psalter (cf. 50:15, 77:3), marking the threshold moment when human solutions fail and the soul stands before God alone. In that moment, David's confidence is not in his eloquence, his worthiness, or his bargaining power—it is purely in God's character. The shift from "I will call" (future tense in English) to "you will answer" (future certainty) transforms a petition into a covenant claim: God has bound himself to hear and respond to his people's cry.

word_study.meaning: Narrowness, confinement, pressure, distress—literally the condition of being hemmed in with no escape. Root meaning suggests being pressed or squeezed from all sides. In the Psalter, tsarah is the condition that drives the soul to seek God alone.
word_study.significance: The word carries spatial imagery: distress is experienced as confinement, a narrowing of possibility. Only God's answer expands the space and restores options. For covenant people, this word describes not just emotional suffering but the theological moment when false supports are stripped away.

word_study.meaning: To answer, respond, reply—literally 'to open one's mouth in response.' The word carries the sense of being heard and receiving a reply, not merely acknowledgment but substantive response. In covenant contexts, 'anah often means God acts on behalf of the one who calls.
word_study.significance: David's confidence rests on God's character as one who answers. This is not abstract faith but relational: God hears and God responds. The Covenant Rendering's present-tense 'for You will answer me' emphasizes that this is David's lived experience of God, not theological speculation.

cross_references.connection: The earlier psalm establishes the same pattern: 'Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee.' David is drawing on an established pattern of God's responsiveness.
Another 'day of distress' psalm where the psalmist 'cried unto God with my voice' and 'he gave ear unto me,' establishing the reliability of calling upon God in extremity.
Samuel intercedes for Israel in crisis, and the cry is answered with thunder and deliverance—a narrative example of the same pattern David invokes here.

Modern revelation echoes this ancient pattern: 'In nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things'—calling upon God in distress is the appropriate human response.

commentary.historical_context: The 'day of trouble' language reflects a historical moment, though scholars debate whether this is David's literal exile (fleeing Saul), his conflicts with Absalom, or a typological representation of Israel's recurring crises. In any case, the Davidic psalms were sung by later Israel during genuine exiles and restorations, making this language perpetually relevant. The confidence David expresses here was tested and proven true in Israel's experience—the temple was rebuilt, the people returned, God's answer came. Ancient Israel understood that calling upon God in distress was not a last resort but the primary recourse of covenant people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-26 records Alma's invocation of this pattern: in the day of his spiritual anguish, he calls upon Jesus Christ for deliverance, and receives immediate answer. Alma's 'day of trouble' becomes the occasion of his conversion. The Book of Mormon demonstrates that this ancient pattern of distress and answered prayer continues in the restored gospel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 records Joseph Smith's cry from Liberty Jail: 'O God, where art thou?' is followed by verses of comfort and assurance. The same pattern—distress, cry, divine answer—appears in the Restoration. The Lord's response in verses 7-25 demonstrates that God still answers those who call in the day of their trouble.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The act of calling upon God in the day of trouble is foundational to temple worship and covenant making. Members covenant to 'hearken to the voice of the Lord' and are assured of God's listening ear. The temple is, in a sense, the House of Answered Prayer where the righteous come to call upon God.

commentary.christological_typology: David's confidence that God will answer his call anticipates the efficacy of Christ's intercession. In the New Testament, believers are told 'if we ask anything according to his will, he heareth us' (1 John 5:14)—an echo of David's certainty. Jesus himself models this pattern in Gethsemane: crying out in distress, yet assured of the Father's answer. The day of Christ's suffering (his ultimate 'day of trouble') is answered by his resurrection.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to distinguish between hoping for an answer and knowing we will receive one. Modern covenant members often face genuine distress—illness, loss, uncertainty, persecution. The question is not whether God can answer, but whether we have cultivated enough covenant memory and trust to call upon him with David's certainty. What 'day of trouble' in your life could become an occasion not of doubt but of deepened covenant claim? The answer comes not to those who ask hesitantly but to those who call knowing God is bound by his own character to respond.

text_kjv: Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works.

commentary.narrative:
This verse shifts from personal petition to cosmic claim. David moves from his own distress to the incomparable nature of God among all other divine beings. The phrase 'among the gods' (ba-elohim) immediately signals that this is not a declaration in a monotheistic vacuum—the Psalter regularly acknowledges the existence of other elohim. What makes this verse distinctive is that it declares them irrelevant through incomparability. The translator notes helpfully clarify: this is not henotheism (worshipping one god while acknowledging others as real threats), but what might be called 'incomparability theology'—YHWH is so categorically different that comparison itself becomes absurd.

The second line shifts the focus from being to doing: 'neither are there any works like unto thy works.' God's uniqueness is not merely ontological (who he is) but functional (what he does). No other divine power in the ancient Near Eastern imagination produced creation, covenant, redemption, and deliverance on the scale and with the character of Israel's God. When David declares that God's works have no parallel, he is thinking concretely: the exodus, the giving of the law, the preservation of Israel, the defeat of enemies, the restoration of the broken. These are not abstract theological propositions but lived history.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'there is no as-you'—a comparative negation that renders something incomparable. The phrase presupposes a category of comparison (other gods) and then declares that within that category, no equivalent exists. Ein kamokha is an affirmation of uniqueness through comparative denial.
word_study.significance: This exact phrase echoes Exodus 15:11 ('Who is like You among the gods, O LORD?') and Deuteronomy 3:24. By using this echoing language, David connects his personal salvation experience to Israel's foundational salvation moments. The incomparability of God is not a new insight but the repeated testimony of covenant history.

word_study.meaning: Gods, divine beings, powers. In the Hebrew Bible, elohim can refer to YHWH, but also to other divine beings (the 'sons of God' in Job 1, the gods of the nations, demons, angels). The plural form indicates multiplicity of divine powers in the ANE cosmology.
word_study.significance: The use of elohim here is important: David does not deny that other powers exist in the cosmos. But YHWH is the only one called Adonai ('Lord'), the only one whose character is justice and mercy, the only one who makes covenant. The acknowledgment of other elohim actually heightens the majesty of YHWH—among all the powers that exist, none approaches him.

word_study.meaning: Works, deeds, acts—the products of action and intention. In covenant language, God's works are the evidence of his character and his faithfulness. Ma'asim are not abstract concepts but concrete historical actions.
word_study.significance: By emphasizing God's works, David grounds his theology in history, not philosophy. He is not making an abstract claim about divine nature but pointing to what God has actually done: created the world, freed the enslaved, sustained the covenant, defeated enemies. The works prove the incomparability.

cross_references.connection: The Song of the Sea uses the identical phrase 'Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?' establishing the incomparability claim at Israel's foundational moment of redemption.

Moses' blessing acknowledges that 'the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance' and 'set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel,' presupposing other divine powers yet affirming YHWH's supremacy.
This entire psalm depicts God standing in the assembly of the gods and pronouncing judgment on them, affirming that other elohim exist but are subject to YHWH's authority.
Later in the exile, Isaiah will ask 'To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?'—extending David's incomparability theology into a polemical argument against idolatry.
Ammon testifies that God's 'matchless power' has wrought wonders among the Lamanites—the Book of Mormon echoes the idea that God's works surpass all comparison.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern literature regularly compared gods, ranking them within a hierarchy of power. The Babylonian Enuma Elish, for instance, portrays Marduk rising to supremacy among the gods through contests of power. David's assertion of YHWH's incomparability is situated in this comparative context—but with a crucial difference. YHWH is not one god among many jockeying for position; YHWH's character (justice, covenant loyalty, creative power) is simply not comparable to other divine beings. The Covenant Rendering's note helpfully clarifies that this is not philosophical monotheism (the denial that other powers exist) but theological monarchism: YHWH's difference is so profound that comparison is meaningless. This would have resonated powerfully with Israel during the exile, when they were surrounded by Babylonian and Persian religion—a reassurance that whatever powers existed in those empires, they bore no real comparison to their own God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 4:34 records Nephi's affirmation: 'O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. Thou hast assuaged my fears.' The incomparability of God is assumed as the foundation of covenant faith in the Book of Mormon. Ether 3:17 records Christ declaring to the Brother of Jared, 'Never have I showed myself unto man whom I have created, for never has man believed in me as thou hast'—suggesting that the works of God in the Restoration surpass all previous manifestations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6-13 asserts that Jesus Christ 'is in all things, and is through all things, and is round about all things'—affirming a form of divine incomparability rooted in the premortal Jesus. Section 76 presents the vision of the heavenly kingdom in terms that surpass all earthly comparison. The Restoration consistently affirms that God's ways and works exceed all human category and comparison.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple presentation of the creation story, covenant, and redemption implicitly declares the uniqueness of God's design and purposes. The endowment demonstrates that God's works (creation, fall, atonement, exaltation) stand alone in their majesty and purpose. No other cosmology, no other pathway to exaltation, can be compared to the way God has ordained.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ himself becomes the ultimate manifestation of God's incomparable works. In John 1, Christ is 'the Word' through whom 'all things were made'—the personal instantiation of the incomparability David celebrates. Hebrews 1:3 declares Christ to be 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person'—Christ is God's ultimate work, the deed that surpasses all other deeds. The resurrection is the incomparable work that no other power, no other god of the nations, could accomplish.
commentary.application: In a pluralistic age, this verse challenges us to think carefully about religious comparison. David is not claiming that other religions are worthless or contemptible—he is claiming that in terms of actual historical deliverance, covenant reliability, and transformative power, God's works stand alone. The question for modern believers is: do our lives bear witness to the incomparable character of God's works? Can others see in our deliverance, our healing, our restored relationships, evidence that our God acts in ways no other power can? This verse invites us to move beyond defensive apologetics into confident testimony born of actual experience of God's unique workings in our lives.

text_kjv: All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name.

commentary.narrative:
The psalm suddenly expands to a vision of cosmic scope. David moves from his personal distress and from God's incomparability among the gods to an eschatological vision: all nations will come and worship. This is striking because Psalm 86 is attributed to David, whose political reality was confined to a small kingdom surrounded by powerful empires. Yet David envisions a future where 'all the nations you have made' (kol goyim asher asita) will bow before Israel's God. This is not political fantasy but theological vision—the conviction that God's incomparability will eventually be manifest to all humanity.

The physical posture of worship matters: 'bow down before thee' (yishtachavu lefanekha) is the most complete act of submission and worship—forehead to ground, the whole body pressed down in acknowledgment of absolute dependence on God. This is not reluctant obedience but joyful worship. And the final phrase, 'shall glorify thy name' (vikhabbedu lishmekha), suggests that these nations will not merely bow but will actively add weight and honor to God's reputation. They will become witnesses to God's greatness among all peoples. This anticipates the vision of Isaiah 2:2-4, where 'many people' shall go to 'the mountain of the Lord's house' in the latter days.

word_study.meaning: All peoples, all nations—the word goy (plural goyim) originally meant 'nation' but came to refer especially to non-Israelite nations. The universality of 'all' (kol) is emphatic, suggesting without exception.
word_study.significance: For David to envision all goyim worshipping Israel's God was radical. Goyim were typically understood as outside the covenant, yet David envisions them not excluded but included in worship of YHWH. This signals a universalist eschatology: God's covenant purposes extend ultimately to all humanity.

word_study.meaning: To bow, prostrate oneself, worship. The root carries the sense of bending, submitting, abasing oneself. Yishtachavu is reflexive, suggesting a voluntary act of self-lowering before God.
word_study.significance: This is the most complete form of worship in Hebrew—the whole self pressed down in acknowledgment. It is not mere intellectual agreement but embodied, physical surrender. The use of this verb suggests that the nations' worship will be total and genuine.

word_study.meaning: To honor, glorify, make heavy—literally 'to weight' something, to add substance and significance. To glorify God is to increase his reputation and honor among the peoples.
word_study.significance: The root meaning of 'making heavy' suggests adding weight and substance. When the nations glorify God's name, they are adding their testimony, their witness, their weight to God's reputation. This is not passive worship but active witness.

word_study.meaning: Your name—in Hebrew, the name represents the character, reputation, and essence of a person. God's name is his revealed character.
word_study.significance: To glorify God's name is to make his character known, to testify to who he is and what he does. The expansion of God's name among all nations is the expansion of the knowledge of his character.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah records a similar vision: 'In the last days...all nations shall flow unto it [the mountain of the Lord's house]...and he will teach us of his ways.' David's vision finds fuller expression in Isaiah's prophecy.
The next psalm celebrates Zion as a city where all peoples will be born anew in God, extending the vision of Psalm 86:9 with even more explicit universalism.

John's vision echoes this psalm: 'All nations shall come and worship before thee; for thy judgments are made manifest.' The eschatological vision of universal worship is central to New Testament revelation.

Joseph Smith's vision of the celestial kingdom indicates that ultimately 'all who have died without a knowledge of this gospel...shall inherit the celestial kingdom,' affirming a universalism rooted in God's incomparable justice.

Christ teaches the Nephites of a future gathering where 'all nations shall be gathered before him' and 'his name shall be blasphemed no more'—the Book of Mormon's version of universal acknowledgment of God.

commentary.historical_context: The vision of universal worship was particularly powerful during the Davidic monarchy, when Israel was ascending as a regional power. But the vision was tested during the Babylonian exile, when Israel was conquered and scattered. Yet the psalm was sung during and after that exile, maintaining the hope that despite present humiliation, God's name would eventually be glorified among all nations. The Covenant Rendering's rendering—'All the nations You have made will come'—emphasizes that this is not David's achievement or Israel's political success, but God's own work of gathering. The emphasis on God as maker of the nations ('whom thou hast made') suggests that the universal worship will come not through conquest but through God's sovereign action. In the Hellenistic period, when these psalms were compiled and sung in the Second Temple, this vision resonated even more powerfully—a small Jewish remnant holding to the faith that their God would ultimately be recognized as the God of all peoples.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
2 Nephi 21 records Nephi's quotation of Isaiah 11, which envisions a time when 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.' The Book of Mormon constantly affirms that God's gospel is intended for all peoples, nations, and kindreds. Alma 29:8 expresses this universalist hope: 'I would that all men could be convinced of the truth and stand before God and be judged.'

The Book of Mormon further develops this vision through the ministry to the Gentiles and the ultimate gathering of all Israel. The teaching that all people have opportunity to accept or reject the gospel reflects the vision that all peoples are invited to worship and glorify God's name.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 88:87-92 records the vision of the gathering of all peoples: 'And plagues shall go forth, and they shall not be stayed until the Lord hath made bare his arm before all nations...that all the nations may see my power.' Section 110 records the appearance of Moses, who committed the keys of the gathering of Israel to Joseph Smith. The eschatological vision of Psalm 86:9 is fundamental to Restoration theology: the gospel is being taken to all nations so that eventually all peoples will have the opportunity to worship the true God.

D&C 84:23-28 teaches that the oath and covenant God makes with the priesthood is that those who receive it shall 'become the sons of Moses, and of Aaron, and the seed of Abraham, and the church and the kingdom, and the elect of God'—a universalism rooted in covenant availability to all.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the house where all peoples are invited to come and worship. The fact that temples are spread across many nations fulfills the vision of Psalm 86:9—the Lord's house is accessible to 'all nations.' The temple represents the eschatological vision made present: a place where all people can come and 'glorify thy name' through covenant making and endowment. Temple work for the dead extends this vision across time: eventually all humanity will have the opportunity to glorify God's name through covenant acceptance.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse prefigures Christ's declaration in Matthew 28:19-20: 'Go ye therefore, and teach all nations...and, lo, I am with you alway.' Christ's Great Commission enacts the vision David expressed—the gospel is to be preached to all nations so that all can come and worship. Revelation 5:9-10 celebrates Christ as the one 'redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.' Christ is the means by which David's vision becomes reality—through his atonement and resurrection, the way is opened for all peoples to approach God.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to align our faith with God's eschatological vision. In a time when we may feel culturally marginalized or insignificant, Psalm 86:9 reminds us that we belong to the people of the only God whose name will ultimately be glorified among all nations. More personally, it challenges us to work toward that vision: how do we help glorify God's name among all peoples? Are we preparing to serve among all nations? Do we truly believe that God's covenant is for all humanity, or do we harbor secret doubts about whether other cultures or peoples can fully embrace God? The vision of this verse should move us beyond tribal religion toward genuine universalism—the conviction that God's incomparable character and works are meant to be known and worshipped by all humanity.

text_kjv: For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone.

commentary.narrative:
This verse distills the theology of the entire psalm into its most concentrated form. After celebrating God's incomparability among other gods (verse 8) and envisioning universal worship (verse 9), David now makes the strongest possible monotheistic claim: 'Thou art God alone' (attah Elohim levaddekha). This appears to contradict verse 8, which acknowledged the existence of other gods. But there is no contradiction—it is a progression of thought. Yes, other elohim exist in the cosmic hierarchy, but only YHWH deserves the title 'Elohim' in its fullest sense. Only YHWH is truly God in the way that matters: only YHWH is worthy of worship, only YHWH makes covenant, only YHWH acts with justice and mercy toward Israel.

The phrase 'doest wondrous things' (oseh nifla'ot) points to the concrete, historical acts that prove this claim. The word nifla'ot comes from pala, meaning 'to be wonderful, to be beyond comprehension.' These are not abstract miracles but the acts that exceed human understanding and possibility: the exodus from Egypt, the parting of the sea, the provision in the wilderness, the defeat of giants, the establishment of the covenant. David's claim that God alone is God is grounded in history, not speculation. It is because God does wondrous things—because God acts in ways no other power can—that he alone deserves the title God.

word_study.meaning: Great, large, significant—in the context of divine attributes, gadol emphasizes magnitude, importance, and supremacy. God's greatness is both quantitative (his power) and qualitative (his character).
word_study.significance: To call God 'great' is to acknowledge that his scale of operation and his sphere of influence surpass all others. David's theology never separates God's greatness (his power) from his character (his justice and mercy).

word_study.meaning: Wondrous things, miracles, acts that surpass comprehension—from the root pala, 'to be wonderful, to exceed normal expectation.' These are acts that appear impossible from a human perspective.
word_study.significance: The use of nifla'ot grounds theology in history. David is not making philosophical arguments but pointing to concrete historical acts: the exodus, the parting of the sea, the defeat of enemies. These wonders are the evidence that only God is truly God.

word_study.meaning: You alone are God—literally 'You God by yourself, alone.' Levaddekha emphasizes solitude, uniqueness, and exclusivity. The claim is not merely that other gods are less powerful, but that only YHWH has the essential nature of true godhood.
word_study.significance: This is the strongest monotheistic statement in Psalm 86. It does not deny that other powers exist but asserts that they do not possess the essential character that makes one truly God. Only YHWH is God in the way that matters for worship, covenant, and salvation.

cross_references.connection: The Song of the Sea records the foundational expression of this claim: 'Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness?' The exodus is the historical act that grounds the claim of God's uniqueness.
Moses teaches Israel: 'Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him.' The revelation at Sinai establishes the unique identity of YHWH.

Isaiah records God's declaration: 'I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD.' The claim of exclusive godhood becomes central to exilic theology.

Nephi affirms that only Christ is the 'Lamb of God, the Eternal Father, the Savior of the world'—the Book of Mormon extends this exclusive claim to Christ as the manifestation of God's redeeming power.

commentary.historical_context:
The historical moment when Psalm 86 was likely sung or compiled was during the Second Temple period, when Jews were returning from exile under Persian rule. In that context, the claim 'thou art God alone' was a radical assertion of monotheistic faith despite living under the rule of a polytheistic empire. The Covenant Rendering's note helpfully clarifies that attah Elohim levaddekha is 'the strongest monotheistic declaration in the psalm.' This was not merely theological preference but an affirmation of national and religious identity: we will not syncretize, we will not dilute our faith, we will not add the gods of the nations to our worship. The wondrous things God did—the exodus, the return from exile—proved that YHWH alone was truly God.

It is also worth noting that this verse represents a development in Israel's theology. In the patriarchal period, the God of Abraham was understood as one mighty God among others (henotheism). By the time of the Second Temple, and certainly by the rabbinic period, the exclusive claim 'God alone' became the central assertion of Jewish faith. Psalm 86:10 stands at a crucial point in that theological development.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
Jacob 4:12 affirms: 'Wherefore, we search the prophets, and we have many revelations and the spirit of prophecy; but we obtain no witness from them that full sufficiency is in any one man.' The Book of Mormon consistently affirms that God alone is sufficient, that salvation depends not on human merit but on God's grace. 2 Nephi 25:23 teaches that grace is 'all we can do...after all we can do'—acknowledging that God alone is the source of redemptive power.

Alma 37:37 instructs: 'And if ye do not remember to be thankful, ye shall be cast out, notwithstanding the Lord's mercies.'—affirming that God alone determines the terms of covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 20:17-36 records a revelatory statement about God's nature and powers: 'And we know that all men must repent and believe on the name of Jesus Christ, and endure to the end in faithfulness, or they cannot be saved in the kingdom of God.' This affirms that God alone (through Christ) has the power to save. D&C 76:23 declares: 'By the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things'—God alone can reveal truth.

D&C 88:15-16 teaches that Christ 'is the light and the Redeemer of the world; the Spirit of truth; who came into the world, because the world was made by him, and in him was the life of men and the light of men.' Christ, as the expression of God's power, demonstrates that God alone is God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple affirms that God alone is the source of covenant, exaltation, and redemption. The temple presentation of the endowment emphasizes that only through God's prescribed pathway (the temple and its ordinances) can exaltation be achieved. God alone sets the terms of worship and redemption; these cannot be modified or altered by human preference. The temple is, in a sense, the physical embodiment of the claim that 'God alone' is God—the place where human will is submitted to divine will.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 10 finds its ultimate expression in John 5:44: 'How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only?' Christ teaches that true faith requires the recognition that God alone is worthy of ultimate honor. In Hebrews 1:1-3, the writer declares that Christ is 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person'—the manifestation of the exclusive claim that God alone is truly God. Revelation 4:11 records the heavenly chorus: 'Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things'—affirming that God alone deserves worship and that his great works (creation, redemption) prove his unique godhood.
commentary.application: In a pluralistic culture, this verse challenges us to hold fast to exclusive claims about God's identity and power. We live in an age that prizes religious tolerance and respects the sincere faith of all traditions. But Psalm 86:10 invites us to distinguish between respecting the sincerity of others' faith and maintaining our own conviction that God alone is truly God in the way that matters for salvation. This is not arrogance but witness: based on the wondrous things God has done in our lives and in the history of the covenant people, we testify that only YHWH is truly God. The application is personal: have we experienced God doing wondrous things in our lives? Can we testify, from lived experience, that God alone has power to save, heal, and redeem? Our testimony to others will be powerful only when it flows from personal encounter with God's wondrous works.

text_kjv: Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name.

commentary.narrative:
The psalm turns from declaration to petition, from theology to transformation. David has affirmed God's incomparability, envisioned universal worship, and asserted God's exclusive godhood. Now he asks for something far more difficult: integration of his own divided will. The request 'Teach me thy way' is straightforward—a petition for instruction in God's path. But the progression becomes more probing: 'I will walk in thy truth' (acknowledging that walking requires more than knowledge—it requires commitment), and then the deepest plea: 'unite my heart to fear thy name' (yached levabi lir'ah shmekha).

The verb yached is exceedingly rare in Hebrew, appearing only here in the Psalter. Its rarity is theologically appropriate because what David is asking for is itself rare and necessary. He is asking God to do something David cannot do himself: make his divided will into a single will. In Hebrew, the heart (levav) is not primarily the seat of emotion but of thought, will, and decision-making. A divided heart is a will pulled in competing directions—loyalty pulled between God and other gods, obedience pulled between God's way and the way of the world, fear pulled between reverence for God and fear of other powers. David asks God to unify him, to make his will coherent and centered on the fear of God's name.

This is the prayer of someone who knows himself well enough to recognize that he cannot simply decide to be whole. The divided heart is not conquered by willpower alone but healed by God's action. The Covenant Rendering captures this perfectly: 'Unite my heart to fear Your name'—the wholeness David seeks is not for its own sake but specifically ordered toward reverence for God. A united heart fears God without distraction or competing allegiance.

word_study.meaning: Teach me, instruct me—from the root yarah, which can mean 'to shoot' (as an arrow) or 'to point the way.' Teaching is a form of directing someone toward the right path.
word_study.significance: David's petition for instruction is a request for direction that will integrate with the petition for a united heart. Teaching is not merely intellectual transmission but a form of guidance that reshapes will and direction.

word_study.meaning: Your way, your path—the manner of living, the direction of life, the specific pathway that God has established. In covenantal language, God's way is the way of obedience to the covenant terms.
word_study.significance: God has a 'way'—a specific path of obedience, righteousness, and covenant fidelity. To walk in God's way is to align one's life with God's revealed will and character.

word_study.meaning: I will walk, I will conduct myself—the fundamental metaphor for how one lives. Walking is not a one-time action but an ongoing direction of life.
word_study.significance: Walking in God's truth is not a momentary decision but a sustained orientation of one's entire life. It requires the kind of integrated, undivided will that David requests in the next line.

word_study.meaning: Unite, make one, make whole—from the root yachad, 'to be one, to unite.' The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (here in Psalm 86:11), making this request unique and singular. The singularity of the verb matches the singularity of the request.
word_study.significance: David is asking for something that is not easy or common: the integration of a fragmented will into coherent, single-minded devotion to God. The rarity of this verb in Scripture suggests that such unity is itself rare and precious. As the translator notes point out, Kierkegaard's famous phrase 'purity of heart is to will one thing' is essentially a commentary on this verse. The united heart is the rare, precious condition that enables genuine worship.

word_study.meaning: Heart—in Hebrew psychology, the heart is the center of will, thought, decision-making, and intention. It is not primarily emotional but volitional. The heart is where one's deepest commitments and allegiances reside.
word_study.significance: When David asks God to 'unite my heart,' he is asking for the integration of his entire volitional being—his will, his affections, his commitments, his deepest allegiances. A divided heart is the condition of someone pulled between competing loyalties; a united heart is the condition of total, undivided allegiance to God.

word_study.meaning: Fear, awe, reverence, respect—the appropriate response of a creature before the God who is both infinitely powerful and perfectly holy. Fear of God is not terror but reverence and submission.
word_study.significance: The fear of God is not the opposite of love but its completion. To fear God's name is to regard God with such reverence and respect that one's will is oriented entirely toward honoring and obeying God. This is the goal toward which the united heart is directed.

cross_references.connection: David previously prayed: 'When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up. Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path'—establishing a pattern of petitioning for instruction in God's way.

The longest psalm expresses the same desire: 'Teach me, O LORD, the way of thy statutes...Incline my heart unto thy testimonies, and not to covetousness'—asking God to align the heart toward obedience.
The Shema requires loving God 'with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might'—demanding the wholehearted devotion that David here asks God to create in him.

Nephi's lament contains the same petition: 'O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. Thou hast assuaged my fears'—asking God to resolve the inner division that threatens devotion.

The Lord teaches Emma Smith: 'And the office of thy calling shall be for a comfort unto my servant, Joseph Smith, Jun., thy husband, in his afflictions, with consoling words, in the spirit of meekness'—showing how united hearts in marriage serve God's purposes.

commentary.historical_context:
The request for a united heart in the context of Davidic kingship is psychologically and politically significant. A king was expected to make decisions of war and peace, justice and mercy, covenant faithfulness and survival pragmatism. David's prayer for a united heart reflects the real inner struggle a leader faces: the pull between different values and duties, the temptation to compromise covenant fidelity for political survival, the division between private faith and public action. The rarity of the verb yached may reflect the rarity of actual integration achieved. The prayer assumes that human will, even the will of a king anointed by God, cannot achieve this integration alone—only God can yachad, can unite, can make whole.

In the Second Temple period, when these psalms were collected and sung, the prayer for a united heart would have resonated with a people returned from exile, struggling to maintain covenant fidelity while living under foreign rule, dealing with internal divisions about how to relate to Persian and Greek culture. The petition 'unite my heart to fear thy name' speaks to the perennial human challenge of integrity—making our inner life and outer life, our private convictions and public actions, cohere around a single center: reverence for God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
Alma 29:1-4 records Alma's desire: 'O that I were an angel, and could have the wish of mine heart...that I might go forth and cry repentance unto every soul'—showing how a united heart directed toward God's work becomes focused and powerful.

Alma 37:37 teaches: 'Let all thy doings be unto the Lord, and whithersoever thou goest, go with all thy heart'—the command to walk with an undivided heart reflects the same principle David seeks.

Moroni 9:25 records Mormon's exhortation: 'And now, the God of peace keep you all in the keeping of his commandments'—peace comes from the integrated life centered on God's will.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 1:32 teaches: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled'—the united heart trusts God's direction completely.

D&C 6:36 teaches: 'Therefore, what are ye that suppress the works of the Holy Ghost?'—division comes when the heart is pulled away from God's direction.

D&C 88:62-63 teaches the covenant basis for a united heart: 'Wherefore, I call upon you to repent, and come unto me, and be baptized in my name, that ye may be sanctified by the reception of the Holy Ghost, that ye may stand spotless before me at the last day.' The united heart is the result of covenant obedience and the reception of the Holy Ghost.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenants explicitly ask the faithful to covenant to live in obedience to God—to 'hearken to the voice of the Lord.' The endowment represents a pathway toward the united heart: as one takes upon oneself the covenants of the temple, the disparate pulls of the world fall away and the heart becomes oriented toward a single center: God and exaltation through obedience. The temple is, in a sense, the place where God's promise to unite hearts is enacted and renewed. Each return to the temple is a fresh petition and a fresh experience of unifying the heart around God's will.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ exemplified the perfect united heart. In Gethsemane, though Christ prayed 'Let this cup pass from me,' he resolved the division by praying 'Nevertheless, not my will, but thine be done'—uniting his will completely with the Father's will. Hebrews 12:2 describes Christ as 'looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame'—Christ's united heart toward the redemption of humanity allowed him to endure the cross. In John 10:29-30, Christ declares: 'My Father...is greater than all...I and my Father are one'—a statement of radical oneness of will and purpose. Christ is the template for the united heart that David seeks.
commentary.application: This verse invites radical honesty about our inner division. Most of us are not as unified as we imagine. We profess faith in God while being pulled by the world's values. We commit to the covenant while being tempted by competing allegiances. We declare our fear of God while actually fearing the opinions of others. The brilliant move of this verse is that it does not demand that we achieve unity through willpower alone—it asks God to do what we cannot do: yached levabi, unite our hearts. The application is to bring our division honestly before God and ask him to integrate us, to make us whole, to unify our conflicting desires around a single center: the fear of God's name. This requires vulnerability, admission of weakness, and trust that God can and will transform the divided heart into a coherent, powerful, directed will. The question is: what is dividing your heart? Where is your will being pulled in competing directions? Can you ask God, as David did, to yached levabi—to unite you at the deepest level?

text_kjv: I will praise thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart: and I will glorify thy name for evermore.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 86 concludes where it began—with a vow of praise—but transformed by what has transpired between the opening petition and this closing commitment. In verse 7, David called upon God in his distress, assured of being answered. Now, having asked God for a united heart (verse 11), David vows to praise God 'with all my heart' (be-khol levavi). This is the answer to the prayer: the fragmented, divided heart becomes whole and capable of undivided praise.

The phrase 'with all my heart' is crucial. David is not committing to praise with his lips while his heart remains divided—he is committing to wholehearted praise, the kind of praise that flows from an integrated self. The Covenant Rendering's rendering—'I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart'—emphasizes the totality of the commitment. The response to God's uniting work is the release of the entire self into praise.

The second half of the verse extends this commitment beyond time: 'I will glorify thy name for evermore' (va'akhabdah shimkha le-olam). The word le-olam ('forever, eternity, perpetuity') suggests not just the remainder of David's life but an eternal orientation. The united heart does not waver back into division; it remains oriented toward glorifying God's name indefinitely. This vow is remarkable because it comes from someone who knows the difficulty of maintaining such commitment. David has not become naive about the challenges of sustained faithfulness—his entire psalter testifies to his wrestling with temptation, doubt, and despair. Yet he vows that his response to God will be permanent praise and glory-giving.

word_study.meaning: I will praise You, confess You, give thanks to You—from the root yadah, which can mean 'to throw, to cast' or 'to confess, to acknowledge, to praise.' The root sense suggests throwing oneself forward or openly acknowledging.
word_study.significance: Praise in Hebrew is not merely emotional expression but public declaration and acknowledgment. When David says 'I will praise You,' he is committing to openly declare God's worthiness before others and before himself.

word_study.meaning: With all my heart, with my whole heart, with complete commitment—the phrase emphasizes totality. Every part of the volitional, decisional self is engaged in praise.
word_study.significance: The direct response to verse 11's prayer for a united heart is the vow to praise 'with all my heart.' The unification of the heart issues in the liberation of the whole self for praise. This is what integration enables: not restraint or constraint but full, whole-hearted expression of devotion.

word_study.meaning: I will honor, I will glorify, I will make heavy—from the root kabad, which carries the sense of weighting something, making it substantial and significant. To glorify God is to add weight to his reputation.
word_study.significance: Glorifying God's name is not merely internal devotion but active witness. David commits to a form of praise that makes God's character and works known to others, adding substance to God's reputation in the world.

word_study.meaning: Forever, eternity, perpetually, to the age—a word that can mean the eternal future or the perpetual present. It indicates time beyond ordinary human measurement, extending indefinitely.
word_study.significance: David's vow is not limited to his lifetime but commits him to a perpetual orientation toward God's glorification. This echoes the eternal covenant theme: just as God's faithfulness extends forever, so David's praise and glorification of God's name extends forever.

cross_references.connection: Another psalm of David begins: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits'—echoing the same commitment to wholehearted praise.

A hymn declares: 'Praise ye the LORD. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD...From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised'—expressing the same perpetual commitment to praise.
Paul calls for 'present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service'—the New Testament echo of David's commitment to wholehearted devotion and praise.
Paul exhorts: 'Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice'—a perpetual call to the kind of wholehearted praise David commits to here.

The Lord teaches: 'If thou art merry, praise the Lord with singing, with music, with dancing, and with a prayer of praise and thanksgiving'—affirming that wholehearted praise and joy are inseparable from covenant life.

commentary.historical_context:
The vow to praise God forever appears in multiple Davidic psalms, suggesting that this commitment was central to David's self-understanding as a covenanted person. In the historical David's life—if we can reconstruct it from the narratives in Samuel—he was a man of intense emotional volatility: capable of deep worship and worship-leading (2 Samuel 6:14-16), but also capable of desperate flight, profound sin, and vengeful actions. Yet in the psalms, David repeatedly vows to perpetual praise and faithfulness. This is not naivety but realism: David knows his own weakness and vulnerability, yet he vows that his response to God will be permanent.

When these psalms were sung in the Second Temple period, the vow to praise God forever would have resonated with a community that had recently experienced the near-annihilation of exile. The commitment to perpetual praise despite historical traumas, despite ongoing hardship and marginalization, was a powerful assertion of covenant hope. It was a declaration that nothing—not conquest, not exile, not political powerlessness—would diminish the people's praise of God. This is the voice not of triumphalism but of tested, proven faithfulness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
Alma 26:8-16 records Ammon's outburst of grateful praise: 'Behold, my joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I am filled with the Spirit'—showing how the experience of God's grace issues in wholehearted praise.

Nephi's final words in 2 Nephi 33:1-15 express a commitment to perpetual witness and testimony: 'And now I write some of the words of Isaiah, that whoso of my people shall see these words may lift up their hearts and rejoice for all men'—a commitment to glorifying God's name forever through testimony.

The Book of Mormon demonstrates repeatedly that those who experience genuine conversion move toward Ammon-like wholehearted praise and commitment to spreading God's name.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 14:7-8 teaches: 'And the day of salvation is extended to all the children of men...And he hath given unto all men knowledge of the truth of my gospel'—affirming that God's covenant extends forever, inviting perpetual praise and response.

D&C 121:45 records the Lord's promise to Joseph Smith: 'Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men...and the Holy Ghost shall be thy constant companion'—describing the kind of wholehearted devotion David vows to.

D&C 76:69 describes the glory of those in the celestial kingdom: 'These are they whose bodies are celestial, whose glory is that of the sun, even the glory of God the highest'—affirming that wholehearted praise and devotion in this life lead to eternal exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment culminates in the commitment to build up the kingdom of God and to receive eternal life. The entire temple journey can be understood as David's journey in Psalm 86: moving from petition (the prayer circle), to the petition for a united heart (the covenants), to the vow of perpetual praise and devotion (the final covenants and commitments). Each return to the temple is a renewal of the vow to glorify God's name forever. The temple's eternal language—'the oath and covenant which belongeth to the priesthood' and the promise of eternal exaltation—grounds the vow in the permanent, unchanging commitments of covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the perfect example of perpetual, wholehearted praise of God. In John 17, Christ's high-priestly prayer is a prayer of ultimate praise: 'I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do' (v. 4). Hebrews 13:15 describes an eternal covenant: 'By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name'—connecting perpetual praise to Christ's eternal work. In Revelation 5:8-14, the heavenly multitude offers perpetual worship to the Lamb: 'Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing'—depicting the eternal praise that David's vow anticipates.
commentary.application:
This closing verse invites us to make the same vow David makes: not in a moment of emotional exuberance, but in deliberate commitment after asking God to unite our hearts. The progression is important: first, petition God to make us whole. Then, commit to wholehearted praise. The question for each of us is: are we ready to praise God with all our heart? Not with the part of us that feels like it, not with the parts that are convenient or comfortable, but with the integrated whole of ourselves—our will, our thought, our feeling, our action unified around a single center: the glorification of God's name.

The perpetuity of the vow is also crucial. We do not commit to praise God when we feel like it, or when circumstances are favorable, or when our faith is strong. We commit to glorify God's name forever—in times of prosperity and in times of devastation, when our faith is vivid and when it is barely an ember, when we understand and when we are deeply confused. This is the vow of a person whose heart has been united by God and who responds by offering that integrated self in perpetual, unchanging praise. The application is both simple and impossibly demanding: Will you praise God with all your heart, forever?
